publicationStmt.p: Generated by `burton ingest`. Do not edit by hand.

div.ed:endnote: Hern: Heron. hie: Urge, hasten.
terse and polite: Neat and polished. indite: Express or dictate words for a literary composition.
take thyself by th’ nose: That is, ‘take a look at yourself’ (following the medieval proverb, ‘Accipe per nasum te, cum me dicis iniquam’: ‘If you call me harsh, take yourself by the nose’).
from’s: ‘From his’.
amain: With full force, violently.

severe Cato: A reference to the ancient Roman statesman and author Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BCE), also known as ‘Cato the Elder’ or ‘Cato the Censor’. He was famous for his severe criticism of the decline of traditional Roman morality, and also, more particularly, for entering the theatre in order to walk out before the start of a performance whose content he disapproved of (a story alluded to by Martial in the preface to the first book of his Epigrams). Eagles don’t hunt flies: A quotation from Erasmus, Adagia (1500–1536), and typical of the kind of moralizing found in the Distichs of Cato, a collection of Latin epigrams, by an otherwise unknown author called Dionysius Cato, which was a standard textbook in Renaissance schools.

A Zoilus and a Momus: The ancient Greek Cynic philosopher and grammarian Zoilus (fourth century BCE) was a notoriously acerbic critic of Homer’s poems who became known as ‘Homeromastix’, or ‘Scourge of Homer’. The figure of Momus was the Greek personification of fault-finding, and was similarly associated with harsh satirical criticism.
The page … virtuous: A quotation from Martial (Epigrams 1.4.8).

antic: Grotesque, ludicrous. personate: Counterfeit, feigned. Primum … coacturus est: In the opening of Seneca’s satirical Pumpkinification of Claudius, quoted here, the narrator tells his readers that he has no obligation to divulge the source of his knowledge of the fantastical and absurd events that he is about to describe.

as that Egyptian in Plutarch … what was in it: The answer given by an unidentified Egyptian is cited by Plutarch in On Being a Busybody (3) as an appropriate rebuke
to someone who is inappropriately inquisitive into other people’s affairs – including the reader, who is told that ‘it would not be concealed, if it were not something bad’ (malum, in the Renaissance Latin translation by Guillaume Xylander which Burton probably used, also carries the senses of ‘mischievous’, ‘harmful’, ‘inappropriate’ and ‘insulting’).
pasquil: Lampoon; see also below, n. 35 (1.2.4). paradox: A barely believable or strange doctrine.
Praxiteles: A celebrated Athenian sculptor of the fourth century BCE.

Mercurius Gallobelgicus: The title of a contemporary Latin newsletter printed in Germany and circulating in England. Mercurius Britannicus: The pseudonym used by the English bishop and writer Joseph Hall in his satirical Mundus alter et idem (1605). Democritus Christianus: The title of the 1616 Latin version of Le Démocrite chrestien (1615) by the French cardinal, bishop and author Pierre de Besse.
wearish: Wizened, shrivelled. Physician: Natural philosopher. Politician: An expert in the theory of politics.

liberales disciplinas: In note ‘l’, the ‘liberal sciences’ – often called the ‘liberal arts’ – were the seven disciplines traced to antiquity and taught in the universities (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy).
Recorder: Someone employed to record civil documents (or, in its original meaning, a magistrate or judge).
reference: Submission to a higher authority.

Xenocrates in Athens: According to Diogenes Laertius (4.2), the philosopher Xenocrates (b. 396/5 BCE) served as head of the Platonic Academy in Athens for twenty-five years, until his death at the age of eighty-two.

Otho Nicholson: In note ‘g’, Otho Nicholson (d. 1622) was a wealthy London lawyer and one of James I’s Examiners in Chancery. He paid for the restoration of the library building at Christ Church in 1610–11, and gave a donation of money for the purchasing of books in 1613.
Card: Plan, or chart.

Saturn was Lord of my geniture … in their houses, &c.: In astrology, the ‘lord of the geniture’ was whichever planet was the dominant influence at the time of a person’s nativity. Burton refers here to his horoscope, a copy of which (drawn up in his own hand) is found in one of his books now held in the Bodleian Library, and reproduced on his monument in the cathedral of Christ Church in Oxford. It shows that at his birth (8 February 1577), Saturn was at the highest point in the sky and in the sign of Capricorn, and that the ‘ascendant’ (the sign rising on the eastern horizon) was Aries, one of the ‘houses’ (the twelve parts of the zodiac with particular significance in human affairs) which was ruled and at that point occupied by Mars. The putatively malign influences of Saturn and Mars were thereby thought to be tempered – and hence were ‘fortunate in their houses’.

I live still … garden: From the third edition (1628) onwards, this passage replaced the following in the earlier versions: ‘although my friends’ providence, care, alacrity, and bounty was never wanting to do me good, yet either through mine own default, infelicity, want or neglect of opportunity, iniquity of times, preposterous proceeding, my hopes were still frustrate, and I left behind, as a Dolphin on shore, confined to my College, as Democritus to his garden, Diogenes to his tub, where I still continue’. In this passage, ‘default’ means ‘defect’ or ‘failure’. The ancient Greek philosopher Diogenes the Cynic is said to have slept in a large ceramic wine-jar – often referred to as a ‘barrel’ or ‘tub’ – exemplifying his scornful rejection of social convention, and contributing to his reputation, as Plato is reported to have said, as a ‘Socrates gone mad’. macerate: Weaken, vex. only: Uniquely, pre-eminently.
spectrums: Phantoms, spectres. monomachies: Duels.
corantoes: Newsletters or newspapers.
fashions: Manners and customs.
several: Different.
day net: A net that can be suddenly pulled shut, used in the hunting of larks and other small birds. passengers: Passers-by.
conceited: Ingenious, clever.
except against: Object, protest.

genius: The Latin term can refer to a tutelary spirit or deity (good or evil), but also, and sometimes simultaneously, to the innate character or nature of a person. impostume: A swelling or abscess, thought to be caused by the superfluity of a humour.

offended: Harmed, hurt. Aegeria: Or Egeria: in Roman mythology, a water-goddess and one of the prophetic nymphs known as the Camenae (later identified with the inspirational Muses of Greek mythology). Egeria was said to have acted as counsellor to the second legendary king of Rome, Numa Pompilius, and was associated with wisdom and oracular inspiration.

private: Intimate (or here, perhaps, discreet and dependable). In note ‘d’, the named individuals refer to contemporaries of Burton at Oxford: Rous was the Head Librarian (‘Protobibliothecarius’) of the Bodleian Library; Thomas Hopper and John Goodridge (‘Guthridge’) bequeathed many medical books to their colleges.

Marius in Sallust … myself: The quotation, adapted slightly from Sallust’s War with Jugurtha (85.13), is from the speech of the Roman general and politician Gaius Marius (157–86 BCE), delivered to his forces in 107 before they leave to fight the Numidian king in North Africa.
just: Full, complete.
disparagement: Degradation.
divine, humane authors: Writers on divinity and the ‘humanities’ – the classically orientated studia humanitatis of poetry, rhetoric, grammar, history and moral philosophy.
set out: Adorn, decorate.

Trium literarum homines: In Plautus’ Pot of Gold (325), the ‘trium litterarum homo’ is the man of the three letters f, u and r, spelling ‘thief’ in Latin. putid: Worthless or foul. close-stool: An enclosed cabinet containing a chamber pot. jakes: Latrine. lap: Wrap up.
vilified: Reduced in value or estimation. collogue: Coax, blandish.
vent their toys: Sell their trifling writings.
Sossius Sinesius: Actually (Quintus) Sosius Senecio, a Roman senator (and consul in 99 and 107 CE).

our Frankfurt Marts, our domestic Marts: The Frankfurt book fair, which was the most important of its kind in early modern Europe and was held twice a year, was far larger than the book fairs in contemporary England.
Chaos: The ‘formless void’ of primordial matter out of which the earth was made.
Maceronicon: A literary work composed of two or more languages; alternatively, a jumble or medley.
Story-dressers: Writers of histories that are embellishments of earlier authors’ works.
likely: Similarly. indite: See above, n. 2 (Preliminaries).
solve: Answer.
Doric dialect: Unrefined speech. rhapsody: A work made up of miscellaneous elements without fixed form, a literary hodge-podge. insolent: Bizarre. indiscreet: Or ‘undiscreet’ – undiscerning.
Momus: See above, n. 7 (Preliminaries). Burton’s loose translation builds on the classical usage of nasus (literally, ‘nose’) to connote mockery or scorn.

parasangs: An ancient Persian unit of length: the distance travelled in one hour (whether by foot or horseback, however, is uncertain), and usually thought to be approximately 3¾ miles. ace: A particle, or the smallest amount possible.
bewrays: Exposes, betrays. old Cato’s rule: This was actually the belief of Plutarch, expressed in his biography of Cato the Elder (7.2) – for whom, see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries).
amaracum sui … another: According to a classical adage, marjoram is repulsive to pigs.

strong lines: Obscure or bombastic writing. the Dominicals: Engravings illustrating the contemplative devotions; they were modelled on places and events taken from the ‘Dominical’ (Sunday) Gospel readings, and included in the Adnotationes et meditationes in Evangelia (1595), a spiritual manual compiled by the Spanish Jesuit Jérôme Nadal (Natalis). explodes: Rejects or condemns.
trivant: A lazy person; or, more strongly, an idle rogue.
brave: Fine, splendid. doctor: An eminently learned person.
Dutch: German.
witty: Wise, ingenious.
painful: Diligent, painstaking. Arena sine calce: The quotation from Suetonius (Gaius Caligula 53) in note ‘b’ refers to the quicklime required to make mortar. propugner: Advocate, champion.
absolute: Perfect. prescription: Ancient or continued custom.
take place: Have effect.
advice: Reflection, deliberation (here, probably without the assistance of another).

as a Bear … doth her young ones: A reference to the ancient belief that newborn bears are not fully formed, but are ‘licked into shape’ by their mothers. fustian: Inflated or inappropriately lofty in expression. Acestes’ arrows … flew: An allusion to the archery competition in the Aeneid (5.519–40), won by Acestes (Virgil’s name for Aegestus, the son of Trojan parents who had fled to Sicily) when his arrow burst into flames to indicate his divine favour. strains of wit: Strained literary constructions (or, alternatively, streams of affective language). brave heats: Expressions of intense feeling. elogies: Eulogies. exornations: Decorations, adornments.

Apollonius, a scholar of Socrates: Apollonius of Tyana (first century CE), a Neopythagorean holy man; ‘scholar’ here means ‘pupil’. According to Philostratus (Life of Apollonius of Tyana 8.2), if called to defend himself in court, Apollonius would have imitated the succinct and apposite speech given by Socrates at his trial.

here champian, there enclosed: Or, ‘here free and open, there constrained’. A ‘champian’ (or ‘champaign’) was an open and level plain, whereas ‘enclosed’ land had been converted from common ownership into private property.

Pontus: In note ‘b’, the Senecan reference is to the ancient region on the south coast of the Black Sea, which had been the heartland of a Persian satrapy, and then a kingdom, before it became a Roman province.

ut canis Nilum lambens: In note ‘d’, ‘like a dog lapping at the Nile’ is a standard trope for dabbling, deriving from the ancient observation that dogs would not stay by the water of that river for any length of time because of its crocodiles.
censure: Judgement, opinion. pleonasms: Superfluities, redundancies.
interpretations: Direct or literal translations. margent: Margin.
interpreters: Translators.
Neoterics: Modern authors.

upon peruse … refuse: The sense of Burton’s poetic translation is clarified by the Latin text (‘ut illa … ut repudias’), which can be rendered as: ‘the result is that you don’t know what you thought you knew,/And what you thought most important for yourself, putting it into practice, you reject.’
But I am now resolved … I have done: This resolution first appeared in the third edition (1628). It remained in, and did not prevent, the editions issued in 1632, 1638 and 1651.
Menedemus … Chremes: Two Athenian characters in Terence’s Self-Tormentor.
deboshed: Debauched.
rillet: A rivulet or stream.

positively: Dogmatically, or engaging in a controversy. Paul’s Cross … St. Mary’s Oxon: Two locations where sermons were commonly preached: the pulpit cross at St Paul’s Cathedral in London and the University Church of St Mary’s in Oxford.

to cut off an Hydra’s head: In classical mythology, when each of the multiple heads of the Hydra were cut off, two more grew back in its place. duplications, triplications: In law, the ‘duplication’ is the defendant’s reply to the ‘replication’ (a claimant’s answer to a defendant’s plea), and the ‘triplication’ is the plaintiff’s reply to the defendant’s duplication.
irrefragable: Obstinate, inflexible.
sciences: Branches of learning.
de lana caprina: A proverbially trivial dispute (referred to in Horace, Epistles 1.18.15) about whether goat’s hair can be called ‘wool’. about moonshine in the water: Proverbially, about nothing.
Drusianus: The learned Italian physician Pietro Torrigiano de’ Torrigiani (d. c. 1319), whose name was Latinized variously as ‘Turisanus’, ‘Trusianus’ or ‘Drusianus’.
T. Linacre: The English humanist scholar and physician Thomas Linacre (c. 1460–1524).
Chirurgeons: Surgeons – in the early modern era, medical practitioners who treated diseases or injuries manually.

driven to their shifts: Pushed to the last extremity, to the point of extreme difficulty or ‘last resort’. mountebanks, quacksalvers, empirics: Types of physician generally regarded by the learned medical community as spurious. ‘Mountebanks’ were itinerant charlatans selling remedies; ‘quacksalvers’ were untrained doctors or ‘quacks’; and ‘empirics’ were untrained doctors who, unlike learned physicians, treated diseases without theoretical knowledge of their causes (the term derives from the ancient medical sect of the Empirici, who drew their rules entirely from experience). taskers: Labourers who work or are paid by the task or piece (as distinct from day-labourers). costermongers: Apple- or fruit-sellers. graziers: People who graze or feed cattle for the market.
prospectives: Scenes or views drawn in perspective. chorographical: Describing, or delineating on a map or chart, a particular region or district.
Jupiter in my sixth house: An indication of suitability for the medical profession, according to some Renaissance astrologers. theoric: Theory.
humanity: Or the ‘humanities’: see above, n. 28 (DJR).

to reconcile those Chronological errors in the Assyrian monarchy: A reference to recent chronological disputes about the reigns of the Assyrian kings, which – as the classical scholar Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) had pointed out – were difficult to reconcile with the accounts given in Scripture. find out the quadrature of a circle: The geometrical process of constructing a square equal in area to that of a circle. the north-east, or north-west passages: Supposed short, direct routes to China and India through the northern polar regions, searched for by explorers such as Henry Hudson (d. 1611) – see below, nn. 5, 6 (2.2.3). that hungry Spaniard’s … Terra Australis Incognita: In 1603, the Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós (1563–1615) had been commissioned by Philip III of Spain to discover ‘the Unknown Southern Continent’ (the mythical terra australis), which had been the subject of speculation since antiquity, and was often seen in the early modern period as a second ‘new world’ to be explored and colonized. perfect the motion of Mars and Mercury: The elliptical orbits of these two planets had been established in 1609 by the astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), who had elaborated them further in 1619. rectify the Gregorian Calendar: The Gregorian calendar was introduced in Catholic Europe in 1582, but the continued adherence
to the Julian calendar in Protestant states (until 1752 in the case of England) led to conflicts over the dating of events in the ecclesiastical year.

that great captain Zisca: The Bohemian general Jan Žižka (c. 1360–1424), a Hussite – that is, a follower of the ecclesiastical reformer Jan Hus (1372–1415) – who led his army to several victories even after he had become completely blind in 1421.
Yet one caution … to their benefit: This warning first appeared in the third edition of 1628, and it remained in the editions of 1632, 1638 and 1651.
gulls: Credulous or gullible people, fools.

Morea may be Moria: The Peloponnese was known as ‘Morea’ in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. In Greek, as Erasmus had remarked to Thomas More in the preface to the Moriae encomium (1511), μωρία means ‘folly’.

vegetal, sensible, and rational: See below, 1.1.2.5; ‘sensible’ creatures are those endowed with sense-perception. Cebes’ table: The Tablet (Pinax) then falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Cebes of Thebes (c. 430–350 BCE), which allegorically represents the correct and false paths in life. actions: Legal processes or speeches. Porcius Latro: Marcus Porcius Latro (c. 55–4 BCE), a famously forceful Roman rhetorician, given the last declamation in the Controversies (a set of fictional legal debates) of Seneca the Elder (c. 55 BCE–39/40 CE).
confound: Mix up, confuse.

the Anticyrae: The plural form refers to the fact that there were three towns named Anticyra in ancient Greece; one of these, a Phocian port on the bay of Anticyra in the Gulf of Corinth, was renowned for its black hellebore, a famous remedy for madness and melancholy. Compostella, our Lady of Sichem, or Lauretta: Santiago de Compostela in Spain, Zichem in the Low Countries and Loreto in Italy, all renowned destinations for Catholic pilgrims and those in search of miraculous cures. a voyage … of Tobacco: There had been several English attempts to colonize Guiana (in what is now Venezuela) in the reigns of Elizabeth I and James I. The region was noted for its abundance of sugar and tobacco.
Agur the son of Jakeh: According to Proverbs 30:1, the author of this chapter of Scripture. The preceding chapters are ascribed to Solomon.

Quis nisi mentis inops, &c.: In note ‘a’, the line being quoted – from the epic poet and theologian Walter of Châtillon (d. c. 1204) – in full is ‘Quis nisi mentis inops oblatum respuat aurum’: ‘Who but the mindless would refuse the offer of gold?’

Socrates … Apollo: According to Plato, the oracle at the temple of Apollo (the Greek god of divination, healing and music, among other things) at Delphi had proclaimed that no one was wiser than Socrates. Brasidas: The Spartan general (d. 422 BCE), who rose to prominence in the Peloponnesian War (431–404), was regarded as a model of bravery. Antenor and Nestor: In classical mythology, two elderly counsellors highly respected for their wisdom, on opposite sides – the Trojan and Greek respectively – during the Trojan War. Pericles: the statesman, orator and general (495–429), portrayed by Thucydides as the patriotic leader of the Athenian democracy in the 430s.

Those seven wise men of Greece: The ‘Seven Sages’ of the early sixth century BCE reputed to have outstanding practical and political wisdom, traditionally Thales of Miletus, Bias of Priene, Cleobulus of Lindus (on Rhodes), Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Chilon of Sparta and Periander of Corinth (sometimes replaced by Myson of Chen, Anacharsis or others). Brachmanni: Brahmins. Ethiopian Gymnosophists: Literally ‘the naked wise men’, the gymnosophists were an ancient ascetic philosophical sect originally from India. Their Ethiopian offshoot was usually regarded as a caste of wise priests.
Empedocles: A Presocratic philosopher (c. 492–432 BCE) from Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily, who was famous for his two poems On Nature and Purifications.

Anaxagoras: In note ‘f’, Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was born in Clazomenae in Asia Minor, and was the first philosopher known to have settled in Athens. Ocean: The metaphor here signifies vastness of knowledge.

As Aelian writ … viris pueri: The ancient Greek sophists Protagoras of Abdera (c. 490–420 BCE) and Gorgias of Leontini (c. 485–c. 380 BCE) had been influentially criticized by Plato in dialogues named after them – the former for his doctrine that ‘Man is the measure of all things’, the latter for his prioritization of rhetoric over philosophy. In the place cited here, Aelian contrasts them unfavourably with Democritus and the Pythagorean philosopher Philolaus (c. 470–390 BCE). in respect: In comparison.
as he censured Alexander: In The History of the World (1614), Sir Walter Ralegh claimed that Alexander the Great ‘had ten thousand in his Army as daring as himself’.
dizzards: Idiots, blockheads.
Aristippus: Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 430–355 BCE), a student of Socrates, and sometimes seen as a bon viveur.

saved him from the plague: Socrates escaped the plague that ravaged Athens in 430 BCE. his Master: His superior. Aristotle was generally regarded as the most accomplished ancient philosopher by Renaissance scholars, although Plato or Socrates were sometimes preferred. opinative: Opinionated. so convict by Anytus: That is, ‘proved to be so’ by Anytus, the Athenian politician who, together with Meletus, prosecuted Socrates at the latter’s trial for impiety and corrupting the young in 399 BCE.
as he said … omnem: Horace, in Satires 2.3.83.

Zenodotus’ heart, Crates’ liver: Zenodotus (c. 325–260 BCE) and Crates of Mallus (fl. second century BCE) were Greek grammarians and scholars of Homer. In the epigram by the Roman poet Marcus Furius Bibaculus (b. 103 BCE) alluded to here, the heart and the liver both represent the physical seat of the intelligence, although the liver was more typically associated with the emotions. Epictetus’ lantern: In a story told in Lucian’s Ignorant Book-Collector (13), a man buys the lantern of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus in the hope of sharing his wisdom.

Crassians: Literally, followers of the Crassus family in ancient Rome, but the term ‘Crassian’ had acquired a double meaning from the meaning of crassus in Latin as ‘thick’ or ‘stupid’. The ancient Roman cognomen ‘Crassus’, which was used in the republican period by several important families (most notably the plebeian Licinii Crassi), had initially been used as an epithet for unusual tallness.

inversorum Apuleiorum … two-legged asses: In the Metamorphoses (sometimes called the Golden Ass), the ancient Numidian writer Apuleius (b. c. 125 CE) portrays the transformation of its narrator Lucius, identified in the final book as the author himself, into an ass. inversorum Silenorum: In classical mythology, a Silenus (or satyr) was a demonic inhabitant of the wild, combining human and animal characteristics, and associated with grotesque hedonism and the god Dionysus (Bacchus); ‘Silenus’ as a singular figure referred to the father or grandfather of the Silenuses/satyrs, also the foster-father and companion of Dionysus, and was traditionally depicted as an old, pot-bellied man. The allusion here, however, derives more specifically from Plato’s Symposium (215B, 216D, 221E), where Alcibiades describes a Silenus as a statue of a satyr containing the image of a god, and then compares one to Socrates – meaning that the philosopher’s external ugliness is belied by his inner beauty and wisdom. An ‘inverted Silenus’ therefore denotes external beauty and inner deformity.
fond: Foolish, silly.
babies of clouts: Rag dolls (‘dolls made of rags’).
get a head: Gain power or ascendancy, become established.
promiscuous: Mixed and disorderly. emmets: Ants.
Thersites: According to Homer (Iliad 2.211–77), a lame, abusive and exceedingly ugly Greek soldier in the Trojan War.
swell: Become ‘puffed up’ or arrogant.
molestation: Affliction, vexation.
conversation: Behaviour, mode of living.
Maecenas: In note ‘a’, Gaius Cilnius Maecenas (d. 8 BCE) was the patron of Horace and Virgil, and a famously wealthy lover of luxury.
prank up: Dress ostentatiously, decorate.
fleer: Laugh at mockingly, ridicule.
Apologues: Moral fables, usually allegorical.

whifflers: Originally attendants employed to clear the way for a procession, but figuratively, swaggerers or bullies. Cuman asses: Fools whose novelties are taken to be signs of talent. The phrase refers to the classical fable of the ass which deceived the inhabitants of Cumae by wearing a lion-skin. outsides: Empty or superficial people.

Jupiter & Juno’s wedding: Jupiter, the sovereign god of the Romans (and the equivalent of the Greek Zeus), was married to Juno (Hera), the goddess of women and marriage (as well as an important civic deity throughout central Italy).

Pluto: The Roman god of the dead and king of the underworld (the counterpart of the Greek Hades). Moronia Pia, and Moronia Foelix: In Joseph Hall’s Mundus alter et idem (1605), the country of ‘Moronia’ (the land of fools, or ‘Fooliana’ in John Healey’s seventeenth-century English translation) contained the regions ‘Moronia Pia’ (‘Fooliana the Devout’), populated by religious heretics and the superstitious, and ‘Moronia Felix’ (‘Fooliana the Fat’), containing the proud and boastful.
the latter end … be worst: The prophecy of Jesus (recorded in Matthew 12:45) about the ‘wicked generation’ possessed by evil spirits.

nec dum finitus Orestes: This phrase from Juvenal (Satires 1.6) originally refers to an incomplete literary composition, but here it signifies the persistent raving of a madman. In Greek mythology, Orestes was driven mad and tormented relentlessly by the Furies after killing his mother Clytemnestra, who had murdered his father Agamemnon with the aid of her lover Aegisthus.

have and hold: Tenaciousness. Father Angelo … to Rome, &c.: Note ‘g’ refers to a famous pilgrimage made by Henri, duke of Joyeuse (1563–1608), a Catholic general in the French Wars of Religion (1562–98) who had become a Capuchin, and taken the name ‘Frère Ange’, after the death of his wife. to tread on Emperors’ necks … stirrup: See below, nn. 91, 92, 93 (3.4.1).

St. Thomas’ Shrine: The shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. Paxes: Precious tablets, depicting the crucifixion or another holy scene, which are kissed by the celebrating priest and then the other participants at mass. cringes: Acts of bowing in a servile or sycophantic manner. knocking: Beating one’s breast. beads: Prayers or devotions conducted with rosary beads.
hallowed beans: Possibly a reference to the Catholic practice of eating beans at Lent, sometimes associated with the commemoration of the dead.

the Golden Legend: The Aurea legenda, or Legenda sanctorum, a collection of hagiographies compiled in the second half of the thirteenth century by the Italian chronicler and archbishop of Genoa, Jacopo da Voragine (1228/9–98). the Turks’ Alcoran: The Qur’an. Rabbins’ Comments: Rabbinical commentaries on the Torah or Talmud.
supererogate: Earn merit for others by doing more than is required by God.

nice & curious schismatics: Both ‘nice’ and ‘curious’ here mean ‘fastidious’, or ‘exceedingly careful and precise’ – qualities often derogatorily attributed to contemporary puritans, who are also the ‘schismatics’ being accused here of destroying the unity of the English Church. things indifferent: Matters that are non-essential to
salvation. tasteless: The Latin adjective insulsus means both ‘tasteless’ and ‘absurd’ or ‘foolish’.
lying at lurch: Lying in wait, lurking. Formalists: People who adhere only outwardly to religious orthodoxy.
gripers: ‘Graspers’ or extortioners.
greenheads: Inexperienced, immature people.

Mahomet the second Turk: The Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II (1432–81), also known as Mehmed the Conqueror, whose military expansion of the Ottoman Empire led to his portrayal as a murderous tyrant in many Christian sources. Sicinius Dentatus: Lucius Siccius (or Sicinius) Dentatus (d. 450/49 BCE), a plebeian military hero later called ‘the Roman Achilles’. M. Sergius: The Roman general – and great-grandfather of Catiline: see below, n. 227 (DJR) – Marcus Sergius Silus, famous for his service in several campaigns in the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE). Scaeva the Centurion: Marcus Cassius Scaeva, who fought in the army of Julius Caesar in the Roman civil wars and distinguished himself in the siege of Dyrrachium (48 BCE).

Cannae: The victory of Hannibal at the Battle of Cannae (216 BCE), during the Second Punic War, was one of Rome’s bloodiest and most ignominious defeats. Battle Abbey: The Battle of Hastings (1066), commemorated in the building of Battle Abbey. as Constantine and Licinius: The Roman emperors Licinius (c. 250–324 CE) and Constantine I (c. 275–337 CE) were initially allies and co-emperors, but became hostile rivals; the allusion here is probably to their struggle at the Battle of Cibalae in 314.

the siege of Ostend: The city of Ostend, at the time occupied by Dutch and English troops, was besieged by Spanish forces between July 1601 and September 1604, during the Dutch Revolt (1568–1648). dorps: Villages.
mine Author: Here, the French historian and bookseller Jérémie Périer (fl. 1588–1624).
condoles: Laments. that immortal Genius: Fame.

When Rhodes was besieged … the top of the walls: The Ottoman Sultan (‘great Turk’) Suleiman I, commonly known as Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566), took Rhodes after a five-month siege in 1522, but his siege of Vienna in 1529 was unsuccessful.

Andromache … Hectorem: In Greek mythology, Andromache was the wife of the Trojan prince Hector. After the fall of Troy she became the slave and concubine of Neoptolemus (or Pyrrhus), the son of Achilles and a warrior infamous for his brutality in the sack of the city.
Collignius: Gaspard II de Coligny (1519–72), a Huguenot leader in the French Wars of Religion (1562–98), who was himself killed in the St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre in Paris in August 1572.

Pharsalian fields: Julius Caesar defeated his rival Pompey the Great at the Battle of Pharsalus in Thessaly (48 BCE). Here the phrase is used to signify the carnage of civil war, specifically at the Battle of Towton (1461) during the Wars of the Roses in England. immanity: Monstrous cruelty.
stupend: Stupendous, amazing.

Sicilian Evensongs: The ‘Sicilian Vespers’, the successful and very bloody rebellion, in 1282, against the rule of the Angevins in Sicily. the Duke of Alva’s tyrannies: Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, the third duke of Alva (or Alba) (1507–82) was the notoriously harsh governor in the Netherlands during the early stages of the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule (1568–1648). those ten persecutions: The persecutions of Christians carried out by the Roman emperors from Nero to Diocletian (64–311 CE).

Niobe was for grief … stone: In classical mythology, Niobe’s grieving and transformation into stone occurs after her children are killed by Apollo and Artemis
(Diana), as a punishment for her boasting about having more children than their mother Leto (Latona).

those fantastical Anabaptists: Protestant sects, originating in Switzerland but spreading to Germany, the Low Countries and England in the early Reformation, who shared the belief that since infant baptism was not authorized by Scripture it should only be performed in adulthood. Their millenarian tendencies, rejection of traditional religious authority, emphasis on the community of believers, and belief in personal revelation – all crystallized in the notorious communal theocracy briefly established by John of Leiden at Münster (1534–5) – led to their widespread association with religious heterodoxy, social unrest and political radicalism.

the Roman Acies: The Roman military term for the front of an army or a line of battle; or figuratively, the whole army drawn up in order of battle. Calgacus’… in Tacitus: Calgacus was one of the leaders of the Caledonian tribes who fought the Romans at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly north of Aberdeen) in 84 CE.
caitiffs: Miserable people, poor wretches. generous: Brave, or noble.

lie sentinel perdue: To be placed as a far-lying outpost or scout (and so to be in a position of extreme danger). battle: Battle array, an army or battalion in array. when Darius’ army … Alexander at Issus: According to the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus, before the Persian king Darius III was defeated at the Battle of Issus (333 BCE) he was warned by an Athenian adviser that his splendidly equipped army would prove no match for the well-disciplined forces of Alexander the Great.
proletaries: Proletarians: the lowest class of citizens (in ancient Rome, those who owned little or no property), or the poor.

Thermopylae, Salamina, Marathon, Mycale … Plataea: Famous battles in the Graeco-Persian Wars, fought between alliances of the Greek city-states against the Persian Empire in the fifth century BCE: at Marathon (490), Thermopylae (480), Salamis (480), Mycale (479) and Plataea (479). Mantinea: The site of three important battles, in 418, 362 and 207, but the reference here is probably to the second of these, fought between the Thebans and the Spartans. Chaeronaea: The site of the decisive victory, in 338, of Philip of Macedon over Athens, Thebes and their allies.

So Africanus … Ennius: The victory of the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus (the Elder) (236–183 BCE) over Carthage in the Second Punic War (218–201) was commemorated in a poem traditionally attributed to the venerated Latin writer Quintus Ennius (239–169), although the authorship of the Scipio is now disputed. feral: Deadly. for: ‘On account of’ (or possibly ‘before’, ‘in front of’).
fact: Deed.
event: Outcome.
pill and poll: Literally, ‘remove the skin and hair’ – and so, figuratively, strip bare by pillage, plunder. turgent: Swollen or inflated with pride or conceit.

funge: Someone who is ‘soft-headed’, like a mushroom or fungus. fumes: Insubstantial, transient or imaginary things – here, words, and possibly with the implication that they ‘go to the head’ and cloud the mental faculties or the reason.
a Gorgon’s head: A very ugly person.
coats: Petticoats or skirts (as worn in this period by young boys as well as girls).

made: Prepared. nose of wax: Something easily twisted or moulded – and so here a person easily influenced. firm in his opinion, cast in his: That is, supported by one judge and ruled against by another.

silly ones … punished: ‘Silly’ here means helpless and innocent, corresponding loosely to the ‘doves’ in the line from Juvenal (Satires 2.63) partially quoted in note ‘f’ (‘It acquits the ravens and persecutes the doves’).
As put case: To put the case, suppose.
policy: Art or practice of government, conduct of public affairs.
compendious: Sparing of time, or economical.

commodity: Self-interest. Eia Socrates, Eia Xantippe: According to Diogenes Laertius (2.5), Socrates imagined his friends encouraging him to fight in the marketplace with his wife Xanthippe, who is traditionally portrayed as a shrew.

omnes hic aut captantur … lacerant: A quotation from Petronius’ Satyricon (116), where Croton (referred to in note ‘f’, now Crotone in Calabria) is depicted as an uncultured and corrupt city, once powerful and flourishing but now dominated by unscrupulous legacy hunters.

Vatinian hatred: The Roman politician Publius Vatinius (b. c. 95 BCE) was publicly attacked in 56 by Cicero, who was then his declared political enemy. Although Vatinius was elected consul in 47, Cicero’s speeches led to his later becoming a proverbial object of intense animosity.

bestead: Assist or relieve. Cato … an old servant: In fact, Cato the Elder was criticized by Plutarch for mistreating his slaves in precisely this manner. Bajazet … make him away: Sultan Bayezid II (1447–1512) had his admiral Gedik Ahmed Pasha executed in 1482 (‘Bassa’ is a variant spelling of ‘bashaw’, itself an earlier form of the title ‘Pasha’). as Silius … Tiberius: The Roman senator and general Gaius Silius was forced by the emperor Tiberius (42 BCE–37 CE) to commit suicide in 24 CE, after claiming that without his help the mutinous Roman legions on the Rhine would have removed the latter from power.

Dea moneta: ‘Moneta’ was one of the epithets of Juno. The Romans had a temple on the Capitoline Hill dedicated to Juno Moneta, probably because of its proximity to the mint. depressed: Lowered, or kept down. Prima fere … &c.: The full quotation from Juvenal (Satires 10.23–4) in note ‘f’ is given below, p. 684 (3.1.2.1).
cogging: Cheating, wheedling.

Qui Curios … vivunt: The quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.3) in note ‘c’ refers to the gens Curia, a Roman plebeian family associated with traditional virtue principally because of the reputation of Manius Curius Dentatus, censor in 272 BCE, for incorruptibility and modesty. ambidexters: Double-dealers, practising on both sides. turning pictures: Pictures which show different images when seen from different angles.

Proteus: In classical mythology, a minor sea-god with shape-shifting qualities. like Mercury the Planet: In Renaissance astrology, the influence of Mercury was thought to oscillate between benevolence and malevolence, depending on its relationship with other planets. garb: Demeanour. baffled: Disgraced, treated with contempt.
the two … glass: In note ‘h’, a ‘perspective glass’ is a magnifying glass, telescope, or optical instrument devised to produce unusual visual effects. livor: Ill-will, spite.
jade: An ill-tempered, worn-out or worthless horse. pined: Starved, tormented.
buy smoke for wares: To be swindled (in Latin fumum vendere, ‘to sell smoke’, means to deal fraudulently). tires: Clothing, attire.
Alphonsus: King Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458).

fortune’s fan turns: ‘Fan’ probably means ‘vane’ or ‘weathercock’, although contemporary poetic usage of the phrase ‘fortune’s fan’ suggests that it could refer to a tool for winnowing grain (via allusion to Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17, where John the Baptist predicts the coming of Jesus as one ‘[w]hose fan is in his hand, and he will th[o]roughly purge his floor’).
an hundred oaks on his back: That is, wearing expensive clothing purchased with the proceeds from the sale of a large quantity of land. Anthropophagi: Cannibals (literally, ‘human-eaters’).
genius: Here, appetite.
ruffle: Brag or swagger. The 1632 edition has ‘russle’ (‘rustle’).

obligation: In law, a written contract or bond. paint Thais: Thais was a famous Athenian courtesan of the fourth century BCE, and was allegedly a mistress of Alexander the Great and subsequently of the Egyptian king Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367/6–282 BCE), but her name here is being used figuratively to refer to any courtesan; ‘paint’ here means ‘adorn with colours’, that is, by applying cosmetics. philologer: A literary scholar.
Aesop’s ape: In the fable ‘Jupiter and the Monkey’, a mother ape is ridiculed when she presents her ugly offspring as the most beautiful beast in the forest. wittol: A contented cuckold, a fool.
colon: Farmer. moil: Work hard, drudge.
insist in: Dwell at length upon.

which Momus … Vulcan’s man: In Lucian’s Hermotimus, or Concerning the Sects (20), the figure of Momus criticizes the design of man by Hephaestus for lacking a means of easily discerning ‘his thoughts and designs, his truth or falsehood’. Hephaestus was the Greek god of fire, blacksmiths and artisans, and the equivalent of the Roman god Vulcan; he was traditionally associated with the creation of Pandora, the goddess of the earth (and the cause of all human miseries), and it is Lucian’s witty extrapolation to give him this role for mankind. On Momus, see above, n. 7 (Preliminaries).

Gallus: The Latin term for a cockerel, and the eponymous character in Lucian’s dialogue. Gyges’ invisible ring: In classical mythology, King Gyges of Lydia (seventh century BCE) had been a shepherd who rose to power by using a magic ring that rendered its wearer invisible. Otacousticon: An ear trumpet, or a similar instrument to assist hearing. species: The bearers of sense-data – see the account of ‘sensible species’ at 1.1.2.7, and n. 34 (1.1.2) below. projectors: Schemers.

Haec sani … juret Orestes: An adaptation from Persius (3.117–18) of ‘dicisque facisque quod ipse non sani esse hominis non sanus iuret Orestes’ (‘You say and do things that even insane Orestes would swear were signs of madness’), which – assuming that sanus is a deliberate replacement for insanus – perhaps builds on the preceding paradox that no one is actually sane.
Seneca’s blind woman: Harpaste, the female clown in the household of Seneca, who reports that she went blind without realizing it (Epistles 50.2–3).
Clodius accusat moechos: The quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.27) in note ‘a’ refers to the notoriously dissolute Roman politician Publius Clodius Pulcher (c. 93–52 BCE).
Atticus … his own spouse: The reference is taken from Cicero’s letters to his friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, but the passage is actually a quotation of the Roman poet Atilius (second century CE).
take himself by the nose: See above, n. 3 (Preliminaries). as Marsyas was … Apollo: In classical mythology, the satyr Marsyas was flayed alive after challenging Apollo to a musical contest.

with Sallust … a most grievous poller himself: Before turning to history-writing, Sallust (86–35 BCE) faced charges of exploiting the Roman province of Africa Nova (Numidia), of which he had been the first governor; ‘poller’ here means ‘despoiler’ or ‘plunderer’.

in Tully’s censure … as mad as himself: In his speech In Defence of Sextus Roscius of Ameria, Cicero presents the politician Gaius Flavius Fimbria (consul in 104 BCE) as an insane criminal, underlining the audacity of his attempted assassination (and then attempted prosecution) of the eminent lawyer and statesman Quintus Mucius Scaevola (c. 140–82 BCE); and see below, n. 6 (3.4.2).
jangling: Babbling or squabbling.

as Ulysses did … a hog still: Drawing on the tenth book of the Odyssey, in which the companions of Odysseus (Ulysses) were transformed by Circe into animals, Plutarch’s Gryllus describes Odysseus’ attempt to restore them to human form,
and relates the argument of Gryllus (now a pig) that animals have greater virtue and intelligence than humans. Elpenor, the youngest companion of Odysseus, is not mentioned in the dialogue. bray: Pound, crush to powder.

Athamas: In classical mythology, the king of Orchomenus in Boeotia driven mad by one of the Furies (Tisiphone), sent by Hera (Juno) out of jealousy because he and his wife Ino had brought up the child Dionysus, the son of Zeus (Jupiter).
good parts: Good qualities. seven wise men: See above, n. 91 (DJR).

Thales sent the golden Tripos … to Solon, &c.: In the traditional story (Diogenes Laertius 1.27), a group of fishermen discovered a golden tripod in the water, and after arguments about its ownership it was determined that the matter should be settled by the ‘Seven Sages’ of Greece. Starting with Thales, each one of the sages passed the matter on to another, with Solon eventually declaring that it should be placed in the temple of Apollo at Delphi.

as the three goddesses … golden apple: A reference to ‘the apple of discord’ in classical mythology, tossed by Eris (the personification of strife) into the feast of the gods at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and triggering the conflict between Aphrodite, Athena and Hera which led to the Trojan War.

temperature of his body: The balance of qualities in the whole body or in a particular bodily part, also referred to as the ‘temperament’ or ‘complexion’. An imbalance of these qualities was sometimes called a ‘distemperature’ (see the editor’s Introduction).

Xerxes … and the like: According to Herodotus (7.35), Xerxes I of Persia (ruled 486–465 BCE) set about whipping the Hellespont (now the Dardanelles strait) in a fit of rage, after two bridges built across it by his men had been destroyed in a storm; their construction of a canal through the peninsula of Mount Athos, however, was successful.
rakest: Scratch (or, alternatively, drag away or pull apart).
afternoon men: Men given to drinking alcohol after lunch, or simply habitual drinkers.

Hours: The classical Horae, goddesses of the seasons. Dionysus: The Greek god of wine and intoxication, but also, among other things, of ritual madness and ecstasy (his Roman counterpart being Bacchus).
bands: Chains.

pauci Promethei, multi Epimethei: According to the ancient Greek poet Hesiod, the name of Prometheus means ‘forethinker’ (and hence signifies forethought), and that of his brother Epimetheus means ‘afterthinker’ (signifying afterthought). In Hesiod’s account, Prometheus was a clever trickster, capable of stealing the fire of Zeus and giving it to man, but the foolish Epimetheus accepted Hephaestus’ gift of Pandora, releasing all manner of evils into the world – see also above, n. 179 (DJR).

Carolus Sapiens, Philippus Bonus, Lodovicus Pius: Charles V (‘the Wise’), king of France (1338–80), Philip III (‘the Good’), duke of Burgundy (1396–1467), and Louis IX (‘the Pious’), king of France (1214–70). an aristocracy … Politicians: For classical political theorists (‘Politicians’), aristocracy is the constitutional rule by ‘the best’ (usually identified as the nobility), as distinguished from monarchy and popular government or democracy.
Apollo consulted … find one: See above, n. 90 (DJR).

multi Thyrsigeri, pauci Bacchi: The contrast between bearers of the thyrsus (a staff tipped with an ornament like a pine cone, carried by votaries of Dionysus or Bacchus) and true mystical followers of the god is drawn by Plato in the Phaedo (69C–D).

Archytas Tarentinus: Archytas of Tarentum, an ancient Greek Pythagorean philosopher (fl. c. 400–350 BCE) said to have invented mathematical mechanics. Geber: Or ‘pseudo-Geber’, the author(s) of an anonymous thirteenth-century corpus of alchemical work that includes material on alphabetical numerology,
now sometimes thought to be the thirteenth-century Italian Franciscan Paul of Taranto, but formerly identified with the ninth-century Islamic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan (the real ‘Geber’). Alkindus the Mathematician: The influential Arabic philosopher, mathematician and polymath Al-Kindi (d. c. 870 CE).
Ptolemaeus: The ancient Greek astronomer and polymath Claudius Ptolemaeus, or Ptolemy (c. 90–168 CE).

he makes Galen fimbriam Hippocratis: Literally, ‘the fringe’ or ‘hem’ of Hippocrates (fimbrias could refer to the border or hem of a cloak, gown or robe, or to tassels hanging from it). The implication – also carried here by the term ‘skirt’, which refers to the lower part of a hanging garment – is that Galen’s works are to be regarded as the ornamental bordering of those of Hippocrates, or simply as their appendage.
idiots: Unskilled or untrained people.
Suisset the Calculator: The English natural philosopher and mathematician Richard Swineshead (fl. c. 1340–54), famous as the author of the Liber calculationum.

deciphered: Represented, portrayed. the sacrifice of Dionysius: A slightly misleading translation of ‘Dionysi sacra’ (‘the rites of Dionysus’) in the commentary on Plato’s Republic (1469) by the Italian Neoplatonist philosopher Marsilio Ficino, who claims that the Dionysian rites signified this kind of spiritual ‘drunkenness’ for Orpheus.
sacerdos Aegyptius: In note ‘h’, the Egyptian priest from Plato’s Timaeus is said to have rebuked the Greeks as perpetual children.
issue: Outcome, result.
Sorites: In logic, a ‘chain’ or series of connected syllogisms, in which the predicate of one proposition is the subject of the next.

Phocion: An Athenian statesman and general, and a politically conservative pupil of Plato. His opposition to democracy is related by Plutarch, and he was executed for his Macedonian sympathies in the brief democratic revolution in 318 BCE. never a barrel better herring: Proverbially, ‘they are all basically the same’, or ‘much of a muchness’.

Copernicus, Atlas his successor: Atlas, the Titan from classical mythology tricked by Heracles (Hercules) into holding up the sky, is presented by Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 4.27.5) as the founder of astronomy.
in sober sadness: In earnest.

creatures: Created things, creations. Rue: A species of ruta, Ruta graveolens. that artificial … them all: At 1.1.3.3 below, Burton explains that ‘artificial’ melancholy is ‘immaterial’, and distinct from the ‘natural’ subspecies of the disease in so far as it is adventitious – that is, principally caused not by black bile but by factors external to the body. The point here is that every organism is susceptible to this ‘artificial’ kind of melancholy.
terse: Refined, cultured.
uncivil: Uncivilized, barbarous.

Lop and Belgian in Asia: ‘Lop’ was the name given by Marco Polo to the kingdom of Charklik (now Ruoqiang in China), located near the Taklamakan Desert. ‘Belgian’ refers generally to Tartary, but also more specifically, according to the Italian cartographer Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), to the obscure promontory on the northeastern cape of Eurasia usually known as ‘Tabin’. Alexandretta: The Turkish city and district of İskenderun, sometimes known as Scanderoon. Bantam: The Javanese port city of Banten. Pisa: On the ‘bad air’ in this city, see below, p. 238 (1.2.2.5). Durazzo: The Italian name for the Albanian city of Durrës. St. John de Ullua: San Juan de Ulúa, a Spanish settlement overlooking the port of Veracruz in Mexico. Podolians: Inhabitants of Podolia, a region in what is now southwestern Ukraine.

Mantua … Cremonae: The phrase in note ‘a’ is a quotation from Virgil (Eclogues 9.26), which laments the land confiscations for the resettlement of military
veterans after the Battle of Philippi (42 BCE), which were extended to Mantua because those from nearby Cremona were not sufficient. Interdum … olim Mauritania, &c.: Note ‘b’ probably refers to the ancient reputation of Mauretania – the territory of the Moors extending from the River Ampsaga in Numidia to the Atlantic – as a land populated by dangerous wild animals (as portrayed, for example, in Horace, Odes 1.22). barred: Blocked up, made inaccessible. Brundisium: The Latin name for Brindisi.
Gerar: The Philistine settlement mentioned in Genesis 20:1–18, possibly in what is now the valley of Nahal Gerar in Israel.

Barcino: The Latin name for Barcelona. Achan’s fault: Achan was stoned and burned for stealing some of the spoils of Jericho, which had been consecrated for the treasury of the Lord’s House; this resulted in the collective punishment of the Israelites by God (Joshua 7:1–26). His name is hence associated with greed or simony.

Sardanapalus: The legendary king of Assyria said to have lived in the seventh century BCE. Dionysius Junior: Dionysius II, tyrant of Syracuse (c. 397–c. 343 BCE). Heliogabalus: The Roman emperor Elagabalus (c. 203–22 CE). Periander: Tyrant of Corinth (d. 587 BCE). Pisistratus: Tyrant of Athens (d. 527 BCE). Tarquinius: Probably Lucius Tarquinius Superbus (ruled 534–509 BCE), the last king of Rome, regarded as a tyrant and exiled – although the reference may be to the fifth king, Lucius Tarquinius Priscus (ruled 616–579 BCE), who was assassinated. Timocrates: Timocrates of Lampsacus (fourth to third century BCE), disciple-turned-opponent of Epicurus (though Timophanes, who became tyrant of Corinth in 366, is perhaps meant here). Childericus: Probably Childeric III (c. 717–c. 754 CE), king of Francia and the last of the Merovingian dynasty, who was deposed in 751 – although possibly his predecessor Childeric II (c. 653–75), who was assassinated. Appius Claudius: Appius Claudius Crassus, said to have led a tyrannical regime in the Second Decemvirate (450–449 BCE), when a board of ten magistrates with consular powers was set up to compile new laws for Rome. Andronicus: Governor of Antioch in the second century BCE, and involved with the Jewish High Priest Menelaus in the assassination of another High Priest, Onias III (2 Maccabees 4:31–8). Galeacius Sforza: Galeazzo Maria Sforza, duke of Milan (1444–76). Alexander Medices: Alessandro de’ Medici, duke of Florence (1510–37).

emulators: Competitors, rivals. Guelphs and Ghibellines: The main rival factions in the city-states of central and northern Italy in the Middle Ages. The former supported the papacy, the latter the Holy Roman Emperor.

Antigonus … all his subjects: The Antigonus mentioned here is Antigonus II Gonatas, king of Macedon (c. 277/6–239 BCE), whose correspondence with the Stoic philosopher Zeno is recorded by Diogenes Laertius (7.1).
mutine: Mutiny. innovations: Revolutions, insurrections.

When Catiline rebelled in Rome: A reference to the notorious failed conspiracy, led by the aristocratic senator Lucius Sergius Catilina (108–62 BCE) to overthrow the consulship of Cicero in 63 BCE. Jack Cade, Tom Straw, Kett: Three infamous English rebel leaders of somewhat lower (or murkier) social status: Jack Cade, of whose origins little is known, led an uprising in Kent in 1450; Jack (not Tom) Straw is a figure of some obscurity who was involved in the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 (according to some accounts it was the pseudonym of Wat Tyler or of one of the other leaders); Robert Kett, whose relatively wealthy family had once belonged to the gentry, led a revolt in Norfolk in 1549.
Mat. Geraldus: Possibly the Italian lawyer Matthaeus Gribaldus (Matteo Gribaldi, d. 1564).

fori tintinabula: This phrase, taken – along with others in this passage – from the third book of the Italian humanist scholar and physician Julius Caesar Scaliger’s
Poetices libri septem (1561), literally translates as ‘bells of the courts’. Scaliger explains that it is an appropriate insult to throw at a soi-disant legal ‘orator’. catchpoles: Tax-collectors or petty officers of justice.
civilian: A practitioner of Roman civil law (rather than canon or common law).
stale: Decoy.
jar: Discord, dispute. causes: Legal cases.
daysmen: Mediators or umpires.
Alfakins or chief Judge: Fuqaha, experts in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh).

scede: Or ‘schede’, a papyrus strip. Scytala Laconica: The skytale, a secret method of communication invented by the Spartans, in which a message was first imprinted by the sender upon a thin strip of leather wound round a wooden cylinder, made illegible by detaching the strip from the cylinder, and then revealed when the recipient rewound the leather on a cylinder of equal diameter.
disannulled: Abolished, annulled.
termers: People who resorted to London during a law term, either for legal business in the courts, or for entertainment or criminality.
incult: Uncultivated, wild.
a discourse … happy reign: The author of this work was the lawyer and poet Sir John Davies (c. 1569–1626), who had served under James I as Solicitor-General in Ireland since 1603.

Parks: Enclosed portions of land held by royal grant or prescription, and reserved for the keeping and hunting of deer and other game. Forests: Woodland districts, typically belonging to the king, also set aside for hunting.

Quinctius in Livy: The Roman statesman and general Titus Quinctius Flamininus (c. 229–174 BCE). the fortunate Isles: The Isles of the Blessed, the residence of heroes in Greek and Celtic mythology, and said to be located somewhere in the Western (Atlantic) Ocean. two of their Captains … round about the world: The circumnavigators Sir Francis Drake (1540–96) and Sir Thomas Cavendish (c. 1560–92).

manured: Cultivated, managed. a wise, learned, Religious King, another Numa … a true Josiah: This passage was present in the first edition of 1621, when James I was on the English throne, but it remained unaltered in the later editions published after Charles I had become king in March 1625. Josiah (c. 649–609 BCE) was a king of Judah, famed, like the legendary Roman king Numa Pompilius, for his religious reforms (2 Chronicles 34–5).
Lycurgus: The legendary founder and lawgiver of ancient Sparta.

Greichgea: Kraichgau, a mountainous region in southwestern Germany. 24 Italian miles over: An ‘Italian mile’ varied in length, ranging between seven-eighths and one and a quarter English miles. According to the traveller and geographer Fynes Moryson, writing in 1617, an Italian mile was 1,000 paces in length (and so identical to a Roman mile), and an English one was 1,500 paces (1,760 yards).
twelve miles over by their scale: A German mile was typically between four and five English miles. According to Fynes Moryson, it was ‘more than three English, or five Italian miles’.
Portugallia interamnis: Literally, ‘Portugal between the rivers’: the region between the Douro and Minho Rivers.

Peru, or Nova Hispania: The Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru, created in 1542, included what is now Peru but also most of the territories of South America under Spanish rule. ‘Nova Hispania’ (literally, ‘New Spain’) included Mexico and its surrounding territories but also extended into what is now the southern USA, as well as parts of South America and Oceania.

any stuff almost: The source upon which this passage is loosely based, Giovanni Botero’s De illustrium statu & politia (1607), suggests that ‘stuff’ here means
raw material. But the term may refer more narrowly to textile or woollen fabric, or alternatively to manufactured material.
Paulus Aemilius: The Roman statesman and general Lucius Aemilius Paullus (c. 229–160 BCE), whose forces, on the orders of the senate, sacked Epirus in northwestern Greece in 167.
Mount Taygetus: The highest mountain in the Taygetus range, in the Peloponnesian peninsula of southern Greece.
the Saxon Heptarchy: The seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of the early Middle Ages (East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria).

Rheti: Or ‘R(h)aeti’, a group of Alpine tribes, identified in antiquity as descendants of the Etruscans, and, since the Middle Ages, the inhabitants of the province of Raetia (roughly speaking the territory of modern-day Grisons). Ragusa: The Republic of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, was an independent maritime state.
Those ancient Massilians: The inhabitants of the ancient Greek colony of Massalia (Massilia in Roman writers), now Marseille.

Selim the first Turkish Emperor: Selim I (1470–1520), Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. Tauris: The ancient name for several places, including the region now known as Crimea and the cities of Tabriz and Hamedan in modern-day Iran. Here, however, Burton has been misled by Robert Peterson’s mistranslation of ‘Taurunum’ (the Latin name for Zemun, now part of Belgrade) in Botero’s De illustrium statu & politia. Henry Duke of Anjou … Poland: Henri of Valois (1551–89) was elected king of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1573, a year before ascending the French throne as Henri III.
James the first in Scotland: James I (1394–1437), king of Scotland.
clothing: Cloth-making. Gaunt: Ghent.
Arabia Petraea: The name of the ‘Arabian Province’ of the Roman Empire, bordering what was then the southern frontier of Syria and the northern frontier of Egypt.
Ormus in Persia: The island of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. opportunity: The advantage given by a suitable or accessible site.
intellectus agens: The ‘agent’ or ‘active’ intellect, an essential component of the rational intelligence of the human being in Aristotelian psychology; see 1.1.2.10 below.
Mexico: That is, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán (now Mexico City).
Tails: Inferior or less valuable parts.
ploughs: Means of earning a livelihood.
riot: Debauchery, dissipation or excess.
Egyptian vagabonds: The Romani people, who first came to England in the early sixteenth century, were sometimes thought to originate from Egypt – hence the name ‘Gypsies’.

Carolus Magnus: Charlemagne, or ‘Charles the Great’ (742–814 CE), king of the Franks and the Lombards, and Holy Roman Emperor. the Duke of Saxony: Burton’s source, the German political theorist Henning Arnisaeus (1570–1636), refers to Augustus, elector (but not duke) of Saxony from 1553 to 1586.
Potosa in Peru: Now Potosí in Bolivia, famous for its silver mines, which were discovered in 1545 and subsequently an important source of revenue for the Spanish Empire.

those stupend works … at Ostium: The artificial enclosed harbour at Portus (two miles north of Ostia), which was linked to the River Tiber by a canal. Initially ordered by the emperor Claudius, it was built in 42–64 CE and then expanded and improved by Trajan in 103. Dioclesiani Therma: The Baths of Diocletian, built in 298–306 CE. Fucinus Lacus: The Fucine lake (Laco Fucino) had been partially drained by Claudius over a period of eleven years, according to Suetonius (The Deified Claudius 20). that Piraeus in Athens: The Athenian politician and general
Themistocles began the development and fortification of the port at Piraeus in 493/2 BCE. Civitas Philippi: Philippi, now Filippoi in northeastern Greece. Heraclea in Thrace: Formerly Perinthus, now Marmara Ereğlisi in Turkey. those Appian and Flaminian ways: The Via Appia and the Via Flaminia, two important Roman roads built in the republican period, and connecting Rome to Brundisium (Brindisi) and Arminium (Rimini) respectively. Moeris and Sesostris: According to Herodotus, the artificial ‘Lake of Moeris’ was named after the Egyptian pharaoh responsible for its construction. He probably had Amenemhet III (who ruled c. 1860–c. 1814 BCE) in mind, but this is a mistake possibly deriving from a misunderstanding of the Egyptian term for ‘canal’ (mi-wer). Sesostris was a legendary Egyptian king whose achievements, based on those of three pharaohs of the Twelfth Dynasty named Senusret, are recorded by Herodotus and Diodorus Siculus. Amasis Aegypti Rex: Note ‘d’ refers to the pharaoh Amasis II, who reigned 570–525 BCE.
corrivations of Waters: Confluences of streams, but here apparently referring to irrigation channels. Moors: Marshes.
Masinissa: King of Numidia (238–148 BCE). battable: Fertile in pasture.

in Egypt, about Babylon and Damascus: ‘Babylon’ here is the city now known as Cairo; Damascus was a provincial capital of the Mamluk Empire, ruled by the Sultan of Egypt, between 1260 and 1516 (Burton is here drawing on an account first published in 1510 by the Italian travel writer Ludovico di Varthema).

cubits: A cubit was an ancient measurement of length deriving from the forearm, usually about eighteen to twenty-two inches. Ptolemy: The Egyptian ruler Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE). absolved: Completed.

Demetrius: Demetrius I Poliorcetes of Macedon (336–283 BCE), whose plans for a canal were never implemented. Herodes Atticus: Tiberius Claudius Atticus Herodes (c. 101–77 CE), a wealthy Athenian sophist and benefactor of Greek cities. our Picts’ wall: Hadrian’s Wall, setting what was then the northern limit of the Roman Empire in the province of Britannia, and beyond which lay the territory of the Picts. Schoenunte: Schoinous (Kalamaki) on the Saronic Gulf, east of Corinth.
Hexamilium, which Amurath the Turk demolished: The Hexamilion (‘six-mile’) wall was reportedly destroyed in 1446 by the forces of Sultan Murad II (1404–51).
Rhodanus: The River Rhône.
from Arar to Mossella: From the River Saône to the Moselle River.
Aurelianus: The Roman emperor Aurelian (Lucius Domitius Aurelianus), who ruled 270–75 CE. some Indian plants: That is, plants (such as potatoes) from the West Indies.
In France … salt: Via the ‘gabelle’, a tax on salt.
Durius: The Douro. Hebrus: The Maritsa.
Bishop Atwater: William Atwater (1440–1521), bishop of Lincoln.
vent and utterance: Opportunity for the selling or bartering of goods.
Aulis: Now Avlida. Ambracia: Now Arta.

Sus Minervam: An abbreviation of ‘Sus Minervam docet’, an ancient proverb deriding the attempt of a stupid person to instruct a wise one. verjuice and oatmeal is good for a Parrot: A comical homophonic translation of ‘veritas odium parit’ that plays on the sourness of verjuice.

general visitor: A visiting inspector-general. Rosy Cross men: The mystical Rosicrucian fraternity: a fictitious secret society, identified in the seventeenth century and allegedly devoted to mysticism and alchemy, for which two anonymous manifestos, the Fama fraternitatis Rosae Crucis and the Confessio fraternitatis, had been published in 1614 and 1615. policy: Civil order, polity.

to strive with Achelous … as he did Hesione: Scenes from the life of Heracles (Hercules) in classical mythology: his defeat of the shape-shifting river-god Achelous, a rival suitor for Deianira – on whom, see below, n. 9 (1.4.1); his fifth labour,
to clean the stables of King Augeas in a single day; his killing of two tyrants, the Thracian king Diomedes, who owned a team of man-eating mares which were kept supplied with human victims (during his eighth labour), and the Egyptian king Busiris, who habitually slaughtered foreigners entering Egypt (during his eleventh labour); his killing of the giant Cacus and the robber Lacinius after they had stolen from him some of the cattle he had been sent to obtain from the giant Geryon (his tenth labour); and his rescue of the Trojan princess Hesione from a sea-monster sent by Poseidon (Neptune). vindicate: Rescue, or liberate. the Torrid Zone: The region situated between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, in which the sun is directly overhead on at least one occasion during the year; see also below, n. 118 (1.2.3). Theban Crates: The Cynic philosopher Crates of Thebes (c. 365–c. 285 BCE), who, according to Diogenes Laertius (6.5), lived in virtuous poverty after giving away his large personal fortune to his fellow citizens.

those mighty Maeotian fens: The marshlands lying northeast of the Sea of Azov (Lake Maeotis in antiquity), which adjoins the Black Sea. Hercynian woods: The Hercynian Forest, which stretched across southern Germany in antiquity. Scorbutum, Plica, morbus Neapolitanus: The epidemical diseases of scurvy, trichoma (or ‘Polish plait’) and syphilis (first identified in Naples, hence morbus Neapolitanus – though it was also known as morbus Gallicus, ‘the French disease’ or ‘French pox’; see below, 1.1.1.2).
L. Licinius: Actually ‘Lycinus’, the character who ridicules the ambitions of Timolaus at the end of Lucian’s dialogue The Ship.

Boccalinus … by Commissioners: Boccalini’s Ragguagli di Parnaso (1612/13), one of whose English translators was Burton’s acquaintance William Vaughan – on whom, see below, n. 52 (2.2.3). It imagines a custom in which Apollo presents princes and potentates with the disorders in their commonwealths, and then challenges them either to defend themselves from criticism or else to implement reforms. The god subsequently appoints the ‘Seven Sages’ of Greece, along with Cato and Seneca, as commissioners to effect a ‘general Reformation’ of the world.

lapis super lapidem sedeat: Probably an adaptation of Christ’s prediction of the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem in Matthew 24:2 (‘non relinquetur hic lapis super lapidem qui non destruatur’: ‘there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone that shall not be destroyed’), suggesting persistence rather than removal.

Pictoribus atque Poetis, &c.: A partial quotation of a maxim from Horace’s Art of Poetry (9–10): ‘Pictoribus atque poetis/quidlibet audendi semper fuit aequa potestas’ (‘Painters and poets have always had an equal right to dare as they please’).

Mare del Zur: The Pacific Ocean (after its Spanish name, ‘Mar del Zur’). the Cyanean Isles in the Euxine sea: The Symplegades (‘Clashing Rocks’) in the Bosporus strait, which in Greek mythology were said to move around randomly, being unattached to the sea bed, and were successfully navigated by Jason and the Argonauts. The ‘Euxine’ is the Greek name for the Black Sea.
coasts: Regions, places or countries.

be it known … these presents: The conventional opening words of a legal proclamation or charter; the phrase ‘these presents’ refers to the present document or its contents. so much money … for casting a Nativity: That is, a very substantial amount. In his De interrogationibus libellus (1555), the Italian polymath and physician Girolamo Cardano warns astrologers not to accept small fees, and says that he once rejected the offer of 200 crowns for drawing up a single horoscope. advowsons: ‘Advowson’ is the exclusive right in ecclesiastical law to present a member of the clergy to a benefice, or more generally to patronage of a church or religious house.

Staples: A town or place granted the right of purchase of certain classes of export goods by royal authority. Hippodamus Milesius: In note ‘e’, Hippodamus of
Miletus (b. c. 500 BCE), was the most famous town-planner in ancient Greece. Rhegium Lepidi: Now Reggio Emilia in northern Italy, built within hexagonal town walls. Cambalu: A corruption of ‘Khanbaliq’, which had been the capital of the Mongol Empire since the reign of Kublai Khan (1260–94), and now Beijing. Palma: Palmanova, a Venetian settlement in northeastern Italy, built as a fortress in the shape of a nine-pointed star and founded in 1593.
baser: Lower in height. after the latest manner of fortification: Complex geometrical arrangements of ditches, moats and projecting bastions made of earth, designed to withstand gunfire.

burses: Or ‘bourses’, commercial exchanges. artillery gardens: Practice grounds for artillery. gymnics: Gymnastics. hospitals: Charitable institutions, or asylums, for the poor, infirm or aged. pest-houses: Hospitals for those suffering from infectious disease, especially plague. a satisfactory almshouse: An almshouse providing ‘satisfaction’ or atonement for sin. benevolences: Voluntary gifts of money. donaries: Donations or votive offerings.
Misnia: Meissen in eastern Germany. Stetein in Pomerland: Szczecin (formerly German Stettin), the capital city of the Polish province of West Pomerania.

Labedum in Ionia: Lebedus, which in Roman times hosted gatherings of Ionian actors and festivals dedicated to Bacchus (Dionysus). pendant: Modern editors have sometimes emended this to ‘pedant’, but in the seventeenth century the term ‘pendant’ could refer to a testicle, and the comical sense of a ‘hanger-on’ may be intended here.

Aediles, Quaestors: Magistrates in the Roman Republic responsible, respectively, for the maintenance of public buildings and festivals, and for the management of public finances. pupils: Orphans who are minors, and consequently, in civil law, wards. all public houses: Communal buildings of all kinds (rather than all taverns).

Mr. Carew … doth raise, &c.: Note ‘c’ refers to discussions about enclosure, which had traditionally been associated with depopulation and the impoverishment of the labouring poor. ‘Cotswold’ refers to the finer wool of sheep from the Cotswolds; Burton’s source, the Cornish antiquary Richard Carew (1555–1620), simply says that after enclosure, ‘Cornish Sheep come but little behind the Eastern flocks’ – that is, those found in counties east of Cornwall.
engrossings: The purchase of land (or other goods) in order to gain a monopoly. fine: In feudal society, the fee paid by a tenant or vassal to a landlord on some alteration of the tenancy.
Fellmongers: Dealers in animal skins or hides. Chandlers: Candle-sellers. curriers: Leather dressers and colourers.
subordinate as the other: Subordinate, that is, to the power of the king, as in civil law.

impropriations: Annexations of benefices (or their revenues) to a lay corporation or lay proprietor. common societies: Shared associations, such as guilds, corporations or charitable foundations. the literati in China: The ‘learned class’ of China, cultured intellectuals who were employed as officials in the Chinese state bureaucracy from the seventeenth to the early twentieth century.
Auditors: People who listen to sermons, or receive spiritual instruction orally.
delegacy: A body or committee of delegates.
to depend: To be suspended, await determination.

Solon’s Areopagites: The Athenian council of the Areopagus, according to the Athenian Constitution (a work often attributed to Aristotle), was instituted by Solon in the early sixth century BCE to act as the guardian of the laws and overseer of the activities of magistrates. proling: Prowling. diapason: Complete agreement, concord.
jument: Beast of burden.

merry-meetings: Festivities, convivial gatherings. that Saccarum festum … Saturnals in Rome: Two ancient festivals in which social norms were overturned, and thereby associated with licentious behaviour: the Persian Sacaea, possibly adopted from the Babylonian New Year Festival, and the Roman Saturnalia, a carnivalesque celebration that took place in December.
En leges ipsi Veneri Martique timendas: The allusion to Mars and Venus in note ‘e’, which is a quotation from Juvenal (Satires 2.31), refers to their adultery – see below, n. 10 (3.1.1).

Aliter Aristoteles … a woman at 30: In note ‘i’, the ages given are incorrect; and, from the second edition of 1624 onwards – where ‘30’ was replaced by ‘20’ – also confusing, as this brought Burton into line with the guidelines in Plato’s Republic (460E). Aristotle, in fact, states in the Politics (7.14) that men should be thirty-seven and women eighteen before they marry.
enormous: Abnormal or extraordinary.
intempestive: Inopportune, untimely.

his tract of usury … anno 1621: In note ‘b’, the author of the Tract against the High Rate of Usury, which had been presented to parliament in 1621 and published anonymously in 1623, was Sir Thomas Culpeper (1577/8–1662).

multiplicity of offices, of supplying by deputies: The same person holding two or more offices or positions, especially ecclesiastical ones (also called ‘pluralism’), and appointing a deputy to discharge duties on his behalf. Burton added this restriction in the second edition of 1624 (the year in which his income from the benefice of Walesby was added to that from Osney). those rectified by the Primum mobile … resolve bodies by Algebra, Stereometry: The process of correctly calculating and determining (‘rectifying’ and ‘resolving’) the measurements of three-dimensional objects by astronomical and geometrical methods: the primum mobile (‘prime mover’) is the outermost celestial sphere – see below, n. 52 (1.2.1) – revolving around the earth in a twenty-four-hour cycle; a ‘geometrical pace’ is the distance between successive stationary positions of the same foot when walking (roughly a length of five feet); ‘stereometry’ is the art or science of measuring solid bodies. Burton’s interest in this area is perhaps related to his earlier service as Clerk of the Market at Oxford (see the editor’s Introduction).

Fabius … not Minucius: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus Cunctator (the ‘Delayer’, d. 203 BCE), the Roman general renowned for his struggle with Hannibal in the Second Punic War with Carthage (218–201), and responsible for the famous ‘Fabian’ strategy of refusing to engage with the enemy except when absolutely necessary; Marcus Minucius Rufus (d. 216), second in command to Fabius and also his political opponent, rejected the strategy by engaging Hannibal’s army at Geronium in 217, and subsequently had to be rescued by his more cautious superior.
defalcations: Deductions. reparations: Repairs.
included: Confined.
corsives: Sources of care or annoyance. Economical body: Household (from the Greek οἶκος, ‘house’).

as Actaeon was by his hounds: In the oldest version of the classical myth, Zeus (Jupiter) punishes the hero Actaeon for raping Semele by sending Artemis (Diana) to turn him into a stag and set his own dogs on him. In other versions, his offence is to boast that he is a better hunter than Artemis, or to see the goddess naked while she is bathing, or to try to marry her in her own sanctuary.
But of this elsewhere: See 1.2.3.10 and 1.2.4.6 below.
naught: Morally bad.
liquorish: Greedy or lecherous. quean: Prostitute. soft: Simple-minded, lacking ordinary intelligence or common sense.

the Thrush and the Swallow in Aesop: In Aesop’s fable ‘Of the Thrush Entering into Friendship with the Swallow’, the thrush, who prefers a cold climate, is told he is incompatible with the swallow, who prefers a warm one. compellations: Names, titles, or words by which someone is addressed.

daughter-in-law: Possibly, stepdaughter (a now obsolete meaning). descend to their present fortunes: That is, deign to stoop, or condescend, to their deteriorated circumstances. when they concur: In note ‘e’, ‘concur’ means ‘coincide’ or, more specifically here, ‘collide’.
casualties: Precarious accidents or uncertainties. drenched: Drowned, overwhelmed.
secure: Free from worry, put at ease. Hieron: The Sicilian tyrant Hieron I of Syracuse (ruled 478–466 BCE). Simonides: The poet Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BCE).

as he said … take it up: Valerius Maximus (7.ext.5) attributes this saying, actually addressed to a diadem not a robe, to an anonymous king. Elsewhere, Stobaeus identifies him as Antigonus, without stating which of the Macedonian kings with this name is meant.
procul a Jove … the nearer the worse: As Erasmus explains in the 1526 edition of his Adagia, the proverb warns against involvement with the very powerful.
casting Counters: Counters used to assist calculation or reckoning up, particularly in book-keeping (the process of ‘casting accounts’).
Minions: Beloved favourites. corculis … ‘little hearts’: An ancient Roman term of endearment, connoting judiciousness or sagacity (the heart was sometimes regarded as the seat of the intellect).

o Medici mediam pertundite venam: To ‘open up the median vein’ is to instigate bloodletting (here, as a treatment for melancholy and madness: see below, 2.5.1.2). The ‘median vein’ was the term for a major vein in the forearm.

Obs and Sols: Objections and Solutions, part of the scholastic disputational method employed in Renaissance theology. School divinity: Scholastic theology, as taught in the universities. intricable: Entangling, perplexing. Wit whither wilt: In note ‘b’, a proverbial phrase addressed to someone whose tongue (or ‘wit’) is running away with him. one calls it: Cicero, in On Divination (2.43.90).
Dr. Resolutus: The nickname of the philosopher and theologian John Baconthorpe (c. 1290–1345/52). Doctor Seraphicus: The title given to St Bonaventure (1221–74).

cere-diminuit-brum: An adaptation of a jocular tmesis (word-splitting), traditionally attributed to Ennius, ‘saxo cere comminuit brum’ (‘he split the brain with a rock’), which splits the term for brain (‘cerebrum’) with the word ‘splits’ (‘comminuit’).
circumvents: Captures, entraps. glozing: Cajoling, coaxing or representing speciously.

grants all Poets to be mad … and who doth not: The classical notion of mad poetic ‘fury’ or ‘frenzy’, the divine rapture experienced by poets while composing their works, was much discussed in the Renaissance. Si furor sit Lyaeus … & Poeta, &c.: The sense of the partial Latin quotation in note ‘e’, which is adapted from the Anacreontica (1554) by Julius Caesar Scaliger, is clarified by the original: ‘Si furor est Cupido,/Si furor est Lyaeus, Si furor est Thalia,/Quoties furor, furor, furor/Amans, bibens, poeta?’ (‘If madness is Cupid,/If madness is Bacchus,/If madness is Thalia,/How often do I become mad, mad, mad/In loving, drinking, {being} a poet?’) ‘Thalia’ is the Muse of comedy and idyllic poetry.
