beray: Befoul. humble-bees, dors or beetles: ‘Humble-bee’ was another name for the bumble-bee; ‘dor’ could refer to the bumble-bee, but also to the hornet or several different species of flying insect, including the dung beetle or may-bug. castigations: Emendations.
Artists: Here, scholars or philosophers, or more specifically those skilled in one of the seven ‘liberal arts’.

draws lines with Archimedes … besieged: Archimedes of Syracuse (287–212 BCE) died when the city was captured by the Romans. In a story related by Plutarch, he was killed by a Roman soldier because he refused to stop contemplating one of his mathematical diagrams. combustion: Commotion, tumult.

They get their wisdom by eating Piecrust some: In note ‘g’, the saying is a version of the proverb ‘Pie lid makes people wise’. Here, the ironic implication is apparently that a full stomach encourages the expression of (unwise) opinions. Traditionally, the saying refers to the removal of the pie lid – which served primarily to protect the pie filling from vermin and insects – as the means by which a person became ‘wise’ as to the contents of the pie.

Semiramis: The beautiful, mythical queen of Assyria whose great achievements and dissolute lifestyle were the subject of many ancient, medieval and Renaissance anecdotes. Her legend is evidently based on the historical figure of Sammu-Ramat, the wife of the Assyrian king Shamshi-Adad V (824–811 BCE).
as Machiavel of Cosmus Medices … in him: Machiavelli actually says this, in the Istorie fiorentine (1532), about Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–92) rather than his grandfather Cosimo (1389–1464).

Richard the rich Duke of Cornwall … like water: Richard, first earl of Cornwall and king of Germany (1209–72), bribed the imperial electors, but having failed to obtain the support of the papacy he was never crowned Holy Roman Emperor.

horn-mad: Originally, with reference to horned beasts, so enraged as to be ready to gore someone with one’s horn (and hence, mad with anger). There is also an allusion to sexual jealousy here, since cuckolds were sometimes said to wear horns on their brows – an idea that may originate in the archaic practice of removing the comb from a castrated cock and grafting its spurs on to the root, which then grew into horns.

Signior Deliro: A character in Ben Jonson’s Every Man out of His Humour (1599), described as ‘a fellow sincerely besotted on his own wife’, called Fallace, ‘& so rapt with a conceit of her perfections, that he simply holds himself unworthy of her’. Hercules Furens, Maenades, and Corybantes: Classical exempla of insane frenzy: ‘Raging Hercules’ – see below, n. 21 (2.4.2); the female worshippers of Dionysus (Bacchus), whose rituals involved ecstatic frenzy; and the semi-divine priests who worship in the orgiastic cults of Dionysus and Cybele with noisy flute music and wild dancing.

Deucalion and Pyrrha’s stones: The stones cast after the great flood, which had been unleashed by Zeus (Jupiter) as punishment for human hubris, by the hero Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha. In Ovid’s Metamorphoses (1.313–47), the stones were said to be transformed gradually into men and women, thereby repopulating the earth. Famian. Strada de bajulis … semisculptis: Note ‘c’ refers to an anecdote told about a fountain on the Via Lata in Rome by the Italian historian Famiano Strada (1572–1649), who observed that its statue of a porter pouring water from a wine-jar was indistinguishable from the real porters who would idly gather around it. that enchanted horn of Astolpho … themselves: In Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (1532), Duke Astolfo has a magic horn that causes his enemies to flee in fright. & laurus insana … insania affecit: In note ‘d’, the ‘laurus insana’ is a species of laurel, said by Pliny the Elder (16.89) to have grown on the tomb of Amycus, the mythical king of the Bebryces in Bithynia: when taken on board a ship, its branches would induce discord and quarrelling among the crew. the mad haven … of Daphnis insana: The port of Daphne on the Black Sea, reportedly named after a large laurel grove nearby (‘Daphne’ means laurel in Greek), and called ‘insana’ through association with the ‘laurus insana’. dementate: Dement, drive out of one’s mind. Midsummer moon: The full moon at the time of midsummer, both of which were traditionally associated with madness. the Dog
days last all the year long: In ancient astrology, the ‘Dog Star’ (Sirius) was thought to induce disease, and it was also traditionally thought to cause madness in dogs. The ‘dog days’ were the hottest part of the summer, when the Dog Star was rising.
sand-blind: Half-blind, dim-sighted.
bored: Trepanned – that is, have a hole bored into the skull to provoke the escape of pathogenic vapours; see 2.5.1.4 below.

Theologues: Theologians. Artists: Here, practitioners of magical arts or occult sciences, particularly astrologers and alchemists. of whom St. Bridget … have prophesied: The mystic and saint Bridget of Sweden (1303–73), the Italian theologian Joachim of Fiore (1135–1202) and the German astrologer Johannes Liechtenberger (d. 1503) were seen by some to have foretold the Rosicrucian movement. Elias artifex their Theophrastian master: The occult philosopher, physician and visionary Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541) was said to have predicted that he would be succeeded by ‘Elias Artifex’ (‘Elias the Artist’, named after the wandering prophet Elijah), a mythical figure who would renovate the arts and sciences.

Ammonius the philosopher: The Platonist philosopher Ammonius Saccas is famous mainly for his teaching of Plotinus at Alexandria in 232–42 CE, but he is also sometimes identified as the teacher of Origen, the Christian Father. Sapientium Octavus: An ironic remark taken from the Satires (2.296) of Horace; see above, n. 91 (DJR).

Gotham parish: The English village of Gotham, in Nottinghamshire, was traditionally labelled the home of stupid people. Lorarios: The lorarius was an ancient Roman official whose job was to flog slaves. Rabelais … Physician: The French satirist François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553) was also a medical doctor.
dry: Miserly, stingy. heteroclites: Abnormal or eccentric people. ordinary: Occurring in the course of regular, everyday life; customary.
winch: Wince.
salve: Heal.

Dionysian feasts: The festivals of Dionysus in Athens took place in the winter months, and started with the rural Dionysia, which involved performances of comedies, tragedies and dithyrambs. Here, in conjunction with the Roman Saturnalia – see above, n. 309 (DJR) – and the comments about leisured idleness and freedom of speech, they carry the implication of carnivalesque comic licence. as he said … periculum est: The Dutch poet and scholar Daniel Heinsius, in an address to the reader printed in the fourth edition of his Poemata (1613).
Vacunal fires: Vacuna was the ancient Roman goddess of the countryside, to whom sacrifices were made by rural worshippers after the harvest had been gathered – hence her association with leisure.

Οὔτις ἔλεγεν: The Greek name derives from the ninth book of the Odyssey, where Odysseus pretends to be called Οὔτις (‘Nobody’) in order to trick the Cyclops Polyphemus. Burton’s immediate source, however, is the Nemo (1510) of the German scholar, poet and satirist Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), which has been explicitly quoted above, at p. 120.
turn the buckle of his girdle: Proverbially, ‘get ready to fight’: a saying that derives from wrestling, in which the combatants would turn the buckles of their girdles behind them before engaging.
an old Poet: The Italian poet and philosopher Lodovico Lazzarelli, in his Crater Hermetis (1505).
castaway: Reprobate, someone rejected. caitiff: See above, n. 143 (DJR). relics: Residues. stupend: See above, n. 138 (DJR).
fabulous: Fond of relating fables or legends.
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
squalid: Parched, marked by drought.
Apollonius: See above, n. 55 (DJR), and below, n. 28 (1.2.1).
the law: The Law of God, as recorded in the Old Testament, and typically counterpoised in Protestant theology with the redemptive Gospel of the New Testament.
botch: Plague.
Astonishing: Dismaying, terrifying.
humiliation: Humbling, abasement.
his friend Marius: This letter of Pliny the Younger (7.26) is actually addressed to Valerius Maximus. period: Purpose, end.
as Peter … daughter’s ague: The source here, Petrarch’s De remediis utriusque fortunae (1366), refers to St Peter.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).

Oppositions, Quartiles, and such unfriendly Aspects: Astrological terms referring to different relationships of stars, or ‘aspects’ – the way in which they look at each other from their relative positions, which may be favourable or ‘unfriendly’. Such ‘aspects’ are measured in terms of fractions of the 360° that comprise the zodiac; an ‘opposition’ is one-half (180°), and a ‘quartile’ one-quarter (90°).

Lake Erno: Lough Erne, in County Fermanagh. According to William Camden in his Britannia (1586), where Gerald of Wales (1146–1223) is cited as a source, Lough Erne was said to have once been well-populated land, but God punished the inhabitants for their ‘abominable sex with animals’ by filling the territory with wild beasts and then flooding it.
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).

like Cadmus’ soldiers: In Greek mythology, Cadmus, the first king of Thebes, had followed the instructions of Athena by sowing in the earth the teeth of a dragon he had slain, from which sprang a race of warriors. Cadmus then threw a stone among the soldiers, causing them to attack each other; with the help of the last five men standing, he built the citadel of Thebes.

brazen bulls: Bulls made of brass, a reference to the torture device invented by Perillus of Athens for the tyrant Phalaris – who ruled Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily c. 570–c. 555 BCE – in which a man was imprisoned and then roasted to death by a fire lit underneath. strappados: The strappado was a form of torture in which the hands were tied behind the back and secured to a pulley. The victim was then hoisted from the ground and dropped halfway down with a jerk.

Hector gave Ajax a sword … hurtless bowels: The exchange of gifts described in the seventh book of the Iliad, where Hector gives Ajax a sword and Ajax gives Hector a belt, is used by Erasmus in his Adagia to illustrate the proverb ‘Gifts from enemies are no gifts’. After Hector was killed, the belt was used by Achilles to tie his corpse to his chariot and drag it around the walls of Troy; Ajax, who was driven into a mad fury by Athena after the council of Greek leaders awarded the armour of Achilles to Odysseus instead of him, then slaughtered a flock of sheep, mistaking them for the council, and killed himself with the sword. As a child Ajax
had been granted the gift of invulnerability (‘hurtless’ in this passage means ‘invulnerable’) by Heracles (Hercules).
surfeiting: Excessive indulgence.
the board: Food and drink served at a table.
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
facility: Laxity.
Pallas: The classical goddess Athena, regularly identified with Minerva.
Affection: Disease, or abnormal bodily condition.
habit: Physical condition or constitution.

Scorbutum … Plica … Morbus Gallicus: See above, n. 285 (DJR). ‘Sweating-sickness’ was an extreme and often fatal kind of fever that had appeared first in England in the later fifteenth century, before spreading to continental Europe.

Xenophilus the Musician: Xenophilus of Chalcidice (fl. c. 400 BCE), a Pythagorean philosopher and theorist of music. Pollio Romilius: Romilius Pollio, an otherwise unknown centenarian who, according to Pliny the Elder (22.53), explained to the emperor Augustus that his longevity was due to drinking honeyed wine and applying oil to his skin. Q. Metellus: The Roman statesman and military leader Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus, who was consul in 143 BCE, and whose four sons also all became consuls. the significators in his geniture fortunate: That is, benign planets were dominant in his horoscope.
Errant: Erratic, moving from one bodily part to another. Connexed: Connected.
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).
Wesel: Oesophagus. Chops: Jaws. furfur: Dandruff, scurf.

Cauls, Kells, Tunicles, Creeks: The first three are all names for membranes, and ‘creeks’ are narrow passages, referring here to those in the brain. passions: Ailments or afflictions. Caro: Usually called ‘carus’, a paralytic condition involving deep sleep and insensibility. Incubus: Or ephialtes, nightmare with palpitations and feelings of suffocation and anxiety. Falling sickness: Epilepsy.

Rheums, Distillations: Defluxions of rheum, catarrh. Frenzy, Lethargy … vigil Coma: ‘Lethargy’, ‘sopor’ and ‘coma’ were all conditions involving insensibility and sleepiness, typically less serious than ‘carus’. ‘Vigilia’ was insomnia, whereas ‘vigil coma’ (usually ‘coma vigil’) was drowsy insomnia. ‘Frenzy’, ‘melancholy’ and ‘madness’ are defined by Burton in 1.1.1.4 and 1.1.3.1 below.
Lonicerus: Actually ‘Lonerus’ (the German physician Johann Philipp Loner, d. 1605), rather than ‘Lonicerus’ (the German botanist Adam Lonicer, 1528–86).
ingenite: Innate or inborn. intended or remitted: Increased or diminished in force or intensity. acquisite: Acquired.
confounded: See above, n. 86 (DJR).

Choler adust, & blood incensed: As with any of the four humours in the body, yellow bile (choler) was termed ‘adust’ when it had been heated or burned. ‘Incensed’ here means ‘kindled’, ‘inflamed’ or ‘burned’.

Henbane: The common name – deriving from its effect on birds – of the toxic, yellow-flowered plant Hyoscyamus niger. Nightshade: Any of the toxic or narcotic plants of the genus Solanum (particularly woody nightshade, black nightshade, or deadly nightshade).

Enthusiasms: Direct divine revelations, often with connotations of insanity or fraudulence: see 3.4.1.2–3 below. obsession or possession of devils: Demonic ‘obsession’, the condition of being controlled or tormented by an evil spirit, was sometimes distinguished from full-blown ‘possession’, on the grounds that, in the former, the sufferer retained some degree of self-consciousness.

King Proetus’ daughters: In Greek mythology, the daughters of King Proetus of Argos were rendered insane by the gods. In one version of the story, Hera inflicted the punishment because they considered themselves to be more beautiful than her.

that fable of Pausanias … Lycaon, &c.: In the classical myth related by Pausanias, the Arcadian king Lycaon was turned into a wolf by Zeus (Jupiter) as a punishment for testing the god’s omniscience by sacrificing a baby on an altar dedicated to him. In Ovid’s version, the punishment is for plotting to murder Jupiter and, when that failed, to feed human flesh to him.
Livonia: A region around the Gulf of Riga, corresponding roughly to modern Latvia and Estonia.
Baldus the great lawyer: The Italian jurist Baldus de Ubaldis (Baldo degli Ubaldi, 1327–1400).
goodwife: The mistress of a household.
the lascivious dance … calls it: In Paracelsus’ account, the symptoms of the disease replicate the voluptuous dancing and leaping of ‘whores and scoundrels’.
forms: Benches.
Equivocations: Ambiguous, uncertain or improper terminological usages.
frowardness: Perversity, stubbornness.
vindicate: See above, n. 284 (DJR).
character: Distinctive feature (or, alternatively, outward sign).
Cato: The Roman statesman and model of Stoic virtue Marcus Porcius Cato the Younger (95–46 BCE), great-grandson of Cato the Elder – on whom, see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries).
proper man of person: Physically attractive man.

Polycrates … dispositions: According to Herodotus, Polycrates – tyrant of Samos c. 540–522 BCE – had been advised by Amasis II of Egypt to dispose of his most precious possession, in order to prevent a reversal of fortune by other means. The Roman historian Aelian mentions the jealousy of Polycrates in his Historical Miscellany (9.4).
ell: A measure of length that varied in different countries; in England it was forty-five inches.

trines, sextiles … quartiles and oppositions: All types of astrological ‘aspect’. A ‘trine’ is one-third of the zodiac (120°) and a ‘sextile’ is one-sixth (60°). Since astral movements were taken to exert influence upon earthly events, the implication here is that everybody and everything is subject to shifts of fate.
celestial powers: See below, n. 46 (1.2.1). interrupt: Hindered, thwarted.
condoles: See above, n. 133 (DJR).
magnanimity: Courage, greatness of spirit.
Affects: Emotions.
Distillation: Catarrh, a defluxion of rheum. Rational soul … make resistance: See below, 1.1.2.9–11, and n. 7 (2.2.6).

complexion: See above, n. 194 (DJR). spirits … Hypochondries: See 1.1.2.2 and 1.1.2.4 below. The hypochondrium (the upper part of the abdomen) was typically bifurcated in medieval and Renaissance anatomy into two ‘hypochondries’, on the left and right sides. crudity: Indigestion.

as the Philosophers … cold: Drawing on Arabic discussions of the quantification of the four primary Aristotelian qualities (heat, coldness, dryness and moisture), medieval philosophers often measured these in ‘degrees’ with a maximum limit of eight. The proverb ‘one swallow does not make a summer’ in note ‘d’ is apparently a warning against generalizing from a single instance (here, with regard to the diverse ‘degrees’ of melancholy).
the vulgar: The common people.
that Royal Prophet: King David, regarded as the author of the Book of Psalms. curiously: See above, n. 125 (DJR).

radical: Naturally inherent. which some call Cambium … Ros and Gluten: The threefold division of alimentary humours into ‘ros’ (‘dew’), ‘cambium’ and ‘gluten’ originates in the Liber pantegni of Constantine the African (d. c. 1087 CE). According to the conventional medieval doctrine, ros is a form of moisture that runs through the veins, and when it passes through the openings at the end of the veins, it begins to whiten and becomes cambium; when fully whitened, as it is incorporated into the bodily member, it transforms into gluten. The first concoction in the Liver: ‘Concoction’ is the technical term in Galenic medicine for the ‘cooking’ of foodstuffs in the process of digestion. In this understanding, food was first concocted in the stomach and intestines, producing chyle, which was then secondarily concocted in the liver into nutritive blood, then sent via the veins to the other parts of the body to be refined into humours. The third concoction involved the secretion and excretion of various substances, such as sweat, hair and tears, from various parts of the body. Referring to the ‘first’ concoction in the liver is thus slightly misleading.
juice: Essential bodily fluid (that is, ‘humour’). peccant: Unhealthy, corrupt.
Meseraic veins: The Mesenteric veins, which carry blood from the intestines to the liver.
feculent: Containing dregs or impurities.
subtle: Very fine or rarefied. For some Renaissance natural philosophers and physicians, the ‘spirit’ was wholly immaterial.
Homogeneal or Heterogeneal: Homogeneous or heterogeneous.
corrivated: Merged into a single stream or channel – but the term is apparently misused here to mean ‘conveyed’ or ‘supplied’.

seminal or emulgent: ‘Seminal’ here pertains to the production of semen; ‘emulgent’ means literally ‘milking out’, and here the term describes the straining or ‘milking’ of serum from the kidneys by its vessels.
hypochondries: See above, n. 61 (1.1.1).
os sacrum: Literally, the ‘sacred bone’, or the sacrum, the large triangular bone at the base of the spine.
animal: Designating the functions of the brain.
Legate a latere: Literally, ‘legate of the side’, the title of a papal legate of the highest rank, with powers virtually equivalent to those of the pope himself.
Rim: The ‘rim of the belly’, that is, the peritoneum, the membrane that lines the abdominal cavity.

watercourse: The name given to the lower part of the lower belly by the source here, the English anatomist Helkiah Crooke (1576–1648), who also identifies it as the hypogastrium, the region of the central abdomen below the stomach.
the shop of blood: Figuratively, the place where blood is produced (referring here to the liver).
a secret virtue: A hidden or invisible force.
constringed: Squeezed together, compressed.
anfractuous: Winding, sinuous. ears: Auricles.
lights: A traditional colloquialism for ‘lungs’.
aspera arteria: Literally, ‘hard artery’, another name for the trachea.
the common sense: See 1.1.2.7 below.
the fourth creek: That is, the fourth ventricle at the base of the brain; see above, n. 32 (1.1.1) on the term ‘creek’.

the Soul is defined to be ἐντελέχεια … which most Philosophers approve: In Aristotelian philosophy, ‘entelechy’ (ἐντελέχεια) involves the actualization of a potentiality, or the complete expression of a function. Here, the notion of the soul as entelechy denotes its definitive characteristic as the ‘perfection’ or completion of the body’s capacity to have life, as commonly understood by Aristotelian natural philosophers in the Renaissance.
Neoteric: See above, n. 62 (DJR).
sensible creatures: See above, n. 85 (DJR).
Semiustulation: Half-burning.
relics: See above, n. 2 (1.1.1).
siccity: Dryness.
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). those six non-natural things: See 1.2.2.1 below.
default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
sensible or passible: Capable of sensation.

the Species of sensible things: In scholastic psychology, ‘species’ are the ‘sensible forms’ carrying sense-data from objects in the external world. They are emitted by these objects, and then received and processed by the various perceptual and cognitive faculties.
Titillation: The sensation of being tickled or touched lightly, tingling or itching.
Diaphanum: A transparent body or transparency (hence the adjective ‘diaphanous’), sometimes used to describe the lower region of the heavens – on which, see below, n. 58 (2.2.3).
exquisite: Highly sensitive.
Musicians: Theorists of music.
resolved: Dissolved, dispersed.
censured: See above, n. 59 (DJR).

Antics: Grotesque or bizarre representations. Ovid’s house of sleep, Psyche’s palace in Apuleius: Two classical loci of fantastical fictional places: the Cimmerian cave that is home to Somnus (the god of sleep) in the ninth book of Ovid’s Metamorphoses; and the opulent palace explored by Psyche in the fifth book of Apuleius’ Metamorphoses.
brutes: Non-human animals.
Register: Registrar.
ligation of senses: Suspension of the senses.
that Aphorism … own good: The maxim is taken from the opening sentence of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.

T. W.: In note ‘a’, the abbreviation refers to the English Catholic controversialist Thomas Wright (c. 1561–1623), from whose Passions of the Minde (1600) the division into ‘concupiscible’ and ‘irascible’ appetites is taken. Impugning: Attacking.
macerates: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
prosecute: Carry out, perform.

the Efficient cause, or End: Two of the four causes in Aristotelian philosophy: the ‘efficient cause’ is the agency, force or means by which something is produced or occurs; the ‘final cause’, or ‘end’, is the purpose for which it is produced.
admirable: Wonderful, astonishing.
the predicament of Situs: ‘Position’ (or ‘situation’) is one of the ten logical categories, or ‘predicaments’, of Aristotelian logic.
reciprocally: Alternately.
ex traduce: By transmission from parent to child.

Orpheus: Orpheus was sometimes regarded in the Renaissance as a founder of an esoteric Greek mystery religion, and was often associated with Pythagorean teachings about the soul. Pherecydes: The mythographer and natural philosopher Pherecydes of Syrus (sixth century BCE). Chaldees: Chaldeans, that is, from the ancient kingdom of Chaldea in the southeastern region of Mesopotamia; ‘Chaldee’ was often used as a synonym for ‘Babylonian’, referring to someone skilled in occult science or magic.

Metempsychosis: The transmigration of the soul. Palingenesia: Or ‘palingenesis’– regeneration or rebirth. epota prius Lethes unda: In Greek mythology, Lethe (‘the waters of forgetfulness’) was one of the five rivers of the underworld. The
association between drinking its waters and reincarnation was most famously expressed in the tenth book of Plato’s Republic.

Lucian’s Cock … Euphorbus eram: In Lucian’s dialogue The Dream, or The Cock, the cock mockingly claims to be a reincarnation of Pythagoras, who was himself (according to his own view recorded in several ancient sources, including Ovid’s Metamorphoses) a reincarnation of Euphorbus, the Trojan hero and son of Panthous in the Iliad.

Leo Decimus that Epicurean Pope: Giovanni de’ Medici, Pope Leo X (ruled 1513–21), was frequently attacked by Protestant polemicists, who portrayed him as impious and devoted to luxury; see below, n. 43 (1.2.2) and n. 80 (3.4.1).

as that Clazomenian Hermotimus averred: According to a story told by Tertullian (On the Soul 44), the soul of the legendary Greek philosopher Hermotimus of Clazomenae was able to depart his body and roam around when he was asleep.

Plato’s Elysian fields: In Elysium, the paradise for the righteous which had traditionally been set aside for heroes in ancient Greek religion, and which is described at the end of Plato’s Republic. that Turkey Paradise: That is, Jannah (‘heaven’) as described in the Qur’an.
rejourn: Refer.
Schoolman: Scholastic theologian (or philosopher).
election: Free choice.

innate notices or beginnings of arts: The innate ‘notions’ (noticiae), according to the Liber de anima (1552) of the German Lutheran theologian and philosopher Philipp Melanchthon, of divine law: ideas, especially of good and evil, which have been implanted in the mind by God, and which also provide the fundamental principles for disciplines (‘arts’) such as geometry and arithmetic.
discoursing: Considering.

Apprehension, Composition, Division: In scholastic psychology, the apprehension of a concept precedes the cognitive processes of the joining and disjoining of a subject and a predicate (‘composition’ and ‘division’ respectively). Invention: The discovery of knowledge or arguments.
there is nothing in the understanding … sense: This Aristotelian formula was frequently quoted, usually in Latin, in medieval and Renaissance theories of intellection.
a bare and rased table: A tabula rasa, or blank tablet (‘rased’ here is a variant form of ‘erased’). capable: Able to receive. forms: Images or representations.
lights: Opinions, information, or capacities that have been acquired by the intellect.
experiments: Experiences, practical understandings.
practic Syllogism: In Aristotelian logic, the application of a rule to a concrete situation.

Regulus the Roman: The Roman statesman and general Marcus Atilius Regulus, consul in 267 and 256 BCE, was captured by the Carthaginians during the First Punic War in 255 and died in captivity. In the patriotic legend that subsequently circulated, the Carthaginians made him swear an oath to the gods that he would secure the terms of a treaty with Rome or go back to Carthage to be tortured to death. In 250, he returned to Rome to negotiate an exchange of prisoners (and, in some versions, a peace agreement), but argued in the senate that the proposal was contrary to Roman interests. After returning to Carthage, he suffered his fate – according to the historian Appian, in a wooden box lined with iron spikes.
So David corrected himself: An allusion to David’s decision, against the urging of his men, to spare the life of Saul (1 Samuel 24). a vantage: An advantage.
oppugners: Assailants.

will and nill: Be willing and unwilling; choose and refuse. our will is free … inevitable and necessary: That is, in particular (contingent) circumstances our actions issue from a free will, but ultimately they are guided by divine necessity.
reluctancy: Internal or mental struggle.

as Phaedra … opposite: This passage is taken from Seneca’s Phaedra (177–9), where the main protagonist is struggling with her lust for her stepson Hippolytus. On the mythological story, see below, n. 10 (3.2.2).
So David knew … Appetite: A reference to David’s affair with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11). fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
cubit: See above, n. 271 (DJR).
feral: See above, n. 147 (DJR).
the Ethics: That is, Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, the central text of moral philosophy in the curriculum of European universities in the Renaissance.

ambages: Circumlocutions, equivocations or, more generally, circuitous paths. Differences: The distinguishing characteristics (in medical logic, the differentia), enabling the condition to be separated from other species of the same pathological genus.
peevish: Obstinate.

Characters: See above, n. 50 (1.1.1). most Melancholy … fear and grief: The insertion of ‘most’ and the passage ‘not all … fear and grief’ first appeared in the second edition of 1624. excepts: See above, n. 21 (DJR).

by consent or essence: A reference to contemporary medical disputes concerning the affection of the brain, whether by means of ‘sympathy’ (‘consent’, from the Latin consensus), in which disease is transmitted from one bodily part to another by means that are typically hidden from the senses, or by a pathology arising within the organ itself (‘by essence’). distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

those six non-natural things: See 1.2.2.1 below. misaffected in their genitures: That is, they have a horoscope in which these planets have a malign influence (or ‘hostile aspect’). are black, or of an high sanguine complexion: With a complexion – see above, n. 194 (DJR) – that is dominated by black bile (a ‘dark complexion’), or with a ‘flushed’ appearance from the predominance of blood.

accident: Accompaniment – or more technically in Aristotelian language, a non-essential property or quality, and often contrasted with an essential ‘substance’. this artificial Malady: See above, n. 216 (DJR), and 1.1.3.3 below.
adventitious: ‘Adventitious kind’ or ‘adventitious disease’ was probably intended.
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR). obnoxious: Susceptible.
macerated: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).
swinish: Coarse or degraded.
ichors & those serous matters: That is, blood serum, and other forms of bodily serum.

Hippocrates in his book of Melancholy (if at least it be his): The landmark Latin translation of the complete works of Hippocrates by Marco Fabio Calvo (c. 1440–1527), published in Rome in 1525, included a spurious work entitled De atrae bilis agitatione, melancholiave (‘On the Disturbance of Black Bile, or Melancholy’), actually written several centuries after the Hippocratic corpus, which is usually dated from the mid-fifth to the mid-fourth centuries BCE. Burton was not the first to doubt the authenticity of this work.
confounding: See above, n. 86 (DJR). in extent: Extended, in degree of seriousness or (perhaps) over time.
mirach: See above, 1.1.2.4. consummate: Finished, completed.
Enthusiasts: Deranged (or fraudulent) claimants of direct divine revelation: see 3.4.1.2–3 below.
Temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Hepatic: Pertaining to the liver.
plunged: Cast into difficulty, puzzled.
Caninus Appetitus: Bulimia (literally, ‘canine hunger’).
the melancholy Duke of Cleves: Johann Wilhelm of Jülich-Cleves-Berg (1562–1609).
Polonian: Polish.

as many Politicians do … and many others: On these ‘pure’ classical constitutional forms, which had been much discussed in political theory since antiquity, see above, n. 201 (DJR). A ‘temperate’ constitution here means one in which government is subject to civil law, or moderated by some other constraint, and typically contrasted with ‘absolute’ rule, which is above the law. The ‘mixed constitution’, influentially theorized in antiquity by the Greek author Polybius and most famously exemplified by Sparta and the Roman Republic, is one which includes some combination of institutions that have a monarchical, aristocratic or popular character. Early modern England was sometimes described by contemporaries as a ‘mixed constitution’, or as a type of ‘mixed monarchy’, in which power was distributed between the supreme office of the king and parliament.
casualties: Matters subject to chance, or uncertainties.
clue: A ball of thread, used as a guide in ‘threading’ one’s way through a labyrinth.
Cardinal Caesius: Cardinal Pier Donato Cesio (1521–86).
Empirics: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
rip … up: Open up, disclose; or, alternatively, ‘lay bare’ or ‘tear up’ satirically. descried: Either ‘discovered’ or ‘disparaged’.
flux: A discharge of blood or excrement, often in relation to dysentery.

Lycurgus … madness: In the version of the myth recounted by Hyginus (132), the Thracian king Lycurgus tried to rape his mother after drinking wine, and then incurred the wrath of Dionysus (Bacchus) because he subsequently attempted to cut down the grapevines he regarded as the ‘bad medicine’ responsible for his actions. Pentheus … sacrifice: The Theban king Pentheus and his mother, the princess Agave, in the most familiar version of the tale given in Euripides’ Bacchae, were both driven insane by Dionysus after the king refused to recognize his deity and banned his worship.

Censor Fulvius … sorrow of heart: The Roman statesman Quintus Fulvius Flaccus committed suicide in 172 BCE after receiving news of the death of one of his sons and the serious illness of another. It was believed, however, that he had been driven mad by Juno Lacinia (Hera) after arranging for the removal of the marble roof tiles of the goddess’s temple in Croton so that they could be used in his own temple of Fortuna Equestris in Rome.

the like happened to Brennus: The military king Brennus, who led the Gallic invasion of Greece in 279 BCE, was wounded in the attack on Delphi (an event reportedly accompanied by various supernatural incidents), and subsequently committed suicide.
Pontificial: Papist.

Clodoveus … body of St. Denis: Clovis II (634–57/8), a Frankish king of Burgundy and Neustria, reportedly opened the tomb of the saint and removed part of his arm. a sacrilegious Frenchman … his own flesh: According to the French historian Robert Gaguin (1433/4–1501), this incident occurred in the reign of Charles VI (1380–1422).
free their own credits: Defend their own reputations.

as in Joshua’s time, as in Pharaoh’s reign in Egypt: Allusions to the hailstones hurled down by God on the Amorites travelling on the road from Beth Horon to Azekah (Joshua 10:11–14), and to the thunder, hail and lightning sent down, at Moses’ request, on Egypt (Exodus 9:22–6).

cry out with Julian … Galileae: According to Theodoret, the dying words of Julian the Apostate – Roman emperor 361–3 CE, and so called because of his conversion to paganism and persecution of Christianity – acknowledged that Christianity would become the state religion of the Roman Empire. with Apollo’s Priest … this: According to John Chrysostom, in 362 CE the emperor Julian had the bones of the third-century Christian martyr St Babylas removed from the grounds of a long-famous oracular temple of Apollo in Daphne – for which, see below, n. 25 (2.2.4) – having been told by the priest that nearby corpses were preventing the god from producing oracles. In October of the same year, the temple was destroyed by a fire, which was interpreted by some as retribution from the Christian God.
stablish: Establish – that is, render secure or strengthen.

When that monster-taming Hercules … yielded: In classical mythology, Heracles (Hercules) is said to have founded the Olympic games by arranging a running race with his four brothers every five years. The tale of his wrestling with Zeus (Jupiter) is recorded in the scholia to pseudo-Lycophron’s Alexandra.
Craterus: In this quotation from the Roman satirist Persius (3.65), ‘Craterus’ is a generic name for a Roman physician, derived from Horace (Satires 2.3.161).

wounded with the spear of Achilles: In classical mythology, when the Greeks stopped in Mysia on their way to Troy, Achilles injured the Mysian king Telephus with his spear. Eight years later, on the advice of the Delphic oracle, Telephus was healed when Achilles applied rust from the spear to the wound.
Schoolmen: See above, n. 61 (1.1.2). Fracastoriana & Ferneliana acies: The followers of the renowned sixteenth-century physicians Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553) and Jean Fernel (1497–1558).

substantia separatae … and intelligences: In scholastic philosophy, ‘separate substances’ (or ‘immaterial forms’) are entities (such as angels, devils and souls) that are separate from matter. ‘Intelligences’ here, which had been described as ‘immaterial forms’ by the controversial Italian natural philosopher Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), are the celestial movers of the heavenly bodies. Platonists Devils … daemones: The Platonist belief in spiritual beings or ‘demons’ said to mediate between the human and divine realms had been authoritatively criticized by Augustine in the City of God, and later Christian authors frequently identified these with malign devils.
insisting in the steps: Following in the footsteps.
Lilis … Devils: Lilith is portrayed as a malevolent mother of demons in Jewish folklore. In the Latin Vulgate, her name (at Isaiah 34:14) was translated as lamia (‘witch’).
The Turks’ Alcoran: See above, n. 123 (DJR).
boni and mali Genii: See above, n. 22 (DJR).

Heroes, Lares … Larvae: In ancient Greece, heroes were a class of beings, usually conceived as powerful deceased humans, who occupied an intermediate category between gods and men and were worshipped in hero cults. In Roman antiquity, lares were household gods; lemures or larvae were ghosts of the restless or malevolent dead.

Saturnian and fiery demon: This description of the demon of Socrates may have been taken from Girolamo Cardano’s De rerum varietate (1557), which relates these astral characteristics to the philosopher’s sublime contemplative wisdom.
Michael Parapinatius, Emperor of Greece: Michael VII Doukas (or ‘Parapinakes’), emperor of Byzantium 1071–8 CE. explode: See above, n. 45 (DJR). admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
aerial: Airy or gaseous – here, referring specifically to the ‘denser’ air of inferior quality mentioned by Augustine in the quotation immediately above.
Animae separatae genii: See above, n. 22 (DJR), and n. 18 (1.2.1).

as the Angel did Habakkuk to Daniel: The apocryphal addition to the Book of Daniel on Bel and the Dragon describes how an angel transported the prophet Habbakuk to the lions’ den, in order to feed Daniel there. as Philip the Deacon … the Eunuch: The transportation of Philip to Azotus (Ashdod) from a road between Jerusalem and Gaza is related in Acts 8:26–40. so did Pythagoras and Apollonius … feats: After the death of Pythagoras, many stories were told about his magical powers, including that of bilocation, although Burton may be thinking of the philosopher’s claims to have travelled to the underworld. In one tale recorded by Diogenes Laertius (8.38), the philosopher once hid himself in a purpose-built underground dwelling before emerging with notes on his experiences in Hades. According to Philostratus, Apollonius of Tyana – see above, n. 55 (DJR) – was arrested as a magician and put on trial before the emperor Domitian, but ended his defence by claiming immortality and then miraculously disappearing from the courtroom (Life of Apollonius of Tyana 8.1–5). spectrums: See above, n. 15 (DJR).

Juno’s image spake to Camillus: In Plutarch’s account (Camillus 6), after the Roman sack of Veii (396 BCE) the general and statesman Marcus Furius Camillus was addressed by the fallen city’s statue of Juno when he asked it for its permission to transport it to Rome so that he could fulfil a vow. Livy (5.22) notes that the assent was actually given by bystanders. Fortune’s statue to the Roman matrons: According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 8.56), the statue of the goddess spoke at the dedication ceremony of the temple of Fortuna Muliebris (‘the Fortune of Women’), built after Coriolanus had been successfully persuaded by his mother, wife and other Roman women to abandon his siege of Rome.

dizzard: See above, n. 96 (DJR). Marcus: The Mesopotamian hermit, reported to have meditated in the desert for twenty years, and whose accounts of spirits are related in the De operatione daemonum of Michael Psellos. of his credit: On his own authority.

A nobleman in Germany … mine Author: The antiquarian and poet Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602) gives the name of his friend Petrus Lepidus (Pierre Joly), a Protestant humanist and lawyer originally from Metz.
Fidem suam liberet: In note ‘b’, the saying playfully challenges the source, Girolamo Cardano, to substantiate his story. juments: See above, n. 308 (DJR).
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR).
blackguard: The lowest class of servant in a household, serving in the kitchen, and perhaps acquiring this name from having coal-stained clothing.

that relation of Thamus: According to Plutarch (The Obsolescence of Oracles 17), Thamus was an Egyptian pilot who, while sailing near the Ionian island of Paxi, heard a voice from the island commanding him to announce the death of the god Pan when his ship reached Palodes. Apollo Pythius: Apollo was given the epithet ‘Pythius’ because of his mythological slaying of the giant dragon Python before his occupation of the site of the oracle at Delphi (according to some sources, Python was the previous custodian of the oracle).
Eremite: Hermit.
policy: See above, n. 283 (DJR).

Gentiles: Heathens, pagans. as that Heathen in Minucius: The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix presents a dialogue between the pagan Caecilius Natalis and the Christian Octavius Januarius. Rabshakeh to the Israelites: Isaiah 36:18–20.
paradoxes: See above, n. 3 (DJR). transposing: Transferring, transplanting.

Pasetis obolus in Suidas: ‘The obol of Pases’, an obol being a small Greek coin. Burton refers to the story, recorded in the tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia
now known as the Suda but formerly attributed to ‘Suidas’, of Pases’ magic coin, which always returned to him after he had spent it.
conjecture: Divine or prognosticate from signs or omens.
Meteors: Any atmospheric or meteorological phenomena.
Ethnics: Pagans. Grazier: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
Plato learned in Egypt: According to Clement of Alexandria (Miscellanies 1.15), Plato had been taught by the Egyptian priest Sechnuphis of Heliopolis.
fret and chafe: Consume and vex.

as Dionysius hath done of Angels: The De coelesti hierarchia of pseudo-Dionysius presents three hierarchies of angels, each containing a further three orders: Seraphim, Cherubim and Thrones; Dominations, Virtues and Powers; Principalities (sometimes translated as ‘Rulers’ or ‘Princes’), Archangels and Angels.

Theutus in Plato: The Egyptian god of the underworld ‘Theuth’ (or ‘Thoth’) is identified by Plato in the Phaedrus as the inventor of writing, numbers, gambling and other arts, but elsewhere he is depicted as a trickster.

above the Moon: That is, in the terms of Aristotelian cosmology, in the higher spheres of the celestial realm which do not come into contact with the changeable, terrestrial matter of the sublunary sphere. ethereal and aerial … Genii: In the City of God (7.6), Augustine relates the view of Varro that the highest heavenly sphere (the ‘ether’, extending down to the lunar sphere) contains ‘ethereal’ souls, and the region between the orbit of the moon and the highest region of cloud and wind (the ‘air’) contains ‘aerial’ souls, which are called ‘heroes’, lares and genii. Manes … Lamiae: In the Roman world, manes were ghosts of the departed and gods of the underworld; lamiae in antiquity were originally female spirits who attacked children, but the term was extended, especially in the plural, to refer to witches.
the middle region: See below, n. 58 (2.2.3).
Chaos: Environment, or space.

Gregorius Tholosanus makes seven kinds … Martial: Pierre Grégoire (Tholosanus) claims in the Syntaxes artis mirabilis (1578) that the types of ethereal demon correspond to the planets, presumably with the seven planets of classical astronomy in mind. He refers to Saturnine, Jovial, Martial, Solar, Venusian and Lunar kinds, but omits the Mercurial.

Principalities: See above, n. 46 (1.2.1). Spheres: In the Ptolemaic astronomy whose influence persisted into the Renaissance, the ‘spheres’ were the eight concentric, transparent and hollow globes thought to revolve round the earth, with each carrying the sun, moon, planets and fixed stars. Some added a ninth clear, ‘crystalline’ sphere above the fixed stars, and a tenth sphere of the primum mobile, said to set the other spheres in motion.
Canidia in Horace: A grotesque witch described by Horace (Epodes 3, 5, 17).

blazing Stars: Comets. Firedrakes, or Ignes Fatui: A ‘firedrake’ is either a fiery meteor, or, like an ‘ignis fatuus’ (literally, ‘foolish fire’), a ‘will-o’-the-wisp’ or ‘jack-a-lantern’. we ought to carry … ancestors: In this passage from the Universae theatrum naturae (1596) by Jean Bodin, which is written as a dialogue between the pupil ‘Theorus’ (‘contemplator’ or ‘tourist’) and his master ‘Mystagogus’ (‘guide to’ or ‘guardian of’ sacred mysteries and objects), Mystagogus refers to the power attributed to amulets – on which, see 2.5.1.5 below – to ward off evil spirits. Dioscuri: In classical mythology, the sons of Zeus (Jupiter), Castor and Polydeuces (or Pollux in Latin), who were said to protect travellers, and whose appearance on a ship’s rigging was thought to foretell a safe escape from a storm. pretend: Signify, foretell. Sancti Germani sydus: Probably a reference to the fifth-century St Germanus of Auxerre, reputed to have calmed a storm, which had been stirred up by demons opposed to his mission to combat the Pelagian heresy in Britain – on which, see below, n. 96 (3.4.1) – by sprinkling oil on the sea and praying to God.
Lipari: One of the volcanic Aeolian Islands, the largest in a chain running between Vesuvius and Etna. Sometimes the name refers to the entire group, which includes Stromboli and Vulcano.
rain stones, as in Livy’s time: Livy’s account of Roman history contains many reports of showers of stones (for example at 1.31.1–4), which were routinely interpreted as supernatural portents.

at Vienna … the Turks: A reference to the siege of Vienna by the Turkish forces of the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566) in 1529. ab urb. cond. 505: Literally, ‘505 years since the founding of the city’ (in 753 BCE), so in 248 BCE.

Mons Draconis in Italy: Mondragone in Campania, so called (according to the Italian scholar and poet Giovanni Pontano, 1429–1503) because of a mountain cave there that was inhabited by a dragon. Anyone who entered was suffocated by its breath and then devoured.
Indians: Here, the Amerindians.

Incubi and Succubi: Although ‘incubus’ had a medical interpretation – see above, n. 32 (1.1.1), and below, 1.2.3.1 – traditionally an incubus was a demon, in male form, who visited someone asleep especially for the purpose of sexual intercourse; a succubus was the female demonic equivalent.

Agrippa’s dog … collar: According to contemporary reports, the occult philosopher Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535) had a black pet dog with a collar decorated with magical symbols. The demonologist and physician Johann Wier (1515–88) records that the dog, named ‘Monsieur’, was falsely rumoured to be the devil in disguise.

Jannes and Jambres: Egyptian sorcerers who competed with Moses for the favour of Pharaoh (2 Timothy 3:8, Exodus 7:11–12). Simon Magus, Cynops, Apollonius Tyaneus: Three ancient magicians: Simon Magus, a Samaritan whose encounter with Peter is described in Acts 8:9–24; Cynops, a pagan sorcerer said to have been defeated by St John on the island of Patmos; and Apollonius of Tyana, on whom, see above, n. 55 (DJR) and n. 28 (1.2.1). Iamblichus: The Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus (c. 240–c. 325 CE), was often portrayed as a magician, mainly because of his defence, in his On Mysteries, of theurgy – the ritualistic art of communicating with beneficent spirits to produce miraculous effects. Trithemius … after she was dead: This necromantic episode involved the German Benedictine abbot and polymath Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) and the apparition of Mary of Burgundy (1457–82), wife of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.
conversant: Dwelling habitually or frequently.
Aegeria … so familiar: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
Hotherus a King of Sweden: According to the Swedish historian and geographer Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), this legendary king ruled in the ninth century BCE.

Dryades, Oreades, Hamadryades: In note ‘b’, three types of wood-nymph: those inhabiting trees in general (dryads), those inhabiting mountain forests (oreads) and those living and dying in particular trees with which they are identified (hamadryads). Foliots: Goblins. Robin Goodfellows: Mischievous sprites or hobgoblins said to haunt the countryside.

range: Rank. Dagon: A Mesopotamian god worshipped (according to Judges 16:23) by the Philistines. Bel: A title given to various ancient Mesopotamian gods, and mentioned as one of the idols of the Babylonians in Isaiah 46:1. Astartes: Astarte, the Greek name for the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar, who was also called Ashtoreth (alternatively, Astaroth or Asteroth). Isis and Osiris: Respectively, the ancient Egyptian goddess of fertility, magic and medicine (among other things), and her brother and husband, the Egyptian god of the afterlife.
pinched: Straitened, or distressed.

sports herself: Amuses or delights herself in a lively way (that is, in producing such abnormal or striking living entities). The phenomenon described here, sometimes called ‘fairy rings’, is now known to be caused by the circular growth pattern of certain fungi.
Barcino: See above, n. 222 (DJR).
Giraldus Cambrensis … deluded: Gerald of Wales (1146–1223) tells the story of a priest from Swansea called Eliodorus (Elidyr), who claimed to have visited an underground fairyland as a child.
They would mend … ages: ‘Irons’ are any tools or utensils made from iron. On the connection of Lipari with metalworking, see below, n. 42 (3.2.3).

Tholosanus calls them Trullos and Getulos: Actually it is Georg Bauer (Georgius Agricola, 1494–1555) who notes the names given by Germans to benevolent fairies as ‘Trulli’ (trolls, or literally, ‘little wenches’) and ‘Guteli’ (literally, ‘little good’ or ‘good-natured ones’).
Telchines: In Greek mythology, skilled metalworkers and malignant magicians who opposed and were eventually destroyed by Zeus. Later, they came to be seen as envious and spiteful subterranean demons.
forlorn: Abandoned, deserted. innoxious: Harmless.

Ziim and Ochim: The King James Bible translates ‘Ziim’ and ‘Ochim’ as ‘wild beasts of the desert’ and ‘doleful creatures’ respectively, but here the terms refer more generically to malign demonic spirits.

Rupes nova in Finland: Literally, ‘new cliff’: Olavinlinna Castle (the model for Kropow Castle in King Ottokar’s Sceptre by Hergé), built on rock on an island in the Kyrönsalmi strait, in the midst of the region of Lake Saimaa. Arion: An ancient Greek lyre-player and poet (seventh century BCE). In a story told by Herodotus (1.24), he was captured by Corinthian sailors, who permitted him to sing a hymn to Apollo before forcing him to kill himself; the music attracted a number of dolphins, and when he threw himself into the water, one of these carried him to dry land. those blocks in Cheshire … family: The surfacing of dead wood in Lake Blackmere (or Brereton’s Lake, in Brereton, Cheshire) was said to have heralded death in the Brereton family. that Oak … as much: ‘Arundel’s Oak’, which according to the Cornish antiquary Richard Carew (1555–1620) was said to bear leaves speckled with white before a death in the Arundel family.
Corse: Corpse.
Ambulones: Another name for ignes fatui – see above, n. 54 (1.2.1). Pucks: Another name for ‘Robin Goodfellows’ – see above, n. 66 (1.2.1).
the Deserts of Lop in Asia: The Gobi Desert.

a great mount in Cantabria: Possibly Mount Aneto in the Pyrenees, although Burton’s source, the Spanish jurist Jeroni Pau (1458–97), situates it near Roussillon. Burton seems to have confused the name of the mountain given by Pau, ‘Canatus’, with Cantabria.
that holy man Ketellus in Nubrigensis: The historian William of Newburgh (1135/6–c. 1198) says that ‘Ketellus’ (Kettle) was from Farnham in Yorkshire.

Getuli and Cobali: In Germanic folklore, underground spirits haunting mines or caves. According to Bauer, ‘Getuli’ (trolls) do domestic work, while ‘Cobali’ (kobolds) imitate the form of human beings, and it is actually the subterranean demons called ‘mountain dwarves’ who dress like miners.
Engines: Plots, snares or wiles.
errs: Compels to vice (an apparently unique usage, or ‘nonce-word’). dejects: Overthrows, weakens or humbles.

vindicate himself for a god: Lay claim to being a god. Aesculapius: In Greek mythology, Asclepius (Aesculapius to the Romans) was the god of medicine and healing. Saturn: In Roman mythology, the god Saturnus was frequently honoured
by human sacrifices (although in the Saturnalia – see above, n. 309 (DJR) – these were replaced by the gift of candles and statuettes, which were said to have been substituted for humans by Hercules). Saturnus was also closely associated with the Greek god Kronos, said to have devoured his children out of fear of a male successor. Moloch: In the Old Testament, Moloch was the name of the Canaanite god worshipped idolatrously by the Israelites by means of child sacrifice; Moloch was also identified by classical authors with Kronos and Saturnus, as well as the god Baal Hammon, to whom the Carthaginians made human sacrifices. Indians: See above, n. 59 (1.2.1). observations of meats, times: Adherence to the customary religious regulations of foodstuffs and the calendar (for example with regard to the Sabbath), viewed by some English Protestants as forms of Roman Catholic superstition, and discussed further below in 3.4.1.2.
Indigetes: Heroes who after their deaths have become gods and patron deities of their countries.

When the Arcades … Metellus the Roman: According to Pausanias (7.15), the slaughter of the Arcadian forces somewhere near Chaeronea in 146 BCE by the Romans under the leadership of Metellus – see above, n. 28 (1.1.1) – was divine vengeance for the Arcadians’ desertion of their allies at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE, who were then defeated by Philip of Macedon. he that is Saturninus, shall never likely be preferred: That is, according to astrological doctrine, those born under Saturn are excluded from ‘preferment’ (promotion) and the acquisition of wealth (the preserve of Jupiter).
Gnathos: Gnatho is the parasitical servant in Terence’s Eunuch.
At Hammel in Saxony … never after seen: In traditional accounts, the story of the Pied Piper of Hamelin is actually dated 26 June 1284.
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
clancular: Secret, clandestine.

Avicenna, si contingat a daemonio … choler adust: Burton glosses the preceding Latin quotation from Avicenna, but adds the notion of the humour being ‘adust’ – see above, n. 37 (1.1.1). The causa propinqua or ‘proximate cause’ of medieval and Renaissance logic (the short-term cause, as opposed to the ‘remote’ or ‘ultimate’ cause) was often termed the ‘immediate cause’ by English authors in this period. complexion: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

Bononia: The Latin name for several European cities, but here it probably refers either to Bologna or Boulogne-sur-Mer. Burton’s source here, Guillaume Durand the Elder (d. 1296), had studied law at Bologna.
fulsome: Disgusting, foul, loathsome.

He had not appeared … alone: The story of the Witch of Endor, who at the request of Saul summons the spirit of Samuel (here interpreted as a manifestation of the devil), is told in 1 Samuel 28:7–25. represented those Serpents … unto it: The story of Moses turning the staff of Aaron into a snake, in a competition with the Egyptian magicians before Pharaoh, is told in Exodus 7:8–12.
Dutch: See above, n. 48 (DJR).

that deal ex parte implicite, or explicite: Apparently a confusion of the phrase ex parte (‘with respect to one side’) with ex pacto (‘by agreement’). The latter had been used by James I in his Daemonologie (1597) to clarify the distinction between witches, who are ‘slaves to the devil’, and necromancers, who are his ‘masters and commanders’.

Nero and Heliogabalus … of old: Elagabalus, Maxentius (c. 283–312 CE) and Julian the Apostate are all included in the account of Roman emperors who made human sacrifices in attempts at divination in Jean-Jacques Boissard’s De divinatione & magicis praestigiis (1616), which also discusses Nero’s consultation of the Delphic oracle.
Ericus King of Sweden … Cap: The mythical king Erik Edmundsson Väderhatt (‘Weatherhat’, also known as ‘Eric of the Windy Hat’), said to have lived in the second half of the ninth century CE.
Monomachies: See above, n. 15 (DJR). make stick-frees: Render invulnerable to the thrust of a weapon.

Crassus’ Chest: An allusion to the Roman general and politician Marcus Licinius Crassus (115–53 BCE), the triumvir whose great wealth was famous in the late Roman Republic, and would subsequently become proverbial.

Eudo de Stellis: Or Éon de l’Étoile (d. 1150), a self-proclaimed prophet and messiah from Brittany, reputed to have magical powers, and who attracted followers from the region’s poor before being condemned, tortured and imprisoned. opinion of: Reputation for.

as that in Hector Boethius of King Duff: According to the Scottish historian Hector Boece (Boethius) in the Historia gentis Scotorum (1527), King Dubh (Duff) of Scotland (d. 966 CE), suffered an illness caused by this kind of witchcraft, but he later recovered. characters: Cabbalistic or magical signs or emblems, or astrological symbols of planets. constellations: Alignments of stars. knots: Knots tied in clothing, a form of maleficent magic.

stand: Stop, or pause. judicial Astrology: The predictive branch of astrology concerned with the influences of astral movements upon earthly and human affairs, and often criticized as deterministic and superstitious. It was commonly distinguished from ‘natural’ astrology, which was concerned with the more strictly physical effects of the stars upon natural phenomena.
Aphorisms: Concise statements of scientific principles.
Scheme: Horoscope.
proper: Particular.
the Ascendant: That is, the horoscope; although for the more specific sense of this term see above, n. 13 (DJR).

This variety … Scorpio: The astrological symbols in note ‘g’ signify the conjunction of Saturn with Jupiter in Libra (‘☌ ♄ et ♃ in ’), and the conjunction of Mars and the Moon in Scorpio (‘☌ ♂ et ☾ in ’). The second of these differs from Burton’s source, Philipp Melanchthon’s Liber de anima (1552), which associates the conjunction of Saturn, Mars and the Moon in Virgo with the debased kind of melancholy suffered by Catiline – on whom, see above, n. 227 (DJR) – in contrast with the noble melancholy of the emperor Augustus.

Mercury in any geniture … irradiated by those quartile aspects of Saturn or Mars: That is, if Mercury is in either Virgo or Pisces (which is in the ascendant), and if it is illuminated by Mars or Saturn at 90°. For ‘aspects’, see above, n. 14 (1.1.1).
quarta luna natos … Eclipses, Earthquakes: That is, to be born on the fourth day after the new moon, or at a time that coincides with an eclipse or earthquake.
the Lord of the geniture: See above, n. 13 (DJR). behold the Horoscope: That is, face the sign of the zodiac containing the ‘ascendant’.
the six non-natural things: See 1.2.2.1 below.

the time of this melancholy … geniture: In the astrological terminology here, ‘directed according to Art’ means to have its time calculated by reference to conjunctions between the ‘significator’ (the planet that signifies the subject of the events him- or herself) and the positions of the ‘promittors’ (or ‘promissors’, planets which prognosticate particular events) in the zodiac; ‘the Hor: moon’ refers to the position of the moon in the horoscope; ‘Hylech’ is the Latin term for the Persian hyleg, which denotes the ruling planet in a nativity, and thereby the determinant of longevity; ‘terms’ are any of the five divisions of each sign of the zodiac, forming the region of increased influence of the planet with which it is associated; ‘fixed stars’ are stars that, in contrast to planets, appear always to
occupy the same position in the heavens; and ‘radical promissors’ are planets that are found in the ‘radix’ (the original geniture of the subject). To paraphrase the passage: ‘the time of this melancholy is when the significators in the geniture, such as the moon in the horoscope or the ruling planet in the nativity, are astrologically calculated to form a conjunction with the hostile rays, or regions of the zodiac, of Saturn and Mars especially, or with any fixed star that shares the characteristics of those planets; or if Saturn moves into a hostile position in relation to the planets found in the original calculation of the geniture.’

Physiognomy, Metoposcopy, Chiromancy: Three forms of divination from, respectively, the features of the face or the body in general, the lines on the forehead, and the palms of the hand. Rotman the Landgrave of Hassia his Mathematician: The astronomer Christoph Rothmann (c. 1560–c. 1600), who served William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel (1532–92), was not actually a ‘mathematician’ in the obsolete sense of ‘astrologer’ meant here; he has been confused with Johann Rothmann, author of Chiromantiae theorica, practica, concordantia genethliaca (1595).

The Saturnine line: Or the ‘fate line’, running through the centre of the palm. Rascetta: Or ‘rascette’, the creases (or ‘bracelets’) running across the wrist at the base of the palm. Saturn’s mount: The fleshy prominence at the base of the middle finger, signifying the influence of Saturn. so if … an acute angle: That is, ‘likewise’, it indicates melancholy in that case.

Saturnine, Hepatic and natural lines: The ‘Hepatic line’ is associated with the liver and the nutritional functions of the body, and so with health, and it runs from the centre of the lower palm towards the base of the little finger. The ‘natural line’, now sometimes called the ‘head line’ because of its association with mental operations, slopes across and down the palm from below the base of the index finger. gross: Indefinite or faint – translating parvus (‘weak’) in the Latin source.
collects: Infers, deduces.
circumforanean: Vagabond, wandering (literally, ‘around markets’). patronize: Support, defend.

Secondary peculiar causes, efficient … precedent: The causes of melancholy now addressed are ‘efficient’ (the means by which the disease comes about) and ‘peculiar’ (particular), in contrast to ‘the other precedent’ ones, namely the general causes that have been discussed in the preceding Subsections. distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

old age … cold and dry: In medieval and Renaissance physiology, the process of ageing involves a gradual loss of warmth and moisture, both of which are essential to life. accident: See above, n. 7 (1.1.3).

as Charles the fifth did to King Philip: The Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (1500–1558) actually abdicated himself from power gradually, bestowing various parts of his empire on his son Philip II of Spain between 1554 and 1556. Carl: Act like a ‘carl’ (or a churl), that is, rudely and coarsely.
Coul-staff: A strong stick for carrying a ‘cowl’ (or tub), usually supported on the shoulders of two people – a common household implement at the time. policy: Stratagem, trick.
habit: Posture, or possibly the general physical appearance or constitution.
Seleucus: The founder of the Seleucid Empire, Seleucus I Nicator (c. 355–281 BCE).
Lepidus … his son: According to Pliny the Elder (7.12), three of the Lepidus family (of the Roman patrician gens Aemilia) were born with a membrane over the eyes.

That famous family of Aenobarbi: The Ahenobarbi were a branch of the plebeian gens Domitia, so named – according to Suetonius (Nero 1) – after their founder Lucius Domitius. His red beard, reputed to be shared by his descendants, was made that colour by Castor and Pollux, who had instructed him to convey news of the Roman victory at Lake Regillus in 499 or 496 BCE in order to prove their
divinity. the Austrian lip: The protruding lower jaw, hereditary in the Habsburg dynasty. Indians: See above, n. 59 (1.2.1). the Bavarian chin: Or ‘Bavarian poke’: goitre, prevalent throughout the Alpine region.

those Galbots in Gascony: Or the ‘Cagots’, a marginalized and persecuted people who had lived for several centuries in western France and northern Spain. They were sometimes thought to be lepers, but were also accused of various crimes including cannibalism and heresy.
symbolizing: Agreeing in nature or qualities, similar.

an inundation … Africk: The Goths who migrated throughout central Europe from the later second century CE onwards were reported in ancient sources to have originated from Scythia or Sarmatia (the western part of greater Scythia, now corresponding to parts of Ukraine, southern Russia and the northeastern Balkans, although here the term probably refers to the Eurasian Steppe). The Vandals, thought to have migrated from southern Scandinavia, entered North Africa in 429 CE and established a kingdom there that lasted until 534.

qualify: Moderate, temper, or bring to a normal condition. the Isle of Maragnan: Now São Luís Island (also Maranhão Island), in the mouth of the Amazon in northeastern Brazil. A French colony was founded there in 1612, but it was expelled three years later by the Portuguese. the Orcades: The Orkney Islands.
temperament: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

megrim: Migraine. Hieronymus Wolfius … Castellio’s: The French theologian Sebastian Castellio (1515–63), famous for his arguments in favour of religious toleration, suffered a period of abject poverty in the 1540s after a dispute with Jean Calvin. Wolf observes that the death of Castellio’s infant was unsurprising in these circumstances.
sentence: Opinion.
fuzzled: Muddled, confused.
Suidas gives instance … Aristachorum: The tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia now known as the Suda actually gives the name of the second son of Aristarchus as ‘Aristagoras’.
resolved: Loosened or relaxed. animal: That is, ‘animal spirits’ – see above, 1.1.2.2.
Pica: In note ‘c’, the tendency or craving of pregnant women for abnormal foodstuffs. humours: Here, the particular qualities of material substances.
defaults: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

Indians: The historian Quintus Curtius Rufus (9.1) refers specifically to the realm of a king called ‘Sopithes’ (‘Sophytes’ in Greek sources), who is probably one of the rulers in the Indian subcontinent in the time of Alexander the Great.
exhaust through riot: Exhausted by debauchery. he said: John Barclay, in his Euphormionis lusinini satyricon (1605–7).

Evident, Remote … some call them: The conventional sequence of causes in Galenic medical pathology, from the ‘immediate’ or ‘predisposing’ cause (causa evidens), through the ‘inducing’ cause (causa antecedens), to the ‘continent’ (or ‘conjunctive’) cause (causa continens) – the last of these being that which leads to the occurrence and continuation of the disease.

consultation: Here, the learned medical consultatio, which is a written case history rather than a personal meeting between physician and patient. objected to: Imputed to, or charged against. offended: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
conversant: Exercised, concerned with.
only: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR).

all four Arabians: Al-Kindi (d. c. 870 CE), Rhazes (or ‘Rhasis’, 865–c. 925), Averroes (1126–98) and Serapion (Ibn Sarabiyun, late ninth century). The last of these was commonly conflated in the Renaissance with another ‘Serapion’, Ibn Wafid (d. c. 1074). peculiar: Distinguished.

cold in the first degree, dry in the second: In Arabic and Galenic medicine, there were four levels or ‘degrees’ used to categorize the effects of drugs and foodstuffs on the body: the first is almost imperceptible and only detectable by theoretical reasoning; the second is readily perceptible by the senses; the third is a strong effect; the fourth is a corrupting or mortifying effect on a bodily member. This scheme was much discussed in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. corned: Preserved or cured with salt. preferred: Recommended.
resty: Lazy, inactive. complexion: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
rammish: Characteristic of a ram; pungent, rank or disagreeable.
qualify: See above, n. 133 (1.2.1).
Parks: See above, n. 240 (DJR).
as Martial’s Epigram testifies to Gellia: ‘Whenever you send me a hare, Gellia, you say, “Marcus, you’ll be handsome for seven days”’ (Epigrams 5.29).
milkmeats: In note ‘b’, foodstuffs made with or from milk. green wounds: Fresh or unhealed wounds.
Banbury cheese: A rich yellow cow’s milk cheese, made in very thin rounds, from Banbury in Oxfordshire.

fenny: Inhabiting fens or swampy areas. Didappers … Curs … and peckled Fowls: A didapper is a small diving waterfowl, also known as a dabchick; a cur is a golden-eye duck; ‘peckled’ is another term for ‘speckled’ or ‘mottled’.
disproves: Authoritatively disallows, disapproves.
Viscosities: Viscous materials that collect in the stomach.
scrupulous: Excessively cautious or meticulous.
soused: Pickled. indurate: Hardened by drying, salting or smoking. Fumades: Smoked pilchards. Stockfish: Air-dried cod. Haberdine: Salt or sun-dried cod. Poor John: Salted and dried hake.
well-liking: Thriving, healthy, plump.

Herbs … Cabbage: The term ‘herb’ is used here in its general sense to refer to a soft and succulent-stemmed plant; gourds are similar to pumpkins or squash; coleworts (or just ‘worts’) are cabbages or any kind of brassica.
Salads: Vegetables (or herbs) that are eaten raw.
Balm: A group of fragrant garden herbs, including balm gentle (or balm-mint), bastard balm and field balm. Succory: Another name for chicory or endive.
Juments: See above, n. 308 (DJR).
Serves: The fruit of the service-tree (Sorbus torminalis).
Sweetings, Pearmains, Pippins: All types of apple (although ‘pearmain’ may also refer to the Warden variety of pear).
naught: Bad, in the sense of unwholesome or harmful. Fitches: Vetch (from the plant Vicia sativa).
obstructive: That is, a cause of pathogenic, and presumably bilious, obstructions in the digestive system.

mine Author: Bernardino Gómez Miedes (Gomesius), author of De sale (1605), who relates the Plutarchan anecdote about Egyptian priests reportedly abstaining from salt because it sharpened the appetite for food and drink.

Muscadine, Malmsey … Metheglin: All sweet drinks: ‘Muscadine’ is muscatel (or ‘muscadel’); ‘Malmsey’, a strong sweet wine originally from Monemvasia in Greece; ‘Alicant’, a Spanish red once produced in Alicante, was similar to Madeira; ‘Rumney’ was another sweet wine from Greece; ‘brown bastard’ was a
sweet Spanish wine similar to muscatel; ‘metheglin’ was Welsh mead that was spiced or mixed with a medicinal substance.
Dutchmen: Germans.

over-stale: Excessively old and strong (drink becomes ‘stale’ in this sense when it has stood long enough to clear, and become freed from dregs or lees). sod: Boiled. frets, and galls: Irritates and erodes.
Spruce: In note ‘c’, Prussia.

a monstrous drink, like the River Styx: In classical mythology, the waters of the Styx, one of the rivers (though sometimes described as a lake) of the underworld, were held to be deadly to humans and animals because of their icy coldness.
creepers: Insects, or ‘creepy-crawlies’. distemperatures: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
fat: Thick, turbid. defecate: Clarify, purify from pollution. paradox: See above, n. 3 (DJR).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
blear eyes: Eyes that are dimmed with morbid matter or inflammation.
Axius … now called Verduri: Today, where the river flows through Macedonia it is known as the Vardar, and after it crosses into Greece it is called the Axios.
Aleacman now Peleca … Thessaly: Today the Haliacmon, the longest river in Greece.

that Struma, or Poke of the Bavarians: Goitre; see above, n. 129 (1.2.1). Bodin supposeth … Labden: In his Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem (1566), the French jurist and polymath Jean Bodin writes of the contemporary inhabitants of the Valdocca valley north of Turin that, like the ‘Labdani’ people in Aquitaine, they are insane and unable to speak ‘on account of labdacismus’ – that is, labdacism (or lambdacism), which involves the frequent repetition of the letter l, and which may be the origin of the otherwise perplexing name ‘Labdani’. ‘Stutting’ is a variant form of ‘stuttering’.
simples: Substances that are unmixed, consisting of one element or ingredient (in contrast to ‘compound’ substances).

condite: Preserved, pickled or seasoned. powdered: Preserved by being salted, pickled or spiced. Simnels: A type of bread or bun made from fine flour and prepared by boiling. Cracknels: Light, crisp biscuits of a curved or hollow shape. as Seneca calls it … Apician tricks: A reference, taken from On Consolation to Helvia (10.8), to the wealthy gourmet Marcus Gavius Apicius (early first century CE), to whom the fourth-century CE cookery book was sometimes attributed. Adrian the sixth … Leo decimus: In this anecdote told by the Italian bishop and historian Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), the ‘accounts’ listed the expenditure on luxuries incurred during the papacy of Leo X – on whom, see above, n. 57 (1.1.2) – which amazed his successor Adrian VI (pope 1522–3); ‘admired’ here means ‘expressed astonishment’.
crudities: Imperfectly digested matter.

oppilations: Obstructions in the stomach. Cacochymia: Unhealthy state of the humours. Plethora: Overabundance of humour, especially blood. Cachexia: A general sickness of the body involving deficient nutrition. Bradiopepsia: Or ‘bradypepsia’, slow digestion.
sink: Cesspool. private: Particular, or specific (often used in opposition to ‘universal’).

Fagos: Or ‘Phagos’: gourmands – from phago, a term used in the Augustan History (The Deified Aurelian 50.4) to describe a gourmand who delighted the Roman emperor Aurelian with his prodigious appetite, and itself deriving from the Greek for ‘glutton’ (φαγών).

to sup in Apollo: That is, to dine in ‘the Apollo’ of the Roman general, and celebrated lover of luxury, Lucius Licinius Lucullus (117–57/6 BCE); the room where, according to Plutarch (Lucullus 41), sumptuous banquets were served. Aesop’s costly dish: Pearl dissolved in vinegar, a drink which according to Horace (Satires
2.239–40) was prepared for the Roman spendthrift Marcus Clodius Aesopus, the son of a famous tragic actor of the first century CE.

Cates: Delicacies. some thousand Crowns: That is, £250 (an English crown being worth five shillings, or a quarter of a pound sterling). Mully-Hamet, King of Fez and Morocco: The Sultan (‘Mully’) of Morocco, Ahmad al-Mansur (1549–1603).
witty: See above, n. 49 (DJR).

In lucem coenat Sertorius: In note ‘f’, a quotation from Martial (7.10) describing the gluttony of Sertorius, a character who is ridiculed on several occasions in the Epigrams. which Dion relates of Vitellius … burst again: This anecdote about the Roman emperor Vitellius (15–69 CE) is related by the historian Dio Cassius (64.2).
make up the mess: Complete the meal.

Ofellius Bibulus … minxit: The Latin passage is taken from an ancient epitaph reportedly inscribed on a tomb outside the Porta Capena at Rome. brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR). Silenus: See above, n. 102 (DJR).
plays it off: Drains or finishes a drink (especially an alcoholic one).

as in like case … honori: In this exchange between Epidicus and Thesprio (from Plautus’ Epidicus 32–3), the former character refers to the cowardice of the master’s son Stratippocles in giving up his arms to the Thebans, and the latter alludes to the cowardice of the Greek poets Archilochus – on whom, see below, n. 18 (3.1.2) – and Alcaeus (c. 625/20–c. 580 BCE), who famously relinquished their shields and fled in the face of the enemy. fox: Intoxicate, make drunk.
Vesper: See below, n. 36 (3.2.3).

Smindyrides … twenty years: Smindyrides was a prominent citizen of the wealthy ancient city-state of Sybaris (on the gulf of Taranto). His luxurious lifestyle was recorded by several historians and commentators.
Verres: Gaius Verres, governor of Sicily, and prosecuted by Cicero in 70 BCE for extortion and corruption.

rendezvous: Possibly here, and with irony, places of sanctuary or seclusion. Centaurs and Lapithae: In Greek mythology, the centaurs and Lapiths fought at the wedding feast of Pirithous and Hippodamia.

a Can of Wine … tombs: Maronis was a fictional elderly drunkard satirized in ancient Alexandrian epigrams, which describe a stone wine goblet carved on her tomb. Burton appears to have mistaken the Greek name for a Latin genitive.
Bonosus: A Roman general and famous drunkard, who rebelled against the emperor Probus and briefly usurped the imperial title before being defeated in 280 CE.

Bitias in the Poet: In Virgil’s Aeneid (1.738–9), Bitias was a member of Dido’s retinue, given a libation of wine by the queen as a challenge at a banquet. According to the ancient commentator Maurus Servius Honoratus, he was the commander of the Carthaginian fleet. clearly: Without embarrassment. if he belie them not: The author being quoted here is the German humanist and jurist Heinrich Petreus (Herdesianus, 1546–1615).
pledge: Drink with someone as a gesture of friendship or allegiance.

servitor: Servant. Brewer’s horse: Slang for ‘drunkard’. City Captains: The commanders of citizen militias, and so – in 1628, when Burton added this passage – not likely to have fought in full battle. Carpet-Knights: Knights whose achievements had taken place in the carpeted bedchamber rather than on the battlefield.

Cockney-like: Squeamish, milksoppy. curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR). Medicina statica: Literally, ‘fixed medicine’, a regular medical regimen. China-broth: A broth made from China root, the rootstock of the climbing plant Smilax china (similar to sarsaparilla), then imported from the East Indies. Plum broth: Made with meat and plums or prunes, along with several other ingredients, and traditionally eaten at Christmas. the Merrythought of a Hen: The wish-bone (furcula), or, as here, the portion of the cooked bird that includes this bone.
put most men out of commons: Exclude them from the ‘common table’ (and so, more loosely, deny them food).
Guipuzcoa in Spain: A province in the Basque Country in Spain.
Cambro-Briton: Cambrian, Welshman. white meats: Foodstuffs prepared from milk, dairy produce.
sit: In note ‘g’, be seated at a table while eating or drinking.
Cicuta, Aconitum: Common hemlock and aconite (or monkshood), both poisonous.
the Nomades of old: Here, probably the ancient nomadic tribes in general, such as the Scythians (rather than the ancient Numidians, often referred to by this term in classical sources).

civillest: Most civilized. the great Mogul’s Court by Land to Paquin … Cataia: The court of the ‘great Mogul’ (the Mughal emperor) of India was located at Agra; ‘Paquin’ (an early version of ‘Peking) and ‘Cambalu’ were both old names for Beijing; ‘Cataia’ was the Latin form for ‘Cathay’ (China).
Palmitos: Hearts of palm, or palm cabbage (also known as ‘swamp cabbage’). Pinas: Pineapples.
