Patagones: In note ‘f’, ‘Patagons’ were a mythical race of giants thought by many explorers to have inhabited the region known sometimes as ‘Chica’, and later as Patagonia. Montezuma himself: The Aztec emperor Moctezuma II (c. 1466–1520), whose name has many variant spellings in this period.
coasts: See above, n. 291 (DJR).
knuckle-deep: Literally, ‘up to the knuckles’, or with the whole hand in – and so, figuratively, ‘deeply’ or ‘with gusto’.

those Indian Capes and Islands: That is, in India and the East Indies. molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR). Calentures: ‘Calenture’ was a tropical disease involving delirium, common among sailors. Fluxes: See above, n. 4 (1.2.1).

Mithridates … to drink poison: According to Pliny the Elder (25.3), the ruler of Pontus – for which, see above, n. 57 (DJR) – King Mithridates VI (ruled c. 120–63 BCE) was learned in the medical arts and invented the idea of rendering poison harmless by drinking it daily after taking remedies. He was sometimes credited with the invention of ‘mithridate’, regarded as a universal antidote to poisons or panacea, whose ingredients typically included opium but otherwise varied widely. a maid … infancy: This story, which seems to have been first recorded in medieval Arabic sources, refers to the ancient Indian practice of employing a ‘Visha Kanya’ (‘poison girl’) as an assassin, and to Porus (d. 318 BCE), king of Paurava (in modern-day Punjab), who fought Alexander the Great in 326 BCE.
a dram … in grains: A dram, in apothecaries’ weight, is worth sixty grains (one-eighth of an ounce or 3.54 grams).
in substance: In a pure or unmixed state, in the natural state.
driven to their shifts: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
disannul: See above, n. 236 (DJR). tender: Attend to.
Nordeling: Nördlingen, in Bavaria. Clyster: Enema or suppository.
Venus: Sexual intercourse.
months: Menses.

Priapismus, Satyriasis: ‘Priapism’ and ‘satyriasis’ were both medical terms for an abnormal condition involving the persistent erection of the penis (or sometimes, more generally, excessive sexual appetite).
stale: Past the prime of life.
conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).
all out: Entirely, totally.
exasperated: Aggravated, intensified.
hothouses: Bath houses with hot baths or steam-baths.

Phlebotomy: Bloodletting was thought to expel noxious or superfluous humours and other substances from the body, and was a common treatment for many different diseases in Galenic medicine; see 2.5.1.2 below. many times neglected: That is, ‘often, if neglected’.
habit: See above, n. 26 (1.1.1).
fuliginous: Sooty (and noxious).

Arabia Deserta: Or ‘Arabia Magna’, the desert interior of the Arabian peninsula. Bactriana, now Charassan: Bactriana (or Bactria) was an ancient kingdom located between the Hindu Kush mountain range and the Amu Darya (formerly River Oxus), in the territory now occupied by northern Afghanistan. Churassan (or Khorasan) is now a province of northeastern Iran, but the name formerly referred to a larger area including parts of central Asia and Afghanistan.
Ormus: See above, n. 258 (DJR).
bleaching: Darkening or blackening.
Diarbecha: Now the city of Diyarbekir in southeastern Turkey. Arabia faelix: South Arabia.
natural melancholy (not this artificial) … dry: See above, 1.1.3.3.
Draughts: Cesspools or sewers.

Alexandretta … Durazzo: See above, n. 219 (DJR). Ditmarsh: The region of Dithmarschen in Germany, now a district in Schleswig-Holstein. Pomptinae paludes in Italy: The Pontine marshes in Italy, which extended along the coast southeast of Rome, and are now drained. Romney Marsh with us: In the English counties of Kent and East Sussex, and now partly drained. the Hundreds in Essex: A ‘hundred’ is a subdivision of an English county or shire, but the reference here is evidently to the marshy hundreds (the ‘continued level of unhealthy marshes, called the Three Hundreds’, as Defoe later referred to them) in southern and eastern Essex.
Regium in Italy: Reggio Calabria. Lynn: King’s Lynn in Norfolk. this new kind of fortification: See above, n. 294 (DJR).

Leander Albertus … qualify the air: In his Descriptio totius Italiae (1567), the Bolognese historian Leandro Alberti claims that the air of Venice is salubrious because of the fire and smoke being continually produced by the furnaces in its glassworks. On ‘Moorish’ here, see above, n. 268 (DJR); ‘qualify’ means ‘mitigate’, or ‘render less unpleasant’. Camden out of Plato … Fens: In his Britannia (1586), William Camden compares the establishment of Cambridge University in the East Anglian Fens to Plato’s decision to found his Academy in an unhealthy part of Attica (actually just outside Athens), on the grounds that the bad climate would suppress physical intemperance.
immund: Unclean, impure.

Tully’s brother Quintus … in Britain: Quintus Tullius Cicero (c. 102–43 BCE) was quaestor some time between 74 and 69, but in Rome rather than Britain. In the late 50s he was a legate on Caesar’s staff in Gaul and in 54 took part in the invasion of Britain, but no letters to his brother from there have survived.
tetric: Morose, or severe.
experiment: Practical proof, example.
Gelidum contristat Aquarius annum: The sun enters Aquarius on 20 January and leaves it on 19 February.
exagitates: Stirs up, excites.

Avicen. lib. 1 … to the 12th: A perplexingly presented reference to Avicenna’s Canon, where the discussion of the element of air is actually, in the terminology of the Latin translation being used by Burton, at ‘Lib. 1, Fen 2, Doc. 2, Cap. 1–11’.
scabbed: Suffering from scabies, or a similar skin disease.
gentry: Good breeding. stepmother of discipline: That is, a false or malign ‘mother’ of (or bad influence upon) discipline.
occasions: Business engagements, affairs.
a hawk in a Mew: In falconry, a ‘mew’ is a cage in which a falcon is placed while moulting.
macerates: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
soothe up: Blandish or cajole by agreement or assent.
Cousin-german: First cousin – but here, figuratively, a near relative. coact: Compelled.
hinds: Agricultural labourers.

shoeing-horn: Something that brings on a condition or facilitates a transaction. Sphinx: In Greek mythology, the hybrid creature that guarded the mountain road to Thebes and devoured those who could not solve its riddle. In Baroque art, the Sphinx was often represented as a female with an alluring décolleté.

Similis a Courtier … retired themselves: According to Dio Cassius (69.19), Servius Sulpicius Similis, who had risen to the position of praetorian prefect under Trajan and played an important role in Hadrian’s assumption of power, resigned his post voluntarily in 119 CE and retired to the country. The emperor Diocletian abdicated, suffering from ill health, in 305, and retired to Salonae in Dalmatia. Vatia … lives alone: A reference to Seneca’s critical account (Epistles 55) of his countrymen’s envy for the idle and secluded life of the wealthy Roman aristocrat Publius Servilius Vatia (c. 65–25 BCE), who owned a famously beautiful villa in the resort of Baiae.

Cleanthes: According to Diogenes Laertius (5.168), the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes (331–232 BCE) supported himself by working at night in a garden as a water-carrier. Pliny’s villa Laurentina, Tully’s Tusculan, Jovius’ study: Three scholarly abodes: the coastal villa of Pliny the Younger by Laurentum, near Ostia; the villa of Cicero at Tusculum, where he composed several of his philosophical works; and the lodgings at the Vatican palace of Paolo Giovio, where he wrote his Historiarum sui temporis libri XLV (1550–52).

Collegiate Cells: Monastic Colleges. After the dissolution of the monasteries in the late 1530s, several Oxford monastic colleges (including Canterbury, Durham and Gloucester) were surrendered to the crown. here and there one: That is, a monastery preserved in various places.

as the Poet … his company: In Aesop’s fable ‘Of the Poet and the Farmer’, the former says that he is never so alone as when he is in the company of the latter – the moral being that bad company is a form of loneliness. Scipio Africanus: Scipio Africanus the Elder – see above, n. 147 (DJR).

for he then followed the Camp: In this passage from Plato’s Symposium (220C–D), Alcibiades reminisces about Socrates during the military campaign against Potidaea in Thrace, which was mounted when the former Corinthian colony revolted against Athenian rule in 432 BCE.

Timons, Nebuchadnezzars: The semi-legendary character of Timon was said to have been a misanthropic Athenian who withdrew from society (to a cave, in Shakespeare’s retelling) after suffering disappointments; according to Plutarch (Antony 70), he encouraged his fellow citizens to hang themselves from a fig-tree in his garden. He reportedly died because he did not want to see a doctor. The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II (ruled c. 605–562 BCE) is portrayed in the Book of Daniel as suffering from divinely decreed madness that involved being driven away from people, eating grass like an ox and growing feathers and claws like a bird (Daniel 4:31–3). default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
good parts: See above, n. 191 (DJR).
swinish: See above, n. 12 (1.1.3). that thinks of waters: Either in dreams or in waking imaginations – see below, 1.3.1.3.
sleep like so many Dormice: That is, deeply – although Burton’s medical source here, the German physician Leonhard Fuchs (1501–66), is referring to the bad effects of sleeping on the back.
hard meats: Foodstuffs that are harder to digest. Incubus: See above, n. 32 (1.1.1) and n. 60 (1.2.1).

that Gymnosophist … the other: In Plutarch’s version of the tale (Alexander 49), Alexander the Great interrogates ten Gymnosophists – see above, n. 91 (DJR) – with difficult questions, and the oldest of them actually delivers the judgement that each has given a worse answer than the others.
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

Cato: Cato the Younger – see above, n. 51 (1.1.1). Jo. Aubanus … look back: The German ethnographer Hans Böhm (Bohemus Aubanus, 1485–1535) says that these people, who lived in the southern part of Africa, were called ‘Cynnami’ by the Greeks and ‘Sylvestres’ by their neighbours; ‘stupid’ here means ‘insensible’.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR). turning it out of the hinges of: Disordering, unhinging.
prosecute: See above, n. 48 (1.1.2). distemperature: In note ‘g’, see above, n. 194 (DJR).
stroke: Influence.
the species of objects: See above, n. 34 (1.1.2).

that Priest … life and sense: Actually from the Venetian humanist Caelius Rhodiginus (Lodovico Celio Ricchieri, 1469–1525), not Celsus. The priest in question is Restitutus of Calama (in Numidia), whose abilities were initially recorded by Augustine in the City of God (14.24).

that Sir Owen … the same Author: The English historian and polymath Matthew Paris (c. 1200–1259) recounts how the knight, who had fought in the service of King Stephen, saw visions of heaven and hell in a cave known as St Patrick’s Purgatory (located on Station Island in County Donegal) in 1153. The reason for the cave’s name was given in the Golden Legend – on which, see above, n. 123 (DJR): God revealed to Patrick that the cave was ‘the place of purgatory’, and that anyone who descended into it would have to perform no other penance or endure any other purgatory for their sins, but that most who did enter would not return. Matthew Paris also tells the story of the monk of Evesham, who experienced visions after a period of fasting in 1196.
Saint Bridget’s revelations: Bridget of Sweden (1303–73) famously experienced religious visions from an early age. as I have formerly said: See above, 1.2.1.5.

Antics: See above, n. 41 (1.1.2). Golden Mountains: The image of the golden mountain, like ‘castles in the air’, was traditionally discussed (most famously by Avicenna and Thomas Aquinas) as an exemplification of the mind’s capacity to create imaginary combinations of nonexistent entities.
Mechanicians: Those skilled in the construction or use of machinery.
Bugbears: Bear-shaped hobgoblins supposed to prey on naughty children – hence also, imaginary terrors.
spectrums: See above, n. 15 (DJR).

Some die suddenly … the battle at Cannae, &c.: The list of sudden deaths collected by Pliny the Elder (7.53) includes that of a Roman mother who died of joy when, contrary to reports, her son returned safely from the Battle of Cannae – on which, see above, n. 130 (DJR).
Jacob the Patriarch … before his sheep: The story is recorded in Genesis 30:37–41; on the word ‘peckled’, see above, n. 15 (1.2.2).
brought to bed of a fair white child: That is, gave birth to a fair- rather than dark-skinned child.
hard-favoured: Coarse-featured.

Dagobertus’ and Saint Francis’ Scars and Wounds: The scars of Dagobert, the Merovingian king of the Franks – probably Dagobert II (ruled c. 676–c. 679) – were said to have been caused by his fear of gangrene; the ‘scars and wounds’ of St Francis of Assisi (1181/2–1226) refer to his five miraculous stigmata.
Sect. 3 memb. 1 subsect. 3: In note ‘f’, the cross-reference should be to 1.3.1.2.
goodwife: See above, n. 44 (1.1.1).
with conceit: By thinking about it.
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

green wounds: See above, n. 13 (1.2.2). Unguentum Armarium … most men controvert: A reference to the contemporary controversy over the so-called ‘weapon-salve’ (unguentum armarium), a magical ointment thought by some to cure wounds when applied to the weapons which caused them, by means of hidden ‘sympathy’ or ‘magnetic’ force. just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).
Mountebanks: See above, n. 76 (DJR).

An Empiric … a silly Chirurgeon: See above, nn. 75, 76 (DJR). Surgery in this era was often denigrated by learned physicians as a crude and bloody form of purely manual labour that lacked a proper theoretical basis.
trenchers: Plates or platters, often round, on which meat was served.
intended or remitted: See above, n. 35 (1.1.1).
macerate: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
as Actaeon … dogs: See above, n. 320 (DJR).
Cebes’ table: See above, n. 85 (DJR).
strappado: See above, n. 18 (1.1.1).

in old Rome … magistracies ceased: The dictator was an extraordinary (but temporary) supreme magistrate in the Roman Republic; while the existing magistrates were subordinate to him, they actually remained in office during his tenure. ‘Ceased’ here may mean ‘ceased from action’: the phrasing follows the passage from Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love (21), quoted below in 3.2.1.1, p. 706, note ‘b’, although the Latin version given there substitutes cessant (‘ceased’) for the unequivocal abdicantur (‘were resigned’) in the sixteenth-century translation of Guillaume Xylander.
rivelled: Shrivelled, wrinkled.

As Elenora … Duke of Gloucester: See below, n. 273 (3.2.2). our English Ovid: The poet Michael Drayton was widely known by this title after Englands Heroicall Epistles (1597), which was modelled on Ovid’s Heroides and is the source quoted here.

like a bottle in the smoke: As the English puritan George Abbot explained the simile in his Brief Notes upon the Whole Book of Psalms (1651), the effects of ‘continual grief’ consume the sufferer ‘into leanness and deformity, like a bladder or a skin-bottle hung up in a chimney, that in tract of time will parch and crack and shrink up into wrinkles not like itself’.

Hecuba … to a dog: In Ovid’s Metamorphoses (13.481–575), Hecuba – the wife of the Trojan king Priam, grieving for her husband and children – is transformed into a furious dog after being attacked by Thracian soldiers for killing their king, Polymestor.
Niobe into a stone … stupid: On Niobe, see above, n. 140 (DJR); ‘stupid’ here means ‘stupefied’, or ‘stunned’.

Severus … died for grief: According to Herodian (3.15), the Roman emperor Septimius Severus (145–211 CE), was ill before his death, but was mainly overcome by sorrow at the luxurious and dissolute lifestyle of his sons. Bothwellius: Note ‘h’ refers to James Hepburn, the fourth earl of Bothwell and the third husband of Mary, Queen of Scots. After being heavily implicated in the murder of Mary’s second husband, Lord Darnley, he eventually died in prison, reportedly insane, in Denmark.
fidus Achates: Achates is the faithful companion of Aeneas in Virgil’s Aeneid; the tag became proverbial.
Angerona Dea: The Roman goddess of suffering and silence. Calends: The first day of the month in the ancient Roman calendar.

amazeth: Stupefies, renders foolish or crazy. Jupiter Tragoedus: Lucian’s dialogue is named after a statue of Jupiter with this epithet at Rome, which itself was probably so called from its location on the city’s Vicus Tragoedus. auditory: Audience.

Faunus: In note ‘e’, which quotes from Andrea Alciato’s Emblematum liber (1536) for the emblem ‘On Sudden Fear’, Faunus is identified with the rustic Greek god Pan, reputed to have invented the military trumpet and the originator of the ‘panic fear’ that descends upon soldiers on the battlefield.
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR).
foiled in the field: Defeated on the battlefield. fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).

Aristotle … the motion of Euripus: The Euripus Strait, which possesses strong tidal currents, runs between the island of Euboea in the Aegean Sea and Boeotia in mainland Greece, and figuratively represented any violent strait or channel. This traditional story about Aristotle is dubious, but was widely believed in the Renaissance. the fisherman’s riddle: The so-called ‘Louse Riddle’ posed to Homer (according to traditional biographies) by some fishermen on the island of Ios. On being asked the question, ‘What was caught?’ the fishermen replied, ‘What we caught, we left behind; what we missed, we bring along’ – namely, lice.
Sophocles killed himself … cap. 12: Valerius Maximus actually reports (9.ext.5) that the elderly Sophocles died from joy when one of his tragedies won a competition by a single vote.

Lucretia stabbed herself … infamy: According to Roman legend, Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, committed suicide after being raped by Sextus Tarquinius – the son of the king, Tarquinius Superbus, who was subsequently expelled by Collatinus and Lucius Junius Brutus, thereby founding the Roman Republic (Collatinus and Brutus were the first two consuls in 509 BCE). Cleopatra VII of Egypt (70/69–30 BCE) committed suicide after learning that Octavian planned to bring her to Rome in a triumphal procession.

Apollonius Rhodius … his Poems: Accounts of the life of the ancient Greek author record that he withdrew to Rhodes after his poetry was poorly received in Alexandria, his probable birthplace; ‘out’ in this passage means in error, or at a loss, from a failure of memory or confidence.
Ajax ran mad … Ulysses: See above, n. 19 (1.1.1).
In China … wits: See DJR, p. 103, and above, n. 303 (DJR).

Hostratus the Friar … made away himself: In 1513, in his capacity as Inquisitor General of the archbishopric of Mainz, the Flemish Dominican Jacob van Hoogstraaten became involved in a controversy about the confiscation of Jewish books as a prelude to their owners’ conversion, which the German humanist scholar Johann Reuchlin had opposed. The satirical Epistolae obscurorum virorum (‘Letters of Obscure Men’, 1515–19) were written in support of, but not by, Reuchlin.
a lask: A bout of diarrhoea. play his prize: Hold its own, play its part (in a contest).
carted: Carried in a cart as a public punishment.
Melicerta: Or Melicertes, a sea-god in classical mythology. In the quotation, Persius (5.103) imagines the reaction of Melicerta to a request by an unskilled ploughman to take command of a ship.

Siculi … tormentum: This quotation from Horace (Epistles 1.2.58) alludes to the notorious cruelty of Sicilian tyrants such as Phalaris – see above, n. 18 (1.1.1) – and Dionysius I of Syracuse (c. 430–367 BCE).
understand of: Learn about (by means of information received).
Lucian’s rock of honour: In Lucian’s Hermotimus, or Concerning the Sects, various philosophers compete to ascend the slopes of the ‘mountain of virtue’.

As he did in Aesop … lose both: In the fable ‘Greedy and Envious’, Jupiter grants each of the characters Greedy and Envious whatever they want, but on condition that the other has twice the amount. Since Envious cannot bear the joy of Greedy, he prays to have one of his eyes put out, so that Greedy would become completely blind.
Chaldee: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2).

Domitian spited Agricola … glorified: Given that the emperor’s jealousy of Gnaeus Julius Agricola (40–93 CE), according to Tacitus, derived from Agricola’s military success in Britain, the reference to him as a ‘private man’ is misleading; Burton is translating the word privatus in Tacitus (Agricola 39.2), where its more accurate meaning is ‘a subject’ (in contrast with a ruler).

Caecina … richly adorned: According to Tacitus (Histories 2.20), the towns and colonies of northern Italy regarded the Gallic dress of the Roman military commander Aulus Caecina Alienus (d. 79 CE) as a sign of arrogance, and were also offended, as Burton notes below, by the sight of his wife Salonina riding a fine horse with purple trappings.

Agrippina-like: Julia Agrippina, or Agrippina the Younger (15–59 CE), whose rivalry with Lollia Paulina over the emperor Claudius’ affections, is recorded by Tacitus: see below, n. 10 (3.3.2). tires: Headdresses. the Roman Ladies … offended: See above, n. 62 (1.2.3). furniture: Decoration, or apparel. bravery: Splendour, or fine clothes.

Myrsine an Attic wench … in beauty: In the Byzantine myth related here, myrtle was once Myrsine, murdered by her jealous peers not only because she was the most beautiful girl in Attica, but also because she was stronger than any of the young men and had the contentious role of bestowing the victory garlands in athletic competitions.
livor: See above, n. 167 (DJR).
Gossips: Friends. jar: See above, n. 232 (DJR).
gentry: See above, n. 112 (1.2.2). the Frog in Aesop … at last: In the fable ‘The Frog and the Ox’, a frog tries to inflate itself to the size of an ox, but bursts in the attempt.

Scotists, Thomists: Followers of the theologians John Duns Scotus (1265/6–1308) and Thomas Aquinas (1225–74). Reals, Nominals: Philosophers who take famously contrasting positions that were elaborated in medieval philosophy: ‘realists’, who hold that universals exist independently of the mind; and philosophical ‘nominalists’, who hold that they do not. Paracelsians: Followers of the Swiss-German physician and occultist Paracelsus – see above, n. 350 (DJR).

ingeniorum cos … wit: The source of the Latin phrase, when applied to emulation, has not been traced (it was more commonly applied by contemporaries to philosophy, or to yellow bile). It may be a paraphrase of ‘alit aemulatio ingenia’ (‘rivalry feeds the wit’), from Velleius Paterculus (1.17.6).

as Themistocles … Miltiades: According to Plutarch, the Athenian politician and general Themistocles (c. 524–460 BCE) said that his envy of the trophies of Miltiades the Younger, who had been celebrated for the Athenian victory over the Persians at Marathon in 490, caused him sleepless nights (Themistocles 3.4). Achilles’ trophies moved Alexander: Another Plutarchan allusion, to an anecdote in which Alexander the Great expresses his preference to see the lyre of Achilles, rather than that of Paris, because the former used the instrument to sing the glorious deeds of courageous men (Alexander 15.9). sue: Follow.

Henry the 8th … that famous interview: The lavish diplomatic meeting (‘interview’) between the two kings that took place in 1520 (not 1519, as note ‘c’ claims) at the so-called ‘Field of the Cloth of Gold’ at Balinghem, on territory that was then English between Guînes and Ardres in northern France, accomplished nothing of substance.

Dionysius the Tyrant … thought: The court of Dionysius I of Syracuse was attended by both Philoxenus of Cythera (435/4–380/79 BCE) and Plato; but according to Plutarch (On Tranquillity of Mind 12), the tyrant envied their respective poetic and philosophical abilities so much that he sent the former to the stone-quarries (then used as prisons), and the latter to Aegina to be sold into slavery. Coriolanus … Alcibiades: Six distinguished aristocratic generals and politicians who were famous in classical history for arousing enmity. From Rome: Gaius Marcius Coriolanus, who by repute was haughtily contemptuous of the plebs, and was banished in 491 BCE; Marcus Furius Camillus, a critic of populist policies for land reform, who was exiled in 391 BCE for embezzling military spoils; and Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus (Scipio Africanus the Younger, 185/4–129 BCE), another opponent of land reform, who was rumoured to have been murdered. And from Athens: Aristides, who was ostracized (that is, expelled for ten years by popular vote, but without conviction for any offence) in 483/2 BCE, perhaps because of his rivalry with the democrat Themistocles; Nicias (d. 413 BCE) – on whom, see below, n. 190 (3.4.1) – who was reportedly unable to win the favour of the Athenian people (though Burton seems to have misremembered Plutarch’s account of how Nicias’ opponent Hyperbolus unsuccessfully attempted to arrange his ostracism and ended up being ostracized himself, probably in 415 but perhaps one or two years earlier); and the notoriously ambitious Alcibiades (451/50–404/3 BCE), who fled twice from Athens but was never formally ostracized or exiled. Theseus: According to Plutarch (Theseus 35.1–4), the legendary king of Athens was imprisoned by the king of the Molossians, Aïdoneus (another name of ‘Hades’) for attempting to steal his daughter; on returning to Athens, Theseus found that in his absence the people had turned against him, and was forced to flee to the island of Scyros, where he was killed by being thrown off a cliff. Phocion: Having been installed as one of the leaders of the oligarchic regime in Athens in 322–318 BCE, Phocion lost popular support because of his friendly relations with the Macedonian commander Nicanor; he was sentenced to death when his regime was deposed, and the democracy briefly restored, in 318.
Acon: Acre, now in the northern coastal region of Israel. The siege of Acre, which was a crucial event in the Third Crusade, took place in 1189–91.
Vatinian hate and rage: See above, n. 161 (DJR).

that Guelph and Ghibelline faction … York and Lancaster in England: Famous enmities: between the Guelphs and Ghibellines – see above, n. 224 (DJR); between the wealthy mercantile families of Adorno and Fregoso, who were political rivals in late medieval Genoa; between the Roman general Lucius (not Gnaeus) Papirius Cursor and his second-in-command Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus, provoked when the latter disobeyed the former’s orders and engaged the enemy in the Second Samnite War in the late fourth century BCE; between Gaius Julius Caesar and Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great), which was at the centre of the civil war of the Roman Republic in the middle of the first century BCE; and between the Orléans and Burgundy factions in France, and the houses of York and Lancaster in England, leading, respectively, to the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War (1407–35) and the Wars of the Roses (1455–85). Carthage and Corinth … as much: Burton is perhaps thinking of the destruction of both cities by Rome in 146 BCE.
strappados, brazen bulls: See above, n. 18 (1.1.1).

Charles the sixth … his life: In the story retold here, Charles VI of France (1368–1422), also known as Charles the Mad, suffered a bout of insanity while on a military expedition against the duke of Brittany (‘Britain’), John IV (1339–99), which had been launched because the latter was harbouring a nobleman who had attempted to assassinate one of Charles’s advisers. The incident actually occurred on 5 August 1392, rather than at the beginning of July, which is when the French army set off.

a story of Herod … a long time after: In the tale told by the early Christian chronicler Hegesippus, Herod the Great (c. 73–4 bce) murdered his uncle Josephus in a jealous rage, falsely thinking that he had being having an affair with his wife Mariamme I (whom Herod executed in 29).
procession: A ‘processional’ book, containing litanies or hymns for use in religious processions.
tetric: See above, n. 106 (1.2.2).
Homer’s Goddess Ate: The goddess in Homer who brings confusion of the senses, and consequently misdeeds and their resultant damage. involved: Entangled, enveloped.
eftsoons: Soon afterwards. arbitrament: Judgement, arbitration.
cark: Burden, anxiety.
mediocrity: Moderate or temperate middle course.

Halcyonian times: Or ‘halcyon days’: a period of calm weather in winter, traditionally associated with the breeding period of the kingfisher, around the winter solstice. In classical mythology the kingfisher was known as the halcyon, and said to charm the wind and waves into calm in order to make its nest on the sea.
bangle away: Squander, fritter away.
precipitiums: Precipices (from the Latin praecipitium).
Emmets: See above, n. 106 (DJR). Sea-cards: Sea charts. The allusion here is evidently to the criss-crossing of the lines that indicate shipping routes on the charts.

Pullus Jovis: A Roman expression, which according to the grammarian Festus (late second century CE) means ‘Jove’s favourite boy’ – that is, someone especially favoured by fortune. Gallinae filius albae: A partial quotation from Juvenal (Satires 13.141–2): ‘Are you the son of a white hen, while we are common chicks hatched from cursed eggs?’

qui fit Maecenas, &c.: A partial quotation from Horace (Satires 1.1.1), which continues ‘no one lives content with his lot, whether it has been brought about by choice, or thrown in his way by chance …?’ On Maecenas, see above, n. 111 (DJR).

Quintus Metellus: See above, n. 28 (1.1.1). P. Mutianus Crassus: The wealthy Roman nobleman, lawyer and orator Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus, who became consul and pontifex maximus in 131 BCE.

Lampido that Lacedaemonian Lady: Lampito (spelled ‘Lampido’ by Pliny) was the daughter of the Spartan king Leotychidas II (reigned c. 491–469 BCE), the wife of King Archidamus II (reigned c. 469–427) and the mother of King Agis II (reigned c. 427–400). Polycrates of Samos: See above, 1.1.1.5, p. 148.

Socrates, Phocion, Aristides: Three classical Athenians with a reputation for outstanding virtue: Socrates, and the statesmen Phocion ‘the Good’ and Aristides ‘the Just’. Aglaus: A semi-legendary citizen of Psophis, said to have been the poorest man in Arcadia but proclaimed by the oracle at Delphi to be happier than King Gyges – on whom, see above, n. 180 (DJR). Cato, Curius, Fabricius: Three statesmen of the Roman Republic regarded as paragons of virtue: Cato the Younger, Manius Curius Dentatus and Gaius Fabricius Luscinus. Fabricius Luscinus, consul in 282 and 278 BCE, was the military leader of the Romans against Pyrrhus of Epirus – on whom, see below, n. 109 (1.2.3) – and was famed for rejecting gifts from Rome’s allies and being content to live in poverty. He and the proverbially incorruptible and modest Curius Dentatus (censor in 272 BCE) were both praised by later generations for their frugality and moral purity. For Cato’s ‘violent death’, see below, n. 155 (1.2.4).

Milo’s strength … Nestor’s years to come: This list of individuals with famous virtues and gifts includes the Greek wrestler Milo of Croton (sixth century BCE), who won six Olympic victories, and whose reputedly superhuman strength enabled him, in contrast with Samson, to support a roof when the columns gave
way; the Albanian military leader and opponent of the Ottoman Empire George Kastrioti Skanderbeg (1405–68), who according to popular folklore, was strong enough to wield an almost impossibly heavy sword; Absalom, who according to 2 Samuel 14:25, was renowned for being the most handsome man in the kingdom of Israel; and Nestor – on whom, see above, n. 90 (DJR). For the obol of Pases, see above, n. 40 (1.2.1); on the ring of Gyges, see above, n. 180 (DJR). absolute: See above, n. 51 (DJR).

as Caesar into Rome, Alcibiades into Athens: Allusions to the famously extravagant military triumphs of Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, and to the celebrated return of Alcibiades to Athens in 407 BCE – see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – after a series of military victories over the Spartans in the Peloponnesian War.

Magnus Gonsalva … banished: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba (1453–1515), a Spanish general who came to be known as ‘the Great Captain’ on account of his successes in the conquest of Granada and the Italian Wars. After falling out of favour at court in later life, he was accused of financial corruption and forced to return to Spain, where he retired to the town of Loja (formerly Loxa) in Granada.

like Xerxes with innumerable armies: In the second Persian invasion of Greece (480–479 BCE), led by Xerxes I. Bajazet the Turk: The Ottoman Sultan Bayezid I (1354–1403 CE) was defeated by Timur (Tamerlane) at the Battle of Ankara in 1402, and died in captivity in the following year. a footstool with Aurelian … to trample on: Probably the Roman emperor Valerian (ruled 253–60 CE) is meant here. According to Lactantius (On the Deaths of the Persecutors 5.3), after losing the Battle of Edessa in 260, Valerian was humiliated by the Persian king Shapur I in various ways, including being made to act as a footstool when the king mounted his horse.
jugglers: Tricksters. naught: See above, n. 322 (DJR). ambidexters: See above, n. 165 (DJR).
Praxinoe and Gorgo … all the rest: In Theocritus’ poem, the two Syracusan women are working their way through the scrum of visitors to see the splendours of the palace in Alexandria.
depress: See above, n. 163 (DJR).

Sulla-like: A reference to the Roman dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla (138–78 BCE), whose additional fourth name ‘Felix’ (‘Happy’ or ‘Lucky’) stood in notorious contrast to his agonizing death from a self-consuming disease. brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR). Demosthenes vow … condemned: In Plutarch’s account, after Demosthenes had been prosecuted for financial corruption (in 323 BCE) and escaped into exile, he summed up his retrospective meditation by saying that had he known the evils attendant on a public career, he would have preferred a direct road to ruin (Demosthenes 26.7).
as I shall prove elsewhere: See 2.3.3.1 below.

pudet lotii: The examination of urine (and faeces) was a common diagnostic procedure in Renaissance medicine. an hungry Jack: A hungry commoner (‘Jack’ here refers to a hypothetical ordinary person). a player: A reveller, or someone who has no serious employment. Chirurgeon: See above, n. 75 (DJR). from’s: See above, n. 4 (Preliminaries). as he could find … hang himself: An allusion to the traditional early Christian story, recorded by the eleventh-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator Theophylact of Ohrid, of the repeated failures of Judas Iscariot in attempting suicide. In this version, after betraying Jesus he ended up living a long, miserable life.
Spretaeque injuria formae: Note ‘d’ is a quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.27), referring to Juno’s anger at the judgement of Paris against her in a beauty contest, which led to the Trojan War.
Talking Fabius: A Stoic windbag ridiculed by Horace (Satires 1.1, 1.2).

that axiom of Silenus … quickly: The ‘wisdom of Silenus’ – for whom, see above, n. 102 (DJR). The reference in note ‘a’ is to Pliny the Elder’s report (7.1) of many
who have committed suicide for this reason. Crates Thebanus: See above, n. 284 (DJR). Cleombrotus Ambraciotes’ 400 auditors: Plato’s account of the soul’s continued life after the death of the body is said to have inspired Cleombrotus of Ambracia, an impressionable young man first mentioned in the Phaedo, to commit suicide (the spelling ‘Theombrotus’, which was used in the early editions of the Anatomy, is found in some ancient manuscripts but is uncommon in early modern English sources). Burton’s version of the story is embellished with the introduction of an audience inspired by his eloquence to follow suit; a more detailed version is given in 1.4.1.1, pp. 423–4.
moth: Something that gradually and silently eats away or diminishes.

cogging: See above, n. 164 (DJR). colloguing: See above, n. 31 (DJR). capping: Taking off the cap as a token of respect. cringing: See above, n. 121 (DJR). fleering: Laughing or smiling – here, in a fawning manner.

about a suit: Engaging in a supplication, petition or entreaty (although a more specific reference to a ‘suit of court’, serving or attending at the court of a lord, is also possible). as Cineas … told Pyrrhus: According to Plutarch (Pyrrhus 14), the Thessalian orator and diplomat Cineas, who worked as an adviser to King Pyrrhus I of Epirus (319–272 BCE), attempted to dissuade him from waging war against Rome by asking a series of questions intended to make him realize that he was already satisfied with his current possessions. Plutarch says that although this troubled Pyrrhus, he was unable to free himself from his ambitious desires.

Lewis Sforza … destruction of Italy: Ludovico Sforza (1451–1508), whose alliance with France initially helped him to ascend to the dukedom of Milan, but also prepared the way for the French invasion of Italy and the First Italian War (1494–8).

from Tribune to Praetor: In the ancient Roman cursus honorum (career path) – the ascending series of magistracies culminating in the consulship – it was customary from the early imperial era to serve as a tribune of the plebs (or as an aedile, if one’s patrician status debarred one from the tribunate) before assuming the more powerful office of the praetorship – a magistracy that was subordinate only to the consuls, and which bestowed wide-ranging legal, administrative and military powers. as Pyrrhus in Plutarch: See above, n. 109 (1.2.3). Sejanus, ad Gemonias scalas: Under suspicion of conspiring against the emperor Tiberius, the praetorian prefect Lucius Aelius Sejanus (20 BCE–31 CE) was strangled and his body thrown down the Gemonian Steps (or the ‘Stairs of Mourning’) on the Capitoline Hill, where it was torn to pieces by a mob. As further punishment, his daughter Junilla was subsequently raped and hanged, and his other children also executed. Evangelus the piper … dead: In Lucian’s Ignorant Book-Collector (8–10), the character of Evangelus is a distinguished citizen of Tarentum who competes in the Pythian games in a musical competition, actually by singing and playing the lyre; his performance is so bad that the judges order him to be flogged and driven out of the theatre. Shortly afterwards (11–12), Lucian relates another story, in which Neanthus, son of Pittacus of Mytilene – see above, n. 91 (DJR) – steals the lyre of Orpheus but plays it so badly that he is torn to pieces by dogs.
have a canvas: Suffer criticism, or a metaphorical ‘drubbing’.
event: See above, n. 149 (DJR).

Qui perjurum … quaerito, &c.: This quotation from Plautus (Curculio 470–72) refers to three places around the Roman Forum (the aforementioned ‘markets’): the comitium, where the people gathered for legislative and judicial decision-making and the election of magistrates; the temple of Venus Cloacina (‘the Purifier’), which was said to govern the Cloaca Maxima (‘Great Drain’) in Rome, and was associated with purification after battle (Plautus’ satirical target was probably boastful soldiers); and the areas around the basilicas, well known for being frequented by lovers, prostitutes and pimps.

Knights of the Post: Notorious or professional perjurers (the ‘post’ perhaps referring to a whipping-post). crackers: Boasters, braggarts. bad husbands: Here, probably people who mismanage their households or resources.
Aesculapius: See above, n. 86 (1.2.1). Plutus: The god of wealth in Greek mythology.
trow: Think, believe.

those intemperate Zones of heat & cold: In Renaissance geography, the earth’s surface is divided into five ‘zones’: the ‘torrid’ or ‘burnt zone’ between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn; the northern ‘temperate zone’ between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle; the southern ‘temperate zone’ between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Antarctic Circle; and the ‘frozen’ or ‘frigid zones’ contained within the two polar circles. The ‘intemperate’ zones referred to here are the ‘torrid zone’ and the two ‘frozen zones’. nasty usage: Either harsh or bad treatment – or, alternatively, the consumption of something nasty as a food or drink.
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR). Ptolemaeus King of Cyprus: Ptolemy of Cyprus, who ruled 80–58 BCE, and was the younger son of the Egyptian king Ptolemy IX Soter II (d. 81).
as Nabal was: According 1 Samuel 25, Nabal was an unpleasant rich man. His name derives from the Hebrew term for ‘wilt’, but came to be associated with shamelessness and folly.

Genius: See above, n. 173 (DJR). like a … dog in the manger: In the fable of ‘The Dog in the Manger’, attributed to Aesop probably incorrectly, a dog chooses not to eat grain, but also prevents a hungry horse from eating. pelf: Wealth, riches.

as Ahab’s spirit … Vineyard: The story of Naboth’s vineyard, in which Ahab, king of Israel in the ninth century BCE, becomes ‘heavy and displeased’ when Naboth refuses to sell the land which Ahab covets, is told in 1 Kings 21:1–25.
wearish: See above, n. 6 (DJR).

dust-worm: A grovelling or mean person, a ‘worm of the dust’. like Pharaoh’s lean Kine … not satisfied: An allusion to the dream of Pharaoh described in Genesis 41:1–4, in which seven ‘ill favoured and leanfleshed’ cows devour seven ‘well favoured and fat’ ones.
cap-case: Casket or box. dark-Lantern: A lantern with a slide, or some other device, which conceals the light.
Lucian … Pythagoras: See above, n. 56 (1.1.2).
scrat: Scratch or rake in the ground with its claws.
deciphered: See above, n. 209 (DJR).
as bitter … their last: An allusion to Proverbs 5:4.
impinge: Strike forcibly upon. Rillets: See above, n. 67 (DJR).
Actaeon-like … dogs: See above, n. 320 (DJR).
Parks, and Forests: See above, n. 240 (DJR). hacker: A cut-throat, or a bully.
impertinent: Here, absurd, irrational or trivial.

he would sometimes live about Ostia … together: The papal residence of the Villa Magliana, about five miles from Rome on the road to Ostia, had hosted hunts since the reign of Sixtus IV (1471–84); but by all accounts these became especially extravagant and frequent in the time of Leo X – on whom, see above, n. 57 (1.1.2).
Tables: Backgammon. tetty: Fractious, testy.
Antony: Marcus Antonius Creticus: praetor in 74 BCE, proconsul in the Mediterranean, and the father of the triumvir Mark Antony.
undiscreetly: See above, n. 40 (DJR).
Tuscans: The ancient Etruscans.
Civilians: See above, n. 230 (DJR).
Sirac.: ‘Siracides’, or the Book of Ecclesiasticus.

Matrem praegnantem … killed his father, &c.: Burton only partially renders the preceding quotation, which translates in full as: ‘He wretchedly suffocated his pregnant mother, tried to rape his sister, nearly killed his father, and mortally wounded his two other sisters.’

aurum potabile: ‘Potable gold’, a controversial substance, reputedly made for medical purposes by alchemists and sometimes identified as the ‘elixir of life’, consisting of gold suspended within a volatile oil in a state of minute subdivision. their Hilary term’s but short: That is, their happiness is fleeting – possibly an allusion to the spring term of the academic year in Burton’s University of Oxford, which is named after St Hilary of Poitiers (and whose name is derived from the Latin hilaris, cheerful); but the more widely circulating phrase ‘keep Hilary term’ also meant ‘maintain hilarity’ or ‘stay cheerful’.
Rhododaphne: Oleander or rosebay.
fond: See above, n. 103 (DJR).
irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR).
swell: See above, n. 108 (DJR).
good parts: See above, n. 191 (DJR).
venditate: Exhibit ostentatiously, as if displaying for sale. in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).

only: See above, n. 14 (DJR). Tympany: Swelling up (and so, figuratively, arrogance). De meliore … Titan: Note ‘g’ is a quotation from Juvenal (Satires 14.35), alluding to the myth of Prometheus’ creation of man from clay. that wise Periander: See above, n. 223 (DJR).

Callisthenes … his insolency: Callisthenes of Olynthus (d. 327 BCE) was the official historian of Alexander the Great, whose military achievements he praised in the Deeds of Alexander. Seleucus King of Syria … certaret: This view is actually assigned by Plutarch (Marcus Cato 12) to the Seleucid king Antiochus III Megas (‘the Great’, c. 242–187 BCE). The mistake has arisen from Plutarch’s claim that the Romans feared Antiochus because he had won back almost all of the dominions in Asia formerly conquered by Seleucus I Nicator – on whom, see above, n. 127 (1.2.1).

Pliny seconds him … O! &c.: Pliny is himself quoting Virgil (Aeneid 5.195), where the sailor Mnestheus, having just renounced his wish to win the boat race at the funeral games of Anchises, announces to his crew that they should nevertheless avoid the disgrace of being last. In the end, they finish in second place. that vainglorious Orator … thy book: In a letter to the Roman historian Lucius (not Marcus) Lucceius written c. 55 BCE, Cicero asked Lucceius to compose a special monograph glorifying his role in the suppression of the Catilinarian conspiracy – on which, see above, n. 227 (DJR).
cracks: Boasts. linenda cedro, & leni servanda cupresso: That is, worthy of these ancient methods of preservation.
Aufidus: The River Ofanto in Puglia, renowned in antiquity for its rapid currents.

Not so much as Demochares on the Topics: A reference to the French theologian Antoine de Mouchy (1494–1594), who borrowed the name of the Athenian orator and statesman Demochares (c. 360–275 BCE), and published a lengthy and self-aggrandizing commentary on Aristotle’s Topics in 1535.

Mausolean tombs: That is, resembling the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the tomb of the satrap Mausolus of Caria (reigned 377–353 BCE), and one of the Seven Wonders of the world. Phryne fecit: According to the ancient grammarian Athenaeus of Naucratis (fl. c. 190 CE) in his Learned Banqueters (13.591D), the wealthy Boeotian courtesan Phryne offered to rebuild the city walls of Thebes after they had been destroyed by Alexander the Great in 335 BCE, on the condition that they bore the inscription ‘Destroyed by Alexander, rebuilt by Phryne the courtesan’. The offer, if made, was apparently never taken up.

De ponte dejicere: In note ‘a’, an adaptation of the classical proverb ‘Sexagenarios de ponte deicere’ (‘To throw the sexagenarians off the bridge’), which, as Erasmus explained in the Adagia, means ‘to consign older people to idleness as if they were doting and useless’. It originates in ancient Rome, perhaps in stories about young men who threw old men off the narrow voting bridges in the Campus Martius at election time, or perhaps in the ancient tradition of killing the elderly during times of famine. Palaemon … literas jactans: Quintus Remmius Palaemon, a leading Roman grammarian in the time of Tiberius and Claudius, was so arrogant, according to Suetonius (On Grammarians 23), that he called the great polymath Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE) ‘a pig’.

funges: See above, n. 151 (DJR). ut Camelus in proverbio … amisit: A proverbial warning against rashly seeking exotic things. Erasmus explained in his Adagia that it is derived from the ancient fable of the camels that demanded horns from Jove, who responded by depriving them of their ears.
sophisters: Sophists, that is (following Burton’s source), the Greek teachers of philosophy and rhetoric in the fifth century BCE, rather than generally specious or fallacious philosophers.

as one told Philip … before: According to Plutarch in his Sayings of Spartans (218F), this was the response of Archidamus III (king of Sparta 360/59–338 BCE) to a gloating letter written by Philip of Macedon after the Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE).

as scant as Alcibiades … Map: An allusion to a tale told by Aelian in his Historical Miscellany (3.28), in which Socrates punctures the pride of Alcibiades by asking him to point to his large estates on a map of the earth.
the 4 Monarchies: As prophesied in the Book of Daniel, the kingdoms of Babylon, Persia, Macedon and Rome (though variations of this list were available).

private: See above, n. 46 (1.2.2). Cadwallader in Wales: The Welsh king Cadwallader (or Cadwaladr) ruled in the seventh century and was mythologized by the medieval historian Geoffrey of Monmouth. Rollo in Normandy: Rollo (c. 846–931) was the first Viking ruler of Normandy and an ancestor of William the Conqueror. Hephaestion: The friend, and probably the lover, of Alexander the Great and one of his most distinguished generals. Brasidas … he was: See above, n. 90 (DJR). he or he: One or the other, either.
sheep’s russet: Coarse woollen cloth, as worn by poor rural dwellers.
animate: Inspire, incite.

the nine Worthies: In medieval and Renaissance chivalry, the nine figures of exemplary virtue drawn from myth, history and Scripture: Hector, Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Joshua, David, Judas Maccabeus, King Arthur, Charlemagne and the Frankish knight Godfrey of Bouillon (1060–1100) – the last of these meriting inclusion on account of his reputation as the leader of the First Crusade, which captured Jerusalem. edictum Domini Deique nostri: A quotation from Martial (Epigrams 5.8.1), itself an allusion to the title, according to Suetonius (Domitian 13), that had been adopted by Domitian in his official correspondence.

Epaminondas: The Theban general Epaminondas, renowned for his part in the Boeotian defeats of Sparta at the Battles of Leuctra (371 BCE) and Mantinea (362), in which he was fatally wounded. duo fulmina belli … both Scipios: The ‘twin thunderbolts of war’ is the name given by Virgil (Aeneid 6.842) to Scipio Africanus the Elder and Scipio Aemilianus – see above, n. 147 (DJR) and n. 72 (1.2.3) – as the Roman conquerors of Carthage. triumviri terrarum … the triumvirs of the earth: That is, the ‘Second Triumvirate’ of 43–33 BCE (the ‘First Triumvirate’ being the alliance between Julius Caesar, Marcus Licinius Crassus and Pompey the Great in 60–53 BCE), comprising Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, and whose ascendancy sealed the end of the Roman Republic.
eviscerate himself like a spider: That is, disembowel or gut himself in the manner that a spider does in producing silk for its web.

impar congressus … Infelix puer: A passage from Virgil’s Aeneid (1.475), where Aeneas is viewing a painting of the Trojan War, and sees the image of Troilus, the young Trojan prince who was ambushed and killed by Achilles (and whose romance with Chryseis, a medieval invention, was the subject of Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde and Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida). as another Philippus … enemies: A reference to Livy’s description (31.13–14) of the actions of Philip V of Macedon (238–179 BCE) during the siege of Athens in 200.
whoa: Stop – as when commanding a horse.
Cotys King of Thrace: Cotys I, who ruled the Thracian tribe of the Odrysae 383–359 BCE.

Jupiter Menecrates: Menecrates of Syracuse (fl. 350 BCE), a physician who attended the court of Philip of Macedon, and whose high estimation of his medical powers led him to call himself ‘Zeus-Menecrates’ (or ‘Jupiter-Menecrates’) and dress up as a god. Maximus Jovianus, Dioclesianus Herculeus: Burton has mixed up the titles taken by the Roman emperors Maximian (Marcus Aurelius Valerius Maximianus Herculius Augustus, c. 250–310 CE) and Diocletian (Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus Jovius, 241/4–c. 313). Sapor the Persian King: Sapor (Shapur) I, who ruled c. 240/42–72 CE.
Xerxes … Mount Athos: See above, n. 195 (DJR).

Plutarch … lost his wits: In Plutarch’s story about the Battle of Cunaxa (401 BCE), fought between the Persian royal brothers Cyrus the Younger and Artaxerxes II, the former died after being struck twice, first by a soldier called Mithridates and then by an unnamed soldier from the city of Caunus in Caria (a region in western Anatolia). When Artaxerxes subsequently claimed to have killed Cyrus himself, the Carian indignantly boasted that he alone had done the deed, resulting in his torture and death by the pouring of molten brass into his ears (Artaxerxes 11). The name ‘Chamus’ given by Burton is probably a corruption of ‘Caunus’.
Epaminondas … Leuctrian victory: See above, n. 166 (1.2.3).
Queen Katherine, Dowager of England: Catherine of Aragon (1485–1536), whose official title after her marriage with the king was annulled was actually ‘princess dowager’.
Maul: Implacable foe, scourge.
institution: Education or instruction.
Corcutus: Prince Korkut (1467–1513), the son of Sultan Bayezid II.
Pencils: Brushes.
President: Presiding deity or guardian.

Boor: An unrefined rustic or peasant. The quotation is from Christopher Marlowe’s Hero and Leander (1598), where the punitive association of Mercury with Poverty, in a fable apparently invented by Marlowe, is ordained by the classical Fates.
Bradiopepsia … Crudities, Oppilations: See above, nn. 44, 45 (1.2.2).

great Tostatus’ … Works: A reference to the influential Spanish theologian and Hebraic scholar Alfonso Tostado Ribera de Madrigal (c. 1400–1455), also known as ‘Abulensis’ after becoming bishop of Avila in 1449.
the other on his Almagest: That is, Ptolemy on his famous astronomical and mathematical treatise, known as the Almagest after the Arabic version that was translated into Latin in the twelfth century.

Thebit Benchorat … to find out the motion of the eighth sphere: The treatise De motu octave sphere was commonly attributed, possibly falsely, to the Mesopotamian mathematician and astronomer Thabit ibn Qurra (c. 830–901). The eighth cosmological ‘sphere’ in question was traditionally held to contain the fixed stars,
located beyond the preceding seven spheres (which contained the planets): see above, n. 52 (1.2.1).
scrubs: Insignificant or inferior people.

Clown: A rustic, or peasant. make congees: Take ceremonious leave. Swasher: Ostentatious braggart or swaggerer. They cannot fiddle … great City: Note ‘b’ relates an anecdote given by Plutarch about Themistocles when taunted about his lack of cultured sophistication, contrasting his inability to play the lyre or harp with his civic achievements (Themistocles 2.3).

King Lewis of France: Louis IX, who reigned 1226–70. conclusum est contra Manichaeos: In the Summa theologiae (1266–73), Thomas Aquinas criticized the ancient belief-system of Manicheanism, which posited a primeval cosmological conflict between the forces of Good and Evil, as an especially grievous form of superstitious idolatry because of its exaltation of two opposed gods. In the thirteenth century, the ascetic heretical sect of the Cathars in southern France were sometimes regarded as Manichean revivalists.

Archimedes in Vitruvius … notice of it: These famous anecdotes about Archimedes arise from his friendship with Hieron II of Syracuse (ruled c. 271–216 BCE), whom he had helped with improvements to the city’s defences. The mathematician was killed by a Roman soldier when the city was sacked after the long siege of 213–212 BCE, because he refused to stop contemplating a geometrical diagram.
St. Bernard … where he was: This story about Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) refers to his journeying around Lake Geneva (named ‘Lacus Lemannus’ by the Romans) in the spring of 1137.
Menedemus Lampsacus: A Cynic philosopher of the third century BCE, who was a pupil of two philosophers from Lampsacus in western Asia Minor, Colotes the Epicurean and Echecles the Cynic.
circumvented: Outwitted, cheated.
Sots: Fools, blockheads.
Paglarensis: The eminent fourteenth-century Sienese jurist Giovanni Pagliarese.
Isaeus: Isaeus the Assyrian, a rhetorician who was famous in Rome c. 100 CE; see also below, 3.2.5.2.
mewed up: Confined or caged up – see above, n. 114 (1.2.2). driven to their shifts: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
saving: Breaking even, or turning a modest profit.

docile: Teachable. Kings can invest Knights … confessed: Sigismund of Luxembourg (1368–1437) who as Holy Roman Emperor knighted the jurist Georgius Fistellus, but then rebuked him at a session of the Council of Basel (1431–5) for seating himself with the knights rather than the doctors of law. The emperor’s point, reportedly, was that he could make a thousand knights in one day, but not even a single doctor in a thousand years.
compass: Lay hold of, obtain.
parable: Procurable.
stump rod: A teacher’s rod used to punish pupils, worn to a stump by repeated use.

trencher Chaplain: A contemptuous term for a domestic chaplain, who eats at the table of a noble patron. Satyricon: In note ‘d’, a reference to the Euphormionis lusinini satyricon (1605–7) by John Barclay (rather than the work of Petronius). a Living to the halves: With a half-share of a benefice. mother of the maids: A housekeeper in charge of the maids, but alternatively, a brothel-keeper. cracked Chambermaid: A morally or physically impaired (by implication, deflowered) lady’s maid – although a maid who cleans bedrooms is also possible.
as Hercules did by Cacus: See above, n. 284 (DJR).
Mathematicians: See above, n. 117 (1.2.1). Sophisters: Here, probably, logicians (without the usual pejorative contrast with philosophers).

in Tythoni … ranas: In classical mythology, at the request of Eos (Aurora), Zeus (Jupiter) granted her lover Tithonus immortality; but when Tithonus became old and helpless, he gradually turned into a cicada. Leto (Latona), the mother of Apollo and Artemis (Diana), arranged for Zeus to turn a group of Lycian peasants into frogs when they refused to let her drink from their pond. viaticum: Travel money or supplies. Manucodiatae those Indian Birds of Paradise … no other food: Since birds of paradise were first brought to Europe from the East Indies in the sixteenth century as skins and with their limbs removed, they were sometimes thought to live perpetually airborne in the highest parts of the sky.

Indians … worth of it: See above, n. 59 (1.2.1). King Hieron … than Simonides did by his: The poet Simonides of Ceos spent his final years at the court of Hieron I of Syracuse – see above, n. 327 (DJR) – where he is said to have helped reconcile Hieron with the tyrant Theron of Acragas (Agrigento).

that Encyclopaedian, all the learning in the world: The word ‘encyclopaedian’ here is used as a noun, its unusual form deriving from the retention of the Greek accusative ending. It refers to the ideal of ‘general’ or polymathic knowledge that was especially prized in Oxford at the time (see the editor’s Introduction).

Dat Galenus opes … by their side: A commonplace saying of obscure origin, with the second line of the Latin verse adapted: literally, ‘But “genus and species”’ (that is, ‘the philosopher’ – other versions give ‘Aristoteles’) ‘is forced to go on foot’). Most commonly, the same line reads ‘ex aliis paleas, ex istis collige grana’ (‘from other disciplines you collect chaff, from these two grain’). ‘Galenus’ and ‘Justinianus’ in the first line are representatives of successful physicians and lawyers respectively.

Poetical divinity: Creative or artistic accounts of the gods – that is, in classical mythology. Helicon: A classical mythological allusion to poetic inspiration. The Boeotian mountain, described by Hesiod as his own inspiration in the opening of the Theogony, was sacred to the Muses as the location of the Aganippe and Hippocrene springs, the drinking of whose waters was said to induce poetic ecstasy.
Calliope: The ancient Muse of eloquence and epic poetry.
fox’d: Intoxicated, drunk – but here, perhaps, also a punning reference to clothing trimmed with fox-fur.
Errant motions: Roving or wandering movements (of the planets, by contrast with the fixed positions of the stars).

For let him be a Doctor of the Law … those all-devouring municipal Laws: The complaint here refers to the domination of the ‘municipal laws’ (the laws of particular states, and so here, English common law) over the ‘civil law’ (the legal system historically derived from Roman law) that prevailed in continental Europe and was studied by learned ‘civilian’ lawyers. In Burton’s time, the number of doctors of civil law graduating from the English universities had declined significantly, after their profession suffered a series of attacks by common lawyers, and the jurisdiction of civil law became diminished by prohibitions issued by superior common law courts preventing them from proceeding with suits. After 1625, however, the role of civil law in ecclesiastical and admiralty courts was restrengthened by Charles I and Archbishop William Laud.
Quacksalvers, Paracelsians: See above, n. 76 (DJR) and n. 68 (1.2.3). cast: Dismissed, sacked. Goodwives: See above, n. 44 (1.1.1).
litigious: Quarrelsome, contentious (not necessarily in the legal sense).

a brief: An abstract or summary. as it was not many years … this land: John Howson (1556/7–1632), one of Burton’s colleagues at Christ Church, became bishop of Oxford in 1619, and subsequently, in 1628, bishop of Durham. The sermon quoted here, on Matthew 21:12–13, was actually delivered on 4 December 1597; for ‘Paul’s cross’, see above, n. 68 (DJR). as Phalaris objected to the Leontines … fear: In the letter quoted here, purporting to be from the Sicilian tyrant Phalaris – see above,
n. 18 (1.1.1) – to the Spartan king Leonidas I (reigned c. 490–480 BCE) in the midst of a conflict over the colony of Leontini, Phalaris claims that a captured spy has told him that Leonidas is destitute of everything except fear and hunger. The ‘Epistles of Phalaris’ were later proved to be spurious, and probably originating in the second century CE.

for the lease of a life: That is, for a lease which remains in force until the death of the person to which it was granted. copyhold: An ancient form of customary tenure, by which lands were held as a portion of a manor, at the will of the landowner and certified only by the transcript (or ‘copy’) of a manorial court record.
Leaping (as he saith) … thunder-clap: A quotation from Ulrich von Hutten’s dialogue Aula sive Misaulus (1518), where the subject is actually the daily routine of the courtier.
Thalia: See above, n. 337 (DJR).

turn our Philosophers’ gowns … millers’ coats: Evidently a loose allusion to the account of Cleanthes given by Diogenes Laertius – see above, n. 121 (1.2.2) – who also reports that the philosopher wore no shirt under his cloak (7.5.169).
except: See above, n. 21 (DJR).

scamble: In note ‘f’, struggle or scramble. non pranderet olus: A reference to a phrase in Horace (Epistles 1.17.13), which itself alludes to a story reported by Diogenes Laertius (2.8.68). When the philosopher Aristippus – on whom, see above, n. 97 (DJR) – walked by Diogenes the Cynic, who was cleaning vegetables, the latter said to him, ‘If you had learned to make these your diet, you would not have paid court to kings.’ Aristippus replied, ‘And if you knew how to associate with men, you would not be washing vegetables.’ baffled: See above, n. 166 (DJR). rich Crassus: See above, n. 103 (1.2.1).

Libanius Sophista … offered unto him: The Greek rhetorician Libanius of Antioch (314–c. 393 CE) is reported by Eunapius, perhaps unreliably, to have refused the honorary title of praetorian prefect when it was offered by unnamed emperors who ruled after Julian, with the comment that the title of sophist was ‘more distinguished’ (Lives of the Philosophers and Sophists 496).
Achan-like: See above, n. 222 (DJR).
embezzled: Squandered.
moil: See above, n. 177 (DJR).

lighten: Flash lightning. as the enchanted Adder … ears: In Psalm 58:4–5, the poison of the wicked is compared to that of a serpent: ‘they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.’
the Bawd in Plautus: Ballio, the pimp in Pseudolus – see above, 1.2.3.6, p. 261. that Miser … in arca: The rich Athenian miser described by Horace in Satires 1.1.
Simoniacal contractors: Greedy traders in ecclesiastical property.

as he said … foul ends: ‘He’ may be the Oxford clergyman and Fellow of Oriel College John Day, in a sermon printed in Day’s Festivals (1615), although William Camden also recorded the proverb in his Remains (1614). as an Eagle’s feathers … substance: According to Pliny the Elder (10.4), the feathers of the eagle, if mixed with those of other birds, will destroy them. aurum Tholosanum: That is, stolen and cursed gold. ‘Toulousain gold’ refers to the treasure of the Tectosages, allegedly plundered from the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi by Gallic invaders in 279 BCE, and taken from Toulouse by the Roman general Quintus Servilius Caepio in 106 BCE. Caepio was disgraced and his family impoverished, and the belief subsequently circulated that touching the gold brought misfortune.
The Eagle in Aesop … all together: The fable of ‘The Eagle and the Fox’.
Church-chopping: Dealing in ecclesiastical benefices.

Flacce Marones: This quotation from Martial (Epigrams 8.55.5) alludes to the
poets Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus) and Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). painful: See above, n. 50 (DJR). Sciences: See above, n. 71 (DJR).
have so much Latin as that Emperor … nescit vivere: The Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund – see above, n. 198 (1.2.3) – had this saying, according to Enea Silvio Piccolomini (Pope Pius II).
trivantly: See above, n. 46 (DJR). Polyanthean helps: A polyanthea is an anthology or commonplace book, collecting excerpts or quotations from literature.
pen and Ink-horn men: Bookish men; the ink-horn was a small container, originally made of a horn, for holding writing ink. humane learning: See above, n. 28 (DJR).
Land-leapers: Or ‘land-lopers’: literally, ‘vagabonds’; but here, figuratively, ‘adventurers’ or ‘explorers’.
Julius Caesar mended the year … Commentaries: By reforming the Roman calendar, in 46 BCE, and composing historical records (that is, works about his military campaigns and the civil war).

Antoninus … Julian: In this list of learned Roman emperors, ‘Antoninus’ is probably Marcus Aurelius (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus) rather than Antoninus Pius, and ‘Severus’ is Septimius Severus; the ostensibly odd inclusion of Nero perhaps relates to his love of poetry and music, or to his relationship with Seneca. Michael the Emperor, and Isacius: Two medieval emperors of Byzantium, Michael VII Doukas – on whom, see above, n. 25 (1.2.1) – and Isaac I Komnenos, who ruled 1057–9. Orion, Perseus, Alphonsus, Ptolemaeus, famous Astronomers: This list begins peculiarly with two Greek heroes with constellations named after them, before introducing the astronomer Claudius Ptolemaeus (Ptolemy) – included, perhaps, because of his occasional (erroneous) association with the Egyptian dynasty of the Ptolemies – and Alfonso X, ‘the Wise’ (1221–84), king of Castile, León and Galicia, who sponsored the creation of the ‘Alfonsine Tables’ of astronomical data, which were influential across Europe until the seventeenth century. Sapor, Mithridates, Lysimachus, admired Physicians: On Sapor – included here because he was credited with the invention of various medicinal syrups, including ‘King Sabor’s Syrup’ for melancholy – see above, n. 171 (1.2.3) and 2.4.1.5, p. 633; on Mithridates, see above, n. 78 (1.2.2); King Lysimachus (360–281 BCE) who ruled Thrace, Asia Minor and Macedon is apparently confused here with the Hippocratic physician Lysimachus of Cos (fl. c. 100 BCE). Evax that Arabian prince … an exquisite Philosopher: Some manuscripts and early printed editions of Pliny the Elder’s Natural History contain a passage describing the Arabian king Evax as having dedicated a book on the subject of medical herbs to the emperor Nero. Burton made this reference in his first edition of 1621, but in 1629 the passage in Pliny was shown by the French scholar Claude Saumaise to have been a medieval interpolation. Evax was also spuriously reported to have written a work on the properties of precious stones.
Anacreon to Polycrates: The Greek lyric poet Anacreon (582–485 BCE) enjoyed the patronage of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos, for whom he was said to have composed laudatory odes.

Xenocrates: See above, n. 10 (DJR). Clerks: Scholars. velut in Lycaeum … University: The Latin word ‘Lyceum’ derives from the name of the ancient Athenian gymnasium dedicated to Apollo Lyceus, which hosted the school of Aristotle, and later became the generic term for a university (or other educational institution). Archelaus … suavi sermone: According to Plutarch (Sayings of Kings and Commanders 177A), the Macedonian king Archelaus (413–399 BCE), on being asked by one of his guests at dinner for a golden cup, ordered it to be given instead to Euripides, saying to the guest, ‘You are just the man to ask and not receive; he to receive even when he does not ask.’ chuff: A coarse, rude person; or a greedy miser.
depression: See above, n. 163 (DJR).
Bavius and Mevius: Two incompetent Roman poets satirized by Virgil and Horace.
elogies: See above, n. 54 (DJR).

Alexander … Hieron: The less well-known names in this list include Demaratus, a prominent Corinthian citizen of the fourth century BCE who, according to Plutarch (Alexander 9.12), helped to reconcile Philip of Macedon with his son Alexander after a domestic quarrel; the Thracian philosopher Anaxarchus (c. 380–c. 320 BCE), who obviously cannot have been a companion of Augustus, but who did accompany Alexander the Great on his Asian campaigns; and the Roman jurists Gaius Trebatius Testa (c. 84 BCE–c. 4 CE) and Gaius Cassius Longinus, who lived in the mid-first century CE. For Simonides and Hieron, see above, n. 327 (DJR) and n. 206 (1.2.3).
as Paterculus of Cato: Cato the Younger – see above, n. 51 (1.1.1).

such another … amongst us: A reference, added in the third edition (1628), to Charles I, who ascended the English throne at the death of his father James I on 27 March 1625. The effect of this passage on readers would have changed dramatically in the sixth edition (1651), issued after Burton’s own death but also after the execution of Charles in 1649.

those Fuggeri … Barocius in Italy: This list of wealthy intellectuals includes the German Fugger dynasty, famous for its patronage of learning, but which also numbered several scholars in its ranks, such as Markus Fugger (1529–97); the Huguenot poet Guillaume de Salluste Du Bartas (1544–90), born into a family of rich Catholic merchants in Montfort; the Huguenot diplomat and author Philippe de Mornay, seigneur Du Plessis-Marly (1549–1623); the Huguenot clergyman and diplomat Antoine de la Roche Chandieu (1534–91), who adopted the name ‘Antonius Sadael’; the Italian nobleman and philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–94); and either the Flemish Jesuit theologian and author André Schott (1552–1629), or his brother, the author and prominent Antwerp lawyer François (1548–1622), who were born into a family of rich merchants.

Sir Huon of Bordeaux, Amadis de Gaul: Late medieval French and Spanish chivalric romances, popular among the gentry and nobility in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and parodied in Don Quixote.
Outlandish: Foreign.
submissness: Humility, submissiveness. censure: See above, n. 59 (DJR).

ingeniously: Ingenuously, honestly. deboshed: See above, n. 66 (DJR). stocks: In the light of the Latin phrase immediately following, probably livestock; alternatively, blocks of wood or tree-stumps, figuratively denoting insensible or stupid people; or just ‘lines of descent’ or family (that is, ‘mere titles’). barbarous Thracians: Thracians were commonly regarded by ancient Greeks and Romans as bloodthirsty barbarians.

take away their straw … brick: An allusion to Exodus 5:6–21, where the enslaved Israelites are commanded by Pharaoh to manufacture their full quota of bricks without their usual supply of straw. no penny, no Paternoster: That is, the priest will not perform without prior payment.

feed, and made: Paid a fee, and have their well-being assured. ut Cerberus offa … to hell: A reference to Virgil (Aeneid 6.417–21), where Cerberus, the dog who guards the entrance to the underworld, is lured by the Cumaean Sibyl into eating a morsel of food covered in honey and imbued with a soporific drug (the Latin phrase means ‘as Cerberus was by a morsel’) – thereby helping Aeneas on his journey.
Omnia Romae venalia: The saying derives from the condemnation of ancient Rome expressed by the Numidian king Jugurtha (c. 160–104 BCE) in Sallust’s War with Jugurtha (20.1).
extraordinary parts: See above, n. 191 (DJR).
indurate: Stubborn.

entertainment: Paid employment or service. he shall serve … Jacob did for Rachel: In Genesis 29:16–30, Jacob agrees to work for Rachel’s uncle Laban for seven years in order to marry her; after Laban tricks him into marrying Rachel’s sister Leah, Jacob has to work for another seven years for the hand of his beloved.
come off soundly: Hand over a large amount of money.
precise: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
serve the turn: Satisfy requirements. hidebound Calves in a Pasture: Calves whose skin clings tightly to the back and ribs, as a consequence of malnutrition and emaciation.

arrearages: Debts, arrears. first fruits … procurations: All types of monetary levy payable to the Crown or the Church. Beginae: Beguine sisters – members of lay sisterhoods, founded in the twelfth century and mainly located in the Low Countries.

Sectaries: (Religious) schismatics. those wild beasts of Ephesus: A borrowing from 1 Corinthians 15:32: ‘If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus’ – Paul was probably referring to the devotees of Artemis in Ephesus – ‘what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not?’ terse: See above, n. 217 (DJR). Graziers: See above, n. 76 (DJR). Chapmen: Merchants or traders. Pontus: Here, the Black Sea, where Ovid was banished by the emperor Augustus in 8 CE, to the town of Tomis (modern Constanta, in Romania). Idiots: See above, n. 207 (DJR).

logic: The study of logic (or ‘dialectic’) was central to the university arts curriculum in Burton’s day. The suitors of Penelope … Alcinous: Vain and dissolute young men. Both allusions are taken from a line in Horace’s Epistles (1.2.28) that refers to the Odyssey: to the multiple suitors of Odysseus’ loving and faithful wife Penelope, who indulged themselves freely in Odysseus’ home for twenty years, before he returned and killed them; and the young courtiers of King Alcinous of Phaeacia, whose palace was famously luxurious.

Let’s take the money … Italy: Differing versions of the satirical criticism of universities in note ‘a’ were in wide circulation in this period – as in Robert Tofte’s translation of Ariosto’s Satyres (1608), George Hakewill’s Answer to a Treatise Written by Dr. Carier (1616), and El Pasajero (1617) by Cristóbal Suárez de Figueroa – but the source of its application to Padua has not been traced.

Philosophasters: Pseudo-philosophers. Philosophaster is also the title of Burton’s own comic drama (see the editor’s Introduction). Note ‘b’ gives the year of its performance in ‘1617’ in old style (that is, according to the unreformed Julian calendar, in which the year began on March 25).
Theologasters: Pseudo-theologians.
both universities: That is, of Oxford and Cambridge.

that which someone once joked … rightly sell: A quotation from an anonymous satirical epigram or ‘pasquil’ – see below, n. 35 (1.2.4) – that was originally directed against Pope Alexander VI (1431–1503) – on whom, see below, n. 80 (3.4.1) – and published in Pasquillorum tomi duo (1544).
For the simoniac … can’t be grateful: A quotation from a decree issued by Pope Leo I (c. 400–461).

rotten fellow: As the note attached to the corresponding Latin passage indicates, this is the English Jesuit and martyr Edmund Campion (1540–81). The allusion is to one of his letters to the Society’s Superior General, Everard Mercurian (1514–80).
ambient: Surrounding, encompassing – here, referring particularly to the air; see 1.2.2.5 above.
entreat: Treat, deal with.
Brach: A hound which hunts by scent; or, more generally, any kind of bitch-hound.
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Cato … agree with them: Cato the Elder – see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries), as reported by Plutarch (Marcus Cato 20.3).
to an hair: With the greatest exactitude.
curiously: See above, n. 125 (DJR). that Queen of France, a Spaniard by birth: Blanche of Castile (Blanca de Castilla, 1188–1252), the wife of King Louis VIII of France.
complexion: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
piece: Here, a derogatory term for ‘woman’, with the connotation of a sexual object.
good parts: See above, n. 191 (DJR).
correct: Bring into a healthy or normal state. qualify: See above, n. 133 (1.2.1).
Micio-like: Like the benevolent and exceedingly lenient uncle in Terence’s Brothers. a noise of Musicians: A company or band of musicians – here, an ironic instance of a ridiculously mild punishment.
Aesop’s Ape: See above, n. 176 (DJR). soothed up: Confirmed or encouraged by the expression of assent or approval. conversation: See above, n. 110 (DJR).
cockering: Indulgence, pampering.
undiscreet: See above, n. 40 (DJR).
close: Private, secluded.
distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
Artemidorus the Grammarian … Crocodile: Artemidorus of Tarsus (fl. first century BCE).
The Massacre at Lyons 1572: The St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre of Huguenots began in Paris in August, but subsequently spread to other French cities, including Lyon.
Orestes … Furies: See above, n. 119 (DJR). spectrum: See above, n. 15 (DJR).
Themison the Physician: The Greek doctor (fl. second/first centuries BCE) who founded the ancient Methodist school of medicine. corse: See above, n. 78 (1.2.1).
offended: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
Hecatas sibi videntur somniare: In Greek mythology, Hecate was the goddess of magic, witchcraft, ghosts and necromancy. The quotation is adapted from Lucian’s Lover of Lies, or The Doubter (39).
Effuso … Faunus ait: On the quotation in note ‘d’, see above, n. 43 (1.2.3).

Hannibal’s army … walls of Rome: Possibly a misremembrance of the panic which, according to Polybius (9.6), was actually induced in the Romans when they heard that Hannibal’s army was camped nearby the walls of Rome – a Carthaginian diversionary tactic during the siege of Capua in 211 BCE.

Augusta Livia … swoon: According to the biography of Virgil attributed to Suetonius (32–3), when the passage containing this line from the Aeneid (6.883) was read to Octavia – the sister of the emperor Augustus, the wife (until 32 BCE) of Mark Antony and the mother of Marcellus (not Augustus’ wife Livia, as stated here) – she fainted but was eventually revived. ‘Dead’ here means ‘insensible’.

Edinus King of Denmark … men: Eric IV (or Eric Ploughpenny), who ruled Denmark 1241–50. According to the German historian Albert Krantz (1448–1517), Eric and his courtiers were driven into a frenzy by a visiting lute-player.
Fuscinum: Now Fushimi.
Meacum: Now Kyoto. stared: Stood on end.
Sacai: Now Sakai.
sanded: Run aground, on to a sandbank.
pasquil: See below, n. 35 (1.2.4). Apologue: See above, n. 114 (DJR).
a railing Aretine: A reference to the notoriously scurrilous Italian satirist Pietro Aretino (1492–1556).

Momus, Homer his Zoilus: See above, n. 7 (Preliminaries). Achilles his Thersites: In the classical tradition deriving from the lost epic poem Aithiopis, Achilles falls in love with the Amazon Penthesileia at the moment of killing her in battle, and then kills Thersites – see above, n. 107 (DJR) – for mocking his love. Philip his Demades: While in captivity after the Battle of Chaeronea (338 BCE), the Athenian orator Demades is said to have rebuked Philip of Macedon for his drunken behaviour.
