Impressed, Philip subsequently made Demades his envoy.

a Rabelais, an Euphormio, a Boccalinus: Three Renaissance satirists: François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553); John Barclay, whose Euphormionis lusinini satyricon (1605–7) is presided over by the character Euphormio; and Trajano Boccalini (1556–1613).

Pasquillers at Rome … that statue: ‘Pasquino’ (or ‘Pasquillo’) was a classical statue of Menelaus carrying the body of Patroclus and the first ‘talking statue’ of Rome. In the course of the sixteenth century, it became customary to decorate it with satirical poems (‘pasquils’) expressing popular grievances. facete: Facetious, witty.
credits: Reputations.

gulleries: Tricks. gulling ex stulto insanum: That is, tricking (‘gulling’) a stupid person in such a way that they become insane. a mope or a noddy: A ‘mope’, like a ‘noddy’, is a fool or simpleton. with them in Apuleius: In the third book of the Metamorphoses of Apuleius, the narrator Lucius has a practical joke played on him by the inhabitants of a city in Thessaly (he is put on trial for the killing of three thieves); this turns out to be part of an annual celebration held there in honour of the god of laughter.
stramineous: Valueless, like straw.
with him in the Comedy: Demea, in Terence’s Brothers.
Peter Dunnius, Earl of Shrine: Actually ‘Petrus Danus’, as given in Burton’s source; ‘Shrine’ refers to Skrzynno in central Poland.

Sophia the Empress … Commonwealth: This anecdote concerns the reportedly handsome Byzantine imperial palace official and army leader Narses (d. c. 574 CE), who had been High Chamberlain of Justinian I and a successful commander-in-chief in the war with the Goths and the reconquest of Italy. In 568, he was ordered back to Constantinople by the new emperor Justin II for financial impropriety, and was said to have invited the Lombard invasion in the same year as revenge for the empress’s insult.
round: Whisper, or murmur.

rumpantur & ilia Codro: A partial quotation from Virgil, Eclogues 7.25–6 (‘Arcadian shepherds, crown your budding poet with ivy, so that Codrus’ guts burst with envy’), Codrus being another poet, and possibly representing Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus (64 BCE–8 CE), a prominent patron of the arts who dabbled in poetry and was the subject of a public panegyric written by one of his protégés.
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).

Varronists: Authors of seriocomic ‘Menippean’ satires, renamed ‘Varronian’ in 1605 by the French scholar Isaac Casaubon after the ancient Roman scholar Varro, who was thought to have instigated the literary subgenre. personate: Mention personally or by name. perstringe: Censure, criticize. Non est Sestius … caballus: This quotation from Martial’s Epigrams (1.41.19–20) puns on the name of the jester Tettius (not Sestius) Caballus: the noun caballus means ‘horse’ or ‘nag’.
The children of Israel … manna: Numbers 11:4–10.
news: New things.
Romae Tybur … Romam: In Horace’s time, it was fashionable to have a villa in the foothills around Tibur (now Tivoli).
Marcus Aurelius and Solomon … mind: For instance in Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations (5.33) and Ecclesiastes 1:14.

Quod tristius morte … bondage: The quotation from the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus (8.7.14–15) is part of the speech of Hermolaus, one of the pageboys of Alexander the Great, after his conspiracy against the king in 327 BCE had been betrayed.
those 30,000 … in Peru: See above, n. 266 (DJR). mouldwarps: Moles.
those women in Turkey … abroad: That is, women in harems (‘abroad’ here means ‘outside the home’). mewed up like Hawks: See above, n. 114 (1.2.2).
Stoves: Rooms heated with stoves.

Huniades, Edward, and Richard the second, Valerian the Emperor, Bajazet the Turk: References to Matthias Corvinus (1443–90), king of Hungary and Croatia (in Hungarian, Hunyadi Mátyás), imprisoned in his youth in Prague by Ladislaus V of Hungary before being elected king himself in 1458; Edward II of England (1284–1327), imprisoned in Berkeley Castle in Gloucestershire, where in traditional accounts he was murdered; Richard II of England (1367–1400), imprisoned in 1399 in the Tower of London and then Pontefract Castle in West Yorkshire, where he died in dubious circumstances; and to the Roman emperor Valerian, captured and imprisoned by the Persians after his defeat at the Battle of Edessa in 260 CE, and the Sultan Bayezid I – on both of whom, see above, n. 97 (1.2.3).
cubbed up: Confined, ‘cooped up’.
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR).

Roger … torments of life: Roger of Salisbury was Chief Justiciar, and so second in authority (‘second man’), to Stephen of Blois, who ruled England 1135–54. After a power struggle, Roger was convicted of treason and died in prison in 1139.
Francis King of France … instant: Francis I was imprisoned in the fortress at Pizzighettone in Lombardy after the French defeat at Pavia in February 1525.
oppugners: See above, n. 73 (1.1.2). censure: See above, n. 59 (DJR).

the silver mines at Freiburg: In note ‘e’, a reference to the famous mining territory at Freiburg, in use since the twelfth century. through all five Zones … cold: See above, n. 118 (1.2.3). depress: See above, n. 163 (DJR).

gripe: A covetous person, or a miser. Lucian’s tyrant: The tyrant Megapenthes, in Lucian’s Downward Journey, or The Tyrant; he denies his crimes, but his bed and lamp are summoned to testify against him.
Maecenas: See above, n. 111 (DJR). Pullus Jovis … albae: See above, n. 89 (1.2.3).

Quando ego te Junonium … golden child: The quotation is taken from the pseudo-Ciceronian Letter to Octavian (6), where Cicero laments his flattering association of Octavian with Romulus (the son of Juno’s son Mars), which is presented as undermining senatorial power and leading to the destruction of the republic. towardly: In note ‘c’, promising, docile or dutiful.

turgent: See above, n. 150 (DJR). Themistocles in the Olympics: According to Plutarch, when the Athenian politician and general Themistocles (c. 524–460 BCE) entered the stadium at the Olympic festival after a victory over the Persians, the audience gave admiring applause to him rather than to the contestants (Themistocles 17).

Veneres: Venuses (and so, beautiful or charming features). as to those Roman Emperors … chamber: According to the account of Septimius Severus given by the Augustan History (23.5), a golden statue of the goddess Fortuna was customarily carried about by the Roman emperors and kept in their bedrooms.

Pythia Philippisat: The sceptical discussion of the Delphic oracle in Cicero’s On Divination (2.57) reports the view of Demosthenes that ‘the Pythian priestess
“philippized”’ – that is, had been bribed by Philip of Macedon to deliver prophecies that suited him.

aufe: A goblin child or changeling left by the fairies (and hence an ‘idiot’ child or simpleton). goose-cap: A numbskull, or fool. uxorem ducat Danaen: A quotation from Petronius’ Satyricon (137), which continues: ‘and he can tell Acrisius to believe what he told Danae’. In Greek mythology, after being told by an oracle that he would be killed by the son of his daughter Danae, King Acrisius of Argos had her imprisoned in a bronze chamber, but Zeus assumed the form of golden rain, which penetrated the roof of the chamber, and thereby impregnated her. Petronius’ point is not only that a rich man can marry any woman he likes, but also, apparently, that he can make her father believe that he is Zeus – in other words, whatever he likes.

he sups in Apollo: See above, n. 48 (1.2.2). Panis pane melior: In note ‘c’, as the Flemish geographer and cartographer Abraham Ortelius reported in his Theatrum orbis terrarum (which Burton owned in the edition of 1584), the proverbial phrase referred to the superior bread – but also the ‘fire hotter than fire’ and ‘iron harder than iron’ – found in the bishopric of Liège.
cabinets: Probably summer-houses or bowers in gardens; but alternatively, museums, picture galleries or ‘cabinets of curiosities’.
Servius … Labeo: The distinguished Roman jurists Servius Sulpicius Rufus (d. 43 BCE) and Marcus Antistius Labeo (d. c. 22 CE), as mentioned in Petronius’ Satyricon (137).

Nummus ait … Romae: Note ‘i’ reproduces a widely circulating allegation, reported by William Camden in Britannia (1586), about Richard, the first earl of Cornwall (1209–72), who harboured the ambition to become Holy Roman Emperor: namely, that he had acquired the title of ‘king of the Romans’, which came to him as the elected king of the Germans, by bribery.
John Medices … Florentine: Giovanni di Bicci de’ Medici (c. 1360–1429), father of Cosimo and Lorenzo the Elder.

those Lacedaemonian Senators … in Plutarch: These meritocratic appointments to the Spartan council of elders are described by Plutarch in his account of the life of Lycurgus – on whom, see above, n. 243 (DJR).
Aristocracies: See above, n. 201 (DJR).
Libertines: Free-thinkers, especially in religious matters.

Claudius … funeral: The reference should probably be to Seneca, who imagines this scene in the Pumpkinification of Claudius. ambubaiarum collegia: A quotation from Horace (Satires 1.2.1), listing the diverse mourners for the Sardinian musician Tigellius (d. c. 40 BCE).

Trimalchionis Topanta: ‘Trimalchio’s be-all and end-all’: The wife of Trimalchio, Fortunata, is described as topanta (from the Greek τὰ πάντα: literally, ‘the whole’ or ‘everything’) in Satyricon 37. quean: See above, n. 323 (DJR).
tires: See above, n. 169 (DJR).

gullish … gull: See above, n. 83 (DJR). Fastidious Brisk: The foppish courtier in Ben Jonson’s Every Man out of His Humour (1599). Sir Petronel Flash: The immoral knight in Eastward Ho! (1605), by George Chapman, Ben Jonson and John Marston. outside: See above, n. 115 (DJR).
under hatches: Or ‘below decks’ – and so, figuratively, in a state of depression, subjection or humiliation.

villains: Base rustics. juments: See above, n. 308 (DJR). pistum stercus … Ulysses’ companions: Apparently a conflation of the episode in the tenth book of the Odyssey, in which Circe feeds Odysseus and his crew acorns and other swine-food after turning them into pigs, with the opening scene of Aristophanes’ Peace, in which two slaves feed a dung beetle with cakes made from mashed dung. as Chremylus objected in Aristophanes: In Aristophanes’ Wealth (Act 4 in the 1542
Latin edition used here), Chremylus complains to Poverty about her various undesirable gifts. salem lingere, lick salt: As Erasmus explained in his Adagia, referring to Persius (5.138–9), the proverb means ‘live a life of great poverty’, originating in the use of salt as a relish by the poor in antiquity. jakes: See above, n. 30 (DJR). fay channels: Clean out gutters.

Socia ad pistrinam … Tristan thresh: In the Comedia de Calisto y Melibea (1499), widely known as La Celestina, by Fernando de Rojas, the young man Calisto attempts to seduce Melibea, the daughter of a local nobleman, with the help of a procuress called Celestina; the story features two of Calisto’s servants, called Sosia (also the name of a female slave in several Roman comedies) and Tristan.
Idiots: Here, uneducated ordinary people.

Qui habitant in Caesia … parat: Note ‘a’ refers to three valleys in Piedmont: that of the River Sesia, the Valle Ossola and the Valle Vigezza. Jakes farmers: Lavatory cleaners. Dirt-daubers: Labourers who use dirt or mud as plaster, or to make cob walls (and also a term of abuse).

polling: Cheating, extortionate. Deux ace … totum: Note ‘f’ quotes a popular rhyme that used the numbers on a die to lament the burden of taxation falling not on the poor (‘one and two’) or rich (‘five and six’), but the ‘middling sort’ (‘three and four’). Genius: See above, n. 173 (DJR).

The feeling and fear … governors: A reference to the first secession of the Roman plebeians in 494 BCE, which according to Livy (2.32.8–12) was resolved when the statesman Menenius Agrippa persuaded them to return to the city by means of the ‘Fable of the Belly and the Members’. jars: See above, n. 232 (DJR).

poor Terence … friends: A reference to the group of Roman friends traditionally referred to as the ‘Scipionic Circle’, said to have been patronized by Scipio Aemilianus – see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – and including Gaius Laelius Sapiens (consul in 140 BCE) and Lucius Furius Philus (consul in 136). Historians are now sceptical of the group’s coherence, or even its existence, but Cicero presented them as philosophically inclined lovers of literature, which would make their reported neglect of Terence, a freed slave, especially shameful.
instant: In note ‘c’, urgent or pressing.
as Ulysses … in Homer: In book 17 of the Odyssey, the treacherous goatherd Melanthius hurls abuse at Odysseus, who at that point is disguised as a beggar. baffled: See above, n. 166 (DJR).
driven to his shifts: See above, n. 76 (DJR).

si miserum fortuna … a liar and a cheat: This quotation, taken from Virgil (Aeneid 2.79–80), of the speech of the Greek warrior Sinon – who pretended to have been cast out of his army and tricked the Trojans into admitting the wooden horse into their city – has been adapted to reflect the truth of the matter by the omission of nec (‘nor’) from the beginning of the first line. In the original, Sinon claims that Fortune will not ‘also shamelessly make him a liar and a cheat’.
counterfeit Cranks: People who feign sickness to gain money from begging. Dummerers, Abraham men: Two terms from beggars’ cant: people who pretend to be, respectively, dumb or insane.
extent: That is, the limit to which it extends; the greatest degree.

A Sybarite of old … valiant men: This anecdote, taken from Athenaeus’ Learned Banqueters (12.518E), concerns a citizen of Sybaris – famous for its luxury – who visited the communal messes (phiditia in Latin) of Sparta, where the staple was the notorious ‘black broth’, made from pigs’ legs, blood, salt and vinegar.
mancipate: Enslave.
Apicius the Roman … to death: See above, n. 43 (1.2.2).

vilified: See above, n. 31 (DJR). amittunt consilium … observed: A reworking of the exclamation given by Gnatho – see above, n. 89 (1.2.1) – on meeting another person who, like him, had wasted an inheritance.
travailer: Labourer. bilem in nares conciunt: Literally, ‘fill the nose with bile’; that is, cause irritation or peevishness.

Philopoemen the Orator … attired: According to Plutarch (Philopoemen 2), the eminent Achaean statesman Philopoemen (c. 253–182 BCE) was mistaken by the hostess of a dinner party for a servant because he was wearing a simple soldier’s cloak. Terentius … outside: At another dinner party, this one hosted by the Roman comic poet Caecilius Statius (c. 230/20–168 BCE), who was, like Terence, a freed slave.

King Perseus … fortune: Perseus of Macedon (212–165/2 BCE) was defeated by the Romans at the Battle of Pydna in 168; he died in captivity, after gracing the triumphal procession of the Roman consul and general Lucius Aemilius Paullus in 167.
Carolus Pugnax … Exeter: Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy (1433–77), and Henry Holland, second duke of Exeter (1430–75).
merry-meeting: See above, n. 309 (DJR).

Conciliator: The Italian philosopher and professor of medicine at Padua, Pietro d’Abano (1257–c. 1315), whose influential work Conciliator litium medicinalium (c. 1303) sought to reconcile apparent conflicts between philosophical and medical doctrine.
as Pliny complains … Virginius: The Roman statesman and general Lucius Verginius Rufus (14/15–97 CE) had been the guardian and friend of Pliny the Younger.
So Stroza … death: Ercole Strozzi (c. 1473–1508), son of Tito Vespasiano Strozzi (1424–c. 1505), who was also a poet.

Gregory Nazianzen that noble Pulcheria: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394 CE) is here mistaken for Gregory Nazianzen (329/30–89/90 CE). The former wrote a consolatory oration on the death of the Princess Pulcheria, the child of the Roman emperor Theodosius I (347–95 CE).

So did Hadrian … Absalom: Like Hephaestion mentioned immediately above, Antinous and Hylas were pederastic beloveds, respectively of the emperor Hadrian – whose mourning after Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130 CE was famously elaborate – and the demigod Hercules – who searched for Hylas at length after his kidnapping by water nymphs. David’s mourning for his third son, Absalom, is recorded in 2 Samuel 18:33. Niobe her children … grief: See above, n. 140 (DJR).

Aegeus … drowned himself: In Greek mythology, King Aegeus of Athens asked his son Theseus to indicate that he had been successful in killing the Minotaur by hoisting white sails on his ship when returning from Crete. When Theseus forgot to do this, Aegeus wrongly assumed that his son had died.
Fallopius: The eminent Italian anatomist and physician Gabriele Falloppio (1523–62).

Vespasian’s death … saith Aurelius Victor: The ‘Vespasian’ referred to by the Roman historian Aurelius Victor is not the emperor now known as Vespasian, but his son the emperor Titus (39–81 CE), whose death was reportedly mourned with popular affection; both bore the full name of Titus Flavius Vespasianus.
great Cham: Khan, the title given to the rulers of the Tartars and Mongols.
vastity: Desolation.
Lewis the 12th: Louis XII of France (1462–1515). planet-strucken: Struck by sudden fear or amazement, as it were by the malign influence of a planet.

Claudia Valesia … the Duke’s wife: Princess Claude de Valois (1547–75), actually the daughter of Henri II, sister of Henri III and wife of Charles III, duke of
Lorraine. She was reported to have been held in great affection by the people of Lorraine for her kindness.

our Titus … Prince Henry’s immature death: The death in 1612 of the eighteen-year-old Henry, prince of Wales, and the eldest son of James I, is here compared with that of the Roman emperor Titus, in whom hopes of future glory had been similarly vested. Scanderbeg’s death: Skanderbeg – on whom, see above, n. 94 (1.2.3) – had been highly esteemed across Europe as a military leader and politician; after his death in 1468 he was glorified for protecting Christendom by holding the Ottoman Empire at bay in Albania.
turtles: Turtle-doves (and here, figuratively, models of constant affection).
the battle of Cannae: See above, n. 130 (DJR). stupid: See above, n. 38 (1.2.3).
The Hungarians … Turks: Władysław III of Poland, who had become king of Hungary (Ulászló I) in 1440, was killed at the Battle of Varna in 1444.

Lauredane Venetorum dux, &c.: According to Pietro Bembo’s Rerum Venetarum ab urbe condita libri (1487), these were the opening words of the declaration of hostilities delivered by the French herald to the Doge of Venice, Leonardo Loredan, which would lead to the War of the League of Cambrai (1508–16). Brixia: Brescia. Forum Julii: Friuli.
Anno 1527, when Rome was sacked by Burbonius: Charles, duke of Bourbon (1490–1527), was leader of the imperial forces in the sack of Rome in 1527.
constuprated: Raped, deflowered. base cullion: Rascal, vile person. as Sejanus’ daughter … in public: See above, n. 111 (1.2.3).

juggling: Cheating, deceptive. a fountain in Greece … a thread: According to Pausanias (7.21.12), the spring next to the sanctuary of Demeter at Patrae contained an oracle whose infallible predictions about sickness could be obtained by lowering a mirror down to its waters. When the mirror was raised, patients would look into it and see themselves as either alive or dead.
Amongst those Cyanean rocks … besides: Pausanias (7.21.130) refers to the predictive powers of the spring at the oracle of Apollo Thyrxeus, at the town of Cyaneae in central Lycia.
Axiochus the Philosopher … like a child, &c.: Axiochus, who is Socrates’ interlocutor in the pseudo-Platonic dialogue Axiochus, was the uncle of Alcibiades – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3).
Clotho: One of the three Fates (her name means ‘spinning’, with regard to the ‘thread’ of life), who is addressed by the tyrant Megapenthes in Lucian’s Downward Journey, or The Tyrant.
Animula vagula … loca: A quotation of the dying words of the emperor Hadrian, as reported in the Augustan History (25.9).

Flavae secreta … Aglauros: Note ‘d’ refers to the story, told in Ovid’s Metamorphoses (12.552–64), of how Athena (Minerva in Roman mythology) hid her child Erichthonius in a box and entrusted it to the three daughters of King Cecrops, the mythical founder of Athens. One of the daughters, Aglauros, defied Athena’s instruction not to open the box, and had her heart poisoned by Envy as a punishment.
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR). as Martha … purpose: Luke 10:40–41.
Humanity: See above, n. 28 (DJR). policy: See above, n. 283 (DJR).
school divinity: See above, n. 333 (DJR).
Reprobation: In Christian theology, rejection by God or damnation.
Genethliacal studies: Astrological predictions of a person’s character and future life and circumstances. elections: Times deemed fit on astrological grounds for undertaking particular tasks.
Indians: See above, n. 59 (1.2.1). pins: Pegs, commonly used in construction.

as the boy … Trinity: A reference to the apocryphal story of St Augustine’s encounter with a boy on a beach trying to empty out the sea with a ladle, in which
the boy told him that this was easier than Augustine’s task of comprehending the doctrine of the Trinity; ‘laved’ here means ‘drawn out’ with a bucket or ladle.

Conradus the Emperor: Conrad III (1093–1152), the first Hohenstaufen king of Germany, and Emperor of the West after 1138. This anecdote refers to his first marriage, to Gertrude of Comburg (d. 1130/31), who bore him two daughters, rather than his second, to Gertrude of Sulzbach (d. 1146), with whom he had two sons. masculine hour: In astrology, a time deemed to be ‘male’ rather than ‘female’ because of some quality (such as strength or activity). success: Result, upshot.
sped: Succeeded.

Aristotle … his life: Both stories actually end in death: Pliny the Elder, who died in 79 CE in the course of rescue efforts following the eruption of Vesuvius, was later portrayed by his nephew, the younger Pliny, as being motivated by scientific curiosity. On Aristotle and the Euripus, see above, n. 46 (1.2.3). Burton is perhaps thinking of Aristotle’s discussion, in the third book of the Nicomachean Ethics, of the case of the sailor who is compelled by a storm to throw his goods into the sea. Pyrrhus … Asia: See above, n. 109 (1.2.3).
Ardelions: Eager meddlers, dabblers or busybodies.
set out: See above, n. 29 (DJR). terse and polite: See above, n. 2 (Preliminaries).
far-fetched: Brought from afar.
trivial: Ordinary, everyday.
nice, curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
macerate: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

A virtuous woman … but she, &c.: In note ‘b’, the second half of Proverbs 12:4 in full is ‘but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones’. as Seneca … Paulina: The mutual care and affection between Seneca and his wife Pompeia Paulina is actually described in Epistles 104. According to Tacitus (Annals 15.43–4), Paulina was prevented by Nero from following her husband into death.
Caecilius: See above, n. 99 (1.2.4).

which made Cato’s son … marry again: In Plutarch’s account (Marcus Cato 24), the implication is that the son of Cato the Elder was upset at least partly because Salonius was one of his father’s under-secretaries (one of his dependent ‘clients’), and so the marriage was to a social inferior.
Chilon’s sentence: That is, the opinion of Chilon of Sparta – see above, n. 91 (DJR).

Mr. Vaughan in his golden Fleece: For more on this work, cited in note ‘e’, see below, n. 52 (2.2.3). cast in a suit: Condemned or defeated in court. Spretaeque … formae: In note ‘f’, see above, n. 104 (1.2.3).

Arius put out … life: The presbyter Arius (c. 250–336 CE) was deemed a heretic when the First Council of Nicaea (325) condemned his position on the Trinity for its privileging of God the Father over Christ. Eustathius of Antioch (d. c. 360) was a notoriously zealous critic of Arius and his followers.

Hipponax … hanged themselves: According to a story reported by Pliny the Elder (36.4), when two men called Bupalus and Athenis created an obscene statue of the poet Hipponax (fl. late sixth century BCE), he responded with a set of invectives that drove them to suicide. Pliny, however, rejects the story as false.
No cut to unkindness: Or, ‘no cut like unkindness’ (proverbial).
disabled: Disparaged, belittled.

Praetextatus a robed Gentleman … chafe: Apparently a misremembrance of Plutarch’s description of Alexidemus of Miletus (son of the seventh-century BCE tyrant Thrasybulus), who storms off after being offended by the seating plan at the banquet described in the Dinner of the Seven Wise Men (3); ‘chafe’ here means ‘rage’ or ‘temper’.
taking of the wall: Walking next to the wall, on the inner side of a pavement or sidewalk (and hence, figuratively, taking precedence).

loss of liberty … intolerable loss: Traditional Roman republican opposition to the ‘perpetual dictatorship’ of Julius Caesar presented it as a form of enslavement. Marcus Junius Brutus (85–42 BCE) and Cato the Younger were both republican heroes: the former, who eventually committed suicide after being defeated by Octavian and Mark Antony at Philippi in 42, for his role in the assassination of Caesar; the latter for his refusal of a pardon from Caesar and consequent suicide in 46.

Polynices … banished man: In classical mythology, Polynices is the son of Oedipus and Jocasta. In the Phoenician Women of Euripides he laments his exile from Thebes, having been betrayed by his brother Eteocles, who refused to abdicate and forced him to flee to Argos. The two brothers, who have been cursed by their father, eventually kill each other in a duel.
rivel: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3).

Lais of Corinth: A famously beautiful, quick-witted and discriminating ancient Greek courtesan, reported by Athenaeus (13.570C–D) to have become an impoverished alcoholic in her old age, and who died in 392 BCE.
hard hap: Bad luck, misfortune (as in ‘mishap’).

henbane … cicuta, mandrakes: See above, n. 38 (1.1.1) and n. 70 (1.2.2). Mandrake (Mandragora officinarum) is a poisonous and narcotic Mediterranean plant with a purple or whitish flower, sometimes thought to have medicinal properties.
stupidity: Stupor.

Part. 1 Sect. 2 Subsect. 3: In note ‘b’, ‘Subsect. 3’ should evidently be ‘Memb. 3’. as Hippolytus … sea-horses: In one version of the classical myth, Hippolytus was killed when a sea-monster sent by Poseidon (Neptune) terrified the horses on Hippolytus’ chariot. Athamas by Juno’s Furies: See above, n. 190 (DJR).
Continent, inward, antecedent, next causes: See above, n. 1 (1.2.2).
Purlieu hunter: Someone who hunts in the purlieu, or outer regions, of a forest.
temperature … distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
radical: See above, n. 3 (1.1.2).
obtrectation: Slander, disparagement. by consent: See above, n. 4 (1.1.3).
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
Dutch: See above, n. 48 (DJR). the French pox: See above, n. 285 (DJR).
Haemorrhagia: Haemorrhage, bleeding. a proper kind … signified: See 1.3.2.4 below.
respected: Considered favourably.
Heart … Meseraic veins: For these bodily parts, see the ‘Digression of Anatomy’ above, especially 1.1.2.3–4.
the shop of humours: Figuratively, the place where the humours are produced; see above, n. 3 (1.1.2).

which the Greeks called φρένες … dotage: In ancient Greek, φρένες can refer either to the midriff or, more generally, to the heart (as the seat of the passions), to the mind (as the seat of perception and thought) and even to ‘will’ or ‘purpose’.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR). fuliginous: See above, n. 94 (1.2.2).
Mirachial: That is, afflicting the ‘mirach’: see above, 1.1.2.4.
the Earl of Montfort in Germany: The counts of Montfort were a Swabian dynasty that belonged to the high nobility in the Holy Roman Empire, and were of equivalent status to English earls.
the mineral: That is, the ‘mine’ (or source).
a medicine of Cantharides: Crushed blister beetle (Cantharis vesicatoria) or ‘Spanish fly’, then considered to be an aphrodisiac.

the mother: Or ‘fits of the mother’, cases of suffocation said to be caused by a uterine disorder – sometimes identified as hysteria, which had been associated with the womb (in Greek, ὑστέρα) since antiquity.

Parrhasius a painter … paint: This story from the elder Seneca (Controversies 10.5) about Parrhasius (fl. c. 440–380 BCE), one of the most important painters in the ancient Greek and Roman worlds, is fictional. The people of Olynthus, located on the Chalcidic peninsula in northern Greece, took refuge in Athens in 348 BCE, when their city was destroyed by Philip of Macedon. On Prometheus, see above, n. 200 (DJR) and n. 149 (1.2.3).
curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR). bewray: See above, n. 43 (DJR).
intended or remitted: See above, n. 35 (1.1.1).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

that herb Tortocolla in Laurentius … some drink, &c.: The eminent French physician André du Laurens (Laurentius, 1558–1609) has been confused with Antonius Laurentinus Politianus, whose De risu (1606) discusses a spider named Tarcotella (probably the tarantula), the bite of which provokes the range of symptoms described here.
flaggy: Drooping, pendulous.
Juniors: That is, modern (rather than ancient) authors.
heartache, or heaviness of the heart: In note ‘f’, chest pain and sluggish movements of the heart. leaping: Throbbing.
twinkling: Blinking.
stut: See above, n. 41 (1.2.2).
mimical gestures: Extravagant gestures, as befitting a mime or a burlesque actor. familiar: Common, habitual. fleering: See above, n. 113 (DJR).
ill-liking: In a bad condition. crudities, oppilations: See above, nn. 44, 45 (1.2.2).
Carotides: The carotid arteries.
respected: Paid attention to, taken notice of.
stupidity: Sluggishness, inertia.
intempestive: See above, n. 313 (DJR).
characters: See above, n. 50 (1.1.1). Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).

Cassandra … the Sibyls: This list of ancient, divinely inspired prophets and seers (‘fanatical’ here means ‘possessed by a deity or devil’) includes Cassandra, the daughter of Priam and Hecuba; Manto, the daughter of the blind Theban prophet Tiresias; Nicostrata, known more commonly as Carmentis (or Carmenta), a goddess said to have originally been a water nymph, and sometimes associated with the Muses; either Mopsus the son of Manto (who gave his name to the town of Mopsuhestia, in the region of Cilicia in Asia Minor), or Mopsus the seer of the Argonauts; the shape-shifting sea-god Proteus; and the Sibyls, female seers who conveyed their typically catastrophic prophecies in hexameter verse.
Enthusiasts: See above, n. 17 (1.1.3), and below, 3.4.1.2–3.
maleficiated: Bewitched.
auditory: Audience (but alternatively, auditorium, which is also possible here).
Bisket: Cognac. deliquiums: Swooning or fainting fits.
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).

Lewis the 11th … officer: Louis XI of France (1423–83), who acquired the nicknames ‘the Prudent’, ‘the Cunning’ and ‘the Universal Spider’ because of his interest in political intrigues and conspiracies.
black men: Evil spirits, devils or bogeymen.
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

individual: Indivisible. Saint Cosmus and Damian, fidus Achates: The third-century Sts Cosmas (the usual spelling) and Damian, born in Cilicia (a region in southern Asia Minor), were traditionally said to be twin brothers and physicians who were martyred together under the rule of the Roman emperor Diocletian; on Achates, see above, n. 40 (1.2.3). Trophonius’ den: The ancient oracle of the god Trophonius, at Lebadea in western Boeotia, was consulted by descending underground, and was said to have involved a terrifying confrontation with the god himself rather than a medium. As Erasmus recorded in his Adagia, the notorious experience of having ‘descended into Trophonius’ cave’ and emerging sombrely dejected later became a proverbial description of someone who has become ‘extremely sorrowful and gloomy’.

Tityus’ bowels: In classical mythology, the giant Tityus was the son of Zeus and Elara. After attempting to rape Leto (Latona), the mother of Apollo and Artemis (Diana), he was punished in the underworld by being stretched out in the abyss of Tartarus; here, in a manner similar to Prometheus, he was tortured by vultures feeding on his liver, which would grow back each night to be devoured again.
Lugubris Ate: See above, n. 81 (1.2.3).
the Poet: Here, Terence, in his Self-Tormentor (122–7).
a spice: A trace or slight touch.
hem: Clear the throat in hesitation, as in ‘to hem and ha’ (or ‘hum and ha’), or ‘ahem’. circumvent: See above, n. 192 (1.2.3).
by odds: By some way, by far.
animated: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3).

vulgar: Ordinary. Dutch-work picture: In note ‘b’, engraving (the reference is to Dürer’s famous Melencolia I of 1514). soft: See above, n. 323 (DJR). witty: See above, n. 49 (DJR). sack: White wine imported from Spain or the Canary Islands.
ex musca elephantem: A version of the proverbial ‘making a mountain out of a molehill’. conceit: Conceive.

that same melancholy Duke of Muscovy: Ivan II (1326–59), grand prince of Moscow and also of Vladimir. Paulus Abbas Eremita: Note ‘c’ refers to Paul of Thebes (d. c. 345), sometimes regarded as the first Christian hermit.
work it out: Bring it about, produce it.
Antic: See above, n. 1 (DJR).
macerating: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

Pet. Blesensis, Christopher Urswick: The French ecclesiastic, statesman and poet Peter of Blois (Petrus Blesensis, c. 1130–1212) declined the archbishopric of Naples in 1168. The English courtier, diplomat and ecclesiastic Christopher Urswick (c. 1448–1522) was rumoured to have refused the bishopric of Norwich in 1499, around the time when he retired from active public life.

Bellerophon in Homer … moan: In Greek mythology, the hero Bellerophon was punished by Zeus for his hubristic desire to search the heavens, and in Homer’s account was condemned to wander aimlessly on the Aleian Plain in Cilicia, blind, lame and in misery.
as Diogenes in his tub: See above, n. 14 (DJR). Timon Misanthropus: See above, n. 125 (1.2.2).

The Egyptians … lib. 12: According to the Hieroglyphica (1556) of the Italian scholar Pierio Valeriano, the hare symbolized wakefulness, trepidation and solitude, among other things (a hare is also depicted on the panel representing ‘solitudo’ in the frontispiece of the Anatomy). Modern scholars regard the primary meaning of the Egyptian hare hieroglyph as the verb ‘to be’ or ‘to exist’.

that which Lod. Vives said … redderet: In his 1522 commentary on Augustine’s City of God, the Spanish humanist scholar Juan Luis Vives records a story in
which the inhabitants of a town imprisoned an ass for drinking water whose surface contained the reflected image of the moon. When the ass was put on trial the next day, one of the men declared that the ass’s stomach should be cut open, so that the moon could be taken out and restored to its former place.
numerical: Identical in all parts.

temperament: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Crisis: The ‘critical’ turning-point in the course of a disease towards recovery or deterioration – although it is possible that Burton intended ‘Crasis’ (the Greek term for ‘complexion’), and it was misread in the manuscript by the compositor.

mutually irradiated, or Lords of the geniture: See above, n. 112 (1.2.1) and n. 13 (DJR). Ptolemaeus in his centiloquy … tract: A reference to the disputed authorship of the pseudo-Ptolemaic Centiloquy, sometimes attributed to Ptolemy and sometimes to ‘Hermes Trismegistus’; the latter was often thought to have been a mysterious pagan prophet contemporary with Moses. Scepticism about the authenticity of the ‘Hermetic’ corpus had increased after the French scholar Isaac Casaubon had argued in his De rebus sacris et ecclesiasticis exercitationes XVI (1614) that many of its texts were actually composed in late antiquity.
buxom: Kindly, amiable.
close: See above, n. 15 (1.2.4).
Monomachies: See above, n. 15 (DJR).

Telephus and Peleus in the Poet: Two characters from Greek and Roman tragedies: see above, n. 16 (1.2.1) and n. 193 (DJR), respectively. Myriads, and tetrarchs: Words that here exemplify pretentious and bombastic speech.
distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
shamefast: Bashful, modest or ashamed. Ajax … poscit: See above, n. 19 (1.1.1).
lye: Acrid fluid.
Siennois: Sienese.
conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).
form: See above, n. 46 (1.1.1).
Such a one … Sophocles: See above, n. 47 (1.2.3).
Enthusiasmus: ‘Enthusiasm’ – see above, n. 39 (1.1.1), and below, 3.4.1.2–3.
irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR). subtle: Clear.
combust: In close conjunction with the sun – ‘burned up’ by it, as it were, or apparently extinguished by its light.
generosity: Courage.
thought every night … devil: See above, n. 60 (1.2.1).
corse: See above, n. 78 (1.2.1).
King Proetus’ daughters: See above, n. 40 (1.1.1).
Dutch: See above, n. 48 (DJR).
constringed: See above, n. 19 (1.1.2).
unguentum populeum: Populeon, a soothing ointment whose ingredients include crushed black poplar buds.
studies: The objects of a person’s interests or endeavours.
makes congees: See above, n. 187 (1.2.3).

as Pamphilus of his Glycerium: In Terence’s Girl from Andros, the character Pamphilus is privately engaged to his lover Glycerium. morning sleep: Or ‘second sleep’: in pre-modern Europe it was common to refer to two intervals of sleep, the ‘first sleep’ evidently starting at some point in the evening and ending around midnight, and the ‘second sleep’ extending from the early to the late morning. Real habits of sleeping, however, seem to have been more complex and varied.
more of these … love-Melancholy: See particularly 3.4.1.3 and 3.4.2.4 below.
during: Lasting, continuing.
as they write of heat … halfway: See above, n. 62 (1.1.1).

superparticular … too little to express it: The proportional terminology belongs to ancient mathematics, but was also employed in Renaissance musical theory. Following the Liber musices (1492) by Florentius de Faxolis, the superparticular ratio occurs when the greater number comprises the smaller plus an exact divisor (factor) of the smaller number (3:2, 6:4 …); sesquialter, when the greater number comprises the smaller plus half of the smaller (3:2, 6:4, 12:8 …); sesquitertia, when the greater number comprises the smaller plus one-third of the smaller (4:3, 8:6, 12:9 …); triple superbipartient, when the greater number comprises the smaller plus two parts, the sum of which is not an exact divisor of the smaller, and is also two-thirds of the smaller, as in 5:3. The quintuple superbipartient ratio occurs when the greater number comprises the smaller plus two parts, the sum of which is not an exact divisor of the smaller, and is also two-fifths of the smaller, as in 7:5. To simplify the passage: ‘the variety of the proportions in which the melancholic humour may occur in relation to the other humours in the body is too great to be graded precisely, even with the concepts provided by geometry’.

ignis fatuus: See above, n. 54 (1.2.1). arthritis or running gout: ‘Arthritis’ here refers to pain in the joints, especially in gout; ‘running’ means ‘moving’ or ‘spreading’, from one part of the body to another.
à la mort: On the point of death – or figuratively, utterly dejected.
shoeing-horn: See above, n. 119 (1.2.2). in Tartara tendit: See above, n. 29 (1.3.1).
incondite voices: Badly composed or crude words. obsolete: Worn-out, hackneyed.
extent: See above, n. 93 (1.2.4).
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR).

hollow: Cry out, or ‘holler’. players: Here, probably ‘revellers’ or ‘merrymakers’, rather than ‘actors’. strike: Here, probably ‘go’ or ‘make their way’, rather than ‘smite’. strut: Here, probably ‘quarrel’ or ‘contend’, rather than ‘swagger’. humorous: Moody, ill-humoured. the Poet: Here, Horace (in Satires 1.3.11).
Orestes: See above, n. 119 (DJR).
that Farmer … Italy: In this anecdote, the physician Prospero Calano refers to his former tutor at Bologna, the philosopher and physician Alessandro Achillini (1461/3–1512).
As Echo … wilt: An allusion to Epigrams 32 by the Roman poet Ausonius (fourth century CE), a meditation on the impossibility of painting the mythological and invisible figure of Echo.

the four and twenty letters: In the Latin alphabet, the classical version of which contained twenty-three letters, but which expanded to twenty-four in the Middle Ages with the addition of the letter w.

confounded: See above, n. 86 (DJR). Part. 1 Subs. 2 Memb. 2: In note ‘f’, the cross-reference should apparently be to 1.1.3.4. Cachexia: See above, n. 45 (1.2.2). Priapismus: See above, n. 86 (1.2.2). caninus appetitus: See above, n. 20 (1.1.3).
humiliate: See above, n. 10 (1.1.1).
distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
tenebrosity: Darkness, obscurity.
high sanguine complexion: See above, n. 6 (1.1.3).
confounded: See above, n. 86 (DJR).
scoffers: Jesters, buffoons. conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).
mirach: See above, 1.1.2.4.
inflation: Gaseous swelling.
obnubilate: Darken, overcloud.
incontinent: That is, sexually incontinent, lustful.
fairybabes: An erroneous variant of ‘fear-babe’ – something that frightens only a baby.

SUBSECT. 4 … Melancholy: This Subsection first appeared in the third edition (1628), probably because Burton came across the works of the Spanish physician Luis Mercado (Mercatus, 1525–1611) and the Portuguese physician Rodrigo de Castro (c. 1546–1627) only after 1624. Mercado’s De mulierum affectionibus libri quatuor (1579) and Rodrigo’s De universa mulierum medicina (1603) are the principal sources used here; the reference to Daniel Sennert in the opening sentence was added in 1632.

just: See above, n. 26 (DJR). having one only … alone: That is, it has one single cause. As explained in what follows, this is corrupted menstrual blood, and is the primary material cause to which other ‘causes’ are subsequently referred.

Cleopatra: Cleopatra VII of Egypt was reputed to have had specialist gynaecological knowledge, although this evidently derived from a confusion with Metrodora, the author (whose full identity remains unknown) of the Byzantine treatise On the Female Diseases of the Womb, which mentions a ‘Berenice, the Queen of Egypt later called Cleopatra’, as one of its sources. Moschion: A Greek physician of the first century CE, to whom the Gynaecology, actually a Latin adaptation of a work by Soranus of Ephesus (fl. c. 100 CE), was wrongly attributed in the Middle Ages. offended: See above, n. 23 (DJR). by consent: See above, n. 4 (1.1.3). intended or remitted: See above, n. 35 (1.1.1).
heartstrings: Here, probably the diaphragm (although any of the cord-like structures attached to the heart, such as the aorta, are also possible). fits of the mother: See above, n. 18 (1.2.5).
forespoken: Enchanted by means of spoken words.
helleborismum Mathioli: Note ‘a’ refers to a famous hellebore treatment devised by the Italian physician and botanist Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–78).
patronize: See above, n. 121 (1.2.1). wanton: Unruly, reckless. flirt: Flighty or frivolous woman. light: Unthinking, frivolous. housewives: ‘Hussies’ – giddy or disreputable women.
temperament: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
well-given: Good-natured, benign. take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR).

as Pallas a Virgin … face: An allusion to Martianus Capella’s Marriage of Philology and Mercury (1.40), where Jupiter’s virgin daughter Minerva blushes with modesty and disapproves of being asked for advice about marriage.
condole: See above, n. 133 (DJR). Pseudopoliticians: False manipulators or schemers (drawing on an early sense of the term ‘politician’ as a crafty schemer or plotter).
humanity: See above, n. 28 (DJR). vain persuasions: Foolish or unwise opinions. temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
Better marry … Apostle: Paul (in 1 Corinthians 7:9).
mastuprations: A seventeenth-century alteration of ‘masturbations’.

Bale’s visitation of Abbeys: The general visitation of the monasteries in England was actually conducted by Richard Layton and Thomas Legh, the agents of Henry VIII’s minister Thomas Cromwell, in 1535–6. The reference here is to the Acta Romanorum pontificum (1558) by the bishop of Ossory, Protestant polemicist and historian John Bale, who mentions the visitation in the preface of this work.
refell: Refute, disprove.
Distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
T. W. Jes.: Thomas Wright, Jesuit – see above, n. 46 (1.1.2).
adry: Thirsty.

the Philosophers of Coimbra: The Jesuits of the University of Coimbra in Portugal, who at the instigation of Pedro de Fonseca (1528–99) and initially under the supervision of Emmanuel de Goes (1542–97), produced a series of commentaries on Aristotelian philosophy (the Conimbricenses) between 1592 and 1606. incend: Inflame, excite. temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
witty: See above, n. 49 (DJR).

that of Heraclitus … mind: The Heraclitean fragment referred to here (‘a ray of light [is] a dry soul, wisest and best’) was commonly taken in the Renaissance to support the association between wisdom and the quality of dryness. In the fragment, the concept of ‘light’, through its association with the sun, possibly refers to ‘life’.
leaping: See above, n. 8 (1.3.1).
pismires: Ants.
pitch: Settle.

Os ventris: Literally, the ‘mouth’ or ‘opening’ of the stomach, below the oesophagus and above the diaphragm (corresponding to the earlier Greek meaning of στόμαχος); on the stomach more generally, see above, 1.1.2.4. intention: Stretching or straining. intentive: Attentive or assiduous.
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
occurse: Approach, meeting.
stayed: That is, restrained or checked – with the implication of being rebuked. molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

Sabini quod volunt somniant: ‘The Sabines dream of what they want’, a proverb recorded by the grammarian Festus (second century CE), referring to the importance of prophetic dreaming in Sabine religion. The Sabines were a people of ancient Italy who were conquered by the Romans, and who featured prominently in early Roman legend.

Sarmiento the Spaniard … in Europe: The explorer and author Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa (1532–92) had been sent to establish a Spanish colony by the Strait of Magellan, which was built in 1584 but failed shortly afterwards. ‘Discover’ in this passage means ‘explore’, and ‘confine’ means ‘neighbouring’ or ‘adjacent’; on ‘brave’, see above, n. 47 (DJR).
the brain … bodies: That is, the brain projects images of solid bodies internally, in the same way as curved glass mirrors reflect images externally (to create visual illusions).
quotes: Writes down, notes; or, alternatively, observes.

thinks he reads … old: In the story alluded to here, Pythagoras is said to have been able to write words in his own blood on a mirror, and then show the same words to be written on the surface of the moon.

Orestes now mad … te putas: In the classical myth dramatized in the Orestes of Euripides (quoted here) – see above, n. 119 (DJR) – Electra tries to bring her brother to his senses when he hallucinates that he is pursued by the Furies and his mother’s ghost.

So Pentheus … troubled: A reference to the temporary derangement of Pentheus – see above, n. 5 (1.2.1) – that occurs when he disguises himself as a worshipper of Dionysus, as described in the Bacchae (918–22) of Euripides.

Albategnius that noble Arabian: The astronomer Muhammad ibn Gabir ibn Sinan al-Battani (d. 929 CE). Baptista Turrianus: Giovan Battista della Torre (d. 1534), who on his deathbed also asked his friend Girolamo Fracastoro to complete one of his works of astronomy.

Eremites: See above, n. 36 (1.2.1). suffites: Or ‘suffiments’: medicinal perfumes that are burned or smoked. suffumigations: Fumes or vapours used for medicinal or magical purposes. mixed candles: Candles made from mixtures of
various ingredients, such as animal fat, fish eyes, tree oil and human blood; when lit, according to the De mirabilibus mundi (formerly misattributed to the medieval philosopher and theologian Albertus Magnus), they have extraordinary effects, including making men appear in the shape of animals or angels, and inducing uncontrollable dancing or flatulence. perspective glasses: See above, n. 167 (DJR). Firedrakes, Meteors … Castor and Pollux: See above, n. 54 (1.2.1). moorish: See above, n. 268 (DJR).

Sanguis upupae … centaurea: Note ‘b’ records a formula from the De mirabilibus mundi, which claims that when centaury (a plant with larger and smaller species, Centaurium majus and Centaurium minus) is mixed with the blood of a female hoopoe and added to the oil of a burning lamp, it makes those present think themselves to be magicians, and also to see themselves upside-down with their feet in the air. Centaury’s uses were traditionally said to have been discovered by the centaur Chiron – on whom, see below, n. 10 (2.2.4). uncouth: Unfamiliar, or marvellous. Catoptrics: Mirrors, or optical instruments designed to produce visual effects by reflection.
antics: See above, n. 41 (1.1.2).

Roger Bacon … his perspectives: ‘They have an old Tale in Oxford’, according to Francis Bacon in the Sylva Sylvarum (1626), ‘that Friar Bacon walked between two Steeples: which was thought to be done by Glasses, when he walked upon the Ground’. As Burton observes here, this is not mentioned by the medieval English philosopher Roger Bacon (1214/20–92), also known as ‘Doctor Mirabilis’ (‘Dr Miraculous’), in his Perspectiva.
Jugglers: See above, n. 98 (1.2.3). Exorcists: Here, those who pretend to call up spirits by magical rites. Mountebanks: See above, n. 76 (DJR).

that whispering place of Gloucester: The ‘Whispering Gallery’ in Gloucester Cathedral, where a circular wall assists sound projection. the Duke’s place … Italy: The Sala dei Giganti, an illusionistic echo chamber designed and painted by Giulio Romano, and built in the Palazzo del Te in 1532–5.
Theophilus … sound: Theophilus was a physician of the second century CE, reported by Galen to have suffered from a hallucination in which a group of musicians continually played flutes in his house.

At Cadurcum … first: In Cahors (Cadurcum) in Aquitaine, according to the French jurist Pierre Grégoire (1540–c. 1597), this effect was produced by directing sound from a plague chapel in the city’s outskirts towards the bank of the River Lot.
seven times … Macedonia: The Echo Stoa at the sanctuary of Zeus in Olympia. some twelve times … France: At the Château de Conflans, in Charenton-le-Pont.

At Delphos … Echo: The ostensibly supernatural-sounding voice of the oracle at Delphi was sometimes sceptically explained – as in Burton’s likely source here, the Dictionarium historicum, geographicum, poeticum (1595) of the French lexicographer Charles Estienne – as a natural echo.

At Barry … forge: Barry Island, now a peninsula adjoined to the town of Barry in South Wales. According to Gerald of Wales (1146–1223), the sounds could be heard coming from a cavity in a rock near the chapel of St Baruc. so at Lipari: See below, n. 42 (3.2.3).
Memb. 1 Sub. 3: In note ‘a’, which refers to the discussion at 1.3.1.3, ‘Sect. 3’ should also be mentioned.

Plato’s reminiscentia: The doctrine of anamnesis, explicated in Plato’s Meno, Phaedo and Phaedrus and mentioned above in 1.1.2.9, according to which human memory contains knowledge acquired during previous incarnations of the soul. all out: See above, n. 89 (1.2.2). Pierleonus: The physician and astrologer Pierleone Leoni of Spoleto (c. 1445–92). Grecian and Barbarian philosophers: Greek and non-Greek philosophers.
varices: Dilated or varicose veins.
Marius the Roman: The surgical treatment of the varicose veins of Marius – on whom, see above, n. 25 (DJR) – is described by Plutarch in his biography of the Roman general and politician (Marius 6).
morphew: A disease (or group of diseases) involving skin discoloration.
relics: See above, n. 2 (1.1.1).
Aesop’s fishes … itself: In the fable of ‘The Fish and the Frying Pan’.

Socrates his cicuta: The execution of Socrates, by the suicidal drinking of hemlock (‘cicuta’), took place after he was convicted of impiety and corrupting the young in 399 BCE. Lucretia’s dagger: See above, n. 48 (1.2.3). Timon’s halter: See above, n. 125 (1.2.2) – a ‘halter’ is a rope with a noose. Cato’s knife: See above, n. 155 (1.2.4). Nero’s sword: Nero committed suicide in the villa of his freedman Phaon in 68 CE, after losing a power struggle and being declared an enemy of the Roman state.
For that deep … tell: Lines from Shakespeare’s Rape of Lucrece (1594).
Megaera’s teat … Alecto: In classical mythology, the sisters Megaera and Alecto were both Furies, representing jealousy and anger respectively.

stung by serpent … Nessus’ blood: In classical mythology, Heracles (Hercules) is killed when his wife Deianira gives him a shirt which, unbeknown to her, has been daubed with the poisonous blood of the centaur Nessus (to which the quotation from Seneca in note ‘d’ also refers). While helping Deianira and Heracles to cross the Aetolian River Evenus, Nessus had tried to rape Deianira, and had been shot dead by Heracles with an arrow dipped in the venom of the Hydra.
strappados … Phalaris’ bulls: See above, n. 18 (1.1.1).

imbonities, insuavities: Malevolences, unpleasantnesses. Euripus: See above, n. 46 (1.2.3). which Ammianus … Palladius: According to the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus (28.17–27), Palladius was a mischievous informer who killed himself after being punished for stirring up trouble in the reign of the emperor Valentinian I (364–75 CE).
upshot: Climax, or extreme limit. Tityus … by a vulture devoured: See above, n. 29 (1.3.1).
distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).

that Laconian lad … misery: A reference to the story, told by Seneca (Epistles 77), of a captive young Spartan who resolved not to be degraded by servitude, and dashed his brains out against a wall when ordered to fetch a chamber pot.

Speusippus … death: According to Diogenes Laertius (4.1.3), this exchange between the Greek philosopher Speusippus (c. 410–339 BCE), who succeeded Plato as head of the Academy in Athens, and Diogenes the Cynic happened when Speusippus had reached a state of paralysis after suffering from a wasting disease. The original account notes that Speusippus went on to kill himself in despair.

Cato, Dido … poisoned themselves: On the suicides of Cato the Younger and Marcus Junius Brutus, see above, n. 155 (1.2.4). The self-immolation of Dido, queen of Carthage, after being left by her beloved Aeneas is described in the fourth book of Virgil’s Aeneid. On Cleopatra VII of Egypt and Lucretia, see above, n. 48 (1.2.3). Sophonisba, the Carthaginian wife of the Numidian prince Syphax, poisoned herself to avoid the shame of appearing in a Roman triumphal procession after Syphax’s defeat in the Second Punic War (218–201 BCE) by the forces of Gaius Laelius (consul in 190 BCE) and the Numidian commander (and future king) Masinissa, in 203 BCE; Masinissa had initially tried to save Sophonisba by marrying her, but when Scipio Africanus forced him to surrender her, he
provided her with the poison. Hannibal poisoned himself in 183/2, after the victorious Romans arranged for his extradition from Bithynia, where he had been in the service of King Prusias I. Vibius Virrius, rebel leader in Capua, having sided with Hannibal in his war with Rome and facing defeat, in 211 persuaded the city’s senators to join him in suicide in order to pre-empt their appearance in a triumph.

Themistocles drank Bull’s blood … enemies’ hands: The Athenian politician and general Themistocles, according to Plutarch (Themistocles 31), drank bull’s blood (supposed to choke the drinker when it coagulated), or some kind of quick poison, in c. 460, to avoid having to fulfil his promise to the Persian king Artaxerxes I (ruled 464–424/3 BCE) that he would subjugate Greece on his behalf. The Athenian orator Demosthenes killed himself in 322 when being pursued by his Macedonian enemies. Publius Licinius Crassus, son of the triumvir Marcus Licinius Crassus – see above, n. 103 (1.2.1) – and his friend Censorinus both committed suicide in the Roman defeat by the Parthians at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE. Lucius Plautius Plancus, who had been proscribed by the triumvirs – see above, n. 166 (1.2.3) – in 43 BCE, surrendered himself to his executioners in order to prevent his slaves being tortured to reveal his hiding place (although some sources say that the strong smell of his perfume betrayed his location to his pursuers).

Razis in the Maccabees … approved: An allusion to the heroic martyrdom of Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, who disembowelled himself in the midst of his Seleucid enemies in 161 BCE. The death of Samson is described in Judges 16:23–31.
So did Saul and Jonah sin: 1 Samuel 31:1–6, Jonah 4:1–9. when Rome was taken: A reference to the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 CE.
Pelagia: St Pelagia of Antioch, who chose to kill herself rather than be dishonoured by soldiers during the persecution of Christians (303–11 CE) in the reign of the Roman emperor Diocletian.

fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR). Maxentius the Tyrant: The Roman emperor Maxentius had been labelled a tyrant by his rival Constantine – on whom, see above, n. 130 (DJR) – after being defeated by him in 312 CE.

Titus Pomponius Atticus … depressit: According to Cornelius Nepos (25.21–2), Cicero’s friend and correspondent Atticus decided in 32 BCE to end his life – against the wishes of his son-in-law Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa (64/3 BCE–12 CE) – by starving himself; ‘dehort’ in this passage means ‘dissuade’.

So did Lycurgus … Empedocles: Lycurgus – on whom, see above, n. 243 (DJR) – is reported by Plutarch to have starved himself to death, satisfied with his life’s work after being told by the Delphic oracle that his constitution would serve Sparta well and bring it honour (Lycurgus 29). On the tale of Aristotle’s suicide, see 1.2.3.6, p. 260. Stories about the suicides of the philosophers Zeno of Citium (335–263 BCE), Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE) and Empedocles are related by Diogenes Laertius: Zeno killed himself by holding his breath after tripping over and breaking his toe (7.1.28); Chrysippus, by drinking himself to death – although in another account the cause is from laughter at one of his own jokes (7.7.184–5); and Empedocles – on whom, see above, n. 92 (DJR) – by throwing himself into one of the craters of Mount Etna, to confirm the belief that he had become a god (8.2.69).
magnanimity: See above, n. 58 (1.1.1).

The Massagetae … that age: The Massagetae were an ancient nomadic tribe, often associated or confused in antiquity with the Scythians, who lived on the plain east of the Caspian Sea. The ‘Barbiccians’ were actually the Derbices, a tribe that lived to the south of the Caspian Sea. Both peoples, after killing their elderly, reportedly then ate them.
Choa: Ceos. prevented: Hastened, brought about.

So did Antony … Ajax: In note ‘f’, Mark Antony committed suicide in 30 BCE after his defeat by Octavian at the Battle of Actium. The Roman senator Gaius
Sulpicius Galba, elder brother of the future emperor, killed himself in 36 CE after he had fallen foul of Tiberius. The senator and military commander Publius Vitellius the Younger attempted suicide in 31 CE, after being implicated in the conspiracy of Sejanus against Tiberius – see above, n. 111 (1.2.3). The emperor Otho killed himself after being defeated by the future emperor Vitellius in 69 CE. On the suicide of Ajax, see above, n. 19 (1.1.1).
Cleombrotus Ambraciotes … first: See above, n. 106 (1.2.3). In this passage, ‘luculent’ means ‘brilliant’ or ‘convincing’, and ‘Plato’s divine tract de anima’ is the Phaedo.

Calanus and his Indians … death: The Indian sage Calanus (c. 398–323 BCE) is reported to have left his home in Taxila and followed Alexander the Great to Persia, where, to complete his spiritual path, he took his own life on a pyre. Circumcellions and Donatists: Christian sects active in North Africa in the fourth century CE, both deemed heretical, and notorious for their pursuit of martyrdom. The former were sometimes thought to be a branch of the latter, who, on occasion, called them ‘Agonistici’. Paradoxes: See above, n. 3 (DJR).

No evil is to be done … Scriptura: An allusion to Romans 3:8. The more common scriptural loci for the prohibition of suicide, on the authority of Augustine, were the descriptions of the sixth commandment (against killing) in Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17.

Jerome to Marcella … Philosophiae: In the letter quoted here, actually addressed to Blaesilla’s mother Paula of Rome (347–404 CE), Jerome chastises her for starving herself while grieving for her daughter, who had died in 384/5 after adopting the ascetic practices of Jerome’s spiritual circle.

to be buried … with a stake: Note ‘g’ refers to the practice of being denied burial in consecrated ground, like a criminal, with a stake driven through the body in order to prevent (according to popular folklore) the suicide’s return to haunt the living. impinge: See above, n. 130 (1.2.3).

as it did the Milesian Virgins of old: According to Plutarch (Bravery of Women 11), when a mysterious suicidal epidemic broke out among a group of girls from Miletus, it was halted by a decree stipulating that the body of anyone who killed themselves should be dragged naked through the marketplace.
Lawful … Unlawful: Permissible or justifiable, and impermissible or unjustifiable (rather than strictly legal or illegal).
Characters: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1). Ligatures: Parts of plants or animals tied to the body of the patient, as sometimes practised in ancient medicine.

those magnetical cures: Here, probably cures that were said to work by a force of attraction that was ‘occult’ or inaccessible to the senses – cf. above, n. 24 (1.2.3); but therapies harnessing the more specifically ‘magnetical’ qualities of the loadstone (iron oxide) were also of interest in late Renaissance natural philosophy and medicine.

Cardan de subt …. Picatrix, &c.: In this list of magical works and their supposed authors mentioned by Girolamo Cardano in his De subtilitate, which Burton used in the edition of 1560, the Ars notoria was a medieval magico-devotional treatise, and was one of the several works attributed to Solomon, who was sometimes reputed to be a magus. ‘Old Hermes’ is Hermes Trismegistus – see above, n. 49 (1.3.1); ‘Artephius’ is the twelfth-century alchemist of uncertain identity to whom various works, including the Clavis maioris sapientiae and the Liber secretus, were attributed; and Costa ben Luca (Qusta ibn Luqa, 820–912) was a Syrian
Christian physician, astronomer and mathematician, and author of a work on ligatures that circulated widely in the Middle Ages and Renaissance. The Picatrix was the Latin translation, commissioned by Alfonso the Wise – on whom, see above, n. 239 (1.2.3) – of a medieval Arabic collection of astral magic, the Ghayat al-Hakim (‘Aim of the Wise Man’).

salve: See above, n. 355 (DJR). young again as the Spanish Marquess … slaves: The French physician René Moreau (1587–1656) does not name the marquess, who in an effort to restore his youthfulness ordered his servants to lacerate him, shut him in a glass jar, and bury him in horse manure. jugglers: Magicians or conjurers. limbecks: Or ‘alembics’, chemical apparatuses used for distillation, consisting of two connected vessels.
commit: Connect, or combine. stupend: See above, n. 138 (DJR). admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2). conclusions: Experiments.

St. Catherine’s wheel … about them: In Spanish and Italian folklore, the imprinting of an image of a St Catherine’s wheel, or a crucifix, either under the tongue or on the roof of the mouth was taken as a distinguishing mark of a magical healer.

that Eleazar did … Vespasian: The Jewish historian Josephus (37/8–100 CE) says in his Jewish Antiquities (8.42) that he witnessed one of his countrymen called Eleazar, who was perhaps an Essene, casting out demons from men in the presence of the emperor Vespasian by means of ‘the wisdom of Solomon’ – that is, by using one of the roots prescribed by Solomon, reciting his incantations and speaking his name.
Jupiter Menecrates: See above, n. 171 (1.2.3).

flectere si nequeant … movebunt: An adapted quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid (7.312), which refers to the Acheron, the ‘river of pain’ in the underworld of classical mythology (and which was used by Freud as the epigraph to The Interpretation of Dreams).
as he prosecutes it: That is, as he (Paracelsus) continues to discuss the subject.
vos estis dii: Psalm 82:6.
others of that sect: That is, jurists.

Schoolmen: See above, n. 61 (1.1.2). cases of conscience: Discussions of how general moral or spiritual rules apply to individual cases, or casuistry – strongly associated at the time with scholastic theology, and in England with puritan authors.
like him in Aesop … wheel: In the fable ‘Hercules and the Wagoner’.
as Christ cured … spittle: John 9:1–7.
Craterus: See above, n. 15 (1.2.1).

non Siculae dapes … cantus: The lines preceding this quotation from Horace (Odes 3.1.18–20), ‘For the man who has a naked sword hanging over his unholy neck’, indicate that the ‘Sicilian banquets’ are of the kind said to have been given to the courtier Damocles by the tyrant Dionysius II of Syracuse as a reward for flattery, in which a sword was suspended over his head by a single hair.

Sint Croesi & Crassi … miseriis: In note ‘c’, which is a quotation from the Flemish humanist Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), the Pactolus was a river in Lydia (the modern-day Sart Çayı in western Turkey) reputed to carry down sands containing gold dust. The proverbially rich Croesus was a king of Lydia (c. 560–547 BCE); on Crassus, see above, n. 103 (1.2.1).
available: Effectual, beneficial.

that unhappy overthrow … death: The French diplomat and historian Philippe de Commines (1447–1511) is commenting upon the decline of Charles the Bold, duke
of Burgundy (1433–77), after his defeat by the Swiss at the Battle of Morat in 1476.
which the Prophet reprehends … amend it: 2 Chronicles 16:12. The books of Chronicles were traditionally attributed to Ezra the Scribe (fifth century BCE).

Minucius that worthy Consul of Rome … God: The speech, as reported by Livy (22.14), was given by Marcus Minucius Rufus in 217 BCE, in order to oppose the delaying tactics of Fabius – see above, n. 316 (DJR). As the quotation in note ‘b’ suggests, Minucius is referring to the Roman allies, but his purpose is to illustrate their desperation and the seriousness of the Roman duty to come to their aid.
receipts: Medicinal recipes, or remedies.

St. Anthony’s Church … the Low Countries: The Basilica of St Anthony in Padua contains a shrine with the relics of the thirteenth-century saint, who was credited with many miracles; the veneration of St Vitus was popular in Germany from the ninth century, when his relics were said to have been brought to the imperial abbey of Corvey; on Loreto and Zichem see above, n. 87 (DJR).
falling sickness: See above, n. 32 (1.1.1).

Tempests: Times, or occasions. dea Vacuna: See above, n. 357 (DJR). dea Cloacina: The Roman goddess Venus Cloacina was associated with the purification of sexual intercourse in marriage; see also above, n. 114 (1.2.3). draught: See above, n. 100 (1.2.2). jakes: See above, n. 30 (DJR). Prema, Premunda, Priapus: The Roman goddess Prema presided over newly weds; by ‘Premunda’, Burton probably means ‘Pertunda’, the goddess that presided over the loss of virginity; Priapus was the phallic god of procreation. bawdy: ‘Filthy’ or ‘soiled’ is possible here, as well as lewd or obscene.
Angerona dea: See above, n. 41 (1.2.3).

Virgo Hallensis: A statue of the Black Madonna in Halle (in the Low Countries, now Belgium), which was believed to have miraculous healing powers and formed the basis for a famous devotional cult of the Virgin. The shrine became a rallying point for Catholics after the Reformation. Laur. Arturus Faunteus: The Jesuit Arthur Faunt (1553/4–91), whose name in religion was ‘Laurence’, was Burton’s uncle (see the editor’s Introduction). The Apologia libri sui de invocatione ac veneratione sanctorum (1589), cited here, defended the invocation of saints against the French Calvinist Daniel Toussain (1541–1602).
St. Hilary’s at Poitiers in France: On St Hilary, see also above, n. 142 (1.2.3).

St. Tubery in another place: St Thibéry, or St Tiberius of Agde, was an early Christian martyr, some of whose relics were interred in the monastery at Saint-Thibéry in the region of Hérault. ‘Gallia Narbonensi’, referred to in Burton’s note ‘b’, was the name of the province of the Roman Empire situated in what is now Languedoc and Provence.

St. Cyricus’ staff: St Cyricus of Tarsus, a Christian child-martyr from the late third century CE, was a victim of the Diocletianic persecutions (303–11 CE). In Wales, he was conflated with St Curig, whose staff, enshrined in the church of St Harmon (near Rhayader in central Wales), was said to have miraculous healing powers.
the three kings of Cologne: Cologne Cathedral has hosted a shrine dedicated to the Magi since their relics were brought there by its archbishop, Rainald von Dassel, in 1164.

that golden legend of Jacobus de Voragine: See above, n. 123 (DJR). Jasper Belga … many such. The Dutch Jesuit Jasper Bartzoen (or Gaspar Barzaeus,
1515–53), who was the subject of the Vita Gasparis Barzaei Belgae e Societate Jesu (1610) by his fellow missionary Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628).
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).

A declaration of Egregious popish impostures … his wicked associates: The author of this work, first published in 1603 by the command of the privy council, was Samuel Harsnett (c. 1561–1631), later the archbishop of York. Weston (alias Edmunds), who had been imprisoned after being implicated in the Babington Plot (1586) to assassinate Elizabeth I, was part of a group of secular priests who had performed exorcisms in the private households of English Catholic recusants in the mid-1580s. Harsnett’s work refuted the accounts of these exorcisms given in a manuscript collection, discovered in 1598, that was known as Weston’s ‘Book of Miracles’.
Aesculapius … that counterfeit God: See above, n. 86 (1.2.1). tables … pendants, donaries: ‘Tables’ are tablets; ‘pendants’ are hanging votive offerings; on ‘donaries’ see above, n. 295 (DJR).
offices: Prayers, or liturgies.
Mountebanks, Quacksalvers, Empirics: See above, n. 76 (DJR).

Chemist: Alchemist. Chemical … Chemistry: Alchemical, and alchemy. The medicine of Paracelsus and his followers – see above, n. 350 (DJR) – represented the most controversial and subversive alternative to orthodox learned Galenism in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Its mixture of esoteric spiritual, astrological and alchemical doctrines had wide appeal across Europe, but especially in Germany, France, the Low Countries and England.
exploded: See above, n. 45 (DJR).
Iatromathematical professors: Those who make their profession from a combination of medicine with astrology (drawing on the obsolete sense of ‘mathematical’ as ‘astrological’).
Chirurgeon: See above, n. 75 (DJR). produce and wire-draw: Lengthen and prolong or ‘spin out’.
oppugn: Conflict with, run counter to.
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR). to the halves: Halfway. molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
extenuation: Under-estimation.
immanity: See above, n. 137 (DJR).
profuse: Extravagant, excessive.
form: Image.
Axiochus sick … health: See above, n. 124 (1.2.4).
difficile: Difficult.
conclusions: See above, n. 6 (2.1.1). receipt: See above, n. 10 (2.1.2).

took one dram for one scruple: A triple dose, since in traditional weighting a dram is roughly one-eighth of an ounce (3.54 grams), and a scruple (twenty grains) is roughly a twenty-fourth of an ounce (1.18 grams). The symbols for ‘dram’ (ʒ) and ‘scruple’ (℈) in medical recipes were easily confused.
exquisite: Accurate, exact.
corrected: Modified, so that any harmful effect is removed. simples: See above, n. 42 (1.2.2).
Aurum potabile: See above, n. 142 (1.2.3). Herba solis: Sundew, which had been used in medical remedies since the Middle Ages.
Furfurs: See above, n. 31 (1.1.1). Agues … Cachexia: See above, n. 45 (1.2.2). Falling sickness … Incubus: See above, n. 32 (1.1.1).
Chirurgery: Surgery – in this era, medical treatment of disease or injury by manual operation.
as the Fox said to the Weasel … subisti: This tale, sometimes included in collections of Aesop’s Fables, is here derived from Horace’s Epistles (1.7); ‘garner’ here means ‘granary’.

Meridian: Particular or special character. with him in Tully … Sicily: Lucilius the Roman satirical poet (d. 103/2 BCE) is portrayed in Cicero’s On Ends (1.3) as writing for the public of Tarentum, Consentia and Sicily – that is, for illiterate provincials rather than the cultured metropolitan elite.
sod: See above, n. 32 (1.2.2).
Boors and Clowns: See above, nn. 181, 187 (1.2.3).
rammy: Rank, pungent.
excepts against: See above, n. 21 (DJR).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
Choaspis in Persia: The Choaspes, now the Karkheh River in modern-day Iran.
Clitorio … undis: This quotation from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (15.322–3) refers to the fountain at Cleitor in northern Arcadia, the drinking of whose waters was believed to destroy the taste for wine.
defecate: Purged of impurities, clarified.

Trunks: This could mean ‘shafts’ or ‘conduits’, but Burton means to refer to Indian ‘tanks’, which were artificial cisterns or reservoirs. that Grecian Calis … Duke of Venice: The wife of the Doge (‘Duke’) of Venice Domenico Selvo (d. 1087) was actually Theodora Doukas (1058–83), sister of the Byzantine emperor Michael VII Doukas.
naught: See above, n. 27 (1.2.2).
Opera gigantum dicit aliquis: In note ‘f’, a reference to the description of the aqueducts given by the Roman poet Rutilius Namatianus in his Voyage Home to Gaul (1.97–100).
That Aqueduct of Claudius … high: The Aqua Claudia, work on which started under Caligula in 38 CE and was completed under Claudius in 52, and whose arches are still partially visible today.
an old cistern: The subterranean Basilica Cistern, built in the sixth century CE in the reign of Justinian I (527–65).
curiously: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
That Segovian Aqueduct in Spain: Work on the Aqueduct of Segovia was started in the reign of the Roman emperor Domitian, but probably not completed until 112 CE.

Sir Hugh Middleton Baronet: In note ‘c’, the wealthy goldsmith Hugh Middleton (or Myddelton, d. 1631) managed and financed the building of the New River, which carried water from the Chadwell and Amwell springs in Hertfordshire to London (a distance of about forty miles), and was completed in 1613. Mr. Otho Nicholson … Oxford: Otho Nicholson – on whom, see above, n. 11 (DJR) – funded the building of the Carfax Conduit, with one of its pipelines reserved for Christ Church, and the modernization of the Hinksey Conduit, in 1616–17.
ceruse: White lead, which was used in paint and cosmetics, and sometimes included in waterproof sealants. fluxes: See above, n. 4 (1.2.1).
Erinaceus Marinus: ‘Sea-hedgehog’, or sea-urchin.
Pearmains: See above, n. 26 (1.2.2). Raisins of the sun: Sun-dried grapes. Muskmelons: Melons with netted rinds, to be distinguished from watermelons.
pistick nuts: Pistachios.
salads: Salad-herbs.
crudity: See above, n. 61 (1.1.1).
betwixt dinner and supper: Until relatively recently, dinner, the main daily meal, was eaten in the middle of the day.
precisely: Strictly.
inanition: Emptiness.
eat and live, as the proverb is: ‘Eat to live, not live to eat’, traditionally attributed to Socrates. concocted: See above, n. 3 (1.1.2).
St. Jerome enjoins Rusticus … thirst: The Rusticus given Jerome’s epistolary advice here was a young monk from Toulouse.
ingurgitate: Swallow greedily, guzzle.

distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Sertorius-like: Sertorius is a fictitious stock character ridiculed in Martial’s Epigrams (7.10.5), quoted here; although the poet’s derogatory use of the name possibly echoes the real Quintus Sertorius (123–73 BCE), the general and governor of Martial’s birthplace Bilbilis, who rebelled against Rome and took temporary control of most of Spain in the early 70s BCE.
inflations: See above, n. 8 (1.3.2).
private: See above, n. 24 (DJR).
which rule Berengarius … his life: The theologian, and archdeacon of Angers, Berengar of Tours (d. 1088), as reported in his poetic epitaph by Hildebert of Lavardin, bishop of Le Mans (d. 1133).
Alexander Severus: Severus Alexander, Roman emperor 222–35 CE.

those Curii and Fabritii: See above, n. 93 (1.2.3). Mauritius, Lodovicus Pius: The Byzantine emperor Maurice (539–602 CE), and Louis the Pious (778–840), king of the Franks and of Aquitaine. Lodovicus Cornarus … Venice: Alvise (or Luigi) Cornaro (1475–1566), whose Discorsi della vita sobria (1558) famously described the strict regimen he had adopted at the age of forty, after a life of excess and debauchery.
excessit medicina malum … in the Poet: A misquotation of Lucan, who in the Civil War (2.142) wrote ‘Excessit medicina modum’ (‘The medicine went beyond bounds’).
mean: Moderately beneficial.

lenitive electuaries: Soothing or gently laxative (‘lenitive’) preparations, in which the main ingredients are mixed with honey or some kind of syrup to form conserves or pastes. condite: See above, n. 43 (1.2.2). turpentine: The semifluid resin of the terebinth tree, Pistacia terebinthus (principally from the Greek island of Chios or Cyprus), which was taken in the form of oil or powder, or in pills, as a purgative. clysters: See above, n. 83 (1.2.2).
forms: Recipes, formulas.
ingeminates: Repeats (for emphasis).
Balneorum usus dulcium: In note ‘b’, ‘sweet baths’, whose waters were perfumed by sweet, aromatic herbs, were commonly recommended in Renaissance medicine.

cracks: See above, n. 152 (1.2.3). Rufus’ pills: Pills made from aloe, saffron and myrrh – spuriously associated with the ancient Greek physician Rufus of Ephesus (fl. c. 100 CE), author of a treatise on melancholy that influenced Galen and many subsequent physicians.
fair water: Water that is clean, clear or pure.
frictions all over the body: Chafing or rubbing the body after exercise or bathing was a common form of medical treatment.
lye: Alkalized water, made from vegetable ashes. capital herbs: That is, herbs suitable for the head.
The Romans … Antoninus and Diocletian: The Baths of Antoninus were built in Carthage in the reign of the emperor Antoninus Pius (138–61 CE); on the Baths of Diocletian see above, n. 267 (DJR).
parietines: Fallen walls, ruins.

Nympheae: In note ‘c’, nymphaea were originally ancient Greek sanctuaries dedicated to nymphs, usually in the form of watery grottoes. Artificial nymphaea with semicircular water basins, and sometimes very elaborate ornamental architecture, were later built across the Roman Empire; in late antiquity the term came to be applied to monumental wells, often fed by aqueducts. There were many of these in Constantinople. absterge: Clean off.
curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
those Porrectan baths: In Porretta Terme, formerly Bagni della Porretta, not far from Bologna. Aquaria: Aquara, not far from Salerno.
Apona: Now Abano Terme, near Padua. holy anchor: Figuratively, a source of abiding spiritual security and confidence.
the waters of St. Helen: The Terme Sant’Elena, in Chianciano Terme, near Siena.
the Chalderinian Baths: In Lucca. coolers: Cooling medicines or agents.
Dutch … Baden: Here, ‘Dutch’ means German, but Burton’s source, the sixteenth-century German historian Johannes Goebel, is actually referring to the baths in the Swiss town of Baden, near Zurich.
