Dr. Turner of old, and Dr. Jones: The English physician, naturalist and priest William Turner (1509/10–68), and the Welsh physician John Jones (fl. 1562–79), both of whom wrote books about bathing.
complexions … temperatures: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
Venus: See above, n. 84 (1.2.2).
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
salacity: Lustfulness, lecherousness.

Thespiadas genuit: In classical mythology the Thespiadae (mentioned in note ‘a’) were the numerous sons of Heracles (Hercules) – by the fifty daughters of Thespius, king of Thespiae in Boeotia – fathered by the eighteen-year-old hero in the course of a single night (jocularly referred to by some as his thirteenth labour). Proculus the Emperor: Famous for boasting about his sexual appetite, Proculus (d. 281 CE) was in fact a Roman usurper who never succeeded in becoming emperor. lusty Laurence: The eponymous protagonist of a traditional English ballad, now lost, about a lascivious womanizer. Messalina the Empress: Valeria Messalina (d. 48 CE), the third wife of the Roman emperor Claudius. Her reputation for lecherous behaviour was well known, but she was specifically associated with prostitution by Juvenal’s description of her nocturnal habit of frequenting brothels and posing as a prostitute named ‘She-Wolf’ (Satires 6.114–32), and by Pliny the Elder’s account (10.83) of how she outdid a famous prostitute in a twenty-four-hour sex contest with a tally of twenty-five men. Triphallus, Marsyas, Herma, Priapus: In note ‘d’, ‘Triphallus’ (literally, ‘Triple-sized Phallus’) was an epithet of Priapus, the god of sexuality and fertility in classical mythology; Marsyas was one of the satyrs, whose characteristics included self-indulgent sexuality; a ‘Herma’ is a herm, a square pedestal or post topped with a bust of Hermes, who was associated with sexuality as a god of transgression. gymnics: See above, n. 295 (DJR).
long-winged Hawk: Falcon. sprung: Made by the hunting hound to fly up into the air, where it is to be seized by the hawk. amain: At full speed, or full force. stoops: Swoops.

the wandering Jew, Elias Artifex, or Lucian’s Icaromenippus: Three mythical or fictional itinerants: the ‘Wandering Jew’, said to be cursed to roam the earth until the Second Coming; Menippus, who in Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man takes a trip up to the heavens to visit the citadel of Zeus; on ‘Elias Artifex’, see above, n. 350 (DJR). such 4 Euripes, and a great rock of Loadstones: ‘Euripes’ here refers generically to straits or sea channels – cf. above, n. 46 (1.2.3). Burton is alluding to the report, made by the Carmelite friar and astronomer Nicholas of Lynne (fl. 1386–1411), that at the North Pole there were four channels of water flowing into a massive central whirlpool, and that at the pole itself there was a black mountain of magnetic rock, thirty-three miles in circumference, which was the source of the earth’s magnetic field. In note ‘g’, ‘Mons Sloto’, which was described as the highest mountain in the world by the Italian philosopher Francesco Patrizi in his Nova de universis philosophia (1591), has not been identified. the variation of the compass: Magnetic declination, whereby the angle on the horizontal plane between magnetic north and true north varies depending on one’s geographical location. some other star in the bear: That is, a star in Ursa Minor, as specified by the Italian philosopher and astrologer Marsilio Ficino (1433–99). magnetical meridian: A distinct locality that is magnetic – in fact a magnetic island, according to the Sicilian astronomer Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575).
it varies 7 grad. by and by 12, and then 22: That is, the magnetic declination varies from 7° to 12° and then 22°, depending on one’s position.
Rasceburg: Raseborg (or Raasepori).

Bartison the Hollander: The Dutch navigator and cartographer Willem Barentsz (c. 1550–97). fretum Davis, or Nova Zembla: Two places that are representative, respectively, of the Northwest and Northeast Passage to Asia (the latter was sought by Barentsz): the Davis Strait, in the Labrador Sea between Greenland and Canada; and Novaya Zemlya, an archipelago in the Arctic Ocean that separates the Barents Sea from the Kara Sea.

Hudson’s discovery … Fox: A list of explorers and navigators who were engaged in the search for a Northwest Passage from what is now Hudson Bay. Henry Hudson (d. 1611) sailed through what would later be called the Hudson Strait into the bay in 1610. ‘Hubbard’s Hope’, now Hubbard Point on the bay’s west coast near Churchill, was named after Josias Hubart (or ‘Hubbard’), the pilot of one of the ships of Thomas Button (c. 1575–1634). The island named by Luke Fox (1586–1635) as ‘Sir Thomas Roe’s Welcome’ – after the diplomat Sir Thomas Roe, who had sponsored the expedition in which it was discovered – was north of the point in latitude 62° 42′ N that had been named by Button ‘Ne ultra’ (‘No farther’), and redescribed by Fox as ‘Ut ultra’ (‘That much farther’) in his North-West Fox (1635); it is now Roes Welcome Sound at the northwest end of Hudson Bay. Cards: See above, n. 12 (DJR). that California is … an Island: The misconception of the Baja California Peninsula as a large island, separated from the mainland by a strait (now the Gulf of California), originated in Spanish reports and maps from the sixteenth century, and persisted into the eighteenth century. Neap tides: These occur shortly after the first or third quarters of the moon, when the high-water level is at the lowest point, and there is the smallest difference between high- and low-water levels (in contrast to ‘spring tides’ after a new or full moon, when the difference is greatest). the straits of Anian … by the Promontory of Tabin:
The Strait of Anian was a mythical passage thought to form the final stretch of the Northwest Passage, sometimes said to run between what is now far-eastern Russia and Alaska, either near the Bering Strait or farther south. On Tabin, see above, n. 219 (DJR).

Quinsay: Or ‘Kinsai’, modern-day Hangzhou. Cambalu: See above, n. 293 (DJR). whether … China and Cataia be all one: By the seventeenth century it had become widely accepted in Europe that China and Cathay (‘Cataia’ or ‘Catai’) were the same place. the great Cham of Tartary: See above, n. 111 (1.2.4). Xuntain … Paquin: ‘Xuntain’ was more usually spelled ‘Xuntien’, another name for what is now Hangzhou; it was sometimes confused with Beijing (Peking), which was also called ‘Paquin’ as well as ‘Cambalu’. Presbyter John: Or ‘Prester John’, a mythical Christian king and patriarch thought, in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, to have ruled a Christian ‘Church of the East’. His kingdom was sometimes located in Asia (particularly India) or Africa (particularly Ethiopia).

Guinea: The island of New Guinea. that hungry Spaniard’s … Terra Australis Incognita: See above, n. 80 (DJR). Magellanica: The regions of Patagonia visited by the Portuguese explorer Magellan (Fernão de Magalhães, 1480–1521) in 1520. Mercurius Britannicus … Lucinia: Joseph Hall’s satirical and fictional Mundus alter et idem (1605) contained lands called ‘Locania’ and ‘Larcinia’, either of which may be intended here.
Schouten and Le Maire: The Dutch navigators Willem Schouten (fl. 1590–1619) and Jacob Le Maire (1585–1616) sailed around Cape Horn in 1616. discovery: Exploration.

that great Bird Rucke: Usually spelled ‘roc’ (or ‘rukh’), a legendary giant bird of prey that originated in Indian mythology and was popularized in Arabic folklore; Marco Polo claimed that it had come to Madagascar from regions farther south. Gryphs: Griffins, which according to a Scythian myth related by Herodotus, guarded gold against the thievery of the ‘one-eyed’ people of the Arimaspians. fountains: Here, founts or sources. flowing: Flooding (the regular overflowing of the Nile had been observed since antiquity). Senega: The Senegal River in northwest Africa, forming the border between Mauritania and Senegal.

those Etesian winds: Northwesterly winds in the Mediterranean, blowing for about forty days in the summer (or, more generally, any winds that blow annually from a particular region). Mount Libanus: Mount Lebanon in northern Syria. Maragnan, Orenoque … Zona Torrida: The Marañón River in Peru, the principal source of the Amazon; the Orinoco River, running through Venezuela and into Colombia; and the ‘Torrid Zone’ – see above, n. 284 (DJR). Cauchinchina: Cochinchina, a region in southern Vietnam that includes Saigon and centres on the Mekong Delta.
Ocean of Zur … pacifico: See above, n. 290 (DJR).

Moabar: The Coromandel Coast in southeastern India. Mount … Pelion … Ossa: Mounts Pelion and Ossa in Greece. Meteors: See above, n. 42 (1.2.1). 1,250 paces … Dicaearchus: Pliny the Elder (2.65) reports that the ancient Greek philosopher Dicaearchus of Messana calculated the height of Mount Pelion as 1,250 paces, which is just over 6,000 feet (or 1,850 metres). 78 miles … Caucasus: On Italian miles – presumably the measurement used by the Italian scholar Jacopo Mazzoni (1548–98) – see above, n. 244 (DJR). 32 stadiums: A ‘stadium’ is a Greek and Roman measure of length, usually one-eighth of a Roman mile, and regarded by later writers as equivalent to a ‘furlong’ (220 yards).

Manoa, or Eldorado in that golden Empire: Manõa, the mythical ‘Lost City of Gold’ renowned for its riches, was often identified in Renaissance sources as El Dorado, the realm of the ‘Golden King’. Confusion reigned about its location, but it was often said to be in what is now Colombia or northern Brazil. gigantical Patagons in Chica: See above, n. 74 (1.2.2). Ybouyapab in the Northern Brazil: The Serra de Ibiapaba, a mountain range on the boundary between the Brazilian
states of Ceará and Piauí. that of Pariacaca … in Peru: Mount Pariacaca in the Peruvian Andes.
The pike of Tenerife: Mount Teide, or the Pico del Teide, a volcano on Tenerife in the Canary Islands.

that strange Cirknickzerksey lake … underground: A reference to Lake Cerknica, a seasonal lake in the region of Inner Carniola in modern-day Slovenia. It is connected to a series of underground caverns, and its size varies throughout the year, with a maximum depth of about twenty feet but sometimes disappearing completely. On a map of Carniola produced by the Austrian cartographer Wolfgang Lazius (1514–65), first published in 1561, a note printed close to the town of Vrhnika (Oberlaibach in German) claimed that the Argonauts travelled from there towards the Adriatic by passing through an underground cave that had been hollowed out of a mountain.

that vast den … in Muscovia: A cave at the Swedish city of Viborg (in present-day Russia), called ‘the Bang’ (in Swedish, ‘Smällen’), perhaps on account of an episode from 1495, famous in local folklore, when the city’s governor created an explosion inside the cave, harnessing the magnifying effect of its echo to scare off Russian invaders. Gilbert’s Cave in Lapland: On the island of Visingsö, on Lake Vättern in Sweden: it is named after the apprentice of the sorcerer Kettil Runske, who, according to a legend recorded by Olaus Magnus in his Historia de gentibus septentrionalibus (1555), imprisoned Gilbert in the cave as a punishment.

exonerates: Discharges. Jaxares, Oxus: The Syr Darya (formerly River Jaxartes) and Amu Darya (formerly River Oxus), originating from what are now the border regions, respectively, of Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, and of Tajikistan and Afghanistan, both used to run into the Caspian Sea. the mouth of Oby: The mouth of the Ob River is in northern Russia, where it flows into the Arctic Ocean.

the Mexican lake: Lake Texcoco, then in the Valley of Mexico. the Titicacan in Peru … Terapeia: Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia, and Lake Tarapaya in Bolivia. exhalation: Evaporation. Mare mortuum: The Dead Sea. Thrasumene: Lake Trasimeno, near Perugia in central Italy.
Padus: The River Po. Rhodanus: See above, n. 274 (DJR).

I would find out … Danubius: According to Strabo (Geography 7.1.5), the sources (‘fountains’) of the Danube were actually discovered by the emperor Tiberius, a day’s march north of Lake Constance, in 15 BCE. Trajan’s bridge: In 105 CE, Trajan did build a bridge across the Danube, near what is now Drobeta-Turnu Severin in Romania; also known as the Bridge of Apollodorus, after its architect, it is thought to be the longest built by the Romans. Grotta de Sibylla: The Grotto of the (Cumaean) Sibyl, part of a network of transport tunnels built in the late first century BCE, was previously thought to run through the acropolis at Cumae, though archaeologists now think it was sited elsewhere in Cumae or at Baiae (a Roman resort on the Bay of Naples). Lucullus’ Fishponds: According to Plutarch (Lucullus 39), the Roman general Lucullus – see above, n. 48 (1.2.2) – had a vast set of artificial waterworks, which included streams for breeding fish, built at his famously luxurious villa at the resort of Baiae. the Temple of Nidrose: Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim, Norway, which was built over period of 230 years between 1070 and 1300, and was historically an important pilgrimage site.
Alpine mice: Alpine marmots, which hibernate for up to nine months in a year.

convicts: Proves. Spanish Kites: Red kites – the Italian historian and travel writer Pietro Martire d’Anghiera specifies the bird called ‘Milvus Regalis’ by the Spanish, in his De legatione Babylonica (1533).

Isthmi, Euripi, Chersonesi: Isthmuses, sea channels and peninsulas; on ‘Euripi’, see above, n. 46 (1.2.3); ‘Chersonesi’ derives from the Greek term for a peninsula (χερσόνησος). baths: Hot or mineral springs. places: Here, perhaps, farms or farmsteads (but several alternative meanings are possible, including battlefields, buildings,
houses, estates and public or residential squares). Remora: The echeneis, or sucking-fish, which attaches itself to ships (and other objects) and thereby was said to delay them (mora means delay in Latin); their apparently magical power was of interest in the Renaissance.

Zoophytes: Plants thought to have some qualities of animals. Herberstein his Tartar lamb: The Austrian diplomat and travel writer Sigismund Freiherr von Herberstein (1486–1566) identifies this plant as ‘barometz’. This was a fake specimen, of obscure origins, often said to be a plant–animal hybrid, and made from the creeping rootstock and frond-stalks of the woolly fern (Cibotium barometz). It was more commonly called the ‘Scythian Lamb’, but its putative origins in Tartary were of continued interest in the seventeenth century. goose-bearing tree in the Orcades: The barnacle goose, or ‘tree goose’, which visits British coasts (including the Orkney Islands) only in winter, was once thought to be produced by a tree growing by the sea-shore, either from its fruit, or from a shell on the tree, or from a kind of mushroom generated by the rotting of its timber in the water. Hispaniola: An island in the Greater Antilles of the Caribbean. those spherical stones … others relate: While the stones in the shapes of animals were presumably fossils, the nature and purpose of the other objects reportedly excavated remains unclear. The carved stone spheres (or man-made ‘petrospheres’), remarked upon by Spanish explorers, were presumably similar to the Diquís spheres in Costa Rica. In this passage ‘Mansfield’ is Mansfeld Land, in southwestern Saxony-Anhalt in Germany, a region once ruled by the counts of Mansfeld; ‘Nokow and Pallukie’ are the villages of Nochowo and Pałuki in central Poland, just south of Poznań and north of Warsaw respectively.

in Lucomoria, a Province in Russia … business: The extraordinary characteristics of the inhabitants of the mythical land of ‘Lukomorye’ (or ‘Lukomorje’), located on some maps in Muscovy or Siberia, were described by several travel writers in this period.
Seamen: Mermen.
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).

that terrestrial Paradise: The Garden of Eden. Ophir … Peruana … Aurea Chersonesus: Ophir is the famously wealthy port from which, according to the Bible (1 Kings 10:22), King Solomon regularly received a cargo of gold and other precious materials. Renaissance commentators speculated whether this lay in Africa, the Americas or Asia. The passage here refers to Peru and the Malay Peninsula (the ‘Golden Chersonese’ in the works of classical geography) as possibilities.

St. Patrick’s Purgatory: A pilgrimage site containing a cave said to be the entrance to purgatory, located on Station Island in County Donegal, Ireland. Trophonius’ den: See above, n. 28 (1.3.1). Hecla in Iceland, Etna in Sicily: See above, 1.2.1.2, p. 196.
his meteors: That is, his Meteorologica.
Equinoctial: Equator. reciprocally: See above, n. 52 (1.1.2).
Trencher: In note ‘a’, see above, n. 27 (1.2.3).
pure element: That is, wholly comprising one of the four natural elements (earth, air, fire and water). Chaos: See above, n. 50 (1.2.1).
that Ambrosian College in Milan: The Biblioteca Ambrosiana, which was named after the patron saint of Milan, opened in 1609 as a centre of Catholic Counter-Reformation scholarship.

schoolmen: See above, n. 61 (1.1.2). Lipari: See above, n. 55 (1.2.1). Hiera … Vulcanian Islands: ‘Hiera’ is the ancient Greek name for Vulcano, one of the Aeolian Islands (themselves sometimes called the ‘Vulcanian Islands’). mount Hecklebirg: Spelled ‘Heckelberg’ in Germanic sources – another name for Mount Hecla, in Iceland, which in the seventeenth century was part of the Dano-Norwegian realm.

Styx: See above, n. 34 (1.2.2). Phlegethon: In Greek mythology, the river of fire in the underworld. Pluto’s Court: See above, n. 117 (DJR). that poetical Infernus … tree: In the fourth canto of the Inferno, Dante places the soul of Homer in the first circle of hell (limbo), where it is found in a wood wielding a sword. Hermione: The port town of Ermioni, in the southeastern part of Argolis on the Aegean coast.

Limbus patrum: ‘Limbo of the Fathers’, one of the four parts of hell according to medieval theology (besides the ‘limbo of infants’, purgatory, and hell of the damned), and the place where those who had died in fellowship with God (and so the Patriarchs of the Old Testament) awaited the coming of Christ for their redemption and entry to heaven. Ignatius’ parlour: The ‘secret’ room in hell reserved for impious and heretical innovators in John Donne’s Ignatius His Conclave (1611).

Virgil, sometimes Bishop of Salzburg … Antipodes: Vergilius (the Latin form of the Irish ‘Fergal’) of Salzburg (c. 700–784) was denounced to the pope by St Boniface (c. 675–754) for several of his beliefs, including that on the other side of the earth there was another race of men. ‘Antipodes’ here refers to this race, rather than to its location, and ‘Mentz’ here is Mainz. Jerusalem where Christ died the middle of it: Medieval maps typically placed Jerusalem at the centre of the world. Delos: An island in the Cyclades archipelago (although Delos here should actually be Delphi, regarded by the ancient Greeks as the centre of the world).
200 Italian miles: See above, n. 244 (DJR).

Lessius … in Diameter: The Flemish theologian Leonhard Leys (Lessius, 1554–1623) calculated that the length of the cavern of hell could be as small as one, presumably Dutch, league, or four Italian miles.
Abraham’s bosom: Heaven (after Luke 16:23).
Let Lucian’s Menippus … voyage: In Lucian’s Menippus, or The Descent into Hades, Menippus travels to the underworld and consults the blind prophet Tiresias about the good life.
accidents: Occurrences, incidents.
Pontus: See above, n. 57 (DJR).
complexions: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
Perioeci: People dwelling on opposing parts of the same meridian.

Quareca: In note ‘c’, Quareca (or ‘Cuareca’) was a mountain range on the Isthmus of Panama, apparently named after its local chieftain, also called ‘Torecha’. Zeilan: Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. Manamotapa: The kingdom of Mutapa, located in what is now Zimbabwe and Mozambique. St. Thomas’ Isle: São Tomé in the Gulf of Guinea. under the line: At the equator.
Ister: The lower course of the Danube. Bithynia: In antiquity, a region, kingdom and Roman province in northwestern Asia Minor.

Quivira, or Nova Albion in America: Quivira was the name for a large region in North America including the area now covered by Oklahoma, Kansas and parts of Colorado, Texas and New Mexico. The precise location of Nova Albion (‘New Albion’) – somewhere on the Pacific coast of North America, and so named by Sir Francis Drake in 1579 during his circumnavigation – is disputed, but it may have been what is now San Francisco Bay.
Norumbega: A mythical city, most commonly thought to be situated in what is now Penobscot Bay in Maine, New England.

Mr. Vaughan … Golden Fleece: In 1616 Burton’s acquaintance William Vaughan, a Welsh scholar and poet who used the pseudonym ‘Orpheus Junior’, attempted to establish a colony in Newfoundland called Cambriol. In The Golden Fleece (1626), in which Burton makes an appearance as ‘Democritus Junior’, Vaughan presented the ‘Cambrioll Colchos’ (the latter term referring to the destination of the Argonauts) as the remedy for all human ills.

Topic stars: Stars whose influence is exerted in a particular place. Dodecatemories: Each of the twelve divisions of the zodiac. the Moon’s mansions: In astrology, the twenty-seven or twenty-eight divisions (or ‘houses’) of the ecliptic, occupied by the moon on successive days.
Spruce: See above, n. 33 (1.2.2).
Spahan: Isfahan in modern-day Iran. 31 gr.: 31°, or ‘grades’.
inhabitable: An obsolete word actually meaning ‘uninhabitable’. the Brise: Or ‘Breeze’, a north or northeast trade wind in the tropics.
evil-inhabited: Sparsely populated.

the middle Region … refractionem: Aristotelian climatology divided the earth’s atmosphere into three regions: the lower region, heated by the sun’s rays refracted from the earth, was warm and moist; the middle region, where water condensed into clouds, was cold and moist; and the higher region, being closer to heavenly fire, was hot and dry.
Sierra de Cadarama: The Sierra de Guadarrama, a mountain range in central Spain running through the provinces of Ávila, Madrid and Segovia.
Lanes: Plains (a corrupted form of the Spanish ‘Llanos’, or ‘Lanos’ in Burton’s source).
La-plate … Potosa: The Río de La Plata (River Plate), in Argentina and Uruguay, and Potosí in Bolivia – on which, see above, n. 266 (DJR).

The fixed stars … follow: The ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus of Nicaea (fl. 162–128 BCE), as reported in the works of Ptolemy, observed that the equinoxes occur earlier in each sidereal year, because of a slow, continuous change of the earth’s axis of rotation. As a result of this phenomenon, known as the ‘precession of the equinoxes’ or ‘axial precession’, the constellations of ‘fixed stars’ are gradually changing position in relation to the signs of the zodiac. The ‘first [point] of Aries’ referred to here, which is used to calculate longitudes in celestial navigation, and which moves westwards by one degree every seventy-three years, had moved into the sign of Pisces in antiquity. Burton’s main point here is that if the earth is the immobile centre of the universe, as in the geocentric model, then over time ‘diverse alterations’ will gradually occur to the regions of the earth as the constellations that influence them change their position.

The Philosophers of Coimbra: See above, n. 5 (1.3.3). Empyrean: The higher region of the heavens. Eccentricity: In Renaissance astronomy, the ‘eccentricity’ of a planet is the numerical measurement of the elongation of its elliptical orbit (a circular orbit would have an eccentricity of zero).

those Medicean, Bourbonian, Austrian planets lately detected: The ‘Medicean stars’ were the four moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo in 1610 and named after his future patrons; the ‘Bourbonian stars’ were sunspots mistaken for planets, named in honour of the French royal dynasty by the astronomer Jean Tarde in 1620; the ‘Austrian stars’ were also sunspots, named in honour of the house of Habsburg by the Belgian Jesuit astronomer Charles Malapert in 1633. Sackbut: A musical instrument with a slide like that of a trombone.
Coele-Syria: Κοίλη Συρία, the ancient Greek name for Syria, or a region of it that included all of the country except Phoenicia. manured: Cultivated, managed.
dog days: See above, n. 347 (DJR).
Lemmer: Lemmings.
Princes of the air: The name given to ‘aerial devils’ in 1.2.1.2 above.

exploded: See above, n. 45 (DJR). Sal, Sulphur, Mercury: According to Paracelsus, the three elements of salt, sulphur and mercury (the tria prima) were the fundamental principles governing the qualities of objects and living things. Salmoneus: In classical mythology, the king of Elis (a region in the northwestern Peloponnese) who imitated the thunder and lightning of Zeus (Jupiter) by attaching bronze cauldrons and dried animal hides to the back of his chariot, and
throwing lighted torches into the air while riding it. Zeus punished him with a real thunderbolt.
angust: Compressed.
Manucodiatae: In note ‘a’, birds of paradise – see above, n. 205 (1.2.3).
Diaphanum: See above, n. 36 (1.1.2).
cast: Vomit violently.

parallaxes: Apparent changes in the positions of the stars when viewed from different points on the earth. orbs: Orbits. ♂ … ☉: The astrological symbols for Mars and the sun. those fictitious first watery movers … Firmament: A reference to the clear, ‘crystalline’ sphere in Ptolemaic astronomy – see above, n. 52 (1.2.1) – sometimes held to lie between the eighth sphere of the ‘firmament’, which contained the fixed stars, and the highest ‘empyrean’ sphere of heaven. Eccentre Epicycles deferentes: In Ptolemaic astronomy, planets moving in small circles (‘epicycles’) with their centres on the circumference of greater circles (known as ‘deferents’) could seem to be moving backwards around the earth.
circles equant: Or ‘equalizing circles’, postulated by ancient astronomers to render planetary movements consistent with the hypothesis that celestial motion was uniform in velocity.

Homocentrics: Spheres or circles concentric with others, or with the earth. Colures: The two principal meridians or ‘great circles’ of the celestial sphere, which intersect at the celestial poles: the equinoctial colure, which passes through the two equinoxes (the first points of Aries and Libra); and the solstitial colure, which passes through the two solstices (the first points of Cancer and Capricorn).

to make wings, and fly up … perform: This anecdote, which ends with a fatal crash-landing and widespread ridicule for the Turkish Icarus, is not recorded by the Flemish diplomat and author Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq (1522–92), but originates in the Byzantine chronicles of Niketas Choniates (c. 1155–1217), who identifies the individual as a purported descendant of the biblical Hagar. Burton may have read about it in the General History of the Turks (1603) by Richard Knolles. lets: Hindrances, impediments. Galileo’s glass: A telescope, as used by Galileo.

ethereal Comets, that in Cassiopeia 1572 … many like: Actually, not comets, but novae (newly discovered stars), which had been observed by Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) and Johannes Kepler (1571–1630). The new star discovered in 1604 by Kepler was actually in ‘Serpentarius’, the constellation now usually called ‘Ophiuchus’. Axle-trees: Or axes, the imaginary or geometrical lines forming the axis of revolution of a planet or celestial body.

An sit crux & nubecula … Antarticum: In note ‘e’, references to the Crux constellation in the Milky Way; and to the ‘Magellanic Clouds’, two large nebulae in the South Pole of the sky. 29,000 Myriads: 290 million (a ‘myriad’ being ten thousand). like those 12,000 Isles of the Maldives: There are actually around 1,200 islands in the Maldive chain of atolls, but the figure of 12,000 was reported in contemporary sources.
a substance or an accident: See above, n. 7 (1.1.3).
Orpheus, Hermes: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2) and n. 49 (1.3.1). in materiam primam: In ancient Greek philosophy, prima materia is the ‘first’, fundamental matter from which all other matter is derived.
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).
paradox: See above, n. 3 (DJR).

when as every point of the Firmament … videtur: The calculations reported here are evidently faulty, or at least based on two incompatible sets of calculations. The Jesuit mathematician Christophorus Clavius (1537/8–1612) claimed that the circumference of the firmament was 1,017,562,500 miles in length, and that therefore – dividing 1,017,562,500 by 24, since the firmament completed its
circular course every twenty-four hours – every star within it travelled 42,398,437.5 miles in one hour. Clavius also claimed, secondarily, that a point on the equator of the firmament travelled 176,660 miles in one unit of time, which he took to be fifteen seconds (the length of time it takes to say an Ave Maria, and equal to a 240th – not a 246th, which may be an error by Burton’s typesetter – of an hour); in one hour, therefore, a fixed point in the firmament would traverse 42,398,400 miles in an hour. Following this calculation gives the same figure as the distance covered by a man who rode for forty miles per day for 2,904 years – but in 203 years, travelling at the same speed, he would cover 2,963,800 miles, which is obviously far greater than the 706,640 (or 706,640.625, using Clavius’ initial calculation) miles covered by a point of the firmament in one minute. (None of these calculations take leap years into account.)

the whole world: Here, the whole universe or cosmos. above ♀ and ☿, beneath ♄, ♃, ♂: ‘Above Venus and Mercury, beneath Saturn, Jupiter and Mars’. absolves: Completes. solve all appearances: Explain the observed facts. those Alphonsine … tables: See above, n. 239 (1.2.3).

Which may be full of Planets … Jupiter, &c.: The speculation in note ‘e’ develops the criticism given by Tycho Brahe of the Copernican theory, discussed here in the main text, on the grounds that it implausibly requires the existence of a massive vacuum between the sphere of Saturn and the firmament. Retrogradations: Similar to parallaxes, but occurring when stars apparently move in a reverse direction from that which is normal.
Kepler, the Emperor’s Mathematician: Kepler became imperial mathematician to the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II (1552–1612) in 1601; on the meaning of ‘mathematician’ here, see above, n. 117 (1.2.1).

those two green children … thence: The ‘green children of Woolpit’, who, according to the chronicler William of Newburgh (1135/6–c. 1198), mysteriously appeared in this Suffolk village in the reign of King Stephen (1135–54), speaking an unknown language and eating only raw broad beans. olymp. 84. anno tertio at Capuae Fluenta: That is, in the third year of the eighty-fourth Olympiad, or 442/1 BCE (Pliny the Elder actually dates this to the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad, or 467/6). The claim that this occurred at ‘Capuae Fluenta’ (‘the streams at Capua’) is probably a slip, as the ancient sources identify the location of the meteorite in Greece as Aegospotami (‘Goat streams’), which in Latin would be ‘fluenta Caprae’. Ancile or buckler in Numa’s time: The small oval shield (ancile) fabled to have fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa Pompilius, the second legendary king of Rome, upon which the prosperity of the city was said to depend. In case the original was lost, Numa ordered eleven exact replicas to be made.
collects: See above, n. 120 (1.2.1). stick not: Do not hesitate.
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).

Kepler … in his perspectives, Lunar Geography: Informal references, which were both present in the first edition of the Anatomy (1621), to Kepler’s Dioptrice (1611) and his Somnium seu opus posthumum de astronomia lunaris, which was published posthumously in 1634 but had been mentioned in the Dissertatio cum nuncio sidereo (1610).
oppugn: See above, n. 6 (2.1.4). two Planets, ☉ and ☾: That is, the sun and the moon.
Daedalian: Like Daedalus (‘Cunning worker’), who in Greek mythology was a supremely ingenious (mortal) inventor and craftsman.
the five upper Planets: In the system of the German astronomer Nicolaus Reimers (Raimarus, 1551–1600), these are Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
Planets without Orbs: Planets unfixed to the spheres surrounding the earth that, in the Ptolemaic theory, carried the planets and stars with them in their revolution.
Jansonius Caesius hath illustrated in a sphere: The Dutch cartographer Willem Janszoon Blaeu (1571–1638) made models of celestial globes in order to compare Ptolemaic with Copernican cosmography.
sound Drums and Trumpets: The militaristic command is an authorial aside, commenting on the intellectual battles under discussion.
hoise: Launch or lift.

Apelles: The Jesuit astronomer Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650) used the pseudonym ‘Apelles’, referring to the celebrated ancient Greek painter Apelles of Cos, in a series of letters written in 1611 to report his observations of sunspots. the Cyanean Isles in the Euxine Sea: See above, n. 290 (DJR).
maculae and faculae: In astronomy, ‘maculae’ are dark spots on the surface of the sun, whereas ‘faculae’ are light spots.

The Hollander … cum Apelle: The author of De maculis in sole animadversis, et tanquam ab Apelle … Batavi dissertatiuncula (1612), calling himself ‘Batavus’ (‘the Dutchman’), is now thought to be Christoph Scheiner. like the Philosophers in Lucian … abroad: In Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man, Menippus, dissatisfied with philosophers’ confused and contradictory speculations about the cosmos and the gods, makes himself wings and flies up to heaven to discover true knowledge. On his way up, he is accosted by the Moon, who asks him to relay her complaints about the absurd speculations of humans about her nature to Zeus, and threatens to remove herself from their view unless Zeus destroys the philosophers. Menippus delivers the message, and the god decrees that he will send his thunderbolt in the spring.

Theologasters: See above, n. 267 (1.2.3). as he saith: The Dutch poet and scholar Daniel Heinsius, in his Hercules tuam fidem (1617). these gigantical Cyclopes will transcend spheres … doth: In the Metamorphoses (1.151–62), Ovid refers to a story in which the giants of classical mythology attempted to seize the throne of heaven by piling mountains up to the stars: see below, n. 10 (2.3.2). But there may be a simultaneous allusion here to Lucretius (5.110–25), where the giants are compared with those who, like Epicurus, give a rational account of the cosmos that is opposed to traditional religious belief.

like Lucian’s Jupiter … Africk: In Lucian’s Icaromenippus, or The Sky-Man (25–6), Zeus receives various prayers and sacrifices from human beings before issuing orders about the wind and weather. The image of Zeus painting the wings of butterflies, a touch of Burton’s own in the second edition (1624), alludes to the classical goddesses of the seasons (Horae), who were the ministers – or sometimes the daughters – of Zeus, and were often artistically depicted with butterfly wings.

the Turks’ Alcoran: See above, n. 123 (DJR). Mahomet … for him: What Burton calls ‘a Pegasus’ is properly identified by his likely source here, Antoine Geuffroy’s Aulae Turcicae Othomannicique imperii descriptio (1577), as the ‘Alborac’. This is the Buraq, the winged horse of Islamic tradition said to have transported the prophet Muhammad into the heavens and back.

They have fetched Trajanus’ soul out of hell: Note ‘b’ refers to the legend, recorded in the Speculum historiale by Vincent of Beauvais (d. c. 1264), that Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) successfully petitioned God to liberate Trajan’s soul from hell, after being moved by a relief on Trajan’s column depicting the Roman emperor’s dispensation of justice to a widow. It became a frequently discussed example of the posthumous salvation of virtuous pagans. bind and loose in heaven: Retain and absolve sins – in contemporary Christian theology, interpreting Matthew 16:19, the power of judgement that belonged to the Church on earth and that would also be upheld in heaven. quartermaster: Someone who shares a quarter of responsibility with another or others. Caecilius: See above, n. 38 (1.2.1).

as Julian did of old … Zacharias the Christian: Allusions to the Contra Julianum by Cyril of Alexandria (c. 375–444 CE), a refutation of Julian the Apostate’s
polemic against Christianity; the Recognitions, written in the fourth century CE and falsely attributed to Pope Clement I (d. 99), which reimagines the confrontation between Simon Magus and the apostle Peter described in Acts 8:9–24; and the Dialogus Ammonius of the lawyer and historian Zacharias Rhetor (465/6–c. 553), which stages a debate between the persona of the Christian author and that of his contemporary, the Greek Neoplatonist Ammonius.
hoo: Similar to ‘how’, or ‘ho’ – an exclamation to attract attention, here also expressing astonishment or bewilderment.
as the Preacher concluded … novum: Ecclesiastes 1:9 in the translation of the Latin Vulgate (where it is verse 10).
my game is sprung: See above, n. 1 (2.2.3).
election: See above, n. 62 (1.1.2).
What harm those extremities … showed: See above, 1.2.2.5.
conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).
the Orcades: See above, n. 133 (1.2.1).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
clownish: See above, n. 187 (1.2.3).
moors: See above, n. 268 (DJR).

Who sees not a great difference … Fens: This list of English locales with contrasting terrains includes the Lincolnshire Wolds, a range of hills in the county of Lincolnshire, and the marshy region of the Fens in East Anglia. On Romney Marsh, see above, n. 101 (1.2.2).
those Tartari Zamolhenses … hordes: Probably the Nenets (or Samoyeds), an indigenous nomadic people in the Arctic region of Russia (‘hordes’ here means ‘nomadic tribes’.)

Sardis: The capital of the ancient kingdom of Lydia and one of the principal cities of the Persian Empire (now Sart in Turkey). Susa: The capital of the region of Elam in what is now western Iran, and now the city of Shush; it was used by Cyrus the Great (reigned 559–530 BCE) as one of his capitals after he defeated the Babylonians in 539. Persepolis: The ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in the reign of Darius I (522–486 BCE), located northeast of Shiraz in modern-day Iran. Pasargada: Pasargadae, built as the Persian capital in the reign of Cyrus the Great, also near Shiraz in modern Iran.
Ecbatana: The ancient capital of the Medes, whose territory became part of the Persian Empire under Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE. It was located in what is now Hamedan in Iran.
Adrianople: Or Hadrianopolis, now Edirne in the European part of Turkey, and the capital of the Ottoman Empire before the conquest of Constantinople in 1453.
Tully had his Tusculan … Village: See above, n. 121 (1.2.2).

The Bishop of Exeter … past: In Francis Godwin’s Catalogue of the Bishops of England (1601), cited in note ‘a’, the bishop of Exeter, John Veysey (c. 1464–1554), is criticized for stripping his see of most of its landed assets – although he was actually complying with requests issued by the royal court during the Reformation for leases and grants of episcopal properties. He was also the founder and benefactor of the grammar school attended by Burton in Sutton Coldfield (see the editor’s Introduction).

So Camden saith of Ewelme … halitus: William Camden refers in his Britannia (1586) to Ewelme Manor, in the Oxfordshire village of Ewelme. The house had been built by William de la Pole, duke of Suffolk (1396–1450), but had become a minor Tudor palace after being confiscated by Henry VII.
as one reports of Venice … smokes: See above, n. 103 (1.2.2).

offends: See above, n. 23 (DJR). Lindley … Drakesly upon Trent: These places, clustered in an area straddling the borders of Warwickshire, Leicestershire and Derbyshire, had a range of familial and personal connections for Burton. The
village of Lindley in Leicestershire was his birthplace, and the nearby villages of Orton-on-the-Hill, Fenny Drayton, Caldecote (‘Caucut’), Amington, Polesworth, Weddington, Swarkeston (‘Swarston) and Drakelow (‘Drakesly’) were home to various members of Burton’s family and his acquaintances.
plat: A patch or plot of land. a Cotswold country: Land like the Cotswolds, a range of hills mainly in Gloucestershire famous for their sheep-pastures.
fielden: Open, level land, suitable for fields.
Champian: See above, n. 56 (DJR).

And he that built that fair house Wollerton … place: The coal owner Sir Francis Willoughby (1546/7–96) chose the position of Wollaton Hall and probably had a hand in its exuberant design, but the main architect was Robert Smythson (1535–1614).
Farmack: Foremark. Mount Edgemond: Mount Edgecumbe.

serenat Boreas … in an excellent prospect: Burton’s source here is the Constantini Caesaris selectarum praeceptionum de agricultura libri viginti (1538), the Latin translation of the Geoponika, a collection of Byzantine works on agriculture attributed by its unknown editor to the scholarly emperor Constantine VII (905–59 CE), although the main author in the original Greek compilation was Cassianus Bassus Scholasticus of the sixth century CE. Cuddesdon in Oxfordshire … matched: Cuddesdon Palace, built in 1634 by the bishop of Oxford, John Bancroft (mentioned in note ‘f’ as Burton’s former tutor), was destroyed in 1644 during the siege of Oxford in the Civil War, but it was later rebuilt.
coast: See above, n. 291 (DJR).
Rustics: Writers on rural matters.
Westchester: Chester.

as at Custoza … Vicenza: Like other aristocratic dwellings in Costozza in the province of Vicenza, the house – described by the travel writer Fynes Moryson in his Itinerary (1617) – was connected to an extensive system of natural and artificial underground caves, the ‘Covoli di Costozza’.

pills: Peels. Benzoin, Ladanum, Styrax: All fragrant resins used in perfumery and formerly in medicine, taken from the Styrax benzoin tree, the cistus plant and the Styrax officinalis tree respectively.
prefers: See above, n. 7 (1.2.2).
sallow leaves: Willow leaves.
fashions: See above, n. 17 (DJR).
stock: A tree-stump, as the type of something lifeless or lacking sensation – and so, figuratively, a blockhead or senseless person. speculation: Viewing or observation.

Seneca the Philosopher … Liternum: In the place cited here, Seneca praises the simplicity of the villa of Scipio Africanus the Elder – see above, n. 147 (DJR) – in Liternum, a Roman settlement in a swampy and malaria-infested region of Campania, and now the village of Lago Patria, near Naples. Elsewhere (Epistles 51), he contrasts it with the luxurious villas built at the resort of Baiae by other statesmen, such as Pompey and Julius Caesar.

Paulus Aemilius … the last king of Macedonia: See above, n. 100 (1.2.4). his son Scipio … Sulpicius Gallus: The historical figures referred to here are Scipio Aemilianus (Scipio the Younger) – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) and n. 87 (1.2.4); the brother and emissary of Eumenes II Soter, king of Pergamum (197–158 BCE); and the Roman politician, general and author of works on astronomy, Gaius Sulpicius Gallus (consul in 166 BCE).
passengers: Travellers.

Hermon and Rameh in Palestina: Mount Hermon, on the border between Syria and Lebanon; and possibly the town called ‘Rameh’, originally a village situated on a hill on the edge of what is now the Beit HaKerem valley in northern Israel (and probably the ‘Ramah’ mentioned in Joshua 19:29). Collalto in Italy: Mount
Collalto, in the South Tyrolean region of northern Italy. the top of Taygetus: See above, n. 250 (DJR). Acrocorinthus, that old decayed castle: The Acrocorinth (‘Upper Corinth’) was the acropolis overlooking the ancient city of Corinth. It had been occupied continuously since at least the eighth century BCE, and had various Byzantine as well as medieval Frankish fortifications – which are probably the ruins referred to here.

Glastonbury Tower, Belvoir Castle, Radway Grange: Glastonbury Tor, a hill near Glastonbury in Somerset; Belvoir (‘Fine View’) Castle in Leicestershire; and Radway in Warwickshire, which is at the foot of Edge Hill. Walesby in Lincolnshire … Countess Dowager of Exeter: In 1624 Burton was granted the benefice of Walesby in Lincolnshire by Frances Cecil, the Dowager Countess of Exeter (1580–1633), but as note ‘d’ records, he resigned it in 1631 (see the editor’s Introduction).

Barclay the Scot commends that of Greenwich tower … other: In his Icon animorum (1614), the poet John Barclay describes the view from Greenwich Hill in London. The word ‘tower’ here may refer to the Palace of Placentia, which was known as ‘Duke Humphrey’s Tower’ (after Humphrey, duke of Gloucester, 1390–1447) and would later make way for the Royal Observatory, although the use of the word ‘tower’ as a synonym for ‘tor’ (hill) is not uncommon in this period.
promiscuous: See above, n. 106 (DJR).
success: See above, n. 135 (1.2.4).
tables: See above, n. 135 (1.2.3).
Amasis: In note ‘d’, see above, n. 267 (DJR).

In our memory … Mahomet the Turk: See above, n. 129 (DJR). This present Sultan: Sultan Ahmet I (1590–1617), who was alive when Sandys went on the trip described in his Relation of a Journey Begun An. Dom. 1610, published in 1615. notches: Or nocks, the small tips of horn affixed to the ends of a bow, with notches for holding the string.
gentry: See above, n. 112 (1.2.2).
frications: Chafing or massaging of the body with the hands.
regiment: Regimen.
gargarized: Gargled.
confounds: See above, n. 86 (DJR).

Aganella … inventor of it: Actually the third-century BCE grammarian Agallis of Corcyra (modern-day Corfu, and thought to be the Homeric kingdom of Phaeacia). She is said to have attributed the invention to Nausicaa, the Phaeacian princess who plays a ball game with her companions in the sixth book of Homer’s Odyssey.

Chiron in monte Pelio … tuebatur: In note ‘j’, in classical mythology the centaur Chiron was said to have had healing powers and to have trained heroes in the arts of medicine, hunting, warfare and music. The Neoplatonist philosopher Maximus of Tyre (second century CE) credits Chiron’s medicine with the ability to strengthen reason and resist the passions.

Herod: According to the early Christian chronicler Hegesippus, after murdering his uncle Josephus in a mad frenzy – see above, n. 78 (1.2.3) – Herod the Great (c. 73–4 BCE) recovered his health by hunting.

The Greek Emperors began it: That is, the Byzantine emperors. Falconry was popular in Byzantium, but is now thought to have spread from western Asia through the Balkans, and was brought to western Europe in the early centuries CE by either the Celts or the Goths.
Adrianople: See above, n. 121 (2.2.3).
stares: Starlings.

reclaim: Train; this meaning derives from use of the term ‘reclaiming’ in falconry, which refers to the recalling of the hawk after it has been released. Pies: Magpies. man them: That is, taming the birds by carrying them on the fist.

stalking-horses: Horses which are trained to allow a hunter to hide behind them, enabling an undetected approach to the game (or a portable screen made from canvas or another light material in the figure of a horse, used for the same purpose). coy-ducks: Or ‘decoy-ducks’: ducks trained to lure wildfowl.
day nets: See above, n. 19 (DJR). chaff-nets: Nets with a fine mesh for catching small creatures. snite: Snipe.
Quail-pipes: Pipes or whistles used to lure quails into a net.

Chorography: See above, n. 77 (DJR). his Isle of Huena: Hven, an island in the Øresund strait, granted in 1576 to Tycho Brahe by King Frederick II of Denmark, and the site of his observatory in the castle of Uraniborg. puts down his nets … ornament: Some of Brahe’s maps of Uraniborg, for instance the one printed in his Epistolarum astrononicarum libri (1596), included depictions of enclosures with nets for bird-catching (an ‘ornament’ here is a visual decoration).
weels: Wicker traps for catching fish, eels especially.
Armholes: Armpits.

just: See above, n. 26 (DJR). Ringing: Either games, such as quoits, that involve the throwing of rings, or bell-ringing. shooting … France: That is, archery, which – according to the historian Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) cited in note ‘b’ – contributed to English military victories in the Hundred Years War (1337–1453) with France.

Keel-pins: Skittles or ninepins. trunks: An early form of billiards, similar to bar billiards. pitching bars: Throwing iron bars. hurling: Similar to handball, and once popular in Cornwall. mustering: Probably ‘muss’, which involves scrambling for small objects that have been thrown down. wasters: Fencing with a single-stick or cudgel. balloon: A game played with a large inflated leather ball, which is struck with an arm fitted with a protective wooden guard. quintain: Tilting at a target post or plank with a lance or pole.

great horses: War horses or chargers. running at rings: Tilting at a ring with a lance on horseback. wild goose chases: Horse-races in which the course of the leader is followed by the others, so as to resemble a flight of wild geese.
that Antiochian Daphne: The grove of Daphne in the Hellenistic–Roman city of Antioch in Syria, which also contained a sanctuary dedicated to Apollo.

Hortus principis … at Ferrara: Alfonso II d’Este, duke of Ferrara (1533–97), built a series of waterways, communicating gardens, baths, and fish and game preserves in the city, connected by a ring-canal filled with swans and other birds. It was flanked by private tree-lined avenues, two of which were called ‘La Montagna’ and ‘La Montagnola’.
St. Bernard … Monastery: The monastery of Clairvaux was founded by Bernard in 1115 in an isolated valley in Champagne.

the Turk’s gardens in his Seraglio: The gardens of the Sultan at Constantinople, described by Pierre Gilles in his De topographia Constantinopoleos (1561), were situated at the foot of the hill on which the palace was located. the Pope’s Belvedere in Rome: The Cortile del Belvedere at the Vatican Palace. that Indian King’s … in Aelian: The extensive royal parks in India, described in antiquity by the Roman historian Aelian, had been built in the period of the Maurya Empire (321–184 BCE), and were maintained in subsequent centuries. those famous gardens … Chantelou in France: The topiary gardens at the Château de Chantelou in the Essonne. ill-apaid: Ill-satisfied, discontented.

the river Peneus: The River Peneus, in the Vale of Tempe in northern Thessaly, was named after the mythological river-god whose daughter Daphne was beloved
of Apollo. It was said to be a favourite place of Apollo and the Muses. passengers: See above, n. 19 (DJR).

that of the Persian Kings … Curtius: The royal palace at Persepolis – see above, n. 119 (2.2.3) – whose treasures were taken by Alexander the Great after his conquest and burning of the city in 330 BCE; cf. 3.2.4.1, p. 856. opiparous: Sumptuous. set out: See above, n. 29 (DJR). curious: Made with care, exquisitely produced. in Trimalchio’s house: In the home, that is, of the ostentatious arriviste whose lavish banquet is described in the Satyricon of Petronius.

as Porus and Alexander: Porus (d. 318 BCE), king of Paurava (in modern-day Punjab), fought Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum River) in 326 BCE. Single combat between the two rulers is not recorded in any account of the battle, but it is depicted on the so-called ‘Porus medallions’ issued by Alexander in commemoration of his victory. Canutus and Edmond Ironside: According to apocryphal accounts given by medieval English chroniclers, after a series of pitched battles in 1016 that had inflicted heavy casualties on both sides, Edmund II (‘Ironside’) of England challenged Cnut (Canute) of Denmark to single combat. When the English king gained the upper hand, Cnut reportedly conceded defeat and agreed to partition the kingdom peacefully. Scanderbeg and Ferrat Bassa the Turk: Firuz Pasha, the general of the Ottoman Sultan Murad II, was reportedly killed in battle in 1445 by the famously mighty Skanderbeg – on whom, see above, n. 94 (1.2.3). nec enim … Hectoris: These lines from the Iliad (22.159–61) refer to the pursuit of Hector by Achilles.

Crecy, or Agincourt, or Poitiers … clariorem: Three famous English victories against the French in the Hundred Years War: at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415). The comment of the chronicler Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1404) refers just to the Battle of Poitiers.
Interview … Francis the first: See above, n. 71 (1.2.3).

Bodin, when he was Ambassador … sight of it: In 1581 Jean Bodin accompanied François, duke of Alençon and Anjou (1555–84), on the latter’s visit to England in order to negotiate his marriage to Elizabeth I. Bodin is reported to have offended the queen.

Pomponius Columna: Actually the condottiere Prospero Colonna (1452–1523). The duel, known as the ‘Challenge of Barletta’, took place in the countryside near Barletta in southern Italy in 1503, after a drunken French knight had insulted the locals. It was won by the Italians.

Breaute the Frenchman, and Anthony Schets: The duel, known as the Battle of Lekkerbeetje, took place near ’s-Hertogenbosch in 1600. It was fought between the French cavalry officer Pierre de Bréauté and Gerard Abrahams, one of the officers of the Dutch commander Anthony Schets van Grobbendonck, with each being supported by twenty-one cavalrymen and two heralds. Abrahams was killed, but de Bréauté was wounded, and he was subsequently captured and executed by Abrahams’s men. The text in note ‘a’ is taken from Abrahams’s epitaph.

like Livy’s Horatii, Torquati and Corvini: According to Livy (1.24–5), the war between Rome and Alba Longa in the reign of Tullus Hostilius (c. 672–642 BCE) was settled by combat between two groups of triplet brothers representing their cities, the Horatii and Curiatii respectively; the sole survivor, and eventual victor, was Publius Horatius. The Roman statesman and general Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus (consul in 347, 344 and 340 BCE) was famously victorious in his duel with a Gaul (perhaps in 361, but alternative dates are given in the sources), from whom he took a gold torque and his cognomen ‘Torquatus’. He subsequently executed his son Titus Manlius Torquatus for going against orders by fighting a duel against the Latin commander Geminus Maecius at the Battle of Vesuvius (340 BCE). The Roman general and consul Marcus Valerius Corvus (Corvinus)
was famous for killing a Gallic warrior in single combat as a prelude to a Roman military victory in 349 BCE.

Cutting the banks of Nilus: That is, making narrow channels in the banks of the Nile to allow water to escape and lower its level. Imbram Bassa: Probably Damat Ibrahim Pasha (1517–1601), Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, and governor of Egypt between 1583 and 1585.
monomachies: See above, n. 15 (DJR).
Iconographies: Drawings, plans. the Escorial in Guadas: El Escorial is situated in the Sierra de Guadarrama in Spain. interpreter: See above, n. 61 (DJR).
Gymnics: See above, n. 295 (DJR). May games: Entertainments and sports associated with the celebrations of May. wakes: Parish festivals held on the feast of the patron saint of a church.
Diocletian … turned gardener: See above, n. 120 (1.2.2).

Lysander … ordines mei: According to Cicero (On Old Age 17), who cites Xenophon for the story, it was actually Cyrus the Younger (c. 423–401 BCE) who said this about his arrangement of trees, to the Spartan general Lysander (d. 395).

Cincinnatus, Cato, Tully: When a Roman army had been encircled in 458 BCE by the Aequi (an Italic tribe) southeast of Rome at Mount Algidus, the Roman statesman Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus was famously called from working in the fields and appointed dictator. He mustered an army that defeated the Aequi, then relinquished his office and returned to his farming. Cato the Elder – see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries) – worked on a farm in his youth, and wrote a book On Agriculture. Cicero described the pleasures of agriculture in his treatise On Old Age.
inoculate: Bud a plant into or upon another one, for propagation.
I am vere Saturninus: See 1.3.1.3, p. 388, where the influence of Saturn is associated with the love of husbandry, and above, n. 13 (DJR).

The Greeks had their Olympian, Pythian, Isthmian, Nemean games … Corinth hers: References to the four main ‘Panhellenic’ games, so called because they were open to all Greeks, held at the sanctuary of Zeus in Olympia, at the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, at the Isthmus of Corinth (in honour of Poseidon) and at Nemea (in honour of Zeus), near Corinth; and to the Panathenaea, the great civic festival of Athens in honour of Athena. our silver games: Rural athletic competitions for silver prizes, organized by church parishes in early modern England for the purpose of charitable fundraising.

in Prytanaeo: The Prytaneum was the official building of the chief magistrates, and the Greek city-state’s sacred centre that hosted many cult activities; Olympic champions were awarded the highly honorific privilege of taking meals there for life. Panathenaeis: The Panathenaic festivals included the ritual of a large sacrifice, from which meat was publicly distributed. Thesperiis: Probably a garbled allusion to the Theseia, a festival held by the Athenians in honour of their hero Theseus, which involved athletic games, the consumption of meat sacrifices and the serving of athara, a special milk porridge. Phiditiis: See above, n. 94 (1.2.4). Naumachies: Mock naval battles staged by the Romans for entertainment in natural and artificial lakes.
In the Low countries … before these wars: That is, before the conflicts of the Dutch Revolt (1568–1648). curiously: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
Ring-doves: Wood pigeons.

Busbequius the Emperor’s Orator: The Flemish diplomat Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq served as the Holy Roman Emperor’s ambassador (the meaning of the word ‘orator’ here) to the Ottoman Empire in 1554 and 1556.

Conradus Gesner … meat: The Swiss naturalist, physician and polymathic scholar Conrad Gessner incorporated some of his own observations in his famous zoological treatise, the Historia animalium (1551–8).
mewed up: See above, n. 196 (1.2.3).

Shovel-board: Or ‘shuffleboard’, a game in which a coin is pushed by hand along a surface with transverse lines. the Philosopher’s game: The Ludus Pythagoreus (or ‘rithmomachy’), a complex mathematical board-game that was often attributed to Pythagoras. small trunks: Or ‘troll-madam’, a ladies’ game similar to bagatelle and billiards. shuttlecock: Or ‘battledore and shuttlecock’, a game in which a shuttlecock is hit with a racket (‘battledore’) between two players, or by one player into the air as many times as possible. yule-games: Christmas parlour or party games. catches, purposes, questions and commands: Kinds of word game. as the old woman … Apuleius: The tale of Cupid and Psyche is narrated by an old woman in the fourth book of Apuleius’ Metamorphoses; this is referenced in note ‘c’ as ‘Miles.’, an abbreviation of sermo Milesius (‘Milesian Tales’), which was a common way of referring to the work that stemmed from its self-description in the opening of book 1. Boccace’s Novels: Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron (1353).

Amaranthus the Philosopher … narration of it: The fictional dialogue entitled in its Latin translation Amaranthus, sive senilis amor, originally written in Greek by the twelfth-century Byzantine author Theodore Prodromos, has the eponymous narrator give a satirical description of the wedding of the elderly Stratocles.
passenger: See above, n. 144 (2.2.3).
ordinary: Inn, tavern, or any other public eating-place.
that great Gonsalva … Andalusia: See above, n. 96 (1.2.3). occurrents: Accounts of events, news.

nicely: See above, n. 125 (DJR). mixed lusorious lots: ‘Mixed lots’ were games involving intelligence or skill as well as chance, in contrast with ‘mere lots’, which were exclusively fortuitous; ‘lusorious’ here means ‘being used in games or pastimes’. sortilegious: In note ‘d’, concerned with the casting of lots (sortilege), often associated with divination and magic, and condemned by English puritans such as Thomas Gataker (1574–1654).
excepted at: See above, n. 21 (DJR).
coney-catching: Swindling, cheating.

Charles the seventh … succeeds: The edict banning games of chance quoted here was issued in 1369 by the French king Charles V (‘the Wise’, 1338–80). Burton, who added this passage in his second edition (1624), was misled by his source, the Palamedes sive de tabula lusoria, alea, et variis ludis, libri tres (1622) by Daniel Souter, who gives the correct date of the edict but misattributes it to the inveterate gambler Charles VII (1403–61).
impertinent: See above, n. 133 (1.2.3).

William the conqueror … betwixt them: In the anecdote told by the historian John Hayward (d. 1627), the game was actually played between Henry (the son of William) and Louis (the son of Philip I of France). The quarrel was reportedly escalated by the latter, the future Louis VI of France (d. 1137), when he called the former, the future Henry I of England (d. 1135), the son of a bastard. The comment here on Louis’s title of ‘prince’ refers to the fact that the heirs apparent to the French throne were given the title of Dauphin only after 1349, when the crown acquired the province of the Dauphiné Viennois.

Cl. Bruxer’s Philosophy game … Ouranomachia: For the ‘philosophy game’, which is here attributed to the mathematician Claude de Boissière (usually Latinized as ‘Buxerius’), see above, n. 54 (2.2.4); the geometrical board-game ‘Metromachia’ was invented by the theologian and philosopher William Fulke (1536/7–89), who also published a manual for an astronomical game called ‘Ouranomachia’ that was similar to the ‘philosophy game’. fictions: Devices or inventions.
severe Catos: See above, n. 6 (Preliminaries).

oppugners: See above, n. 73 (1.1.2). ignoratio Elenchi: Literally, ‘ignorance of a refutation’, which in Aristotelian logic refers to the fallacy of failing properly to address the question at hand. as he did in the comedy: Here, Terence in his Self-Tormentor (214).

the King’s declaration … permitted: The ‘Declaration of Sports’, issued by James I in 1617 and 1618, and again by Charles I in 1633, permitted various sports and recreations on Sundays and other holy days, including ‘May games’, ‘Whitsun ales’ (parish celebrations at Whitsuntide involving ale-drinking and other entertainments) and, in 1633, ‘wakes’. It was published in order to resolve a dispute that had arisen in Lancashire between puritans and gentry.
hobby-horses: Figures of horses in morris-dancing. tabors: Small drums. crowds: Fiddles. barley-breaks: A flirtatious game of ‘catch’, in which one couple chases two other couples.
Gladiators: Here, professional swordsmen or fencers.
deboshed: See above, n. 66 (DJR). relish: Understand, or regard.
Evil is not to be done … of it: See above, n. 31 (1.4.1).
Roman Saturnals: See above, n. 309 (DJR).
Philippus Bonus … Burgundy: See above, n. 201 (DJR).
snorting on a Bulk: Snoring on a shop stall.

Antiochus Epiphanes: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes (c. 215–164 BCE). The following story originates in Polybius (26.10), where he is called ‘Epimanes’ (‘the Madman’) because of his eccentric behaviour. Clown: See above, n. 187 (1.2.3).

those that Phidias made of old: The Athenian sculptor Phidias (fl. c. 465–425 BCE) was especially renowned for two statues: the Athena Parthenos on the Athenian Acropolis and the Zeus at Olympia. These were made from gold and ivory, and embellished with jewels, silver and glass. molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

Francesco Francia’s pieces: The Bolognese painter, goldsmith and medallist, whose real name was Francesco Raibolini (c. 1447–1517). Architectures: Architectural drawings. Devices: Emblems or heraldic designs. Scutcheons: Or ‘Escutcheons’, shields depicting coats of arms. perspective glasses: Here, probably mirrors that produce optical illusions – see above, n. 167 (DJR).

Cabinets: Rooms in which collections of works of art and objects of curiosity were exhibited. the great Dukes in Florence: The grand dukes of Tuscany – in this period, of the Medici dynasty. of Felix Platerus in Basel: The Swiss physician Felix Plater (1536–1614) had a herbarium and a famous collection of curiosities at his home in Basel. Dutch-works: See above, n. 36 (1.3.1). cuts: Woodcuts. Sadeler … Vrients: This list of Flemish and German engravers, in which Dürer was by far the most famous, includes Gilles Sadeler (1570–1629), who spent most of his career in Prague in the service of the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II; Hendrik Goltzius (1558–1617); and Jan-Baptista Vrients (1552–1612). Indian pictures made of feathers: These were among the several adaptations of traditional Amerindian handicrafts brought to Europe by the Spanish in this era. China works: Porcelain. frames: Probably decoratively carved picture frames. Thaumaturgical motions: Devices showing magical illusions.
junkets: Cakes, confectionery or any sweet dishes.
Libanius the Sophister: The renowned pagan Greek rhetorician Libanius (314–93 CE).

that Geometrical tower … in Italy: The Torre Garisenda, the smaller and apparently ‘leaning’ one of the ‘Two Towers’ of Bologna, built in the early twelfth century. the steeple and clock at Strasbourg: Strasbourg Cathedral’s high north tower, built in the early fifteenth century, and its astronomical clock, built in the mid-sixteenth century. corrivate: See above, n. 9 (1.1.2).
Chaldee: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2).
Charles the great: See above, n. 265 (DJR).

Americus Vesputius … Lod. Vertomannus, Aloysius Cadamustus: Italian explorers: Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512); Ludovico di Varthema (c. 1470–1517), famous for his journey to Mecca and his travels around Persia and India; and
Alvise da Cadamosto (c. 1428–83), credited with the discovery of the Cape Verde Islands and various places on the Guinea coast of West Africa.
accurate: Carefully made. Bartison: See above, n. 5 (2.2.3). Oliver à Nort: The explorer Olivier van Noord (1568–1627), the first Dutchman to circumnavigate the world.
dials: Sundials – or possibly nautical compass roses, as depicted on maps.

Epaminondas, Pelopidas: Two ancient Theban generals idealized for their courage and virtue: on Epaminondas, see above, n. 166 (1.2.3); Pelopidas (c. 410–364 BCE) contributed to the famous victory over the Spartans at Leuctra (371 BCE) and was killed in the Theban defeat of Alexander of Pherae at Cynoscephalae. Hercules or Bacchus: In classical mythology, Heracles (Hercules) was conceived, born and raised in Thebes (his mother was Alcmene, the wife of the Theban king Amphitryon). Dionysus (Bacchus) was the son of the Theban mortal Semele and was said to have invaded and conquered India.

in imitation of Alexander: The account of the visit of James I to Oxford given by the university’s public orator Isaac Wake in Rex Platonicus (1607), the work cited in note ‘b’, portrays the king as imitating Alexander the Great ‘both in purpose and in voice’ while he strolled through the library.
as Aesop’s Cock … dunghill: In the fable of ‘The Cock and the Jewel’.
Lecture: Lectureship.

Munificent Ptolemys: The Egyptian king Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367/6–282 BCE) founded both the library of Alexandria (although that was mostly built in the reign of his successor Ptolemy II Philadelphus) and the encompassing scholarly research institution known as the Musaeum. bountiful Maecenates: See above, n. 111 (DJR). our public Academies: The universities of Europe – in light of the reference here to their presence in ‘most Cities’, which suggests that Burton may also be thinking of learned societies on the continent. our private Colleges: That is, the colleges of the universities and religious institutions in England.

Otho Nicholson: See above, n. 11 (DJR). the right reverend John Williams … Lincoln: The bishop of Lincoln and dean of Westminster, John Williams (1582–1650), who became archbishop of York in 1641, donated several thousand pounds to St John’s College, Cambridge, and Lincoln College, Oxford, for their libraries. He also paid for the redecoration of the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster Abbey, and endowed the library there with manuscripts, books and bookcases. The phrase ‘in Fieri’ in this passage means ‘proceeding’, or more literally, ‘in the process of being made’; ‘corporate towns’ are those that act by means of a corporation and have municipal rights.
Amadis de Gaul … Huon of Bordeaux, &c.: Chivalric romances of the kind satirized in Don Quixote – see above, n. 249 (1.2.3).

Nepenthes: An Egyptian drug mentioned in the Odyssey (4.220–21), and said to relieve sorrow and mental pain. alterative: A type of drug thought to change the bodily temperament. diverter: A drug thought to alter the course of the humoral flow. plashed: Intertwined, to create an overarching cover.
Paul bids Pray continually: 1 Thessalonians 5:17.
Ferdinand and Alphonsus kings of Aragon and Sicily: Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452–1516) and Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458), who was also Alfonso I of Sicily. take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR).
Laurence Medices: Lorenzo de’ Medici (1449–92).

Niceratus in Xenophon: In Xenophon’s Symposium (3.5), the character of Niceratus, who was an Athenian naval commander in 410/9 BCE, says that his father Nicias – on whom, see below, n. 190 (3.4.1) – forced him to memorize all of Homer.

Qui quid sit pulchrum … dicunt: This quotation from Horace (Epistles 1.2.3–4) refers to two Greek philosophers, both from Soli in Cilicia and renowned for their
focus on ethics: the Stoic Chrysippus (c. 280–207 BCE) and the Platonist Crantor (c. 335–275 BCE), the latter being known particularly for his consolatory work On Grief.
corroboratives: Medications that fortify the body. lenitives: See above, n. 2 (2.2.2).
humane and divine authors: See above, n. 28 (DJR). Brachygraphy: Shorthand, stenography.

diverb: Proverb, or proverbial expression. Colossus: The Colossus of Rhodes. In note ‘e’, the weight is given in pounds, and is calculated from the report of the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes the Confessor (d. 817/18 CE), who says that after being melted down by Arab invaders, its metal was loaded on to 900 camels (one camel was traditionally said to be able to carry 1,200 lb.). Domitian’s Amphitheatre: The Colosseum, the building of which was begun by Vespasian and continued by Titus; probably only the arena’s substructures were built in the reign of Domitian.
the 23 letters: See above, n. 88 (1.3.1). complicated: Combined, mixed together.
apogeums, perigeums: Apogees and perigees: the points at which a planet is, respectively, at its greatest and smallest distance from the earth. eccentricities: See above, n. 63 (2.2.3).

Archytas’ Dove: Archytas of Tarentum – see above, n. 204 (DJR) – was said to have made a self-propelling wooden bird. Albertus’ Brazen head: The medieval German philosopher and theologian Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280 CE) was reputed to have owned a magical brass head, a mythical automaton capable of answering any question posed to it.

Baptista Porta … Mydorgius: References to the philosopher and polymath Giovan Battista della Porta (1535–1615), who had a public dispute with Galileo over who had first invented the telescope; the astronomer and mathematician Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), another of Galileo’s rivals who worked with telescopes; and the mathematician Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), who had strong interests in optics and astronomy, and who commissioned the production of many different kinds of lenses, including those used in telescopes.
Otacousticons: See above, n. 180 (DJR). intend: See above, n. 35 (1.1.1).

Rosy Cross men: See above, n. 283 (DJR). Geber, Lullius, Bacon: References to pseudo-Geber – see above, n. 204 (DJR); the Catalan Franciscan philosopher, theologian and mystic Ramon Llull (or Lull, 1232–1316); and Roger Bacon – see above, n. 26 (1.3.3).

Crollius: the German alchemist and professor of medicine at Marburg, Oswald Croll (1563–1609). aurum fulminans, or aurum volatile: ‘Fulminate of gold’, which Croll called ‘aurum volatile’ – an explosive precipitate produced by adding ammonia to a solution of auric chloride. Cornelius Drebbel: The famous Dutch inventor and engineer Cornelis Jacobszoon Drebbel (1572–1633). linum non ardens: Incombustible linen was first invented, according to Pliny the Elder (19.4), in the deserts of ancient India. petards: Small bombs made of a metal or wooden box filled with gunpowder.

another Tract of Mumia: According to Paracelsus, the ‘mumia’ (also referred to as ‘mummia’ or ‘mummy’) was an immaterial vital substance in the body that served as the vehicle of the vital life force (‘archeus’), and was capable of warding off disease or injury. Alexipharmacum: Antidote for poison; originally for snake-bite but, according to some medieval and Renaissance writers, for any noxious substance or debilitating condition.
Martial Amulets: Amulets said to protect against poisoning, which was associated with the influence of Mars. unguentum armarium: See above, n. 24 (1.2.3).

Napier’s Logarithms: The Scottish mathematician John Napier (1550–1617) first published his discovery of logarithms in his Mirifici logarithmorum canonis
descriptio (1614). those tables of artificial Sines … division: The mathematician Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), one of Burton’s friends at Christ Church, presented the first table of logarithms of trigonometrical functions, calling them ‘artificial sines and tangents’, in his Canon triangulorum (1620). These superseded the tables of tangents, computed from tables of sines by division, produced by the German mathematician Johann Müller (Regiomontanus, 1436–76). his Sector, Quadrant and Cross-staff: The work referred to in note ‘c’, Gunter’s De sectore & radio (1623), discussed the use of various mathematical instruments, including the geometrical figure of the sector for various problems, the quadrant for angular measurements in geometry or astronomy, and the cross-staff for calculating the altitude of the sun or a star.
Ephemerides: A collection of astronomical tables, showing the predicted positions of stars and planets for each day in a given period.

Impresses: Devices or emblems, often with accompanying verses. Epithalamiums: Wedding poems or songs praising the bride and groom. Chronograms: Inscriptions or sentences in which a date or epoch is expressed by the numerical values of letters. Aelia Laelia Crispis: The first line of what was apparently a Roman funerary inscription on the ‘Bologna Stone’, which was discovered near the city in the mid-sixteenth century and of great interest to Renaissance alchemists and hermeticists. Tot tibi sunt dotes … caelo: The verse quoted in note ‘e’ is taken from a work of ‘combinatorial’ poetry, in which the word order of an invented line of verse is multiply varied. This one was composed and given 1,022 variations by the Flemish Jesuit Bernardus Bauhusius, in a volume of poetry edited in 1617 by the scholar Erycius Puteanus (‘Putean’). Rainnerus of Luneburg: Actually the poet Heinrich Reimers (Reimarus) of Lüneberg, author of Proteus poeticus (1619), which presents 2,150 variations of the verse quoted in note ‘f’. Chrysolithus: Probably the pseudonym of Carol Goldstein, another combinatorial poet and author of Versum quem Protea Poeticum vocant (1618).
Cut-works: Embroidery or appliqué. bone lace: Fine lace made using threads wound on bone or ivory bobbins.
pelf: Here, valuable objects or material possessions.
beads: See above, n. 121 (DJR).
mediocrity: See above, n. 84 (1.2.3).
molesting: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
competent: Adequate.
fascinations: Spells or enchantments.
hollows: See above, n. 84 (1.3.1).

arches, falls of water, like London Bridge: In the seventeenth century, the tidal ebb and flow of the River Thames under London Bridge was restricted by its multiple narrow arches and wide pier bases. The allusion here is to the sound of gushing water when the levels on either side were substantially different. available: See above, n. 6 (2.1.2).
frications: See above, n. 5 (2.2.4). a good draught of muscadine, with a toast: That is, toasted bread dipped in muscadine – on which, see above, n. 30 (1.2.2).
fomentations: Medicinal applications to the surface of the body of flannels soaked in hot water, or of other warm and soft substances.
Incubus: See above, n. 32 (1.1.1) and n. 60 (1.2.1).
as he said in Lucian: The narrator Tychiades, who is told a series of superstitious stories in Lucian’s Lover of Lies, or The Doubter. Hecates: See above, n. 22 (1.2.4).
when Ptolemy King of Egypt had posed the 70 interpreters … daytime: In this tale about Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE), ‘posed’ means ‘questioned’ or ‘interrogated’.
Morpheus: In classical mythology, the god who sends dream visions of human forms, and one of the sons of Hypnos (or Somnus), the god of sleep.
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

his furious desires carry him from Lyceus … to Athens: This paraphrase of a passage from the Neoplatonist philosopher Maximus of Tyre (second century CE) refers to details from the life and career of the famously ambitious Alcibiades – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3). In Plato’s portrayal, Alcibiades frequented the Athenian gymnasium, which was located in the Lyceum, with his friend Socrates; the other places mentioned here refer to his exile and military exploits abroad. Critias tyrannizeth … city: Critias (c. 460–403 BCE) was one of the ‘Thirty Tyrants’ of Athens, a notoriously oppressive oligarchy that wielded power there in 404–403, after the Peloponnesian War. Sardanapalus is lovesick: The legendary Assyrian ruler (said to have lived in the seventh century BCE) was often portrayed as archetypally licentious and pleasure-seeking.
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
fond: See above, n. 103 (DJR).
default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
an upright shoe … on the other side: An ‘upright shoe’ is one that fits either foot, and is transferable from one to the other when it wears down.
let the moving faculty overrule her: Being commanded, that is, by the will in the rational soul – see above, 1.1.2.8 and 1.1.2.11.
admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
mandrake wine: Wine infused with mandragora root: see above, n. 160 (1.2.4).

Democritus’ Collyrium: The ‘collyrium’ (eye salve) was actually named after the ancient Greek physician Demosthenes Philalethes, who was a renowned ophthalmologist active in the first half of the first century CE.
exonerating: Unburdening.
available: See above, n. 6 (2.1.2).
he and he: One and the other, both of them. that old man in the Comedy: Chremes, in Terence’s Self-Tormentor (574–5).
semper habens Pylademque … Orestem: In Greek mythology, Pylades was the companion and cousin of Orestes – for whom, see above, n. 119 (DJR). His name was proverbial for a close and faithful friend.
by occasion of: Because of. Charles Duke of Burgundy … perplexed: See above, n. 7 (2.1.2)
witty: See above, n. 49 (DJR).
alienate: Divert, distract.
secure: See above, n. 327 (DJR).
aspects: Sights, appearances.
manned by art, and animated: Trained to seat a rider, and encouraged. generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR). away with: Bear, endure.

green: Fresh. good Chirurgeons, bold Empirics: See above, nn. 75, 76 (DJR). a horse starts at a rotten post afar off: At night time, that is, because of the phosphorescence emitted by certain kinds of fungi that grow on rotting wood (‘rotten posts’ are sometimes mentioned alongside glow-worms in contemporary sources).
