those Roman Matrons … breathe out their last: In A Reply to the Address of Symmachus (1091–1101), the Roman Christian writer Prudentius criticizes the
Vestal Virgins, who had privileged seats at the gladiatorial shows, for delighting in the deaths of the combatants.
proud Jacks: Vulgar commoners, ‘knaves’ (‘Jacks’ here refers to hypothetical ordinary people).
stupid: See above, n. 38 (1.2.3).
dehort: See above, n. 23 (1.4.1).

Socrates in Plato … eyes: In the Charmides (156B–157E), the headache of the eponymous character (Plato’s uncle) serves to introduce the doctrine, frequently referred to by Renaissance authors, that the cure of the soul is necessary for the cure of the body; this is attributed to the Thracian king Zalmoxis, who is usually referred to as a god in classical sources; see below, n. 68 (3.4.1).

that true Nepenthes of Homer: See above, n. 95 (2.2.4). Epidamna Thonis’ wife: Actually Polydamna, wife of the Egyptian nobleman Thon. Helena’s bowl, Medea’s unction, Venus’ Girdle, Circe’s Cup: Magical enchantments from classical mythology: the bowl of wine into which Helen of Troy poured nepenthe, before giving it to her husband, the Spartan king Menelaus, and his companions in the Odyssey; the herbal concoction used by Medea to bring Aeson, father of her husband Jason, back to life as a young man; the girdle, possessing the power to inspire love, given by Hephaestus (Vulcan) to Aphrodite (Venus); and the cup of Circe, filled with a potion that turned Odysseus’ companions into swine.

Maximus the Philosopher: Maximus of Ephesus (fourth century CE), who encouraged the emperor Julian to renew the pagan religion by infusing it with Platonism. Paeon: An ancient Greek god of healing, and often one of the epithets of Apollo (‘Apollo the Healer’). He also appears in the Iliad as the physician to the gods.
Chremes … Menedemus: See above, n. 65 (DJR).

Q. Fabius Maximus … ague: The consul Quintus Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus defeated the Gallic tribe of the Allobrogians at the mouth of the River Isère in southwestern France (not the Isaurus, which is now the Foglia in northern Italy) in 121 BCE.
an Advocate of Paris before mentioned: See, 1.3.1.3, p. 392.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
roaring meg: Large cannon – the term comes from the name of the great fifteenth-century cannon, now more commonly known as ‘Mons Meg’, at Edinburgh Castle.
animates: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3).

Hercules Gallus, Orpheus, and Amphion: Mythological figures associated with the powers of speech and music: Hercules Gallicus (or Ogmius), the Gallic god of eloquence, who civilized the populace by rhetorical persuasion; Orpheus, who tamed wild animals and moved trees and rocks with his lyre; and Amphion, son of Zeus and Antiope, who helped to build the citadel at Thebes by charming the stones into place with his golden lyre. stocks and stones: The context suggests that tree-stumps and stones may be meant literally, but this phrase was also used to refer contemptuously to pagan idols, or ‘gods of wood and stone’.
Arion … follow him: See above, n. 77 (1.2.1).

in Lydia in the midst of a lake … dance: The German scholar Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa refers in his De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533) to the account given by the Roman scholar Varro of the Lydian ‘Islands of the Nymphs’ in Lake Koloe (now Marmara Gölü) near Sardis. At the sound of flutes, these ‘islands’ – actually floating reed-beds – moved out into the middle of the lake and danced around before returning to the shore.
Apollonius: See above, n. 55 (DJR).

Ismenias the Theban: A famous flute-player of the fourth century BCE. According to Boethius in the Principles of Music, Ismenias’ music cured the maladies of many of his fellow Boeotians, who had been particularly tormented by sciatica. St. Vitus’ Bedlam dance: See above, 1.1.1.4.

Timotheus the Musician: Timotheus of Thebes, a musician frequently confused in the Renaissance with the citharist and poet Timotheus of Miletus, who also lived in the fourth century BCE. the tale of the Friar and the Boy: A sixteenth-century English ballad, in which an old man gives a magical pipe with the power to induce uncontrollable dancing to a young boy, who uses it to take revenge on his stepmother and her accomplice, a friar.

Asclepiades the Physician: Asclepiades of Bithynia, active in Rome in the early first century BCE, and famous for advocating musical therapy for mental illness. Cleinias and Empedocles: The Pythagorean philosopher Cleinias of Tarentum (fourth century BCE) was said to have assuaged his anger with a lyre. According to Boethius (The Principles of Music 1), Empedocles – on whom, see above, n. 92 (DJR) – calmed the anger of a young man, who had been intent on killing one of his dinner guests, by changing the musical mode of the singing at the feast.

Homer brings in Phemius playing: In the first book of Homer’s Odyssey, the Ithacan singer Phemius performs in the house of the absent Odysseus, upsetting Penelope with a song about the return of the Greek heroes from Troy.
liberal sciences: See above, n. 7 (DJR).

Gnaeus Manlius: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, Roman consul in 189 BCE. According to Livy (39.6), after defeating the Galatians in Asia Minor, Vulso’s soldiers were corrupted by the luxurious booty which they brought back to Rome. Anno ab urb. cond. 567: Literally, ‘567 years since the founding of the city’ (in 753 BCE), so in 186 BCE.
absolute: See above, n. 51 (DJR).
concent: Harmony of sounds.

Ionic and Lydian tunes: The ancient Greek Ionic (or Ionian) and Lydian modes were associated with cheerful and effeminate music. have a ––––––: The omission mark refers to the favours from the women of Paris, which, according to the French diplomat and historian Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), were included in the promises made by King Louis XI to Edward IV of England during the negotiations for the Treaty of Picquigny in 1475. In the event, Edward settled for a payment of 75,000 crowns.
Sonnets: Songs or ballads.
a free horse: That is, one that is already willing or keen to go.

Astolpho’s horn in Ariosto: See above, n. 347 (DJR). Mercury’s golden wand in Homer: In classical mythology, Hermes (Mercury) gave his lyre – the gift of music – to Apollo, who in return gave him a golden wand or ‘caduceus’, a winged staff entwined with two serpents, which possessed various magical powers and was later associated with the healing power of physicians.
prorogues: Extends.

the three Salernitan Doctors … Dr. Quiet: A quotation from Sir John Harington’s 1607 translation of the Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a didactic medical poem attributed (possibly inaccurately) to the renowned medieval medical school of Salerno in southern Italy.
patron: See above, n. 121 (1.2.1).

pieces: Women or girls. ‘Pieces’ here is probably used in a non-derogatory sense – cf. n. 8 (1.2.4) above – although some scholars believe that at least some of the women in the circle of Epicurus were originally prostitutes.
cock-horse: A stick with a horse’s head, or hobby-horse.

Valorous Scipio and gentle Laelius: Two Roman statesmen reported by Cicero to be close friends. On Scipio Aemilianus, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) and n. 87 (1.2.4); Gaius Laelius (b. c. 190 BCE) acquired his nickname ‘Sapiens’ (‘the Wise’) because of his reputation for political prudence, but Cicero connected it to his philosophical interests.
Machiavel in the 8th book … in him: See above, n. 343 (DJR); ‘note’ here means ‘reproach’.

as Themistocles … carriage: Plutarch (Themistocles 2) describes the passage of the Athenian politician and general Themistocles (c. 524–460 BCE) from youthful intemperance to ambitious public service, although this may be an allusion to Aelian (Historical Miscellany 2.12), who also remarks on his enthusiastic dedication to Athenian politics.

Castruccius Castrucanus: The condottiere and duke of Lucca, Castruccio Castracani degli Antelminelli (1281–1328). cushion-dance: A wedding dance, in which the women and men take turns to kneel on a cushion and be kissed.

Lucretia toto sis … volo: In the quotation from Martial (Epigrams 11.104.21–3) in note ‘d’, Burton has replaced the courtesan Lais – on whom, see above, n. 158 (1.2.4) – with Thais, a fictional character mocked elsewhere by Martial for her ugliness and loose morals, and named after another famous Greek prostitute (Martial himself refers to substituting the two names in Epigrams 3.11.3). On Lucretia, see above, n. 48 (1.2.3).
which was used in Thessaly … laughter himself: See above, n. 37 (1.2.4).
facete: See above, n. 35 (1.2.4).

Ctesias reports of a Persian king … by turns: This anecdote, related by Athenaeus (The Learned Banqueters 12.530D) from the Greek historian Ctesias (late fifth century BCE), refers to the Babylonian satrap Nanarus, who was the viceroy under Artaeus, an early king of the Medes. Lil. Giraldus of an Egyptian prince … Muses: The Italian scholar Giglio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552) took this tale from the account given by Diodorus Siculus of an ancient Egyptian prince called Osiris (Library of History 1.18.4).
Sophies: The Persian emperors of the Safavid dynasty. Moguls: See above, n. 72 (1.2.2).
curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR).

Si Numerus … jocisque: In this quotation from Horace (Epistles 1.6.65–6), ‘Numerus’ should actually be ‘Mimnermus’ – a Greek elegiac poet and symposiast of the seventh century BCE who was renowned for his love poetry.

rings: Proclaims aloud. Modern editors have sometimes emended this to ‘brings’, but the sense and imperative mood of the subsequent quotations suggest that Burton has in mind the spoken advice of physicians to their patients.
goodfellows: Carousers, revellers.
Volupia, Rumina, Edulica, Potina, Mellona: The Roman goddesses of (respectively) sensual pleasure, suckling, children’s nourishment, drinking, and bees and honey.

Philoxenus’ neck: The legendary late-fifth century BCE Greek gourmand and poet Philoxenus of Leucas was ridiculed in classical comedy for praying for a long tongue and a neck like a crane, in order to increase the pleasures of eating and drinking. Jupiter’s trinoctium: The space of three nights in which Zeus (Jupiter) slept with Alcmene, who thereby conceived Heracles (Hercules). that the Sun … Joshua’s time: A reference to God’s granting of Joshua’s request to give the Israelite army more time to defeat the Amorites (Joshua 10:12–13).
Timocreon of Rhodes: A Greek poet of the early fifth century BCE, most of whose verses were probably recited at drinking parties (symposia).

calentures: Deliriums – cf. above, n. 77 (1.2.2). complexions: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Funges: See above, n. 151 (DJR). Casks: Hollow shells or empty-headed people – as well as barrels for holding liquor.

a terrible battle … killed: An episode from the brief intersection of the Hundred Years War between England and France with the first Castilian Civil War (1351–69), fought between Pedro the Cruel (also known as Pedro the Just) and his illegitimate brother, Count Enrique of Trastámara. After the former had been deposed, in 1367, the army of the latter, a French ally, was defeated at Nájera by the forces of Edward of Woodstock (the ‘Black Prince’, and son of King Edward III of England).

As Hermione lamented … malam: In the Andromache of Euripides, Hermione plots to kill the child of Andromache and Neoptolemus (now Hermione’s husband) out of jealousy. In the line quoted here (946), she blames her wrongdoing on women in her household who stoked up her passion. For Andromache and Neoptolemus, see above, n. 135 (DJR).
except: See above, n. 21 (DJR).
paraenetical: Advisory, admonitory.
orbities: Losses of children.
Glycypicron: Cf. 1.1.1.5, p. 149.
Bellona’s whips: Bellona, the ancient Roman goddess of war, was often depicted riding into battle with a whip or torch. Epithalamiums: See above, n. 115 (2.2.4).

Grave nihil … an old Poet: The line quoted here is a fragment of the Hypsipyle of Euripides, taken from Plutarch’s Letter of Condolence to Apollonius (16). The similar quotation of Euripides used by Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations (4.29) is actually from the Orestes.

as Minucius Felix the Roman Consul … adverse: According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 8.22–8), the Roman statesman Marcus Minucius Augurinus (consul in 497 and 491 BCE), here confused with the author Minucius Felix, was the leader and spokesman of the Roman legation sent to halt Coriolanus’ attack on the city in 488.

even to that happiness of Augustus: A reference to the ancient Roman ‘Felicitas Augusti’, a goddess said to have accompanied the emperor on his enterprises, bringing him good happiness and fortune. The phrase also featured on Roman coins, denoting the peace and prosperity of the empire. Burton here seems to allude to the violent deaths of many of the emperors, or perhaps more generally to the fall of the Roman Empire. Almoner: An official who distributes alms or charitable donations. Pluto’s Treasurer: That is, Plutus’ treasurer – see above, n. 116 (1.2.3).
Alcibiades’… Gonsalvus’ fortune: On these figures, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3); 1.2.4.4, p. 336; and 1.2.3.10, p. 273. default: See above, n. 14 (DJR). circumvented: See above, n. 336 (DJR).

Retrograde: See above, n. 86 (2.2.3). in Apogeo, Perigeo: See above, n. 105 (2.2.4). combust: See above, n. 63 (1.3.1). feral: Ungoverned by the influence of another planet, and on a course that has no conjunctions with other planets. fortitudes & debilities: Positions or circumstances which strengthen or diminish the influences of planets. terms: Parts of each of the signs of the zodiac, assigned to particular planets. case: A planet ‘in case’ is in declension, that is, in the sign opposite to its exaltation, and over which it exerts its greatest influence. detriments: Positions where planets are in the sign opposite their own house, when their influence is weak.
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
as the mouldwarp in Aesop … quiet: In the fable of ‘The Ass, the Ape and the Mole’; on ‘mouldwarp’, see above, n. 51 (1.2.4).

Endymion: There are different accounts of Endymion in classical mythology. Some sources identify him as the king of Elis, who desired Hera (Juno) and was punished by Zeus (Jupiter) by being made to fall asleep for eternity; others refer to him as a hunter or a shepherd from Caria, desired by the moon goddess Selene, who obtained a wish for him from Zeus, and his choice was for eternal sleep in youth and immortality.

that of our Apostle … loveth: Paul, identified in the King James Bible as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, which is quoted here (12:6); this attribution, however, was a matter of ongoing dispute.
as gold in the fire: An allusion to 1 Peter 1:7.
ingeminates: See above, n. 4 (2.2.2).

as it was said to Hagar in the wilderness: The Egyptian slave Hagar was given as a wife by Sarah to Abraham and mistreated by her before bearing Abraham’s son Ishmael (Genesis 16:1–16). vindicate: Protect, or support.

Cornelius Mussus: Cornelio Musso (1511–74), bishop of Bitonto, whose renown as a rhetorically accomplished preacher earned him nicknames such as ‘the modern Demosthenes’ and ‘the Chrysostom [literally, “golden mouth”] of Italy’.

Hannibal had one eye: Hannibal lost his right eye after contracting an infection while crossing the Arno marshes in 217 BCE. Appius Claudius: Appius Claudius Caecus, Roman censor in 312 BCE and builder of the Appian Way, who acquired his cognomen Caecus (‘the Blind’) from his blindness in old age. Timoleon: The Greek ruler and military commander Timoleon of Corinth, who reportedly resigned his generalship because of blindness in 337 BCE. Muleasses king of Tunis: Muley Hassan (d. 1545 CE), said by Cervantes to have had his eyes burned out with hot irons by his son, who dethroned and imprisoned him in 1542. John king of Bohemia: John of Bohemia (1296–1346 CE) famously fought and died at the Battle of Crécy in 1346, having been blind for ten years.
evirated: Castrated.
Angelus Politianus: The renowned Italian scholar and poet Agnolo Ambrogini (1454–94), more commonly known as Angelo Poliziano. tetter: Pustular eruption. fulsome: Disgusting, nauseating.
purblind: Partially blind or short-sighted.

Marsilius Ficinus, Faber Stapulensis … Melanchthon: Three major figures of the Renaissance scholarly world: the Italian Neoplatonist philosopher Marsilio Ficino (1433–99); the French humanist scholar and theologian Jacques Lefevre d’Étaples (c. 1450–1536); and the German Lutheran theologian and philosopher Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560).
beads: See above, n. 121 (DJR).

Agesilaus: Agesilaus II, king of Sparta (400–359 BCE), was born lame in one leg, but famed for his typically Spartan military bravery and efficiency; cf. below, n. 37 (3.2.2). Bocchoris: Or Bakenranef, ruler of Lower Egypt (c. 720–715 BCE), traditionally regarded as a sage and great legislator.

Vladislaus Cubitalis: King Władysław the Elbow-High of Poland (1261–1333), whose military successes included the reconquest of Lesser Poland and parts of Gdansk Pomerania. His Polish nickname ‘Łokietek’ means ‘Little Elbow’ or ‘Little Ell’, the łokieć being a unit of measurement worth twenty-four inches. The Latin name ‘Cubitalis’ refers to the similarly small cubit – on which, see above, n. 271 (DJR).

Otus and Ephialtes … nine acres long: The ‘Aloads’ in Greek mythology, two giants who attempted to confront the gods by piling Mount Ossa on Olympus and then Mount Pelion on Ossa. In the Odyssey (11.305–20), they are said to have grown by the age of nine to a height of nine fathoms (sixty-four feet, or nearly twenty metres), which is substantially less than the ‘nine acres long’ (590 feet, or 180 metres) stated here.

Qui ut magnus Orion … undas: This passage from Virgil’s Aeneid (10.763–5) refers to the famously beautiful and gigantic mythical hunter Orion – who was sometimes said to be a son of Poseidon (Neptune) – and to the old sea-god Nereus, a shape-changing son of Pontus (the mythological personification of the sea), and said to live in the depths of the sea. Maximinus … Caligula: The great size of the Roman emperor Maximinus Thrax (Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, 172/3–238
CE) is noted in the Augustan History (28); the Iliad describes Ajax as a man of colossal size, and the strongest Achaean soldier; and the emperor Gaius Caligula (12–41), according to Suetonius (50), was very tall. those great Zamzummims, or gigantical Anakims: Biblical giants who inhabited Palestine (Deuteronomy 2:20–21). lubbers: Large, clumsy and stupid people.
Jovianus Pontanus: See above, n. 58 (1.2.1).
contain: Maintain chastity.

Bilibaldus Pirkimerus: Willibald Pirckheimer (1470–1530) was a councillor and ambassador of the important imperial city of Nuremberg (‘ruled’ here means ‘counselled’ or ‘guided’, rather than ‘governed’). He was also a lawyer, humanist scholar and friend of Dürer.

Simon in Lucian … Simonides: This vignette from Lucian’s Dream, or The Cock (14) refers to the high social standing denoted in ancient Greece by the patrilineal suffix -ides (literally, ‘son’ or ‘descendant of’).
scutcheons: See above, n. 78 (2.2.4).
outsides: See above, n. 115 (DJR). match with them: Be equal to them.
gentry: See above, n. 112 (1.2.2).

Tiberius preferred … drinkers: According to Suetonius (42), after spending two days feasting and drinking with his plebeian friends Lucius Pomponius Flaccus and Lucius Calpurnius Piso, the emperor Tiberius made the former the governor of Syria and the latter the prefect of the city of Rome. Suetonius also says that he awarded the quaestorship to an obscure candidate because he had risen to the emperor’s challenge of drinking a whole amphora of wine at a banquet. parchment row: Or ‘parchment people’, a loose rendering of the phrase ‘regnum carthaceum’ (‘paper kingdom’) from Johann Valentin Andreae’s satirical Menippus (1618), where the mockery is directed at those who arrogantly flaunt their learning after a little reading. Here, the sense is apparently of people whose claims to social standing rest purely on genealogical documents; the phrase ‘paper kingdom’, however, is used to mock scholarly pretension in DJR, p. 24.
a cracked piece: A morally or physically impaired woman (with the connotation of a sexual object).
form: The nest or lair of a hare – and so here, figuratively, the origin.
infra quatuor maria: That is, within the British Isles.
a lawyer, & then a –––––– a … gentleman: The self-bowdlerizing dashes in this passage are apparently designed to encourage readers to provide their own insults or expletives.
Those Roman knights … so much: In imperial Rome, a minimum census qualification of 400,000 sesterces was required for a Roman citizen to be included in the equestrian order.
fine for it: That is, pay a fee to purchase the title without its usual obligations.
mard: Turd.

Bends, fesses: Both heraldic devices (or ‘charges’) in the form of a band. A bend runs diagonally across a shield, from top right to bottom left – as seen from the bearer’s point of view – whereas a fess runs horizontally across its middle.
with a grace: Along with a short prayer or blessing. fustian: See above, n. 54 (DJR). mimical: See above, n. 11 (1.3.1).
a gull, a dizzard: See above, nn. 83, 96 (DJR).
coiners: Forgers, dissemblers.
brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR).
polls: Heads.
the Ragusian Commonwealth: The Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik), an independent maritime state. those Athenian Areopagites: Members of the Areopagus – see above, n. 307 (DJR).

Loysii, Manderini, literati, licentiati: Chinese magistrates: those who, in the terminology reported by the Italian Jesuit missionary Matteo Ricci (1552–1610), are given the title of ‘Lauye’ or ‘Lautie’ (signifying ‘mother’ or ‘father’), as well as mandarins, literati – on whom, see above, n. 303 (DJR) – and licentiates.

Cathesbeius Sultan of Egypt and Syria: Sultan Qaitbay (ruled 1468–96). All the Mamluks were emancipated slaves; Qaitbay was freed on the basis of his descent from the thirteenth-century Ayyubid Emir of Damascus, al-Ashraf Musa, and he subsequently ascended to power through the Mamluk military hierarchy.

That poor Spanish Pizarro … Anatillo: The Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro González (c. 1475–1541), marquess of Los Atavillos in Peru. Bashaws: See above, n. 162 (DJR). Pertinax, Philippus Arabs, Maximinus, Probus, Aurelius: Roman emperors said in various sources to have risen from provincial obscurity to political prominence through careers in the army: Publius Helvius Pertinax (126–93 CE), the son of a Ligurian freedman and emperor of Rome for three months in 193; Marcus Julius Philippus, or ‘Philip the Arab’, emperor 244–9, whose father is described in the Epitome of the Caesars (attributed to the historian Aurelius Victor) as being of lowly origin and the leader of a group of brigands; Maximinus Thrax, who, according to the Augustan History (1), was once a shepherd-boy from a semi-barbarous Thracian tribe; Marcus Aurelius Probus (emperor 276–82), whose father, according to the Epitome of the Caesars (35), was a rustic farmer; and the emperor Aurelian – on whom, see above, n. 276 (DJR) – who is reported by the Augustan History (3) to have come from a humble family.
Cato, Cincinnatus: Consuls in 195 and 460 BCE respectively; see above, n. 44 (2.2.4).

Pius secundus, Sixtus quintus, Johan. secundus, Nicholas quintus: Pius II (Enea Silvio Piccolomini), pope 1458–64, was born into an impoverished aristocratic family, and had worked as a farmer in his youth. Sixtus V, pope 1585–90, came from a poor family, and was said to have worked as a swineherd as a boy. John II, pope 533–5, was born into a Roman family about which little is known – it did own property on the Caelian Hill, but although his father had the aristocratic-sounding name ‘Proiectus’, he was probably not of senatorial rank. Nicholas V, pope 1447–55, was the son of a Ligurian physician who died when he was young.

Socrates, Virgil, Horace … natus: Socrates was the son of a stonemason; Virgil was said by Macrobius (Saturnalia 5.2.1) to have had a peasant father, although he is now known to have been born into an equestrian family; Horace’s father, who oversaw his education, was a freed slave.

The Kings of Denmark … bear: The bear ancestry of the eleventh-century Danish nobleman Ulf Thorgilsson, the father of King Sweyn II (c. 1019–76), was discussed in the Gesta Danorum of the medieval chronicler Saxo Grammaticus.

Alexander … bastards: Alexander the Great, according to Plutarch (Alexander 3), was rumoured to have been told by his mother Olympias of Epirus that the god Ammon was his real father. The identity of the mother of the Athenian politician and general Themistocles is uncertain, but she is reported by some sources to have been non-Athenian. The Numidian king Jugurtha (c. 160–104 BCE) was the illegitimate son of Mastanabal, who reigned 148–140 BCE. King Arthur, according to the medieval chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth, was the son of Uther Pendragon and Igraine, the wife of Uther’s enemy Gorlois. William the Conqueror was the son of Robert I, duke of Normandy (1000–1035 CE) and his mistress Herleva. The mother of the Athenian orator Demosthenes, according to his rival Aeschines (Against Ctesiphon 172), was a Scythian. According to a medieval legend, the theologians Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160) and Peter Comestor (d. c. 1178) were brothers, the illegitimate sons of an adulterous mother; the twelfth-century Italian monk and jurist Gratian was also included in this story, and Burton has perhaps confused him with the eminent lawyer Bartolo da
Sassoferrato (Bartolus, 1313–57), who did discuss the rights of bastards in detail. The father of Pope Adrian IV (born Nicholas Breakspear, c. 1100–1159), was the poor English clerk Robert de Camera, but nothing substantial is known about his mother, who probably died when he was young; his inclusion in this list may be an echo of early modern anti-Catholic propaganda.
Arpinas: An Arpinian, born in the provincial hill-town of Arpinum (Arpino), about seventy miles southeast of Rome.
Agathocles: Agathocles (361–288 BCE) – tyrant king of Syracuse, and from 305 the titular king of Sicily – whose father Carcinus had owned a pottery manufactory.

Iphicrates and Marius: The father of the important Athenian general Iphicrates (c. 415–c. 353 BCE) was a shoemaker; and, like Cicero, the famous Roman general and politician Gaius Marius was born in Arpinum.

Abdalonymus was a gardener … king of Syria: According to the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus (4.19–20), Abdalonymus (d. 312 BCE) was descended from one of the kings of Sidon, but was working there as a gardener. He was appointed king of Sidon by Alexander the Great after the Macedonian conquered the city and absorbed it into his empire in 332.
degeneres Neoptolemi: An allusion to Virgil (Aeneid 2.549), where Neoptolemus – on whom, see above, n. 135 (DJR) – describes himself as ‘degenerate’, before killing Priam during the sack of Troy.

Udalricus Earl of Cilia … the baseness of his birth: The Slovenian Ulrich II, count of Celje (1406–56 CE), and the Hungarian John Hunyadi (c. 1406–56) had a long-running feud. The doubtful allegation that Hunyadi was the illegitimate son of the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund was said by some commentators to have been manufactured by Ulrich.

quod prodest Pontice … censeri: In this quotation from Juvenal (Satires 8.1–2), the aristocratic Ponticus is a generic figure, although the name suggests someone descended from a general who had triumphed in the region of Pontus – for which, see above, n. 57 (DJR).

Thersites: See above, n. 107 (DJR). dum modo … Aeacidae similis: The grandson of Aeacus – on whom, see below, n. 10 (3.2.1) – referred to in this quotation from Juvenal (Satires 8.269–71) is Achilles. non natus, sed factus: A phrase borrowed from the theological commentator Ambrosiaster (Questions on the Old and New Testaments 81), where it refers to Christians.

Send them both … difference: The quotation in note ‘h’ from Francis Bacon’s essay ‘Of Cunning’ (1612) refers to Aristippus of Cyrene – on whom, see above, n. 97 (DJR). funge: See above, n. 151 (DJR). Polynices in his banishment: See above, n. 156 (1.2.4).

Tontonteac: Or ‘Tusayan’, a region inhabited by the Hopi people in present-day northern Arizona. villain: See above, n. 81 (1.2.4). Saldanian: From the Bay of Saldania, now Table Bay on the Cape peninsula of South Africa. Dasamonquepeuc: Dasamongueponke, a village then in Virginia (but now in North Carolina), and also the name of the Secotan people inhabiting the region. The term ‘Virginian’ might refer, alternatively, to a European colonial settler there.

terrae filius: Although here the classical phrase is being used generically, it was also the title of an official jester who customarily gave a satirical speech at the annual Oxford Act (the ceremony to mark the completion of degrees). insult at: Boast or brag insolently.
the Euxine sea: See above, n. 290 (DJR). default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
magnanimous: See above, n. 58 (1.1.1). currish: Like a cur – mean-spirited, quarrelsome.
as the cat in the fable … mice: In Aesop’s fable ‘The Cat and Venus’ (or ‘The Cat-Maiden’). likely: See above, n. 38 (DJR).
descried: See above, n. 3 (1.2.1). garb: See above, n. 166 (DJR). kickshaws: Fancy culinary dishes.

Hephaestion … Armies: Four generals under Alexander the Great, three of whom – the exception being Hephaestion – ascended to kingship. Antigonus I Monophthalmus (382–301 BCE) had served both Philip and Alexander before he proclaimed himself king of Macedon. On Hephaestion, Ptolemy and Seleucus, see above, n. 162 (1.2.3), n. 175 (DJR) and n. 127 (1.2.1).
ingenuously: Befitting a person of honourable standing.
Those Curii and Fabritii: See above, n. 93 (1.2.3).
bravely: See above, n. 47 (DJR).
Saturnal feasts: See above, n. 309 (DJR).

collogue: See above, n. 31 (DJR). as Seneca by Nero was served: Nero compelled Seneca, who had been his tutor and adviser, to commit suicide in 65 BCE, on the probably false suspicion that he had been involved in a failed conspiracy against the emperor. Sejanus by Tiberius: See above, n. 111 (1.2.3). Haman by Ahasuerus: The fate of Haman, counsellor of the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) – on whom, see above, n. 195 (DJR) – is described in Esther 5–7.
vindicate: See above, n. 284 (DJR). Craterus: See above, n. 15 (1.2.1).
Pactolus: See above, n. 5 (2.1.2).

mihi curto … Tarentum: Note ‘a’ is a quotation from Horace (Satires 1.6.104–5), in which the poet’s freedom to make a trip in as comically lowly a manner as he wishes is contrasted with the expectation placed upon the ambitious praetor Tillius – possibly a reference to Lucius Tillius Cimber, one of Julius Caesar’s assassins – that he should travel with an expensive entourage. In the previous satire (1.5), Horace describes a trip he made to Brundisium with his patron Maecenas – see above, n. 111 (DJR) – who probably went on to Tarentum to conclude a treaty between Mark Antony and Octavian.
Tartarian Chams: See above, n. 111 (1.2.4).
bawdy: See above, n. 3 (2.1.3). cloyed: Surfeited, satiated to the point of disgust.
success: See above, n. 135 (1.2.4).
Mr. Recorder: See above, n. 8 (DJR).

Nonius the Senator … sesterces: According to Pliny the Elder (37.21), Nonius (the son of Marcus Nonius Sufenas, quaestor in c. 62 BCE) was outlawed by Mark Antony for the sake of one of his rings, which contained a precious opal. Perox the Persian King … gold: In a story related by the Byzantine historian Procopius (History of the Wars 1.4), when Peroz I, king of Persia 459–84 CE, was about to fall into a deep trench dug by his Hephthalite (White Hun) enemies, he removed an enormous and valuable pearl (‘an union’) from his ear and discarded it, to prevent it being owned by anyone else.
tissues: Items of rich cloth, often embroidered with gold and silver.

Tartar Lamb’s-wool: See above, n. 25 (2.2.3). dyed in grain: Dyed in scarlet grain, or kermes, which was made from the dried bodies of scale insects found on the kermes oak in the Mediterranean region. a gown of Giants’ beards: Possibly a muddled allusion to the cloaks made of the beards of vanquished kings, as sometimes worn by the monstrous giants in Arthurian legend.
Dives: The name given in the Latin Vulgate to the rich man in the parable at Luke 16:19–31.

enforcing: Strengthening. naenias: A naenia (or nenia) was an ancient Roman funeral dirge with flute accompaniment. Ad generum Cereris … tyranni: Note ‘b’ quotes
Juvenal (Satires 10.112–13), where the son-in law of Ceres is Pluto – on whom, see above, n. 117 (DJR).

poor Lazarus … behind him: In the parable of ‘Lazarus and Dives’, told in Luke 16:19–31, after death the poor beggar Lazarus is comforted in heaven, and the unnamed rich man is tormented in hell. The name ‘Lazarus’ was sometimes used to refer generally to a beggar or a leper.

Crassus and Sulla … victories: The reference here is presumably to the military achievements of both Crassus and Sulla – on whom, see above, n. 103 (1.2.1) and n. 101 (1.2.3) – in the Social War (91–87 BCE) between Rome and its allies; they shared a famous victory against the Samnites at the Porta Collina in 82. Croesus for his end: After defeat and capture by the Persians in 546 BCE, King Croesus of Lydia was reputedly placed on a pyre to be burned to death, but was saved when Apollo extinguished the flames with a rainstorm.

Etiam servi diis curae sunt … sight: This allusion to the Saturnalia of Macrobius (1.11) inverts the opinion of the character Evangelus, who remarks on the absurdity of the idea that the gods might care about slaves.

parasangs: See above, n. 42 (DJR). Claudius his Narcissus, Nero’s Massa, Domitian’s Parthenius: Narcissus was a wealthy Greek freedman favoured by the Roman emperor Claudius; Baebius Massa was an informer and favourite of the emperor Domitian (not Nero); and Parthenius was the chamberlain of Domitian, associated with the latter’s assassination. curious: See above, n. 30 (2.2.4).

Amaltheae cornu: In classical mythology, Amalthea was the nymph who fed Jupiter with goat’s milk; alternatively, it was the name of the goat herself – one of whose horns was placed in the stars as the ‘Cornu Amaltheae’ or ‘Cornu Copiae’ (‘cornucopia’ or ‘horn of plenty’), from which nectar and ambrosia flowed. cinis aequat … at last: The saying attributed here to King Alfonso V of Aragon (1396–1458) derives from Seneca (Epistles 91.16), who notes that irrespective of the disparity between people’s funeral monuments, ‘their ashes level everyone’ (‘aequat omnes cinis’).

my nobility … tail: In this rendering of a witty insult recorded by the Italian jurist Giovanni Nevizzano in his Sylva nuptialis (1518), ‘tail’, like the Latin word cauda which it translates, refers both to the penis and to the train or tail-like part of a robe or coat.

whether Monarchies … absolute: See above, n. 23 (1.1.3). whether Peter were at Rome: In early Christian tradition, St Peter is said to have founded the Church at Rome, where along with St Paul he was martyred and buried. This belief, which was important in early modern Catholicism, had been disputed by Luther, who argued that the bodies of Peter and Paul were probably not in Rome, and that the Church there had most likely been founded by someone else well before Peter’s arrival. or Constantine’s donation be of force: The ‘Donation of Constantine’, the decree in which the emperor Constantine I (c. 275–337) transferred the authority of Rome and the Western Roman Empire to the papacy, had been shown to be an eighth-century forgery by the Italian humanist scholar and Catholic priest Lorenzo Valla (1407–57). This discovery was often cited by Protestant polemicists, although by Burton’s time the decree’s inauthenticity had been almost universally acknowledged by Catholics.
macerates: See above, n. 14 (DJR). swelling pelf: See above, n. 108 (DJR) and n. 121 (1.2.3).
Gyges regno Lydiae … contentus: On Gyges and Aglaus in note ‘a’, see above, n. 93 (1.2.3).
as Simonides objecteth to Hieron: See above, n. 206 (1.2.3). in lectis eburneis dormit … viol: Amos 6:4–6, where the prophet Amos is denouncing the complacent luxuriousness of Israel.
Loblolly: Thick gruel.
so far from giving thanks … Consul: See above, n. 111 (1.2.3).
Expect: Wait.

Rome … two myriads of inhabitants: In the Admiranda, sive de magnitudine Romana (1598), cited in note ‘g’, Justus Lipsius actually estimates the population of imperial Rome to have been 4 million. The figure of ‘two myriads’ (20,000) is perplexing; ‘myriad’ here may mean, very loosely, a million, or it may be a mistake. in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
humanity: See above, n. 28 (DJR).
Scaliger: The Scaligeri or Della Scala family, who had ruled in Verona and the Veneto mainland in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.
Maximinus: See above, nn. 11, 36 (2.3.2). Agathocles: See above, n. 43 (2.3.2). bare: Bare-headed (here, as a sign of respect).

Frescobald and Cromwell: After going bankrupt, the Florentine banker Francesco Frescobaldi (1495–c. 1535) was said to have been given money and a horse by his childhood friend, the English lawyer and royal minister Thomas Cromwell (c. 1485–1540). Frescobaldi had generously supported Cromwell earlier in life, who had risen from relatively humble origins as the son of a cloth merchant.
descents: Generations.
cells: Probably storerooms (such as granaries or animal stalls), rather than small private rooms or apartments.
Non est volentis … Dei: Romans 9:16.
Abraham’s servant … Isaac’s wife: Genesis 24. the Samaritan woman: John 4:4–26.
Choaspis that runs by Susa: See above, n. 8 (2.2.1) and n. 119 (2.2.3).

It was no Epicurean speech of an Epicure … have enough: The Roman Lucretius, who is quoted immediately below (‘Divitiae grandes … animo’), was a follower of Epicurus – but not, the suggestion is here, an ‘epicure’ devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure to excess.
Socrates in a Fair … not want: This is one of the anecdotes about Socrates recorded by Diogenes Laertius (2.5.25); ‘convented’ here means ‘assembled’.
kicked her up: Ejected her, kicked her out.
Son of Maia: Maia was the mother (by Jupiter) of Mercury.
Sebastian Foscarinus: The Venetian philosopher, nobleman and senator Sebastiano Foscarini (c. 1478–1552).

Lord Treasurer: Shortly after the publication of the first edition of the Anatomy in 1621, this post, which was one of most important and powerful in the English government (and had only recently returned from being held in commission to a single person), would be occupied by Lionel Cranfield, earl of Middlesex (1575–1645). On his minor contribution to the frustration of Burton’s pursuit of ecclesiastical patronage, see the editor’s Introduction.
prevented us of: That is, ‘obtained before us’.

Ulubrae: A small town in the Pontine marshes southeast of Rome, known for its decrepitude and depopulated state as well as its noisy frogs. It was eventually abandoned because of its unhealthy location.
Pyrrhus would first conquer Africk … folly: See above, n. 109 (1.2.3).
as Censorinus well writ to Cerellius: The Roman grammarian Censorinus (third century CE) addressed his work De die natali, quoted here, to his patron Quintus Caerellius.

mare ad Barbaros, Barbari ad mare … Barbarians: A quotation from the Groans of the Britons, the appeal made by the British to the Romans in the mid-fifth century CE for aid against the marauding Picts and Scots, and recorded by the sixth-century monk Gildas.

those lazy Philosophers: That is, philosophers in antiquity who propounded the so-called ‘Lazy’ or ‘Idle Argument’, which justifies total inactivity on the grounds
that everything is determined by fate. It was most famously refuted by the Stoic Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE), and criticized by Cicero among others.
as he said: The German theologian and satirist Johann Valentin Andreae, in his Menippus (1618).

When Crassus the Roman Consul … death: Marcus Licinius Crassus – see above, n. 103 (1.2.1) – who was consul in 70 BCE and again in 55, fled after the Roman defeat by the Parthians at Carrhae in 53. However his enemies captured him, and cut off his head and hands. The allusion to ‘Homer’s Mars’ refers to the bellow of Ares on being struck by the spear of Diomedes in the Iliad (5.855–61).

serpens, sitis … the better: The quotation is from the speech given by Cato the Younger – on whom, see above, n. 51 (1.1.1) – and reported in Lucan’s Civil War (9.402–3), to encourage his troops before their heroic march across Africa to join forces with King Juba I of Numidia.
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
the very hairs … numbered: Matthew 10:30.

The tyrant took the city … freed them: The tyrant referred to here is Nebuchadnezzar II (ruled c. 605–562 BCE), whose conquest of Jerusalem and subsequent actions are detailed in the Book of Daniel. In this homily addressed to the citizens of Antioch in 387 CE, John Chrysostom draws the parallel in order to quell their recent revolt against taxation imposed by the emperor Theodosius I.

Mutium ignis … tormenta: In note ‘c’, the Roman heroes are Gaius Mucius Scaevola (‘Left-handed’), who after failing in an assassination attempt against the Etruscan king Lars Porsenna in 507 BCE, burned off his own right hand to prove his courage; Gaius Fabricius Luscinus – on whom, see above, n. 93 (1.2.3); and Regulus – on whom, see above, 1.1.2.10 and n. 71 (1.1.2).
bands: See above, n. 199 (DJR).
offended: See above, n. 23 (DJR).

Servus Epictetus … superis: These lines attributed to the Greek epigrammatic poet Leonidas of Tarentum (late fourth to mid-third century BCE), himself famously impecunious, refer to the crippled Stoic philosopher Epictetus and to Irus, the greedy and cowardly beggar in the house of Odysseus at Ithaca.
Spera Batte … spera: In this quotation from Theocritus (Idylls 4.41–2), the momentarily lovesick character Battus (‘Chatterbox’) is consoled by his friend, the goatherd Corydon.

as Machiavel relates of Cosmus Medices … cloud: In his description of Cosimo de’ Medici in the Istorie fiorentine (1532), Machiavelli emphasizes his great wealth and liberality, and notes that ‘all those who had charge of his property in all Europe shared in his prosperity’ – which probably explains Burton’s description of him as a ‘fortunate and renowned Citizen of Europe’.
Huniades … Henry the third … to be crowned kings: See above, n. 54 (1.2.4). Henry III of Portugal (1512–80) was a Catholic cardinal before ascending the throne in 1578.

Nondum omnium dierum … not yet set: According to Livy (39.26.9), these words of Philip V of Macedon – on whom, see above, n. 168 (1.2.3) – were issued in anger in a dispute with the Thessalians about his control of conquered territory, and were taken by them, as well as by the Romans, as a threat.
this made Timon half mad … misfortunes: See above, n. 125 (1.2.2).

Zeno the Philosopher … good turn: According to Diogenes Laertius (7.1.2–4), after Zeno of Citium (335–263 BCE) was shipwrecked on a voyage from Phoenicia to Piraeus, he came across the philosopher Crates of Thebes – see above, n. 284 (DJR) – whose pupil he became.

Alexander sent an hundred talents … as I am: In Plutarch’s anecdote about Phocion – on whom, see above, n. 213 (DJR) and n. 72 (1.2.3) – he repeatedly refuses the money, but eventually asks Alexander the Great to release several of his associates from prison in Sardis instead (Phocion 18).

generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR). speech of Cotta in Sallust: The Roman politician and orator Gaius Aurelius Cotta (124–73 BCE), whose speech attempting to calm the popular violence caused by a grain shortage, delivered when he was consul in 75, was recorded by Sallust.

Non cuivis contingit adire Corinthum: A quotation from Horace (Epistles 1.17.36) of a Greek proverb, referring to the wealth required to enjoy the luxurious life and sacral prostitution reportedly on offer in Corinth – for which, see below, n. 14 (3.2.2); for the Roman poet, though, the reward is for moral virtue. all Catos, or Laelii: On Cato the Younger, see above, n. 51 (1.1.1); on Laelius, see above, n. 56 (2.2.6).
parcels: Parts, or divisions, of a whole. crewel: Thin yarn used for embroidery and tapestry. exornation: See above, n. 54 (DJR).

Croesi and Darii: ‘Croesuses’ and ‘Dariuses’. The latter might refer to the famously rich and powerful Persian king Darius I (ruled 522–486 BCE), who introduced the Persian gold coin (the ‘daric’) named after him; or alternatively to Darius III (ruled 336–330 BCE), whose treasury in Persepolis – which was reported to have accumulated thousands of tons of gold and silver since Cyrus the Great (ruled 559–530 BCE) founded the Persian Empire – was looted by Alexander the Great in 330 and subsequently dispersed through the Near East and beyond.
As Menenius Agrippa … Rome: See above, n. 86 (1.2.4). Apologue: See above, n. 114 (DJR).
vegetals, sensible creatures … reasonable souls: See above, n. 85 (DJR).
Corollary: Proposition, tenet.

Maecenas in pluma: See above, n. 111 (DJR). Regulus in dolio: See above, n. 71 (1.1.2). those poor starved Hollanders … An. 1596: Willem Barentsz – on whom, see above, n. 5 (2.2.3) – actually died with his crew in Novaya Zemlya, an archipelago in the Arctic Ocean north of Russia, in 1597. those eight miserable Englishmen … death itself: While on a whaling expedition to the northwest coast of Greenland in 1630, the English sailor Edward Pelham and seven other members of the crew of the Salutation were dispatched to meet another ship, but went missing and were given up as lost. In Pelham’s account, they spent the winter at Bell Sound in a timber cabin, within which they built another enclosure (‘stove’ here literally means ‘box’), and survived by eating whale meat before being rescued in May 1631.
old Chremes: See above, n. 65 (DJR).
indefinitely: Unlimitedly, infinitely.

as birds with henbane: See above, n. 38 (1.1.1). Nero, Otho, Vitellius, Heliogabalus … imperassent: Burton here extends the remark made by Tacitus about Galba (Histories 1.49) to four more emperors that were famously intemperate and dissolute.

’twas Cato’s note … contain: According to Plutarch (Marcus Cato 8), when King Eumenes II of Pergamum (d. 158 BCE) visited Rome, Cato the Elder – on whom, see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries) – viewed him with suspicion on the grounds that ‘the animal known as king is by nature carnivorous’. On the word ‘note’ here, see above, n. 57 (2.2.6).

Eutrapelus … behind: This quotation from Horace (Epistles 1.18.31–5) refers to the wealthy Roman patron Publius Volumnius Eutrapelus, who, when he wanted to bring about the demise of one of his clients, fed his desire for luxury. ‘Fly out’ here means ‘burst out into improper conduct’.
If Adversity hath killed … thousand: An allusion to 1 Samuel 18:7: ‘Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.’

Demetrius in Seneca: Demetrius the Cynic, a Corinthian philosopher of the first century CE and friend of Seneca, who portrays him as the model of the Cynic–Stoic sage. He was critical of the emperors Caligula, Nero and Vespasian, who banished him – along with most of the other philosophers in Rome – to an island in 71 CE.

bestow a whole Manor on a thread: That is, establish a large estate with great ease. The phrase derives from Jerome’s Life of Paul, the First Hermit, where the passage reads ‘with a single thread stitch together manors out of farms’ (‘uno filo villarum insuunt praedia’).
stoves: Rooms heated with stoves.

Ptolemaeus King of Egypt … Strato’s scholar: Ptolemy II Philadelphus (308–246 BCE) was tutored in Egypt by the Greek philosopher Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335–c. 269 BCE), who went on to become the head of the Lyceum in Athens. that renowned Library at Alexandria: See above, n. 92 (2.2.4).
Joseph … Pharaoh’s house: In Genesis 39:7–23, Joseph is imprisoned after refusing to sleep with the wife of Potiphar, but in recognition of his virtue the warden puts him in charge of the jail.

The rain is a stranger … India: In this passage from Philostratus the Elder (Letters 8), the original Greek refers to the nightingale being foreign to the season of spring (because in Greece it arrived in the summer); but in the 1608 Latin translation by Fédéric Morel, which is used here, the Greek ἔαρ (‘spring’) is rendered oddly as aer (‘air’). The inclusion of Ganymede, a famously beautiful Trojan prince in classical mythology, refers to the tale of his abduction from Mount Ida by Zeus (Jupiter) to serve as cup-bearer on Olympus.
hone after: Pine for, hanker after.

There is a base nation in the North … Rome: The Chauci (or Chauken) were an ancient Germanic tribe from the region between the Rivers Ems and Elbe. Pliny the Elder’s point (16.1.4) is that they are fortunate to have been conquered and absorbed into the Roman Empire, so it is ridiculous for them to complain about being reduced to slavery. in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).

land-leapers: See above, n. 237 (1.2.3). Polus Venetus … Schouten: This list of explorers (and pirates), alongside the more famous names of Marco Polo, Christopher Columbus, Vasco da Gama and Francis Drake, and those others identified above at n. 9 (2.2.3) and nn. 85, 86 (2.2.4), also includes Vicente Yáñez Pinzón (c. 1462–c. 1523), who sailed with Columbus on his first voyage to the Americas, and Thomas Cavendish (c. 1560–92), who followed in Drake’s footsteps by raiding Spanish ports in the Pacific and circumnavigating the globe.

Tully, Aristides … banished: In 58 BCE Cicero’s enemy Publius Clodius – on whom, see above, n. 183 (DJR) – introduced a law that banished anyone who had a Roman citizen killed without trial. Cicero, who as consul in 63 BCE had summarily executed the Catilinarian conspirators – see above, n. 227 (DJR) – on grounds that were at best legally dubious, fled to Macedonia; he stayed in exile for fifteen months before being recalled by a law of the people to Rome, where he was warmly welcomed on his return. During the struggle of Themistocles with Aristides – on whom (along with Theseus), see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – the former left Athens for Argos after being ostracized (exiled for ten years without conviction for any offence) in the late 470s. Codrus was the mythical last king of Athens, reputed to have ruled in the eleventh century BCE; Burton is perhaps thinking of his father Melanthus, who was exiled to Messenia before he became the Athenian ruler. Codrus was, however, reported to have left Athens heroically on one occasion: after the Delphic oracle prophesied that if he was not harmed then a Dorian invasion of Athens would succeed, he is said to have voluntarily sacrificed himself by turning himself over to the enemy soldiers.
as a horse at a rotten post: See above, n. 21 (2.2.6).

Say what you can … Indian Prince: The specific source of this reference – presumably to the Aztec emperor Moctezuma II (c. 1466–1520) – has not been traced. Girolamo Benzoni, cited in note ‘b’, discusses Peruvian sun-worship, human sacrifice and belief in the immortality of the soul in his Historia del Mondo Nuovo (1565). Bonum est esse hic: The words said by Peter to Jesus at his transfiguration, as recorded in the Latin Vulgate (Matthew 17:4).
O Hone, as those Irish women: ‘O hone’ is an Anglicized version of ochone, a Scottish Gaelic exclamation of grief and sorrow (akin to ‘alas’ or ‘woe’).

Mezentius would not live … linquam: Mezentius was a mythical, and famously cruel and bloodthirsty, Etruscan king, also sometimes portrayed as a blasphemer. In the passage quoted here from the Aeneid (10.855–6), he laments the death of his son Lausus, who has just been killed by Aeneas in combat after saving his father. He is eventually killed himself, after begging to be buried with his son.

violenta luctu … passions: This passage in Tacitus (Annals 3.1) refers to the grief of Agrippina the Elder (c. 14 BCE–33 CE) after the death, not of one of her sons but of her husband the general Germanicus (15 BCE–19 CE), ostensibly from illness, and perhaps from poisoning by his adoptive father, the emperor Tiberius.

subitus miserae color … Rutuli: Two quotations from Virgil’s Aeneid (9.475–8, 493–4) describing the lamentations of the mother of Euryalus (the Trojan companion of Aeneas) after he is killed, together with his friend Nisus, while on a scouting expedition to the camp of the Rutuli tribe, who are resisting the settlement of the Trojan exiles in Italy.
prank: See above, n. 112 (DJR).
vindicate: See above, n. 284 (DJR).

say with old Simeon … in peace: In Luke 2:25–35, Simeon, an elderly man from Jerusalem, who has been told by the Holy Spirit that he will not die before seeing Christ, meets the young Jesus in the temple and embraces the prospect of death; ‘well-affected’ here means ‘positively disposed’ or ‘inclined’ (that is, towards death). with Paul … Christ: Philippians 1:23.

Beata mors … aperit: This, along with the passage quoted in note ‘f’, is taken from the pseudo-Ciceronian De consolatione (1583), which had been ‘discovered’ by the Italian scholar Carlo Sigonio (c. 1524–84) and purported to be the entirety of a work that had been preserved only in fragments. Several contemporaries rightly doubted its authenticity. blessed are they … Lord: Revelation 14:13.

Servetus the heretic … the people: The Spanish theologian and scholar Miguel Serveto (Michael Servetus, 1509/11–53) was condemned as a heretic for his views on Christ and the Trinity by the Catholic Church in France, and also by the governing council in Calvinist Geneva, where he was executed in October 1553. The bibliographical reference in note ‘g’ is to the Contra libellum Calvini in quo ostendere conatur haereticos jure gladii coercendos esse (1562) by Sebastian Castellio, which was published anonymously and labels each section ‘Vaticanus’.
the pike of Tenerife: See above, n. 15 (2.2.3).

When Jupiter himself wept … good: A reference to the Iliad (16.459–60), where Zeus weeps for his son Sarpedon, one of the leaders of the Lycians, who is about to meet his fate by being killed by Patroclus.
Non decet … Germanicus’ advice: A quotation from Annals (2.71). Tacitus portrays the death of Germanicus, and his subsequent funeral, as a model of virtuous restraint.
macerate: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
the first statute in Magna Carta: Figuratively, the fundamental principle of the constitution (of human affairs).

Ladislaus King of Bohemia … died: Ladislaus the Posthumous (1440–57), duke of Austria and king of Hungary, Bohemia and Croatia – and so called because he was the posthumous son of Albert II of Germany – died before he could marry his betrothed, Magdalena of Valois (1443–95). Obeunt noctesque diesque, &c.: In note ‘f’, a quotation from Statius (Silvae 2.1.210), referring to the mortality of the universe.

Calliopius recensui: In a misunderstanding, common in Renaissance scholarship, of the concluding passage found in several of the manuscripts of Terence’s comedies, the Terentian editor Calliopius is treated as if he were the reciter in the play. The error stems from confusion about the abbreviation of recensui (‘I edited’ or ‘I reviewed’) as rec., which some commentators read as a shortening of recitavi (‘I recited’), and led to the treatment of the former as synonymous with the latter.

that Assyrian Nineveh: The destruction of the capital of the Assyrian Empire in 612 BCE is described in Nahum 2:1–13. Delos … council-house of Greece: The Cycladic island of Delos, which had been the meeting-place and treasury of the Delian League (the fifth-century BCE Greek alliance against the Persians), was sacked in 88 BCE by Archelaus, the general of Mithridates VI of Pontus, and in 69 BCE by pirates. Its decline was frequently mentioned in Roman literature.

Quid Pandioniae restat … Atheniae: This quotation from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (15.430), which is part of a speech given by Pythagoras about the inevitable decline of powerful civilizations such as Troy, Sparta and Thebes, refers to Pandion I, one of the semi-mythical kings of Athens.
Cyzicus: A wealthy ancient Greek city in the Anatolian region of Mysia, located on what is now the south coast of the sea of Marmara in northwestern Turkey.
Hieron: Probably Hieron I of Syracuse – see above, n. 327 (DJR). Empedocles: See above, n. 92 (DJR).
One Anacharsis … Scythians: A legendary Scythian prince sometimes included in lists of the ancient Greek ‘Seven Sages’ – see above, n. 91 (DJR).
vindicate: See above, n. 17 (2.3.1).

Nondum sustulerat … crinem: Virgil (Aeneid 4.698) here refers to the sacrificial practice in which the priest plucked hairs from the brow of an animal and threw them into the fire, indicating the beginning of the actual killing. At this point in the poem, Proserpina (Persephone), the wife of Pluto (Hades), has evidently refused to consign the fair-haired Queen Dido of Carthage, who has stabbed herself, to the underworld. lethaeoque … sarcophago: A quotation from an epigram inscribed on an ancient Roman marble funerary altar, dedicated by a man called Donatus to his recently deceased fiancée Pedana; on Lethe, see above, n. 55 (1.1.2).

he did either so find … another … & bona tam … fuit: Passages from the De remediis fortuitorum, a work spuriously attributed to Seneca in the later Middle Ages. as Critobulus … did by his: In Xenophon’s Symposium (2.3), Socrates remarks that the wives of his fellow symposiasts Critobulus and Niceratus – on whom, see above, n. 99 (2.2.4) – do not need to use any more perfume than they do already. Burton may have meant the description in Xenophon’s Economics (7) of how Ischomachus trained his wife. good cheap: Cheaply. inform: Shape, train.

as that Ephesian widow in Petronius: An allusion to the tale, told in the Satyricon (111–12), of a woman from Ephesus who mourned the death of her husband with prolonged intensity, but was eventually seduced by a sympathetic soldier (who had been guarding the nearby bodies of some crucified thieves, to prevent anyone from removing them for burial).

dignus Apollineis lachrymis … lament: The quotation, from the funeral oration composed by the sophist Aelius Aristides in 161 BCE for the handsome youth
Eteoneus, refers to the mythological portrayal of Apollo as a lover of beauty, and more particularly of beautiful young men. Aristides quotes the poet Pindar (c. 518–438 BCE) in his speech. On ‘witty’ here, see above, n. 49 (DJR).
Eteocles and Polynices: See above, n. 156 (1.2.4). another Ganymede: See above, n. 4 (2.3.4).
Condole: See above, n. 133 (DJR).

Cardinal Brundusinus: The archbishop of Brindisi, Girolamo Aleandro (1480–1543), who was also a scholar and a poet, was buried in the church of San Crisogono in Rome, but his remains were later transferred to his hometown of Motta di Livenza in Treviso.
undiscreet: See above, n. 40 (DJR).
Styx: See above, n. 34 (1.2.2). Acheron: See above, n. 10 (2.1.1). the Elysian fields: See above, n. 59 (1.1.2).

transpose: Disturb, discompose. as Ulysses that wept for his dog … obfirmato: This quotation from Plutarch refers to the behaviour of Odysseus when he returns to Ithaca in disguise after his twenty-year absence, openly weeping when his neglected old dog Argus recognizes him (Odyssey 17.290–327), but maintaining his composure as Penelope mourns the death of her husband in ignorance of her companion’s true identity (19.203–14).
fortuit: Fortuitous.
disannul: See above, n. 236 (DJR).

The Beaver bites off’s stones to save the rest: Since antiquity, when beavers were hunted for castoreum – see below, n. 64 (2.5.1) – they had been believed to evade capture by biting off their own testicles (‘stones’).
wasters: See above, n. 23 (2.2.4). cudgels: Bouts of combat with cudgels, or clubs.

as he confessed to Zopyrus the Physiognomer: Zopyrus was a magus, probably of Syrian origin, who lived in Athens at the time of Socrates; on physiognomy, see above, n. 117 (1.2.1). froward: See above, n. 48 (1.1.1).

nunc Maecenates & Agrippas: The powerful Roman patrons Gaius Cilnius Maecenas – see above, n. 111 (DJR) – and Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa (64/3 BCE–12 CE). The former claimed royal descent, but the latter had humble origins.
collogue … fleer: See above, nn. 31, 113 (DJR).
I have had some … benefactors: On Burton’s patrons, including those mentioned in note ‘d’, see the editor’s Introduction. Suffenus: A bad poet with delusions of grandeur, ridiculed by Catullus (22).

beating: Running around in an attempt to escape (a term used in hunting). Distichon ejus … in Rome: Note ‘a’ refers to ‘a couplet on the Christian soldier, from the Greek’, used as an epitaph on the tomb of the humanist scholar Francesco Pucci (1463–1512) in the Church of Sant’Onofrio in Rome. Its authorship is actually uncertain, but its use in varying forms on funeral monuments is documented in antiquity and the Renaissance.

Paedaretus … meliores: Pedaritus, who is quoted in note ‘b’ from Plutarch’s Spartan Sayings (231), was a Spartan military commander in charge of the island of Chios. His execution of the pro-Athenians there prompted the Chians in Sparta to bring an action against him, and he was killed by the Athenians in 411 BCE.

Indignissimus plerumque … laudatissimo: This passage from the second book of Petrarch’s De remediis utriusque fortunae (1366), which follows Seneca’s On
Providence (3.14), refers to the ostensible injustice of Publius Vatinius – an outspoken supporter of Julius Caesar – being awarded the praetorship in 55 BCE ahead of the more qualified Cato the Younger. On these two figures, see above, n. 161 (DJR) and n. 51 (1.1.1).

Salarium non dat multi salem: This witticism, taken from Johann Valentin Andreae’s Menippus (1618), plays on the fact that the Latin salarium was originally the allowance given to Roman soldiers to buy salt.

Hieron of Syracuse … Kingdom: According to the Roman historian Justinus in his Epitome of the Philippic Histories of Pompeius Trogus (23.4), the future Hieron II of Syracuse – on whom, see above, n. 189 (1.2.3) – displayed great promise, and ‘seemed to lack nothing kingly except a kingdom’. On ‘brave’ in this passage, see above, n. 47 (DJR). Perseus of Macedon had … govern it: See above, n. 100 (1.2.4). The comparison between these two ancient rulers is taken from the dedication of Machiavelli’s Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio (1531).
collogue: See above, n. 31 (DJR).

which Tiresias advised Ulysses in the Poet … ditescere: In Satires 2.5, Horace imagines a continuation of the discussion in the underworld between Ulysses (Odysseus) and the blind prophet Tiresias (Odyssey 11), with the latter offering various strategies for successful legacy hunting; cf. n. 43 (2.2.3) above.

Gesner was a silly old man: Gessner – see above, n. 52 (2.2.4) – was forty-nine, which was viewed by contemporaries as old age, when he died from the plague in 1565. swelling: See above, n. 108 (DJR). foot-cloths: Ornamented cloths laid over the back of a horse and hanging down to the ground on both sides, considered a mark of dignity.
Brutus: Marcus Junius Brutus – see above, n. 155 (1.2.4).
Moronia pia, or Moronia faelix: See above, n. 117 (DJR).
painful: See above, n. 50 (DJR). Certificate: Attestation, certification.
in conceit: In high esteem or favourable opinion. private: Secluded. compass: See above, n. 199 (1.2.3).
a jury: A dozen. motion: Inclination, emotion. fame: Report, or rumour.

scamble: See above, n. 222 (1.2.3). the star Fomahant: Fomalhaut, the brightest star in the Piscis Austrinus constellation, and associated in Renaissance astrology with eternal fame (when in a benevolent aspect).
Canvas: See above, n. 112 (1.2.3).

Magna petis Phaethon … viribus istis: A quotation from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (2.54–5), in which Phaethon is warned by his father, the sun-god Sol, that his request to drive the chariot that pulls the sun is dangerous. Phaethon is subsequently unable to control the horses, and is killed by Jupiter to prevent the earth being consumed by fire. James and John … not what: Their request to Jesus is to sit alongside him in glory, at his right and left hands (Mark 10:35–7).
a block: An idol. turgent: See above, n. 150 (DJR).
Eia Socrates, eia Xantippe: See above, n. 159 (DJR). animate: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3).
Durum & durum non faciunt murum: That is, proverbially, bricks placed against each other without mortar will not adhere. diverb: See above, n. 103 (2.2.4).

the Columni in Rome: The Colonna, a powerful Italian aristocratic family, left Rome after being persecuted by Pope Alexander VI because of their support for Frederick I of Aragon (1452–1504). They were excommunicated and had several of their fortresses confiscated in 1501, the same year that Frederick was deposed as king of Naples. Impress: Here, the image produced by a seal or stamp – see also above, n. 115 (2.2.4). Flecti potest, frangi non potest: A misquotation of Seneca’s tragedy Thyestes (200) which reverses the sense of the original: ‘flecti non potest, frangi potest’ (‘unbendable, but breakable’).
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR).

infestus infestis … Emmanuel Philibert Duke of Savoy: The motto (‘symbol’) of Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy (1528–80), whose military exploits earned him the moniker ‘Testa di Ferro’ (‘Ironhead’), was presented on a medal of 1553 beneath an image of an elephant with lambs.

Edward Senior, and Leolin Prince of Wales: Actually Edward the Confessor (c. 1003–66) and Gruffudd ap Llywelyn (d. 1063). Their meeting, as described by the English writer and royal clerk Walter Map (d. 1209/10), may have occurred in 1056.
brangling: Quarrelsome, contentious.
Anytus and Meletus … hurt me: See above, n. 98 (DJR).

which Asinius Pollio … provoked him: According to Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.4.21), the Roman politician and historian Gaius Asinius Pollio (c. 76 BCE–c. 5 CE) made this remark with regard to the invective poetry written against him by Octavian before the latter became the emperor Augustus. ‘Ware’ in this passage means ‘cautious’.
One of Chilon’s three difficult things … injuries: Attributed by Diogenes Laertius (1.3.69) to Chilon of Sparta – see above, n. 91 (DJR).

Conradinus that brave Swabian Prince: After his supporters had been defeated at the Battle of Tagliacozzo (1268), Conradin, duke of Swabia (1252–68), was imprisoned and executed by Charles I of Anjou, king of Naples and Sicily (1226–85). The latter’s son, Charles II of Naples (1254–1309), was captured in a naval battle in the Gulf of Naples in 1284; but rather than being beheaded in the manner of Conradin, as was demanded by an angry crowd when he was taken to Messina, he was eventually released and later died peacefully in Naples.
hie: See above, n. 1 (Preliminaries).
as an Ichneumon doth a Crocodile: The ichneumon, related to the mongoose, was noted for eating the eggs of crocodiles, but was also thought to enter their bodies and devour them from within.
as Haman … for Mordecai: Esther 7:1–10. Thre.: The Book of Lamentations (indicated by the abbreviation of ‘Threnodia’).

Dionysius of Syracuse: Actually Dion (409–354 BCE), the son-in-law and chief minister of the Syracusan tyrant Dionysius I, and a friend and disciple of Plato; he was banished in 366 by his former master’s son, Dionysius II. without door: Outdoors.
self do, self have: A version of the proverb ‘you reap what you sow’.

a Thistlewarp’s nest: A ‘thistlewarp’ is another name for a goldfinch, or thistle-finch. the Humble-bee in the fable … lap: The mention of a ‘humble-bee’ – see above, n. 338 (DJR) – is a mistake. The allusion here is to Aesop’s fable ‘The Eagle and the Beetle’, in which an eagle refuses the request of a beetle to spare a hare, and the beetle takes revenge by destroying the eagle’s eggs – even when laid in the lap of Jupiter, who admits the justice of the beetle’s cause.
Brasidas: See above, n. 90 (DJR).
fidus Achates: See above, n. 40 (1.2.3).
that upright Cato: In fact, Cato the Younger, not his great-grandfather Cato the Censor – see above, n. 51 (1.1.1).
the gains go to the box: A forerunner of ‘the bank always wins’.
the Elephant and Dragon’s conflict … ruined: In this passage, drawn from the discussion of the cunning predatory methods of snakes in Pliny the Elder (8.12), ‘dragon’ means ‘large snake’ or ‘python’.

an Hydra’s head: See above, n. 69 (DJR). as Praxiteles did by his glass … moment: This story about the ancient Athenian sculptor Praxiteles is taken from Girolamo Cardano’s De consolatione libri tres (1542), where the choleric artist smashes a mirror after seeing his ugly face reflected in it, and then becomes further enraged by seeing more images of his deformity in the broken pieces.
pasquilling libels: See above, n. 35 (1.2.4).
Socrates was brought … Aristophanes: In the Clouds.
exploded: See above, n. 45 (DJR).
as Themistocles did … exploits: See above, n. 58 (2.2.6). For ‘deboshed’, see above, n. 66 (DJR).
so Tully was in Rome, Alcibiades in Athens: See above, n. 8 (2.3.4) and nn. 72, 95 (1.2.3).

Latrantem curatne … canem: This line, taken from the Symbolorum et emblematum centuriae tres (1605) of Joachim Camerarius the Younger, alludes to Artemis (Diana) as the classical goddess of the moon and hunting.

that Albanian dog … present: According to Pliny the Elder (8.61), Alexander the Great was given a huge dog as a present by a king of Albania (whose territory lies in what is now northern Azerbaijan and Dagestan); but when bears, boars and hinds were released for it to hunt, it lay ‘contemptuously motionless’. The dog was destroyed and a second one, prodigiously proficient at fighting, was sent in its place. vindicate: See above, n. 17 (2.3.1).

J. Kevenheder a Carinthian Baron: In note ‘a’, ‘Kevenheder’ refers slightly misleadingly to Johann Khevenhüller (1538–1606), from the duchy of Carinthia in southern Austria. He was the legate of the Holy Roman Emperor at the Spanish court, and an avid collector of animals and plants from around the world. Urchin: Hedgehog. The symbol of Gonzaga duke of Mantua: Note ‘b’ refers to Vincenzo Gonzaga, duke of Mantua (1562–1612). The heraldic device depicted a lizard with a tree-stump and camomile plant; the latter was associated with the power of virtue to rejuvenate and restore strength, deriving from the belief that it was the unnamed herb that Pliny the Elder (8.41) claimed was used by lizards to cure their wounds after being bitten by venomous snakes.

O Jane a tergo … by a stork: Janus, the ancient Roman god of passage and beginning, could not be mocked behind his back because of his two faces (Persius, Satires 1.58). Antevorta and Postvorta: In Roman mythology, the goddesses of past and future respectively, as well as childbirth, and said by Macrobius to have been worshipped as the companions of divination. Macrobius associated them with Janus, but the mention of Jupiter here probably derives from the Roman view, discussed by Augustine in the City of God (7.9), of the latter’s ultimate power over everything that comes about in the world. Moses had a Dathan … Shimei: Dathan and Korah both rebelled against Moses (Num. 16:1–33); Shimei cursed and pelted David with stones (2 Samuel 16:5–8).
that lusty courser in Aesop … same Ass: In the fable ‘The Horse and the Ass’.

a good conscience … feast: Proverbs 15:15. the Poet … iratis: Seneca, in Hercules (33–4). posy: Motto. Palladium: An image of the goddess Pallas (Athena) said in classical mythology to have guaranteed the safety of the city of Troy (and so, by extension, signifying any kind of protection or safeguard). Livor: See above, n. 167 (DJR).
Bion: Note ‘b’ refers to the ancient Greek philosopher Bion of Borysthenes (c. 335–c. 245 BCE), who had been influenced by the Cynics.
Cotys King of Thrace: See above, n. 170 (1.2.3).
baffle: See above, n. 166 (DJR).
defaults: See above, n. 14 (DJR). humane Authors: See above, n. 28 (DJR).

Siracides: See above, n. 140 (1.2.3). Fear God … remember thy last: A series of quotations from 1 Peter 2:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:6, 17; Ephesians 4:26; and Ecclesiasticus 7:40. fashion not yourselves to this world, &c., apply yourselves to the times: To avoid self-contradiction, the second instruction, added in the second edition of 1624, can be understood as a subordinate clause governed by the negative scriptural injunction (1 John 2:15) preceding it – that is, read as ‘{nor} apply yourselves to the times’: the commonplace Christian warning against conforming
to worldly values. strive not … thy neighbour as thyself: Quotations from Ecclesiastes 6:10; 1 Peter 3:9; Ephesians 4:31–2; and Luke 10:27. and whatsoever … motto: According to the Augustan History (51), the Roman emperor Severus Alexander had heard this from a Jew or a Christian.
Had I wist: Or ‘Had I known’: a proverbial expression that was common in early modern literature, and figurative in Middle English for something done in heedlessness or ignorance, or vain regret.
opinative: See above, n. 98 (DJR).

Be not a neuter … passions: According to the Athenian Constitution (8.5), often attributed to Aristotle and cited in note ‘k’, Solon passed a law, intended to facilitate compromise, that disenfranchised any citizens who chose to remain neutral in a situation of civil strife. On Solon, see above, nn. 91, 307 (DJR).

Ocymum ne terito: Or, ‘be gentle’. The Latin phrase is taken from Joachim Camerarius the Younger’s Symbolorum et emblematum, ex re herbaria desumtorum centuria una collecta (1590), where the full saying is given as ‘Officium ut faciat, nimis, o Rex, ne preme plebem, Suavius ut spirent, Ocyma ne terito’ (‘So that they do their duty, O king, don’t press the common people too hard; so that they smell more sweetly, don’t crush the basil leaves’). Camerarius explains that the herb is most pleasantly fragrant when handled gently, and also refers to the belief, recorded by Pliny the Elder (20.48), that if basil is crushed and left beneath a stone, it produces scorpions.
cheese trenchers and painted cloths: Seventeenth-century cheese plates and wall-hangings were sometimes decorated with moralizing tags.

as the Veientes were to the Romans … gravis: This quotation from Livy (2.48.7) refers to the persistent conflict between the Romans and the inhabitants of the Etruscan city of Veii, which was said to stretch back to the time of the Roman kings and ended only when Veii was destroyed in 396 BCE.
tetters: See above, n. 4 (2.3.2).
sharkers: Cheats, swindlers. Coney-catchers: See above, n. 61 (2.2.4). prowlers: Impostors or cheats. smell-feasts: People who scent out feasts and come uninvited, greedy spongers.
circumvented: See above, n. 336 (DJR).
roaring boys: Noisy and riotous boys or men, hooligans, or drunks.
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR).
that illiterate Virginian simplicity: The uncultivated simplicity of contemporary (native American) Virginians. macerated: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
the Isles of Orcades: See above, n. 133 (1.2.1). the Forest of Arden: The Ardennes Forest, in what is now mainly the territory of Belgium and Luxembourg. painful: See above, n. 50 (DJR).
Martianus Capella … before his time: Martianus Capella, who is himself using the account of Pliny the Elder (7.2.27–30), is referring to the inhabitants of Sri Lanka.
Finmark, Biarmia, Corelia: The northern half of Fennoscandia (the peninsula bordering the Norwegian, Barents and White Seas), comprising Finmark, Bjarmaland and Karelia.
stall-fed: That is, fattened up in the manner of an animal kept and fed in a stall. lubbers: See above, n. 11 (2.3.2).
kitchen Physic: Nourishment for invalids from the domestic kitchen.

preposterous: Here, probably ‘unseasonable’ or ‘untimely’ (by inverting the proper order of treatments), although ‘foolish’ or ‘contrary to reason’ are also possible. Themison: A famous ancient physician (fl. second or first century BCE) from Laodicea in Syria, who founded the Methodist school of medicine. The Methodists had been criticized by Soranus of Ephesus – on whom, see above, n. 14 (1.3.2) – for their treatment of patients suffering from mania, which involved locking them up in chains and depriving them of food and light (cf. the depiction of the maniacus in the frontispiece of the Anatomy).
liberal science: See above, n. 7 (DJR).

what was Apollo but the Devil: In early Christianity it was common to claim that the pagan gods were actually devils. Later descriptions of Apollo as Satan derived from the former’s identity as the god of the sun and light, and his conflation with Lucifer – the morning star (‘bringer of light’) in Latin antiquity, which from the fourth century CE onwards was identified with the biblical figure of Satan.

Phaon: An ancient physician who was identified by Galen as one of the pupils of Hippocrates, and who is sometimes thought to have contributed to the Hippocratic corpus. Like some of his contemporaries, Burton is evidently associating him with the Greek god Paeon – on whom, see above, n. 28 (2.2.6). Podalirius: In Greek mythology, a son of Asclepius and a heroic or divine physician. Melampus: A mythical seer and miracle healer. Menecrates (another God): See above, n. 171 (1.2.3).
Fimbriam Hippocratis: See above, n. 206 (DJR).
Mountebanks, Empirics: See above, n. 76 (DJR).

singularity: Conspicuous dissent. as he said of Hadrian: The Byzantine historian Joannes Xiphilinos (eleventh century CE), in his epitome of the sixty-ninth book of Dio Cassius. The emperor is said to have made this exclamation, which was adapted from a popular saying, after ceasing his medical regimen for dropsy and deciding to eat and drink himself to death.
adulterine: A product of adulteration or admixture (and so impure or debased).
Chirurgeons: See above, n. 75 (DJR). facete: See above, n. 35 (1.2.4).
Strangury: A disease of the urinary organs, involving slow and painful urination.
Critic days: ‘Critical days’, involving the ‘crisis’ of a disease: see above, n. 48 (1.3.1). Indications: Suggestions for treatment of a disease, derived from its symptoms.

Cambyses in Xenophon: The Persian king Cambyses I (c. 600–559 BCE), who, according to Xenophon’s Cyropaedia (1.16), dispensed this advice to his son, the future Cyrus the Great, who founded the Persian Empire.
latitude: Range, extent.
take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR).
that learned Fuchsius of Nuremberg: The German physician Leonhard Fuchs (1501–66). limbeck: See above, n. 5 (2.1.1).

Sena Cassia: Cassia fistula, also known as the ‘golden shower tree’ or ‘pudding pipe tree’, whose fruit has purgative properties. Zocotora: The island of Socotra, or the archipelago of the same name, in the Indian Ocean. Turbith: Or turpeth, the purgative root of the tropical vine plant Operculina turpethum. Agaric: The tree fungus Fomitopsis officinalis. Myrobalans: The astringent, plum-like fruit of myrobalan trees (various species of the genus Terminalia), said to have a range of beneficial effects on the stomach, blood and mind, and often recommended for melancholy. Hermodactyls: Roots of the Asiatic autumn crocus (or meadow saffron), Colchicum luteum, which were used as laxatives and purgatives. the Anticyrae: See above, n. 87 (DJR).

Mariola and Renagolosa: The range of the Sierra de Mariola, and Mount Peñagolosa, both in the region of Valencia in Spain. Baldus … lake Benacus: Monte Baldo in the Italian Alps, bordering Lake Garda (known in Latin as Benacus).
Munster Mons maior in Histria: The Učka mountain range (Monte Maggiore in Italian) in northwestern Croatia, on what is now the peninsula of Istria at the head of the Adriatic.
beyond the Garamantes: Or ‘to the ends of the earth’ – an allusion to Virgil (Aeneid 6.795), which refers to the powerful ancient Berber tribe that inhabited what is now southwestern Libya.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).

that Fernelius much laboured … T.
