B. with us: References to the famous French physician Jean Fernel (1497–1558), the German physicians Janus Cornarius (born Johann Haynpol, 1500–1558) and Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602) and the English physician Timothy Bright (1549/50–1615), author of A Treatise Wherein is Declared the Sufficiencie of English Medicines (first edition 1580) as well as A Treatise of Melancholy (1586).

ours in Oxford: The Botanic Garden of Oxford University, the oldest of its kind in England, was founded in 1621 by Henry Danvers, earl of Derby (1573–1644), a wealthy army officer and administrator who was probably inspired by the Jardin des Plantes in Paris. in fieri: See above, n. 93 (2.2.4).

Satyrium … extinguunt: Satyrium is a genus of orchid; ‘eruca’ is either a genus of Brassica (Brassica eruca) or rocket; ‘priest pintle’ (in note ‘f’) is any of several orchids (especially early purple orchid, wild arum, or cuckoo pint, Arum maculatum) – and all are putative aphrodisiacs. vitex … agnus Castus: The chaste tree (Vitex agnus-castus), or Abraham’s balm, like the water lily, was sometimes thought to have anaphrodisiac properties. Sabina: Note ‘g’ refers to savin, a small bushy juniper (Juniperus sabina), which was used to stimulate contractions and assist delivery, but also to facilitate termination. The passage ‘some again … quite extinguish seed’ translates the second half of the preceding Latin quotation. foalfoot: Coltsfoot (Tussilago farfara). eyebright: A plant of the genus Euphrasia, used to treat the eyes. Rue: See above, n. 216 (DJR).
Enula campana: Elecampane (Inula helenium).
Balm: See above, n. 23 (1.2.2).
Centaury: See above, n. 24 (1.3.3).
Darthspine or Camaepitis: Ground-pine or yellow bugle (Ajuga chamaepitys). Succory: See above, n. 23 (1.2.2). Barberries: The berries of the Berberis shrub.

Maidenhair: A fern – either black maidenhair (Adiantum capillus-veneris) or maidenhair spleenwort (Asplenium trichomanes). finger fern: The rusty-back fern (Asplenium ceterach). dodder of thyme: A parasitic plant of the genus Cuscuta that grows on flax, clover, thyme and other plants. hoppe: The seed vessel of flax. rind: Bark.
gromwell: The plants of the genus Lithospermum, with hard stony seeds. plantain: The low-growing plant of the genus Plantago, rather than the type of banana.
featherfew: Feverfew (Tanacetum parthenium).
organ: Plants of the genus Origanum, especially wild oregano or marjoram.
Melissa Balm: Balm gentle or balm-mint (Melissa officinalis). admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
Scorzonera: Black salsify (Scorzonera hispanica).
Lupulus, hop: The climbing perennial Humulus lupulus, the female of which produces hops.
as I shall after show: See below, 2.5.3.1. sod: See above, n. 32 (1.2.2).

Fumitory: A small whitish and blue-green plant of the genus Fumaria. Scolopendria: Ferns of the genus Scolopendrium (hart’s-tongue). Cuscuta: Dodder. Ceterach: A genus of ferns with scaly fronds, including the rusty-back fern. Tamarisk: A shrub or small tree of the genus Tamarix, especially the common tamarisk. Genista: The common broom (Cytisus scoparius), or any of the yellow-flowered, spiny shrubs of the genus Genista.

Scordium: Water germander (Teucrium scordium). Stoechas: French lavender (Lavandula stoechas). Ros Solis: Sundew (or rosa solis), a plant of the genus Drosera. Ocyme: Basil (Ocimum basilicum). Sanders: Sandalwood.

Chamico: The evergreen shrub chamiso (Adenostoma fasciculatum). Linschoten’s Datura: The thorn-apple (Datura stramonium), or any plant of the genus Datura – as described by the Dutch merchant and travel writer Jan Huyghen van Linschoten (1563–1611). Guaiacum: A genus of trees and shrubs found in America and the West Indies. China: See above, n. 65 (1.2.2). Sassafras: The dried bark of the Sassafras laurel or Ague-tree, Sassafras officinale. Carduus Benedictus: Blessed (or holy) thistle, Centaurea benedicta.
Herba solis, or Dutch Sindaw: Sundew.
Homer’s Moly: The herb with magical powers given by Hermes to Odysseus as a protection against Circe.
censured: See above, n. 59 (DJR). explode: See above, n. 45 (DJR).
salt of coral: The term ‘salt’ refers to the solid and soluble substance obtained from an object by a chemical process of dissolution, distillation and evaporation.
Granatus: Garnet. Calicut: Or Calico, now the city of Kozhikode, on the Malabar coast in southern India.

veni mecum: Literally, ‘come with me’, a variation of vade-mecum (literally, ‘go with me’ – a handbook or reference manual), and the title by which the extremely popular De medendis humani corporis malis enchiridion (1560), by the Turin physician Pietro Bairo (Bayrus, 1468–1558), was commonly known.

Chelidonius: Or Chelidony, the ‘swallow stone’: a stony substance found in the stomach of the swallow, which was said in medical folklore to have therapeutic properties and the power to ward off evil spirits. lapped: See above, n. 30 (DJR).
The Eban stone: Or the ‘exhebenus’ stone, mentioned by Pliny the Elder (37.58) as a handsome white stone described by Zoroaster (probably in a treatise on stones).
Emmetris: Also spelled in Latin eumetris or eumitres – possibly amazon-stone, tourmaline or a kind of emerald.
viper’s wine: Or Benzoardicum Thericale, wine medicated by an extract obtained from vipers, and a popular beauty potion on account of its supposedly rejuvenating properties.

the bone in a Stag’s heart, a Monocerot’s horn, Bezoar-stone … East Indies: Three forms of protection against – or antidote for – poisoning in medical folklore: the powdered ‘bone’ (actually degenerated artery) from the heart of a stag, which was said to have made the animal immune to snake venom; the horn of a unicorn (‘Monocerot’), which in practice was the tooth of a narwhal or powdered rhinoceros horn, and was also said to have a number of beneficial and therapeutic properties; and bezoar-stone, which was principally used to detect poisons, and was a solid lump found in the intestines of goats, sheep or deer (the most valuable ‘East’ or ‘Oriental’ bezoar came from the Persian wild goat).
Lapis Lazuli … mentioned in their place: See below, 2.4.2.2.
Unions: See above, n. 12 (2.3.3). cordial: Invigorating to the heart.
at mihi plaudo … as he said in the Poet: The wealthy Athenian miser described by Horace in Satires 1.1.66–7.

Aurum potabile: See above, n. 142 (1.2.3). he discommends … used in it: The Swiss physician and theologian Thomas Erastus (Thomas Lüber), who criticizes the Paracelsian use of aurum potabile on these grounds in his Disputationes de medicina nova Philippi Paracelsi (1572). which argument our Dr. Gwinne … Dr. Antonius: A reference to the refutation of the Paracelsian alchemist Francis Anthony (1550–1623) by the Oxford professor of physic Matthew Gwinne (1558–1627), in his In assertorem chymicae, sed verae medicinae desertorem (1611); this is also the source of the text in note ‘d’.

digged out of that broody hill … ubi nascetur ridiculus mus: An allusion to Horace’s Art of Poetry (139) – which also forms the basis for Aesop’s fable ‘The Mountain in Labour’ – where the image exemplifies a bathetic composition that begins with great promise but delivers little.

Alexipharmacums … Amuleta Martialia: On ‘Alexipharmacums’ and ‘Mummias’, see above, n. 111 (2.2.4); on ‘Amuleta Martialia’ and other ‘Magnetical cures’, see above, 2.2.4.1, p. 514; on ‘unguentum Armarium’ see above, n. 24 (1.2.3).
Heteroclitical: Deviant, anomalous.
Euonymus: The pseudonym of Conrad Gessner – on whom, see above, n. 52 (2.2.4) – in his Thesaurus Euonymi Philitria de remediis secretis (1552).
botch: An ulcer, tumour or sore.
bewray: See above, n. 43 (DJR).
exolete: No longer effective, obsolete.
Mithridate: See above, n. 78 (1.2.2). Treacle: Or ‘theriac’, a medicinal compound that was similar to mithridate, and said to be an antidote to poisons and a protection against various diseases.
Simon Eitover: Actually ‘è Tovar’, one spelling of the name of the learned Portuguese physician Simón de Tovar (1528–96).

Hamech, and Philonium Romanum: Two kinds of electuary – on which, see above, n. 2 (2.2.2) – with many ingredients. Confectio Hamech was a purgative containing myrobalans, Philonium Romanum was a narcotic containing opium.
Theriacum Andromachi: A compound medicine and antidote to poison, said to have been invented in the first century CE by the Greek physician Andromachus the Elder.

Magistrals: Medicinal formulae devised and compounded by particular physicians. Augustana Pharmacopoeia: The official pharmacopoeia adopted in 1564 by the imperial city of Augsburg (founded by the Romans as Augusta Vindelicorum). meridian: See above, n. 2 (2.2.1). London hers: The Pharmacopoeia Londinensis, was issued by the College of Physicians in 1618; later editions bore the subtitle The London Dispensatory.
paradox: See above, n. 3 (DJR).
consisting: Firm, cohering.
foreigner: Stranger.
regiment: See above, n. 6 (2.2.4).
temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

de pomis … King Sapor: See above, n. 171 (1.2.3). Epithyme: Dodder of thyme. Byzantine: An unidentified herb used in medicinal syrups, or perhaps the Syrupus Bizantinus commonly attributed to the Assyrian physician Mesue the Elder (c. 777–857).
preparatives: ‘Preparations’, or treatments administered before further medication.
Eclegmes, or Linctures: Both terms for linctus, a semifluid medicine licked off the spoon.

Diambra, Diamargaritum calidum, Dianthus, Diamoschum dulce … Diagalinga, Diaciminum, Dianisum, Diatrion piperion, Diazinziber, Diacapers, Diacinnamonum … Diamargaritum frigidum, Diacorolli, Diarrhodon Abbatis, Diacodion: Compound electuaries (hence the prefix ‘dia-’) with the main ingredients, respectively, of amber, pearl (in a hot mixture), carnation, musk, galangal, cumin, aniseed, three kinds of pepper, ginger, capers, cinnamon, pearl (in a cold mixture), coral, red roses, poppy-heads. Electuarium de gemmis: The ‘gem electuary’, reputedly devised by Mesue the Younger (d. 1015), which was a blend of precious stones and herbs. laetificans Galeni & Rhasis: ‘Laetificant’ (cheering) mixtures usually containing gold and sometimes silver,
attributed to Galen and Rhazes respectively. tables: Pills (that is, tablets). Condites: Conserves or electuaries.
Stechados: French lavender (another term for ‘stoechas’). Nymphaea: Water lily.
Alablastritum: Ointment containing unexpanded flower-buds. Populeum: See above, n. 70 (1.3.1). accidents: Symptoms.
Emplasters: Pastes or salves applied on linen or leather.
Cataplasms: Plasters (the word can also refer to poultices).
Cerotes: Or ‘cerates’ – stiff ointments made of wax, lard or oil, and other ingredients. Frontals: Treatments applied to the forehead.
Epithemata: Or ‘epithems’ – moistening or softening medicines.
balls: Perhaps perfumed soap-balls. as shall be showed: See below, 2.5.1.5, 2.5.3.1.
Asarum, or Asarabacca: Hazelwort (Asarum europaeum). Diaserum Fernelii: A purgative syrup of mint and violet, named after the French physician Jean Fernel (1497–1558).

vinum Scilliticum: Squill is the bulb or root of the sea onion (Urginea maritima), or of any plant of the genus Scilla. Rubell: Or vinum rubellum, which in the contemporary medical context refers to claret mixed with cloves and antimony.
goodwives: See above, n. 44 (1.1.1). iid. weight: Two pennyweight, that is, forty-eight grains in traditional weighting, or approximately one-ninth of an ounce (3.11 grams).
so bold as blind Bayard: In medieval romance, the bay-coloured horse named Bayard given by Charlemagne to Renaud was blind (and so rashly courageous).
undiscreet: See above, n. 40 (DJR).
Godefridus Stegius the Emperor Rodolphus’ Physician: The Dutch physician Gottfried Steegh (1550–1609) attended the court of the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II (1552–1612) in Prague.
Trent: Trento, in northern Italy.
admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
explodes: See above, n. 45 (DJR).
like Scanderbeg’s sword: See above, n. 94 (1.2.3).
Polypody: The fern Polypodium vulgare. Epithyme: Dodder of thyme – see above, n. 32 (2.4.1).

herb Mercury: Probably French mercury (Mercurialis annua), used in medical enemas, or ‘good King Henry’ (Chenopodium bonus-henricus), with which it was sometimes confused. Origan: Or ‘organ’: see above, n. 35 (2.4.1).

alypus: Or alypum: globe daisy or southern European gutwort (Globularia alypum). dragon-root: The root of dragonwort. dittany: There were several herbs called ‘dittany’ that were held to have medicinal properties, including Origanum dictamnus (or ‘dittany of Crete’), Marrubium pseudodictamnus (‘bastard dittany’) and certain plants of the genus Dictamnus. Colutea: Or bladder-senna (Colutea arborescens), a yellow-flowered shrub with bladder-like pods. Sene: Senna.
Lapis Armenus: Armenian stone, or lapis stellatus, a blue Azurite stone that resembles lapis lazuli.
Pulvis Hali: ‘Powder of Haly’, a mixture named after the Arabic physician Haly Abbas (d. 994).
noisome: Noxious, harmful.
Elege and Celane … fountain Clitorius: See above, n. 40 (1.1.1). Proetus was actually said to be the king of Argos; Lake Clitorius, however, was in Arcadia.
P. Aegineta, Galen’s Ape: The Byzantine physician Paul of Aegina (c. 625–89) was sometimes regarded as a slavish imitator of Galen. the Anticyrae … Achaia: See above, n. 87 (DJR).
dizzard: See above, n. 96 (DJR).
Menecrates ὁ ζεὺς: See above, n. 171 (1.2.3).

Hercules … wife and children: In classical mythology, the goddess Hera (Juno) struck Heracles (Hercules) with a temporary fit of madness, in which he murdered his children by his first wife, the Theban princess Megara; in some versions, he killed Megara as well.

Ennius of old: See above, n. 147 (DJR). sack: See above, n. 36 (1.3.1). Carneades the Academic … Hellebore first: The ancient Greek philosopher Carneades (214/13–129/8 BCE), regarded as the head of the Sceptical ‘New Academy’. According to Aulus Gellius (17.15.1–3), he took hellebore in order to prevent any corrupt humours in his stomach from rising up to his brain and interfering with his thoughts. which Petronius puts upon Chrysippus: In the Satyricon (88), the old poet Eumolpus claims that the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BCE) purged his brain with hellebore three times in order to continue his investigations.
lustres: Five-year periods. oppugned: See above, n. 6 (2.1.4). Junior Physicians: Modern (rather than ancient) doctors.
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).

Solon … what city: This story originates in the account given by Pausanias (10.37) of the destruction of the town of Crisa – identified in ancient tradition with Cirrha, and a close neighbour of Anticyra in Phocis: see above, n. 87 (DJR) – at the end of the First Sacred War in the early sixth century BCE.
Euonymus: See above, n. 61 (2.4.1).
Vidus Vidius a Dutch Physician: Vidius (Guido Guidi, 1509–69) was actually Italian.
upshot: See above, n. 12 (1.4.1).
except against: See above, n. 21 (DJR).

Oxymel Scilliticum: An ‘oxymel’ (a potion with a base of vinegar and honey) made with bulbs of squill (sea onion, Urginea maritima). Syrupus Helleboratus … in Quercetan: The elaborate recipe for the Syrupus helleboratus major given by the French physician Joseph Duchesne (Quercetanus, c. 1544–1609) includes one and a half ounces (42.5 grams) of black hellebore leaves and one dram (one-eighth of an ounce, or 3.54 grams) of hellebore root. The more straightforward Syrupus helleboratus minor contains ten drams of black hellebore leaves.

electuaries: See above, n. 2 (2.2.2). Pil. Indae: ‘Pillulae Indae’, medicinal pills containing black hellebore and lapis lazuli, attributed to Mesue the Elder. Confection of Hamech: See above, n. 67 (2.4.1). Diasenna, Diapolypodium, Diacassia, Diacatholicon: Compound electuaries (indicated by the prefix dia-) made from, respectively, senna, polypody, cassia, and a mixture of ingredients (including liquorice, senna, cassia and fennel). Hieralogodion: An electuary whose ingredients usually included colocynth (bitter-apple) and white and black hellebore, and here attributed to the ancient Greek astronomer Ptolemy – on whom, see above, n. 205 (DJR).

Hieram Rufi: The ‘Hiera Rufi’ (‘Electuary of Rufus’), a famous drug that was spuriously attributed to the ancient Greek doctor Rufus of Ephesus – see above, n. 6 (2.2.2) – was a purgative compound of many ingredients, usually including aloes, white and black hellebore, colocynth, saffron, cassia bark and mastic, mixed together with honey.

pil. Aggregat …. Pil. Ind. Mesue … Pilulae sine quibus esse nolo, Pilulae Cochiae cum Helleboro, Pil. Arabicae, Foetidae, de quinque generibus mirabolanorum:
Kinds of Pilulae aggregativae or ‘Aggregative pills’, made from several ingredients and usually devised to treat diseases affecting more than one part of the body. These include the ‘Pillulae Indae’ attributed to Mesue the Elder, as well as the following: Pilulae sine quibus esse nolo (literally, ‘pills I don’t want to be without’), the proverbial name given to pills containing aloes, senna, rhubarb and other ingredients, prescribed especially for purging phlegm from the brain; Pilulae Cochiae cum Helleboro, colocynth pills with hellebore; Pilulae Arabicae, pills made from aloe, bryony root and several other ingredients, for purging yellow bile from the head; Pilulae Foetidae, ‘fetid pills’ made from galbanum, a gum resin from Persian species of Ferula (giant fennel); and Pilulae de quinque generibus mirabolanorum, ‘pills from five kinds of myrobalans’. Turbith: See above, n. 21 (2.4.1). Manna: Dried sap or gum, especially from the branches of the manna ash (Fraxinus ornus), and used as a laxative. Elescophe: Possibly sun spurge (Euphorbia helioscopia).
choler is to be purged because it feeds the other: That is, because yellow bile nourishes black bile.
coined: Perhaps ‘produced’ (as a synonym for ‘quoted’), or ‘made valuable’.
boles: Large pills (or boluses).
Gargarisms: See above, n. 7 (2.2.4).
Apophlegmatisms: Treatments for purging phlegm from the head. Pellitory: The perennial herb Anacyclus pyrethrum.
Errhina: Or ‘errhines’, medicines which produce sneezing. Pimpernel: Any of several plants of the genus Pimpinella, especially burnet saxifrage. Castor: See below, n. 64 (2.5.1).
Castilian soap: Castile soap, a hard white soap made with olive oil and soda. Scammony: A purgative gum-resin taken from the roots of Convolvulus Scammonia.
Chirurgical: See above, n. 20 (2.1.4).
habit: See above, n. 26 (1.1.1).
what do I?: ‘What would I know?’, or ‘What business is it of mine?’
scarification: Slight surgical incisions.
Dropax: Pitch-plaster, a depilatory mixture of pitch and oil. Sinapismus: Or ‘sinapism’, a mustard plaster.
Issues … kept open: ‘Issues’ are surgical incisions made to drain an accumulation of fluid, then often kept open by the insertion of a pea. as shall be showed: See below, 2.5.1.4, 2.5.3.1.
This diet, as I have said … non-natural things: See above, 2.2.1.1.
avoided: Voided, emptied.
preparatives: See above, n. 76 (2.4.1). averters: See below, 2.5.1.4.
immaterial melancholy: See above, 1.1.3.3. distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
the median or middle vein of the arm: See above, n. 332 (DJR). a good season: A good while, a long time. the head vein: The cephalic vein in the arm.
months: See above, n. 85 (1.2.2).
Augeae stabulum purgare: See above, n. 284 (DJR).
lenitives: See above, n. 2 (2.2.2).

Electuarium lenitivum: Or the ‘Confectio sennae’, a lenitive electuary – on which, see above, n. 2 (2.2.2) – containing senna and polypody. Diaphenicum: An electuary containing dates and honey. Diacatholicon: See above, n. 31 (2.4.2).

Cassia: The pulp from the fruit of the Cassia fistula or ‘golden shower’ tree. Catholicon: A purgative electuary considered to evacuate every humour, with many varying ingredients (such as senna, rhubarb, hellebore, aniseed and fennel). Pil. Indae, Fumitoria, de Assaieret: See above, n. 33 (2.4.2). The ingredients of the pills known as ‘Pillulae fumitoria’ included fumitory – see above, n. 40 (2.4.1) – and myrobalans; those of ‘Pillulae de Assaieret’ included mastic, myrobalans and aloes.
Hieralogodion: See above, n. 31 (2.4.2).
cracks: See above, n. 152 (1.2.3).
invention: Discovery, finding out.
admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
4 scruples: A scruple is twenty grains in traditional weighting, or approximately a twenty-fourth of an ounce (1.18 grams).
Pinetus: ‘Penottus’ (the French physician and alchemist Bernard Georges Penot, 1519–1617) is probably meant here.
Aqua Chelidonia: A mixture containing the juice of the common or greater celandine plant (Chelidonium majus), said to remedy weak eyesight. Aurum potabile: See above, n. 142 (1.2.3).
Dutch: See above, n. 48 (DJR). sets light by: Accounts of small value, despises.
oppugn: See above, n. 6 (2.1.4).

As Thessalus of old … his own doings: The ancient Greek doctor Thessalus of Tralles (fl. c. 60 CE), a fiercely polemical member of the Methodist school who was active in Rome, declared himself superior to all his medical predecessors; his tombstone bore the inscription ‘champion physician’. The ‘Asclepiadeans’ were the followers of Asclepiades of Bithynia, a Greek physician who had developed his theories in Rome in the late second century BCE, and were the contemporary rivals there of the Methodists.
Mart: See above, n. 34 (DJR).
bastard Saffron: Safflower (Carthamus tinctorius). Sene: See above, n. 13 (2.4.2).

our natural Philosophy Reader: Edward Lapworth (1574–1636), who was also a physician and a poet, was appointed the first Sedleian reader in natural philosophy at Oxford in 1618, and became the Linacre physic lecturer in the following year.
Sneezings … nasals: Or errhines, medical preparations that induce sneezing. masticatories: Medical preparations that are chewed in the mouth.
Empiric: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
fuliginous: See above, n. 94 (1.2.2).
corroborating: Fortifying, refreshing. relics: See above, n. 2 (1.1.1). Temperament: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
sacrificed to Bacchus and Pallas: In other words, they venerated wine as well as wisdom.

Legitur & prisci Catonis … virtus: In note ‘a’, the quotation from Horace (Odes 3.21.11–12) probably refers to Cato the Elder – on whom, see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries) and n. 44 (2.2.4) – who was reported by Plutarch (Marcus Cato 25) to have enjoyed conviviality with neighbours on his country estate. However, Cato the Younger – on whom, see above, n. 51 (1.1.1) – was also said to have been a heavy drinker.

Demetrius in Plutarch … Seleucus’ hands: This anecdote, from Plutarch’s biography of Demetrius I of Macedon, refers to his captivity after surrendering himself in 286 to Seleucus I Nicator; on these two kings, see above, n. 272 (DJR) and n. 127 (1.2.1). Plutarch claims that Demetrius eventually ate and drank himself to death (Demetrius 52).
parable: See above, n. 200 (1.2.3). molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

habes, Serene charissime … pertinent: The last line of Seneca’s On Tranquillity of Mind, addressed to his younger relative and friend Lucius Annaeus Serenus (d. 62/3 CE), refers to the contents of the treatise rather than to wine.
exploded: See above, n. 45 (DJR). ventilated: Examined, discussed.
hear the Scriptures … occasion: Proverbs 31:6, 1 Timothy 5:23.
goodfellows: See above, n. 68 (2.2.6).
incensed: See above, n. 37 (1.1.1).
that black … Lacedaemonians: See above, n. 94 (1.2.4).
Scorzonera roots condite: See above, n. 37 (2.4.1) and n. 43 (1.2.2).

Datura: A genus of toxic plants, especially Datura stramonium, with hallucinogenic properties – see also above, n. 42 (2.4.1). Bang: Or ‘bhang’, the leaves and seed capsules of the female cannabis plant.

One of the Roman Emperors … exhilarate himself: Galen’s On Antidotes (14.4) records that Marcus Aurelius took mithridate – see above, n. 78 (1.2.2) – every day, in a dose measured to the size of an ‘Egyptian bean’ (the seed of the Indian lotus plant, Nelumbo nucifera). According to Galen, the emperor adjusted the amount of opium in each dose, depending on whether he needed to sleep or to endure his imperial duties.

Bezoar-stone: See above, n. 53 (2.4.1). the confection of Alkermes: The dried bodies of scale insects, formerly thought to be berries or grains, found on the kermes oak (Quercus coccifera) in the Mediterranean.
Amber: Ambergris.
Ox-tongue: Bugloss or borage (so called because of the shape and roughness of the foliage).
except against: See above, n. 21 (DJR).
as Thucydides of the plague at Athens: Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War (2.7.3–54) gives an influential account of the famous ‘plague of Athens’ (430–426 BCE). Catholic: Universal.

Diamargaritum frigidum, Diambra … Electuarium laetificans Galeni & Rhasis, de Gemmis, Dianthus, Diamoschum dulce: See above, n. 78 (2.4.1). Diaboraginatum … Diamoschum … amarum: Compound electuaries with the main ingredients of borage and bitter musk respectively. Electuarium Conciliatoris: An electuary named after Pietro d’Abano (‘the Conciliator’) – see above, n. 103 (1.2.4) – that includes juice of apples and borage, myrobalans, cinnamon, galangal and several other ingredients. syrup. Cidoniorum de pomis: Syrups of quinces and apples. Enula campana: See above, n. 28 (2.4.1). Satyrion: A name for various kinds of orchid, reputed to have aphrodisiac qualities.
diabuglossatum: A compound electuary containing bugloss.
form: See above, n. 3 (2.2.2).
spagirically: Alchemically.
wether’s head: Possibly the head of a ram, but more probably here the chickpea plant, whose Latin species name (arietinum) means ‘ram’s head’.
exenterated: Disembowelled, eviscerated.
Epithems: See above, n. 84 (2.4.1).
Melilot: Or ‘sweet clover’: any plants of the genus Melilotus, which usually have yellow or white flowers.
on a Friday in the hour of Jupiter: In the system of astrological hours, in which each planet is considered to ‘rule’ over particular parts of the day, this was the fifth hour after sunrise.
lapped: See above, n. 30 (DJR).
Chirurgery: See above, n. 20 (2.1.4).
Verbasco: Verbascum, or mullein.
dioscordium: An electuary made with scordium (water germander).

Requies Nicholai: An electuary containing opium, nutmeg and mandrakes – see above, n. 160 (1.2.4). Triphera magna: An electuary containing opium, mandrakes, cinnamon, galangal and other spices. pilulae de cynoglossa: Cynoglossum (hound’s-tongue) pills. Laudanum Paracelsi: An electuary containing opium, henbane, spermaceti and other ingredients.
Nenuphar: Water lily.
nodules: Small bags containing medicaments, often tied up with a knot.
virgin wax: Fresh or unused bees-wax.
Frontlets: Cloths or bandages to be worn on the forehead, and containing medicaments that were sometimes called ‘frontals’ – see above, n. 83 (2.4.1).
Castoreum: Or ‘castor’, an unctuous medicament made from the exudate of the castor sacs of beavers. water of life: That is, aqua-vitae.
stillicidia: ‘Stillicides’, medicinal drops.

flect: Or ‘flected’ – bent over, bowed. Nam qua parte … Statius: ‘Statius’ in note ‘b’ should be ‘Stasinus’. The line is a Latin translation of a verse sometimes attributed to the ancient epic poet Stasinus of Cyprus.
a waiting-Gentlewoman: A female servant of a lady of high birth. offended: See above, n. 23 (DJR).

id populus curat scilicet: A sarcastic observation, quoted from Terence’s Girl from Andros (185). Mr. Doctor Ashworth: Note ‘e’ refers to one of Burton’s contemporaries at Oxford, the learned physician Henry Ashworth (1552–1633) of Oriel College, who had a medical practice in Catte Street.
consent: See above, n. 4 (1.1.3).
Litharge … litharge of silver: Lead monoxide, and the same substance when it is specifically produced by the separation of silver from lead ore (galena), in which silver is often found.
Aron: Arum.
indurate: See above, n. 19 (1.2.2).
intentive: See above, n. 11 (1.3.3).
deliquium: See above, n. 22 (1.3.1).

Hieram Archigenis: That is, ‘the Electuary of Archigenes’, a purgative containing colocynth (bitter-apple), agaric, scammony and many other ingredients. It was named after the Syrian physician Archigenes of Apamea, who practised in Rome during the reign of Trajan (98–117 CE).
salvatella: A vein on the back of the hand near the ulnar edge, often used in bloodletting.
Ptolemaeus Philadelphus … King of Assyria: Berenice Phernophorus (285/80–246/5 BCE), the daughter of the Egyptian pharaoh Ptolemy II, was married to Antiochus II Theos of Syria in 252.
Lamb’s-wool: Hot ale mixed with roasted apple pulp, sugar and spices.
Chalybs praeparatus: Water mixed with iron. Alexipharmacum: See above, n. 111 (2.2.4).
ground-Pine: See above, n. 31 (2.4.1).
inunctions: Rubbing in of oil or ointment.
of them I have spoken: See above, 2.2.2.1.
Southernwood: The shrub Artemisia abrotanum. Cerotes: See above, n. 83 (2.4.1).
calastic Cataplasms: Laxative poultices. Dropaces … sinapisms: See above, n. 5 (2.4.3). Dutchman: See above, n. 48 (DJR).

Calamus Aromaticus: Lemongrass. Valerian: Any of the plants of the genus Valeriana. Zedoary: The aromatic root of the Curcuma genus of plants. Aristolochia: A genus of shrubs, including the common birthwort (Aristolochia clematitis). Cicliminus: Cyclamen. Dittander: Dittany. Ammi: Bishop-weed. Cary: Caraway. grana Paradisi: ‘Grains of paradise’, which commonly referred to cardamom, although this was sometimes confused with the closely related West African spice Aframomum melegueta. Diacalaminth, Electuarium de baccis lauri: Compound electuaries containing, respectively, calamint and bayberries. Benedicta laxativa: ‘The blessed laxative’, made with turbith, scammony, spurge roots and many other ingredients. Pulvis ad flatus Antid. Florent.: ‘A powder for wind from the Florentine Antidotary’, containing coriander, aniseed and other ingredients. pulvis Carminativus: ‘Carminative powder’, made of a mixture of spices to expel wind. Aromaticum Rosatum: ‘Rose spice’, made of red roses, liquorice and several spices.
Spikenard: An aromatic oil or ointment obtained from the plant Nardostachys jatamansi, which is of the honeysuckle family and grows in the Himalayas.
Empirics: See above, n. 76 (DJR). bullet: A small round ball.
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
℞ Elect. lenit …. misce: This prescription is apparently missing some ingredients. lenitive electuary: See above, n. 2 (2.2.2).
pilulae mastichinae: Pills containing mastic, aloes, agaric and other ingredients.
Turpentine: See above, n. 2 (2.2.2).

dissembling with him in Petronius … grave Philosophers: In the Satyricon (85), the character Eumolpus describes how in Pergamum he warded off suspicion that he intended to seduce the son of his host, by feigning offence whenever the topic of taking advantage of pretty boys came up in dinner conversation.
Love-toys: Amorous playing, or light caresses.

Erubuit, posuitque meum Lucretia librum … legit: This slightly modified quotation from Martial (Epigrams 11.16.9–10), refers to Lucretia – on whom, see above, n. 48 (1.2.3) – as a model of the sexually virtuous wife.

counterfeit Catos: See above, n. 6 (Preliminaries). as the Lord John answered … Guazzo: An allusion to La civile conversazione (1574) by the Italian writer Stefano Guazzo, in which the elderly secretary, Signor Giovanne Cane (‘Lord John’ in the English translation of 1586) addresses Giovanna Bobba, who has been named as the ‘queen’ of the banquet. resolve: Examine, analyse. divert: Ward off, avert.
excepted at: See above, n. 21 (DJR).

the second of the Aeneids … heroical subject: The second book of the Aeneid is devoted to Aeneas’ telling of the story of the Trojan War to the Carthaginian queen Dido. Their love affair is described in the fourth book. the Canticles … a Ballad of Ballads: Both names for the Song of Solomon, the second of these appearing in both the Great Bible (1539) and the Bishops’ Bible (1568).

Jacob and Rachel … Shechem and Dinah … Judah and Tamar: Genesis 29, 34, 38. the fornications … Moabites: Numbers 25:1. Samson and Delilah’s embracings: Judges 16. David and Bathsheba’s adulteries … Amnon and Tamar: 2 Samuel 11, 13. Solomon’s Concubines: 1 Kings 11:3.
Susanna: Daniel 13, a chapter regarded by Protestants as apocryphal, tells the story of a beautiful and virtuous Hebrew wife who is falsely accused of adultery and successfully defies her accusers.

that dalliance with Agathon … abitura fuit: The ancient Athenian tragic poet Agathon, whose works are lost, appears as a character in Plato’s Symposium. The attribution of the epigram quoted here to Plato was spurious.

that Plato and Socrates … from their City: In book 10 of Plato’s Republic, where the character of Socrates is describing the ideal city. quod Junonem cum Jove in Ida … contectos: In book 14 of the Iliad, Hera (Juno) distracts Zeus (Jupiter) on Mount Ida (overlooking Troy) by making love to him and then inducing him to sleep, permitting her to help the Achaeans. Vulcan’s net: Book 8 of the Odyssey describes how Hephaestus (Vulcan) forged an unbreakable chain-link net, which he used to capture Ares (Mars) and his wife Aphrodite (Venus) while they were together in bed, and then drag them to Mount Olympus to be ridiculed and punished by the other gods. Apollo fled, when he was persecuted by Achilles: In book 21 of the Iliad, Apollo disguises himself as the Trojan hero Agenor, who has been engaging Achilles in single combat, and runs away from Troy in order to allow his compatriots to return safely into their city. as Mars that roared … his fall: On this allusion, combined here with a reference to the Greek warrior Stentor, whose powerful voice was said to be equivalent to those of fifty men, see above, n. 53 (2.3.3). Vulcan was a summer’s day … broke his leg: In book 1 of the Iliad, Hephaestus (Vulcan) tells Hera how Zeus once caught him by the foot and hurled him down from Olympus to the island of Lemnos. to admire Autolycus … Charmides: Allusions to Autolycus, a young Athenian athlete whose admiration by Callias is portrayed in Xenophon’s Symposium; the poet Agathon; and four Athenians portrayed as Socrates’ interlocutors in Platonic dialogues named after them (the famously beautiful Alcibiades – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – along with the aristocrats Phaedrus, Charmides and Lysis).

Callias, Thrasymachus, Polus, Aristophanes: The Athenian comic poet Callias (fl. first half of the fifth century BCE), who mocked Socrates in his ‘Prisoners’; the sophist and rhetorician Thrasymachus of Chalcedon (fl. c. 430–400 BCE), depicted as the withering critic of Socrates in Plato’s Republic; Polus, a sophist from Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily whose views on rhetoric clash with those of Socrates in Plato’s Gorgias; and Aristophanes – on whom, see above, n. 41 (2.3.7). emulators: See above, n. 224 (DJR). Anytus and Meletus … for teaching Critias to tyrannize, his impiety: See above, n. 98 (DJR); on Critias, whose association with Socrates was the real reason for the latter’s trial according to Xenophon, see above, n. 2 (2.2.6). juggling: See above, n. 122 (1.2.4).
overseen: Imprudent; but also, perhaps, drunken or intoxicated (with love).

as he said of Cato’s drunkenness … to be drunk: Probably an exaggeration of the defence given by Seneca (in On Tranquillity of Mind 17.9) of the inebriation of Cato the Younger – cf. above, n. 29 (2.5.1).
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

Heliodorus a Bishop … Theagenes and Chariclea: Little is known for certain about the author of the third- or fourth-century CE Greek novel also known as the Aethiopica, which tells the story of the Ethiopian princess Chariclea and the Thessalian noble Theagenes, other than that he was a Phoenician from the city of Emesa, and that he adopted the pseudonym ‘Heliodorus’ (‘Gift of the Sun’) because his family claimed descent from the sun-god Helios. The view that he was bishop of Tricca in Thessaly, and wrote the novel in his youth, was first related by the early Christian historian Socrates Scholasticus.

indited: See above, n. 2 (Preliminaries). that wanton history of Euryalus and Lucretia: Enea Silvio Piccolomini (1405–64) wrote the extremely popular Historia de duobus amantibus, which details the illicit affair between a married Italian
lady and a German courtier, in 1444. He became Pope Pius II in 1458, and the Historia was first published in 1467–70.
Alpheratius: Guzmán de Alfarache, a picaresque novel by Mateo Alemán, published in two parts in 1599 and 1604.

aspersion: Sprinkling. edulcare vitam … nugis: This passage loosely reproduces verses by the Roman poet Gnaeus Matius (early first century BCE) that are quoted by Aulus Gellius (15.25.2), although Burton probably meant the poet Lucius Accius (b. 170 BCE) – cited in note ‘b’ – to whom the lines were attributed in the Dialogus de amoribus (1554) by the French jurist Pierre Godefroy (Godefridus, d. 1573).

Babylonius & Ephesius … Suidas: Note ‘e’ refers to three Greek authors called Xenophon mentioned in the tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia now known as the Suda: Xenophon of Ephesus, author of the Tales of Ephesus or Habrocomes and Anthia (probably second century CE); and two shadowy figures about whom almost nothing is known: Xenophon of Antioch, said to have written the lost ‘erotic history’ Babyloniaca, and Xenophon of Cyprus, whose lost Cypriaca told the mythological story of Myrrha, Cinyras and Adonis (more famously related by Ovid in the Metamorphoses).
enarrations: Commentaries, expositions.

Aretine’s Antonia: The character of Antonia, the friend of the elderly prostitute Nanna in Pietro Aretino’s Ragionamento della Nanna & dell’Antonia (1534). Burton used this work in the Latin translation (1623) by Caspar von Barth, which renames Nanna as Lucretia.

that famous testament … Porcellus: In the Testamentum Porcelli, an ancient parody of a will, a piglet (‘Grunter Roast-Pig’) bequeaths his bodily parts to various parties: his ears to the deaf, his tongue to lawyers and the verbose, his loins to women, and so on.
The Comical Poet: Terence, in the prologue to his Girl from Andros.

Madaurensis: Apuleius, whose full name was Lucius Apuleius Madaurensis. Annianus, Sulpicius, Evenus: The three poets mentioned by Ausonius are the Latin lyricist Annianus, who wrote obscene verses in the second century CE; Sulpicia – on whom, see below, n. 9 (3.3.4) (Burton apparently confuses her with Servius Sulpicius Rufus, whose licentious poems are mentioned by Ovid, and who was the grandfather of another Sulpicia who wrote love poetry: see below, n. 63 (3.3.1)); and Evenus of Paros, probably from the fourth century BCE, and known for his erotic poetry. Fescennines: Verses or songs, traditionally sung at weddings and frequently obscene. Atellans: Ribald or licentious farces.

Virgil in Priapeiis: Poems about Priapus – on whom, see above, n. 3 (2.1.3) – attributed to Virgil, Ovid and others. Petronius in Catalectis: The group of poems collected and published by the classical scholar Joseph Scaliger as the Catalecta (1573), twenty-three of which were by Petronius, was also included in the edition of the Satyricon published by the Pithou brothers in 1587.
heroical or Herculean love: See below, 3.2.1.1.

censure: See above, n. 59 (DJR). a naked man … as Augusta Livia truly said: According to Dio Cassius (58.2), Augusta Livia (the wife of the emperor Augustus) thereby saved the lives of some men who were to be executed for meeting her when they were naked. Honi soit qui mal y pense: In note ‘c’, the motto of the medieval English chivalric Order of the Garter is cited to complement an expression, quoted in the main text, given by the character Simo in Terence’s Girl from Andros (164).
Extremum hunc Arethusa … laborem: In this quotation from Virgil’s Eclogues (10.1), the mythological nymph and Muse Arethusa is invoked as the inspirer of pastoral poetry.

in the Olympics … Wrestlers in Philostratus: An allusion to the Life of Apollonius of Tyana (4.29) by Philostratus, where Apollonius – on whom, see above, n. 55 (DJR) – is reported to have approved the Eleians’ careful management of the
rites at the Olympic games, but also to have said that ‘I don’t know if they are wise; they are certainly sophists’ (that is, they pretend to be wise).
in the first Partition … Sections of Perturbations: See above, 1.2.3.1, 1.2.3.11, 1.2.3.14, 1.3.1.2, 1.3.1.3, 1.3.1.4, 1.3.3.1.

Plato calls it the great Devil: A reference to the speech of Diotima in Plato’s Symposium, also quoted in note ‘b’, which describes love as a ‘great demon’ (202E) because of its power in the spiritual realm that mediates between the gods and men; cf. above, n. 18 (1.2.1).
the Ethics: See above, n. 80 (1.1.2). naughty tree: An inferior tree that proverbially can produce only bad fruit.
several: See above, n. 18 (DJR). as the species … inner soul: See above, n. 34 (1.1.2).
Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR). just: See above, n. 26 (DJR). paraenetical: See above, n. 2 (2.3.1). admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
extreme parts: Powerful or pronounced personal qualities. that speech of Pausanias … two loves: As related by the character in Plato’s Symposium (180D–E); on ‘Veneres’ see above, n. 65 (1.2.4).

One Venus is ancient … commonly we call Venus: The Platonic bifurcation of Aphrodite (Venus) to represent the division between the higher and the common forms of love, which was fundamental to Renaissance Neoplatonism, derives from two of the epithets by which the goddess was worshipped in ancient Greece: Aphrodite ‘Ourania’, said to have been produced in the sea by the genitals and seed of Uranus, the divine personification of heaven; and Aphrodite ‘Pandemos’, the daughter of Zeus and Dione.
those four cardinal virtues: In classical philosophy, the moral virtues of prudence, justice, courage and temperance.

that golden chain … from heaven: An allusion to the ‘golden chain’ stretching from heaven to earth, described in the Iliad (8.19–27); Zeus says that using it in a tug-of-war with all the other gods, he would be able to pull the earth, sea and gods all together up to Olympus. It was the subject of much subsequent allegorical commentary as a link between the divine and human realms, and here, in the Platonic interpretation given in pseudo-Lucian’s In Praise of Demosthenes (13), it is associated with the ascent of the soul that occurs in ‘divine fury’.
as shall be showed in his place: See below, 3.4.1.2, 3.4.2.3.

confound: See above, n. 86 (DJR). Sensible … Love: ‘Sensible’ love, which as the following paragraph explains, is that which belongs to all sentient creatures or ‘brute beasts’, is a passion produced by the activities of the ‘Sensible’ or ‘sensitive’ soul (see above, 1.1.2.5–6).

as a Stone to his centre: In this pre-Newtonian phrase, which is probably taken here from the English Catholic controversialist Thomas Wright’s Passions of the Minde (1600), the ‘centre’ of a stone is the point towards which it naturally moves when dropped.
Jet, chaff: Medieval and Renaissance discussions of gemstones often noted the power of jet, when polished or chafed by rubbing, to attract lightweight objects such as chaff or straw.
Bur: Burdock.
Maecenas: See above, n. 111 (DJR).
Achan in the camp: See above, n. 222 (DJR).

Apelles, Phidias: The highly acclaimed painter Apelles of Cos (fl. fourth century BCE) was very well paid for his works, and the similarly celebrated Athenian
sculptor Phidias – on whom, see above, n. 77 (2.2.4) – was famous for his use of gold, some of which he was charged with misappropriating.

tied … by the teeth: That is, bound by the need or desire for food – a figurative expression deriving from Plautus (The Two Menaechemuses 94–5), who refers to the power of vincla escaria (‘edible chains’) to keep men from running away.
abject: Outcast.

Geryons: In classical mythology, the giant Geryon had three bodies (or one body and three heads in some versions); his form was taken to symbolize the unity of separate persons in friendship. turgent: See above, n. 150 (DJR). depress: Disparage, put down. rupto jecore exierit Caprificus: The original line from Persius (1.25) compares the outbreak of poetic inspiration to the dislodging of rock by the shoots of the wild fig-tree, and incorporates the idea (preserved here) that the soul’s passions issue from the liver.
golden apple: See above, n. 193 (DJR).
e contra: Contrariwise, vice versa. Caterpillar: Rapacious or predatory person, extortioner. Hog rubber: Yokel, country bumpkin.
Desinit in piscem … superne: A famous description of grotesque visual imagery from Horace’s Art of Poetry (4), referring to literary works that are composed out of mismatched elements.
Thessala Tempe: A phrase taken from Horace (Odes 1.2.4), referring to the famously beautiful valley of Tempe in Thessaly – see above, n. 29 (2.2.4).
Credo equidem … vultus: Note ‘b’ quotes Virgil (Aeneid 6.849), where the Roman poet refers to the superior artifice of Greek sculpture. curious: See above, n. 30 (2.2.4).

Non amo te Sabidi, &c.: In full, Martial’s epigram (1.32) reads ‘Non amo te Sabidi, nec possum dicere quare:/hoc tantum possum dicere, non amo te’ (‘I don’t love you Sabidius, and cannot say why; all I can say is this, I don’t love you’).

Alexander admired Hephaestion, Hadrian Antinous: See above, n. 162 (1.2.3) and n. 107 (1.2.4). Nero Sporus: Sporus was a young freedman who bore a remarkable resemblance to the recently deceased second wife of Nero, Poppaea Sabina (d. 65 CE) – on whom, see below, n. 137 (3.2.2) – who was said to have been kicked to death by the emperor. Nero had Sporus castrated, used him as a sexual surrogate and then married him in a ceremony that renamed him ‘Sabina’.
temperament: See above, n. 194 (DJR). trine and sextile aspects: See above, n. 55 (1.1.1). Ascendents, Lords of their genitures: See above, n. 13 (DJR).

Aemilius Lepidus & Julius Flaccus: Note ‘a’ includes references to the Roman statesmen Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior (sometimes mistakenly called Flaccus), former political opponents who were reconciled in 179 BCE, when both assumed the censorship.

Isocrates Demonico precipit … simultatum: In To Demonicus (33), referred to in note ‘d’, the ancient Greek orator Isocrates (d. c. 338 BCE) instructs Demonicus, who was possibly the son of Hipponicus, a wealthy Cyprian.

as the golden shields … heaven: See above, n. 88 (2.2.3). so vile and base … de Burdonum familia: In 1601, the German scholar Caspar Schoppe (Scioppius, 1576–1649) published a detailed debunking of the claim by the classicist Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) to be descended from the aristocratic Della Scala family – on whom, see above, n. 32 (2.3.3). According to Schoppe, Scaliger was the grandson of the relatively lowly Paduan cartographer and miniaturist Benedetto Bordone (1460–1531).

Ovid in Ibin: Ovid’s Ibis is a long (644-line) curse, addressed to an unknown former friend of the poet. Archilochus: An ancient Greek lyric poet (fl. 670–640 BCE) from the island of Paros, renowned for his fierce invectives – particularly against a nobleman called Lycambes, who had refused the poet permission to marry his daughter.

as jet draws a straw: See above, n. 42 (3.1.1). fucate: Artificial, counterfeit. form: Beauty. those two Venus’ twins, Eros and Anteros: In classical mythology, Eros
(the personification of love as sexual desire) and Anteros (‘Mutual love’, the personification of requited love and avenger of unrequited love), were both sons of Aphrodite (Venus) and Ares (Mars).
Gnathos: See above, n. 89 (1.2.1). outsides: See above, n. 115 (DJR).

he that Caelius Secundus met by the highway side: The Augustinian friar Agostino Mainardi (1482–1563), friend and former teacher of the heterodox religious reformer and writer Caelio Secondo Curione (1503–69), and the latter’s interlocutor in the dialogue De amplitudine beati regni Dei (1554).
glozing: Cajoling, coaxing. Rehoboam’s Counsellors: The young counsellors whose advice Rehoboam favours over that of the elders, leading to the rebellion of the Israelites (1 Kings 12).
characters: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1). I shall elsewhere discuss: In 3.2.2.5; see also 3.3.1.2.
astonied: Stunned, benumbed.

Mercury the Gentleman-usher … from above: In classical mythology, the messenger-god Mercury (Hermes) was associated with the Graces because of his role as the god of eloquence. Hesiod’s Theogony (907) states that Eurynome, the daughter of the sea-god Oceanus, bore Zeus the three Graces – goddesses that came to be proverbial models of grace, talent and beauty.
who was more grim … to look upon: The ugliness of Socrates was proverbial, but Plato’s Theaetetus (143E–144A) specifies that he had a snub nose and especially protruding eyes.
Politianus, Melanchthon, Gesner: See 2.3.2.1, p. 547, and 2.3.7.1, p. 602. Sileni Alcibiadis: See above, n. 102 (DJR). impolite: Unpolished, rough. terse: See above, n. 217 (DJR).

Alcibiades … deformed soul: Boethius’ judgement of Alcibiades – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – probably derives from the description of his youthful ambitiousness and self-conceit in Plato’s Alcibiades I.
Abdalonymus in Curtius: See above, n. 45 (2.3.2).
Titus Pomponius Atticus … Rome: See above, n. 23 (1.4.1).
Q. Cincinnatus … Dictator of Rome: See above, n. 44 (2.2.4).

Cato, Fabricius, Aristides, Antoninus, Probus: See above, n. 51 (1.1.1), nn. 93, 239 (1.2.3), and n. 36 (2.3.2). Parmenio the King: The Macedonian general Parmenion (400–330 BCE) achieved considerable military success on behalf of Alexander the Great, who executed him after he was implicated in a series of conspiracies. The historian Quintus Curtius Rufus (3.6.4) emphasizes Parmenion’s loyalty. Titus deliciae humani generis: See above, n. 115 (1.2.4). dilling: Darling. Edgar Ætheling: Edgar Ætheling (b. c. 1052, d. in or after 1125) was the grandson of King Edmund II Ironside, and in 1066 the only candidate for the throne who was of English royal descent. He was elected as king by an Anglo-Saxon assembly of nobles and leading citizens, but was never crowned.

I do mightily love Calvisius … to Sossius: Pliny actually expresses his affection for Varisidius Nepos, whom he identifies (Letters 4.4) as a near relative of a close friend of his from Comum, Gaius Calvisius Rufus. On ‘Sossius’, see above, n. 33 (DJR).
Cato in … de Finibus: Cato the Younger, as he appears in Cicero’s On Ends; see above, n. 51 (1.1.1).
Magdalen Queen of France … the 11th: Actually Margaret of Scotland (1424–45), who married Louis XI – on whom, see above, n. 24 (1.3.1) – in 1436.

that prediction of Sibylla Cumea: Virgil’s fourth Eclogue records the prophecy of the Cumaean Sibyl that a ‘golden race’ will appear after the birth of a child (later taken to be Christ) and the advent of a golden age.

Plato and Pythagoras … Egyptian Priests: See above, n. 44 (1.2.1). Pythagoras is reported in ancient sources to have come into contact with various oriental sages
when he travelled to Egypt. Apollonius travelled … Gymnosophists: See above, nn. 55, 91 (DJR).

Multi Romam … profecti sunt: According to the Flemish travel writer Frans Schott (1548–1622), these lines were inscribed over one of the doors in the Palazzo della Ragione in Padua (Livy’s birthplace), where a cenotaph to the ancient historian had been erected in the mid-sixteenth century. The lines did not come, as note ‘e’ suggests, from the portrait bust.
A true love’s knot: In note ‘f’, a ‘true-love knot’ was an ornamental knot (a double-looped bow or two intertwined loops) symbolizing true love.

Diapason: See above, n. 307 (DJR). Damon and Pythias: When the Pythagorean philosopher Pythias was sentenced to death for treason by the tyrant Dionysius I of Syracuse – cf. above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – his friend Damon took his place while Pythias returned home to say farewell to his family. When Pythias returned, Dionysius freed them both. Pylades and Orestes: See above, n. 14 (2.2.6). Nisus and Euryalus: See above, n. 6 (2.3.5). Theseus and Pirithous: The legendary king of Athens and the king of the Lapiths in Thessaly became friends after they fought each other. prosecute: Follow, accompany (or possibly, honour or cultivate – from the Latin prosequor).
Naenias: See above, n. 16 (2.3.3).
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).
from teeth outward: Pretendedly; in profession but not in reality. by-respects: A ‘by-respect’ is a side aim or motive, for a reason other than the ostensible one.
currish: See above, n. 54 (2.3.2).

blear the world’s eyes: See above, n. 38 (1.2.2). the Gemonian scales: See above, n. 111 (1.2.3). Eusebius: Chief minister to the Roman emperor Constantius II (ruled 337–61 CE). He was executed in 361, after being condemned for corruption by the extraordinary court set up by the new emperor Julian at Chalcedon.
dilection: Spiritual love. circle equant: See above, n. 75 (2.2.3).
reference: See above, n. 9 (DJR).

the Decii: Father and son of the same name (Publius Decius Mus), both Roman consuls who sacrificed themselves in battle, in the Latin War at Vesuvius (340 BCE) and in the Third Samnite War at Sentinum (295 BCE) respectively. In the former’s act of self-sacrifice, according to Livy (8.9), he devoted himself and his enemies to the spirits of the dead in the underworld (di manes). Horatii: See above, n. 37 (2.2.4). Curtii: An ancient Roman family given heroic status on account of their mythical connections with the ‘lacus Curtius’, a pond or pit in the Forum. In the legend, when the crevice opened up in 362 BCE, an oracle declared that it would not be closed until sacrifice was made of Rome’s greatest possessions; Marcus Curtius saved his country by leaping into it, on horseback and in full armour. Scaevola, Regulus, Codrus: See above, n. 58 (2.3.3), n. 71 (1.1.2) and n. 8 (2.3.4).

the Fabii: One of the oldest patrician families at Rome, who volunteered to fight on behalf of the city against the forces of the Etruscan city of Veii – see above, n. 1 (2.3.8). After some success, all but one of them eventually perished in an ambush at the Battle of the Cremera (477 BCE).
Battle Abbey: See above, n. 130 (DJR).

six Senators of Calais … die for the rest: A reference to the story of the burghers of Calais from the Hundred Years War, in which the besieged city, in 1347, was compelled by Edward III of England to send out six of its leading citizens, wearing
nooses around their necks. According to contemporary chroniclers, the citizens’ lives were spared after Edward’s wife, Philippa of Hainault, interceded on their behalf. Modern historians, however, have interpreted the episode as a traditional symbolic act of surrender.
Maro: See above, n. 233 (1.2.3).
dispart: Cleave, break up.
complicated: See above, n. 104 (2.2.4).

those seven works of mercy: Here, apparently, the seven corporal works of mercy (bury the dead; visit the sick; visit the imprisoned; feed the hungry; give drink to the thirsty; clothe the naked; and shelter the homeless), rather than the spiritual ones (teach the ignorant; counsel the doubtful; admonish sinners; bear wrongs patiently; forgive offences; comfort the afflicted; and pray for the living and the dead).
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR). impertinent: See above, n. 133 (1.2.3).

offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR). upon his knees, as Sarpedon … in Homer: An allusion to the Iliad (16.491–501), where Sarpedon, just before being killed by Patroclus, begs his cousin Glaucus, the other leader of the Lycians at Troy, to avenge his death. made dice of his bones, as they say: A proverbial phrase referring to the English practice of delivering dice, which in this period were often made from bones, to creditors of executed prisoners, representing all that the latter were likely to own at their deaths.

Hircanaeque admorunt ubera tigres: Note ‘c’ quotes Dido’s reproach of her lover Aeneas’ cruelty (Aeneid 4.367). Hyrcania (‘Wolf’s Land’) was a region on the southeast corner of the Caspian Sea, known for its animal life. animate: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3). Eris dea: See above, n. 193 (DJR).
common societies: See above, n. 303 (DJR).
myriads: Innumerable coins (or, more strictly, tens of thousands of them). as the Fox told the Ape: In Aesop’s fable ‘An Ape and a Fox’. ingurgitate: See above, n. 30 (2.2.1).
the dog in the manger: See above, n. 121 (1.2.3).
Poor Lazarus: See above, n. 17 (2.3.3). chippings: Crusts. offals: Crumbs, leftovers.
counterfeit crank: See above, n. 92 (1.2.4).
Spittle: Or ‘spital’ – a charitable house for the indigent or diseased, a lower-class hospital.
default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

The lantern in Athens … Xenocles: According to Plutarch, whose Life of Pericles is evidently the main source for the following list of ancient Greek architectural accomplishments, the wealthy Athenian citizen Xenocles arranged the building of the lantern over the Periclean shrine of the mysteries at Eleusis (Pericles 13). the Theatre by Pericles: Pericles – see above, n. 90 (DJR) – had a colonnaded hall built for the Odeon, a space for reciting songs and poetry, on the southern slope of the Athenian Acropolis. the famous port Piraeum by Musicles: This should be Mnesicles, an Athenian architect active in the second half of the fifth century BCE, although he was famous for designing the Propylaea, the monumental gateway to the Acropolis. The layout of the city of Piraeus was traditionally attributed to Hippodamus of Miletus in c. 450 BCE, but Burton may be thinking of Callicrates, another fifth-century architect whom Plutarch notes (Pericles 13) as the designer of the ‘Long Walls’ of Athens, linking the port to the main city. Pallas Palladium by Phidias: The ancient wooden cult statue of Athena Polias in the Erechtheum has here been confused with Phidias’ sculpture of Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon – on which, see above, n. 77 (2.2.4). the Pantheon by Callicratidas: Actually the Parthenon, one of whose architects was Callicrates. brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR).

that Marian Oak: Named by Cicero after Marius – on whom, see above, n. 25 (DJR) – in an epic poem (now lost) about the Roman general and politician, and symbolizing poetic inspiration and immortality.
Maecenates: See above, n. 111 (DJR).

a Caleb or a Joshua: Of all the Israelites who escaped from Egypt, only Caleb, son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, son of Nun, were permitted to enter the Promised Land, because they had remained faithful in their worship of God (Numbers 32:11–12).

Astraea: In classical mythology, Astraea was the goddess of justice who lived on earth in the golden age (the first, harmonious and abundant age in Hesiod’s scheme of the five ‘Ages of Man’, the miserable ‘iron age’ being the last of these), but she abandoned it for heaven.

designments: Plots, schemes. Italian blaspheming, Spanish renouncing: Burton’s probable source here, the Relation of the state of the religion (1605) by Sir Edwin Sandys, criticizes the ‘renouncings’ (of God) and blasphemies expressed by Spanish and Italian soldiers, drawing on the commonplace Jacobean association of Roman Catholicism with atheism.
monomachies: See above, n. 15 (DJR).

Gallienus in Treb. Pollio … Vopiscus of Aurelian: Note ‘b’ refers to the Roman emperors Gallienus (c. 218–68) and Aurelian – on whom, see above, n. 276 (DJR). Both were reported in the Augustan History to have had carried out prodigious acts of slaughter. The note also incorporates a line from Juvenal (‘Rabie … Praecipites’: Satires 6.648–9).
Bills: Halberds.

Bioneis sermonibus & sale nigro: A quotation from Horace (Epistles 2.2.60), which refers to the famously caustic satirical wit of the ancient philosopher Bion of Borysthenes (c. 335–245 BCE). those ten persecutions: See above, n. 139 (DJR).
combustion: See above, n. 340 (DJR).

which Josephus once said … peevishness was such: This quotation from the historian Josephus (The Jewish War 5.6) refers to the plundering of the Temple of Jerusalem by John of Gischala, the leader of the Jewish revolt against the Romans, during the Roman siege in 70 CE.
generous: See above, n. 143 (DJR).
vegetal and sensible creatures: See above, n. 85 (DJR).

Hesiod makes Terra and Chaos to be Love’s parents: In Theogony (116), Hesiod only says that Chaos – on which, see above, n. 35 (DJR) – and Gaia, the Greek personification of the earth and roughly the equivalent of the Roman Tellus or Terra – came into existence before Eros; cf. above, n. 36 (3.1.1). Ante deos omnes … Amorem: This quotation from Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love (13) is itself taken from the Cosmogony of Parmenides (fifth century BCE), which says that Eros was produced by Aphrodite. As is intimated in note ‘e’, Plutarch gives final approval to Hesiod’s description of Eros as the first-born of all the gods.
Iris and Favonius: The goddess of the rainbow, and the west wind (also called Zephyrus). Agathon: See above, n. 9 (3.1.1). well-whittled: Drunk, intoxicated.
out of Aristophanes: That is, from the speech of the character Aristophanes in Plato’s Symposium (189C–193D), rather than the plays of the Athenian comic poet.
Phornutus: The Roman Stoic philosopher and scholar Lucius Annaeus Cornutus (first century CE), sometimes called ‘Phornutus’.
Magnus Daemon … Plato calls him: See above, n. 31 (3.1.1).

the lion, the deer … the Stymphalian birds: Allusions to various mythical figures fought by Heracles (Hercules): the Nemean lion, the hind of Ceryneia, the Erymanthean (not Aetolian) boar, the giant Antaeus and the Stymphalian birds (man-eaters with bronze beaks). Caecilius: See above, n. 99 (1.2.4).
Stesichorus: Stesichorus was a Greek lyric poet of the sixth century BCE, traditionally said to have been struck blind for insulting Helen of Troy.

quartermaster: See above, n. 105 (2.2.3). Tenet Thetide aequor … Jove: In the original source, Seneca’s Trojan Women (345–6), these lines refer to Achilles. The sea-goddess Thetis was the mother of Achilles; Aeacus, a judge in the underworld, was his paternal grandfather; and Jupiter, the father of Aeacus, was his great-grandfather.

Jupiter himself was turned into a Satyr … for love: Some of the many transformations of Zeus (Jupiter) in classical mythology, in order to seduce, respectively, Antiope of Thebes, the daughter of the river-god Asopus; Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory; Europa, usually said to be the daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor; Leda, the daughter of the Aetolian king Thestius; and Danae, the daughter of King Acrisius of Argos – see above, n. 67 (1.2.4).

the Moon lamenting … Endymion: See above, n. 13 (2.3.1). Venus herself confessing … youth’s sake: The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite describes the seduction of the Trojan shepherd-prince Anchises by Aphrodite (Venus) on Mount Ida, leading to the birth of Aeneas. The Phoenician shepherd Adonis was also the lover of Aphrodite, and was said to have been killed by Ares (Mars) out of jealousy on Mount Libanus (Mount Lebanon in northern Syria) – see below, n. 56 (3.2.2).
pantofle: Slipper.

Stheneleius hostis: In this quotation from Ovid (Heroides 9.25–6), the ‘Stheneleian enemy’ is Eurystheus (the son of Sthenelus), the mythical ruler of Argos and adversary of Heracles, who charged the latter with his twelve labours.
Dictator quo creato … magistratus: On the Roman dictatorship mentioned in note ‘b’, see above, n. 33 (1.2.3).

Jovianus Pontanus … his Secretary of State: The scholar and poet Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503) was the tutor to the duke of Calabria and the future Alfonso II, king of Naples (1448–95), and was also employed in the Neapolitan court as chief secretary – first to the duke’s wife, Ippolita Maria Sforza, and subsequently to the duke himself and his successor, King Ferrante, who ruled 1495–6.
corrival: Rival in an equal position.
a Triton: An inferior sea-god in classical mythology, or (which is the sense here) a sea-monster in semi-human form.

Saxo Grammaticus … Northern Kings: See above, n. 40 (2.3.2). that common tale of Valentine and Orson: A medieval, originally French, romance, in which twin brothers are brought up separately in an aristocratic court and a bear’s den.
Leucadia: A Greek island, which in antiquity had a city of the same name, in the Ionian Sea; now Lefkada.
Puteoli: Now Pozzuoli, near Naples.
Telchines: See above, n. 74 (1.2.1).
facts: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

Apollonius: See above, n. 55 (DJR). Tantalus’ gold described by Homer: In the Odyssey (11.582–92), the fruit which is placed punitively beyond the grasp of Tantalus is not golden. Burton may have been reading Spenser’s Faerie Queene (2.7.51–6), which describes the apples on the tree of Hesperides, by which ‘greedy Tantalus’ is tormented in the garden of Proserpina, as being inedibly golden. Alternatively, the association of Tantalus with miserliness in Horace’s Satires (1.1.68–79) may have exerted influence here.
an honest Historian of our nation: Matthew Paris, in his Flores historiarum. thereby: Nearby.

Philinnium and Machates: A story set in the reign of Hadrian. Machates, an impoverished young man who was forbidden to marry his beloved, an aristocratic Corinthian girl called Philinnium, died of despair and returned to haunt her.
Teuchedy: Possibly the Japanese Buddhist goddess Benzaiten, enshrined on the island of Enoshima.
Jupiter Belus: The Babylonian god Bel Marduk was often identified as ‘Zeus Belos’ and ‘Jupiter Belus’ in Greek and Roman sources. brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR). Chaldean: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2).
juggling: See above, n. 122 (1.2.4).
King James: James VI and I was the author of a treatise entitled Daemonologie (1597).

Dares Phrygius, and Dictis Cretensis: Dares Phrygius and Dictys Cretensis were both purported authors of eyewitness accounts of the Trojan War. Joan of Naples: Giovanna I (1328–82), queen of Naples, who was reputed to have murdered her husband András of Hungary in conjunction with her lover, Louis of Taranto (whom she subsequently married). Fredegund and Brunehaut: Fredegund (d. 597) was the consort of the Frankish king Chilperic I (ruled 561–84); she was reported to have persuaded him to divorce his first wife, and to have murdered his second, Galswintha, before becoming queen herself. She had a running feud with Brunehaut, or Brunhilda (c. 534–613), the Visigothic queen of the Merovingian kingdom of Austrasia, who was the sister of Galswintha, and who had the mayor of the palace of Burgundy, Berthoald, murdered in 604 in order to make way for her lover Protadius.
monomachies: See above, n. 15 (DJR). calentures: See above, n. 77 (1.2.2). combustions: Inflammations.
e contra: See above, n. 8 (3.1.2).

Semiramis … horse: This story about Semiramis – on whom, see above, n. 342 (DJR) – derives from her mythological association with Ishtar, the Mesopotamian goddess of sex and fertility. Pasiphae with a bull: In classical mythology, Pasiphae, the wife of the Cretan king Minos, was induced by Poseidon to fall in love with the bull which the god had created for her husband to sacrifice, but which the latter had kept for himself; the product of their union was the Minotaur. Aristo of Ephesus with a she-ass, Fulvius with a mare: The Greek and Roman Parallel Stories (29), sometimes attributed to Plutarch, claims this about the ancient misogynists Aristonymus of Ephesus and Fulvius Stellus. Sylvans: Forest-dwelling spirits, who typically consort with satyrs, fauns and nymphs in the trains of deities such as Pan or Bacchus, and who are sometimes described as lascivious and having the feet of animals.

Hercules had Hylas … Phryga: This list has some inaccuracies. Burton’s source, the Herculis vita (1539) by the Italian writer Giglio Giraldi – who evidently referred to an inventory of the male lovers of Heracles given by a scholiast on the Argonautica of Apollonius of Rhodes – names Hylas, Philoctetes, Diomus, Perithoas, Abderus and Phrix. On Hylas, see above, n. 107 (1.2.4); Philoctetes was a Thessalian hero and a companion of Heracles; Diomus was the eponymous hero of the district of Diomea in Attica, with whom Heracles is said (by the grammarian Stephanus of Byzantium) to have fallen in love while visiting Diomea’s father Colyttus; Abderus, another companion of Heracles, was the son of Hermes or Poseidon, and the eponymous hero of the Thracian city of Abdera; Phrix was said to have founded a city in Libya, but nothing else is known about him; and the identity of Perithoas is a mystery. others suggest … Eurystheus: Also noted by Giraldi, with reference to the claim made in the Struggles of Heracles by the ancient Greek epic poet Diotimus.

Plato himself … Agathon: See above, n. 9 (3.1.1). Xenophon his Cleinias: Xenophon discusses the beauty of Cleinias, the young cousin of Alcibiades, in his Symposium (4.12–26). Virgil his Alexis: Alexis is the beautiful boy loved in vain by the shepherd Corydon in Virgil’s Eclogues. Anacreon his Bathyllus: Bathyllus is a beautiful young man who appears several times as the author’s beloved in the extant fragments of the Greek lyric poet Anacreon (582–485 BCE).

Sodomy is the Diana of the Romans: The goddess Diana (Artemis) was often identified as the guardian of female chastity. wives … turning their shoes around the wrong way: In protest, since they were not permitted to give evidence against their husbands.

Giovanni della Casa … kind of sex: The Protestant enemies of the Florentine poet, archbishop and writer on etiquette Giovanni della Casa (1503–56) invented a rumour, which circulated widely across Europe, that he had written a book called De laudibus sodomiae seu paederastiae (‘In Praise of Sodomy or Pederasty’). The title referred to verses from his poem Capitolo Il Forno (1538).

Angelo Poliziano … love of boys: Several stories about the demise of Poliziano – on whom, see above, n. 4 (2.3.2) – were in circulation. The most sensational, recorded in a letter written a few weeks after the events in 1494 by the Sienese banker Antonio Spannocchi, told how the famous scholar and poet had fallen in love with a beautiful boy, who fell ill, became mad and died. Shortly afterwards, according to Spannocchi, Poliziano himself started raving, tried to strangle his former student Piero de’ Medici (who in reality may have poisoned Poliziano), and also eventually died.
Ganymedes: Catamites or young male prostitutes – senses which derive from the homoerotic aspect of the mythological tale related above, n. 4 (2.3.4).

The story of Pygmalion in Ovid: In Ovid’s version of the tale in book 10 of the Metamorphoses, Pygmalion is a Cypriot artist who falls in love with an ivory statue of a beautiful girl, named Galatea, that he has sculpted. When Galatea is brought to life by Venus, Pygmalion marries her, and their daughter Paphos gives her name to the island (of Cyprus). Mundus and Paulina … Bk 2 ch. 4: The reference here should be to the Jewish Antiquities (18.65–80) of Josephus, which tells the story, set during the reign of Tiberius (14–37 CE), of the young equestrian Decius Mundus, who seduced a married noblewoman called Paulina by pretending to be the god Anubis in a temple of Isis at Rome. Pontius the legate of Gaius Caesar … allowed it: Pliny the Elder actually says this of Caligula (‘Gaius Caesar’) himself, but Burton is translating ‘Pontius legatus Caii principis’, which is erroneously printed in Renaissance editions of the Natural History (35.3.17–18); in classical mythology, Atalanta is the beautiful daughter of the Boeotian king Schoeneus – see below, n. 60 (3.2.2). Bona Fortuna … Bona Dea: Aelian (Historical Miscellany 9.39) tells the story of a young man who fell in love with a statue of Good Fortune – which from its partial remains appears to have been semi-nude and unusually titillating – in Athens. When the council refused to let him buy the statue, he decorated it with crowns and garlands and killed himself. With regard to the Bona Dea (‘Good Goddess’), there are several accounts of agalmatophilia (‘statue-love’) in ancient literature, most famously in Ovid’s retelling of the myth of Pygmalion; but Burton has perhaps been misled by a memory of the antics of Publius Clodius – on whom, see above, n. 183 (DJR) – who notoriously disguised himself to infiltrate the Roman nocturnal ceremony of the Bona Dea, from which men were rigorously excluded, in 62 BCE.
Heliogabalus: See above, n. 223 (DJR).

Someone called Hostius … detestable to mention: According to Seneca (Natural Questions 1.16.1–2), the sexual obscenity of Hostius Quadra, who lived in the reign of Augustus, prompted his own slaves to murder him, and was so notorious that it became the subject of a contemporary theatrical farce.
as Gryllus reproached Ulysses in Plutarch: See above, n. 189 (DJR).
a Nebuchadnezzar: That is, a madman; see above, n. 125 (1.2.2). pepon: Fruit of the gourd family – probably a type of melon or pumpkin.

As Seneca lived with his Paulina: See above, n. 144 (1.2.4). Arria and Paetus: A reference either to Arria the Elder and her husband the Roman senator Caecina Paetus – the former killed herself when the latter was sentenced to death for conspiracy by the emperor Claudius in 42 CE; or to Arria the Younger and her husband Thrasea Paetus – the former was prevented by the latter, who was prominent in the Stoic Opposition to Nero, from joining him in suicide in 66. Artemisia and Mausolus: Artemisia II of Caria (in western Anatolia) was famously grief-stricken when her husband (and brother) Mausolus died in 353 BCE; cf. above, n. 155 (1.2.3). Rubenius Celer … fell out: The harmonious matrimony of the Brescian Publius Rubrius (not Rubenius) Celer and his wife Gaia Ennia, which is mentioned in several Renaissance works but not in any ancient sources, was recorded in the epitaph inscribed on Ennia’s tomb at Rome.
will and nill: See above, n. 74 (1.1.2).
Nestor or Tithonus’ life: See above, n. 90 (DJR) and n. 205 (1.2.3).

irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR). Marcus Antoninus … sororem: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus) married Faustina the Younger (Annia Galeria Faustina), who was the daughter of his adoptive father, the emperor Antoninus Pius, in 145 CE. Caracalla Juliam Novercam: In the Augustan History and other hostile ancient sources, the Roman emperor Caracalla (188–217 CE) is said to have married his mother – falsely identified as his stepmother – Julia Domna (d. 217 CE, the Syrian wife of the emperor Septimius Severus). Cinyras with his daughter Myrrha: In classical mythology, the incestuous union of Cinyras, king of Cyprus, with his daughter Myrrha led to her transformation into a myrrh tree and the birth of Adonis.

Quartilla in Petronius … a maid: In the Satyricon, Quartilla is a priestess of Priapus – see above, n. 3 (2.1.3) – who hosts an orgy, during which she delivers the speech loosely quoted in note ‘d’. ‘Milo’ here is the ancient Greek wrestler Milo of Croton – see above, n. 94 (1.2.3); Burton has inserted this allusion into the proverb ‘He may carry a bull that has carried a calf’, following the association made by the commentary on this saying in the Adagia of Erasmus.
Aretine’s Lucretia: See above, n. 21 (3.1.1).
Rahab … hid the spies: Joshua 2:1–21. quean: See above, n. 323 (DJR).
linger: Have an urgent desire or craving.
the middle age: That is, the middle-aged – or, alternatively, the period of the Middle Ages.
Bonosi: See above, n. 61 (1.2.2).

Caelius Auphilenum … depereunt: This quotation from Catullus (100.1–2) reworks the proverbial idea of ‘brotherly love’ by referring to the love of the characters Caelius and Quintius for a Veronese brother and sister.
town Bulls: Figuratively, promiscuous men.

Solomon’s wisdom … Amnon towards his sister: 1 Kings 11:1–3; Judges 16:1–18; Genesis 19:30–35; 1 Samuel 2:22; Daniel 13:5–27 (considered apocryphal by Protestant Churches); 2 Samuel 16:21–2, referring to the concubines of his father David; 2 Samuel 11, 13.
Ad Taniam fugias: A reference to the River Tanais, now the Don in Russia, and in antiquity sometimes regarded as the border between Europe and Asia.
writhen: Deformed, contorted. bursten-bellied: That is, with a stomach swollen to the point of bursting. flickering: Hankering, flirting.
beldam: A grandmother; or (depreciatively) a repulsive old woman, a hag.
high-fed: Fed to excess or richly, well-fed.
Ilishi: Usually given in Latin as Ilisci, from the Arabic al-ishq (love).
his Commentator: The German physician Nicolaus Taurellus (1547–1606).
Medium ferit … in Anacreon: This quotation from the Anacreontea (33.27–8) refers to the ancient Greek view of the liver as the seat of passions, especially bodily desire.
Homer feigns Tityus’ liver … by love: See above, n. 29 (1.3.1).
Temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).

mutually aspected: Subject to each other’s ‘aspects’ – on which, see above, n. 14 (1.1.1). of Venus’ complexion: That is, share a ‘complexion’ – see above, n. 194 (DJR) – with the planet Venus, regarded as generally cold and moist, but warmer when oriental and more moist when occidental.

Plutarch interprets … Mars and Venus: In How the Young Man Should Study Poetry (4), Plutarch disparages the common astrological interpretation of the mythological tale that the sun reveals Aphrodite (Venus) in the arms of Ares (Mars) – see above, n. 10 (3.1.1). For the astronomer Claudius Ptolemaeus (or Ptolemy, c. 90–168 CE) and others, this signifies that the conjunction of Mars and Venus presages births conceived in adultery, which will be discovered by the sun when it returns in its course (that is, the secret will be revealed in the light of day). queans: See above, n. 323 (DJR).
in the dignities: In a situation in which its influence is heightened (here, by its aspect with Mercury).
Gregory Nazianzen … Chilo his scholar: The quotation is actually from one of the letters of St Basil (329/30–79), addressed to his pupil Chilo.

the Girdle of Venus, and the Mount of Venus: In palmistry, the Girdle of Venus is the line shaped like a crescent moon that runs from between the first and second finger to between the third and fourth finger. On its classical mythological name see above, n. 27 (2.2.6). The Mount of Venus is the area in the palm at the base of the thumb.
atomi: Particles.
the colt’s evil: Penile swelling in young horses – and hence, figuratively here, youthful priapism.

Iolaus: In classical mythology, the nephew and friend of Heracles (Hercules), who helped the latter’s killing of the Hydra – see above, n. 69 (DJR) – by cauterizing its multiple necks and burying the last, immortal head under a rock.

what Hippolytus am I: In classical mythology, Hippolytus rejected Aphrodite (Venus), who retaliated by inducing his stepmother Phaedra (the wife of Theseus) to fall in love with him. On his death, see above, n, 162 (1.2.4). Telchine: See above, n. 74 (1.2.1). Genius: See above, n. 22 (DJR).
propend: Incline, tend towards. Napthe: Or naptha – liquid petroleum.

which book … third Edition: Burton is concerned to ward off any suspicion of plagiarism, because of similarities in form and content between his discussion of love-melancholy and that given by Ferrand in De la maladie d’amour ou mélancolie erotique, which was published in 1623 (not 1624, as claimed in note ‘a’). Burton’s copy of Ferrand’s work, which has no annotations but is inscribed with the date 1629, indicates that he acquired the book in that year, after the publication of the third edition of the Anatomy (which, as note ‘a’ records, was seven years after its first edition).

stall-fed: See above, n. 4 (2.4.1). rank: Flourishing, abundant. hirquitallire: This Latin term, derived from hircus (he-goat), was usually used to denote the breaking of the voice in male puberty, and thereby came to be associated with the advent of adolescent sexual desire.

In that one Temple of Venus … besides Lais: The temple of Aphrodite at Corinth was notorious for sacral prostitution, although some scholars now doubt whether this was really practised.
