Lais here is probably the Corinthian prostitute mentioned in 1.2.4.7, p. 364, but another beautiful Lais of the same profession, who was born in Sicily in 422 BCE and came to Corinth in 415 as a prisoner of war, is also possible. school of Venus: Slang for brothel.

Capua in Italy … Hannibal’s soldiers can witness: After Hannibal’s victory at the Battle of Cannae (216 BCE) – on which, see above, n. 130 (DJR) – his troops reportedly became demoralized while encamped for the winter in the wealthy Campanian town of Capua, famous for its perfume. For Cicero in On the Agrarian Law, the episode demonstrated the corrupting power of luxury. Canopus in Egypt, Sybaris, Phaeacia, Baiae … Lampsacus: The list includes ancient places famous for their luxury and hedonism: Canopus, a coastal settlement in the Nile Delta; Sybaris, situated on the Gulf of Taranto in southern Italy; Phaeacia (or Scheria), a mythical region mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey; Baiae, on which, see above, n. 21 (2.2.3); and Lampsacus, a Greek city on the eastern side of the Hellespont (Dardanelles strait) in Anatolia, and traditionally the birthplace of Priapus.
that whore in Spartian … licet: A reference to the alleged relationship between Caracalla and Julia Domna – see above, n. 50 (3.2.1). brag with Proculus: See above, n. 24 (2.2.2).

Sardanapalus: The legendary Assyrian king (said to have lived in the seventh century BCE) was notorious for his multiple male and female concubines, and for his general decadence. Messalina: See above, n. 24 (2.2.2). Joan of Naples: See above, n. 32 (3.2.1). Solomon … Concubines: See above, n. 7 (3.1.1). Ahasuerus his Eunuchs: A reference to the eunuchs attending the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) – on whom, see above, n. 195 (DJR) – described in the Book of Esther; two of them plotted to kill the king (Esther 6:1–7). Tigillinus: Ofonius Tigellinus (c. 10–69 CE), praetorian prefect in the time of Nero, and one of the emperor’s favourites. In 39, he had been banished from Rome by Caligula for sexual misdemeanours with Agrippina the Younger – for whom, see below, n. 10 (3.3.2) – and Julia Livilla, two of Caligula’s sisters, and is depicted as a thoroughly debauched character in the Annals of Tacitus. Moguls: See above, n. 72 (1.2.2). Shereefs of Barbary: The emperors of Morocco (or the rulers of any of its districts). Persian Sophies: See above, n. 64 (2.2.6).
Amore abundas Antipho: A line from Terence’s Phormio (163), spoken by Phaedria to Antipho – newly married to an unsuitable girl, Phanium.
Aegisthus: See above, n. 119 (DJR).

Ismenodora stole Bacchon: In Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love, the desire of the rich widow Ismenodora for the handsome young man Bacchon prompts her to abduct him and arrange their marriage. as Aurora did Cephalus: In classical mythology, the goddess of the dawn Eos (Aurora) abducted the hunter Cephalus, by whom she had a son, Phaethon – on whom, see above, n. 15 (2.3.7). as Jupiter did by Europa, Neptune by Amymone: In classical mythology, Europa, daughter of the Phoenician king Agenor, was abducted by Zeus (Jupiter) when he turned himself into (or sent) a bull to entice her; Amymone, one of the daughters of Danaus, was rescued from a satyr and seduced by Poseidon (Neptune).
For all to sicker: ‘For as surely’. liquorish: See above, n. 323 (DJR).
diasatyrion: A compound electuary containing satyrion – see above, n. 46 (2.5.1).

he, prompted by Cressida: Encolpius, the narrator who has been advised in the Satyricon (130) by a maid (actually called Chrysis) to explain his impotence in a letter to her mistress, an aristocratic Crotonian woman calling herself ‘Circe’.
After dinner, take Callirhoe: A quotation from Persius (1.134), which is probably referring to the title of a romantic novel by the ancient Greek writer Chariton, Chaereas and Callirhoe.

Bacchic apples: Traditionally apples were lovers’ gifts. They are associated with Dionysus (Bacchus) in Theocritus, Idylls 2.118 – a passage interpreted by Athenaeus (Learned Banqueters 3.82D) as confirming that the god discovered the fruit.

Cubebs: Or ‘Java pepper’ – aromatic berries of the climbing shrub Piper cubeba or Cubeba officinalis, found in Java and Sumatra. Surax: Or ‘Surnag’, said to grow in the Atlas Mountains in northwestern Africa.
China root: See above, n. 65 (1.2.2).
prevented: See above, n. 27 (1.4.1). incensed: See above, n. 37 (1.1.1).

Lucian confesseth … present with her. Lucian’s Essays in Portraiture details the exquisite beauty and wisdom of the mistress of the Roman emperor Verus (d. 169 CE), a Greek woman from Smyrna who shared the name Panthea with the wife of Abradatas, a (fictitious) king of Susa. The latter Panthea was said to have been captured by Cyrus the Great after a victorious battle with the Assyrians, and her beauty was described in the fifth book of Xenophon’s Cyropaedia.
the species of love: See above, n. 34 (1.1.2).
admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
That Persian Xerxes … magnificence of it: According to Strabo’s Geography (14.1.5), Xerxes I spared the temple of Artemis in Ephesus; those destroyed ‘in Greece’ were in the Greek cities of Ionia.

Eryximachus the Physician: An Athenian doctor from the fifth century BCE, who delivers a speech in honour of Eros in Plato’s Symposium (185E–188E). S. L.: Note ‘g’ refers to the English antiquary Sampson Lennard, whose 1606 translation of I problemi della bellezza (1605) by Tommaso Buoni is quoted above.
speak Autolycus … Alcibiades though drunk: On Autolycus and Alcibiades, see above, n. 10 (3.1.1). The godlike appearance of Telemachus is described at the start of the second book of the Odyssey.
when the said Alcibiades … sweet sake: On Anytus, who was one of the lovers of Alcibiades, see above, n. 98 (DJR). fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
the properest man of person: See above, n. 52 (1.1.1).

Agis King of Lacedaemon … little wife: According to Plutarch (Agesilaus 2), it was actually Archidamus II (ruled c. 469–427 BCE) who was fined by the Spartan ephors for marrying a small woman, on the grounds that she would bear ‘not kings, but kinglets’. Their son was indeed short and lame, but reigned successfully as Agesilaus II (400–359).
Adrian the fourth … bastard: See above, n. 41 (2.3.2).

he ploughs with his heifer: An allusion to Judges 14:10–20, where Samson sets a riddle for the thirty Philistine men chosen to be his companions at his wedding feast. When they are unable to solve it they threaten Samson’s wife, who persuades him to give her the solution, which she then reveals. Samson retorts, ‘If ye had not plowed with my heifer,’ referring to the exploitation of his wife, ‘ye had not found out my riddle.’
Saul was a goodly person and a fair: 1 Samuel 9:2. Maximinus: See above, n. 11 (2.3.2).

Branchus the son of Apollo … Demigod: This story about Branchus – in classical mythology, a lover of Apollo who introduced the worship of the god at the temple at Didyma on the Ionian coast, and the eponymous ancestor of the aristocratic family of priests and prophets known as the Branchidae – derives mainly from the commentary on the Thebaid of Statius by its editor Lactantius Placidus (late fourth century CE). Ancient sources identify his mother as a woman from Miletus, who during her pregnancy had a vision of the sun entering her belly; Renaissance works such as the Dictionarium historicum ac poeticum (1567) by Charles Estienne, refer to her as Jaucis, the daughter of Sucron.
That Idalian Ganymede … to Hadrian: See above, n. 4 (2.3.4), n. 162 (1.2.3) and n. 107 (1.2.4).
a dumb comment: A ‘silent treatise’ or ‘silent commentary’.
cringe: See above, n. 121 (DJR).

Those intemperate young men … Venus’ picture from her: This passage refers to the most famous work by the celebrated Athenian sculptor Praxiteles (fourth century BCE), the marble statue of Aphrodite in Cnidus, and the most famous painting by his equally celebrated contemporary Apelles of Cos, the ‘Aphrodite Anadyomene’. On Phryne, see above, n. 155 (1.2.3).
Zerubbabel: The Jewish governor of the former kingdom of Judah on behalf of the Persians in the sixth century BCE – here addressing Darius I.
Chariclea … preserved for her person: See above, n. 15 (3.1.1).

When Constantinople … the grand Signior himself: According to early modern legend, Sultan Mehmed II – on whom, see above, n. 129 (DJR) – neglected his duties as a ruler after falling in love with a beautiful Greek slave named Irene (or ‘Hyerenee’). The Ottoman army under his command conquered Constantinople in 1453.

So did Rosamond … King Henry the second: Rosamund Clifford (c. 1140–75/6), sometimes called ‘the Fair Rosamund’ or ‘the Rose of the World’ – the famously beautiful mistress of Henry II of England (1133–89), and later a figure of romance and legend.
O noble piece of Justice, mine author exclaims: This account of the trial of Phryne comes from Athenaeus’ Learned Banqueters (13.590D–F), but the exclamation is apparently Burton’s addition.

Parthenopaeus: In Greek mythology, the famously beautiful son of Atalanta, and one of the seven Argive captains, led by and including the betrayed Polynices, who marched against Thebes (the ‘Seven against Thebes’) and were all killed in the process. On Polynices, see above, n. 156 (1.2.4); and on Atalanta, see below, n. 60 (3.2.2).

Sinalda was a woman … would not hurt her: In Germanic and Norse legend, the fourth-century Gothic king Ermaneric executed his wife Svanhildr (or Swanhild), the beautiful daughter of Sigurd and Gudrun, by having her trampled to death by horses. The animals carried this out only when a bag was put over her head, having initially been captivated by her beautiful eyes.
Apostrophe: A rhetorical figure of speech: turning away from the audience to address another person or thing.
trick: Adorn, dress up.

A fly lighted … by his divine looks: The anecdote given by Athenaeus (Learned Banqueters 6.249D–E) refers to a flatterer called Nicesius attached to Alexander II, king of Molossia (ruled c. 271–240 BCE). Burton has taken the tale from the French Jesuit scholar Nicolas Caussin, who adapts and embellishes it in De eloquentia sacra et humana libri XVI (1619), where the semi-fictional (at least) ‘Malthinus’ is described as a wealthy degenerate.

When Venus ran … Adonis: In classical mythology, Aphrodite (Venus) falls in love with the beautiful young Phoenician shepherd Adonis, the son of Myrrha – on whom, see above, n. 50 (3.2.1) – and hides him in a chest entrusted to Persephone. When Persephone refuses to give Adonis back, Zeus (Jupiter) orders that after spending four months in the underworld he may be returned to Aphrodite for four months. But after dying in a boar hunt, Adonis changes into an anemone flower.

Boreas ventus … two sons of her: In classical mythology, Boreas is the personification of the north wind. He abducts the mountain nymph Orithyia, originally the daughter of the mythical Athenian king Erechtheus (sometimes identified with King Erichthonius); the products of their union, Zetes and Calais, are both wind-gods.

The River Alpheus … Arethusa: In classical mythology, the river-god Alpheus, whose name was given to the longest river in the Peloponnese, was a hunter who loved and pursued the huntress and nymph Arethusa, who fled to Syracuse by escaping under the sea.

Inachus and Peneus: In classical mythology, Inachus was the founder king of Argos, said to have married the water nymph Melia. His name is given to the personification of the main river on the plain of Argos, now the Panitsa River. On Peneus, who was married to Creusa, the nymph of the springs of the River Peneus, see above, n. 29 (2.2.4).

Peneia: In classical mythology, the nymph Daphne, daughter of the river-god Peneus, was a chaste huntress who fled from the affections of Apollo – see below, n. 270 (3.2.2). Atalanta: In one version of her myth, the beautiful Boeotian princess is permitted to remain a virgin only if she defeats her suitors in a race. One of them, Hippomenes, wins by dropping three golden apples obtained from Aphrodite into her way during the contest. as they did to gaze on Psyche … object of her age: An allusion to and quotation from the Metamorphoses of Apuleius (4.28–9), which describes the effect of the extraordinary beauty of the mythical princess Psyche, the beloved of Amor (Cupid, or Eros). Coroebus to Troja … incensus amore: In classical mythology, Coroebus was a proverbially foolish and inept Phrygian ally of King Priam, whose journey to Troy in amorous pursuit of Cassandra is referred to by Virgil in this quotation from the Aeneid (2.342–3).

King John of France … his dear mistress: This story about Jean II (le Bon) of France (1319–64) and Katherine Montagu, countess of Salisbury (d. 1349) – with whom Edward III of England was also reputed to have been infatuated – is a false rumour of obscure origin. Jean II had been imprisoned after his defeat at the Battle of Poitiers in 1356; he was released to raise funds to pay a ransom, but when this proved impossible he returned to England in 1363.

Plutus: That is, Pluto – see above, n. 117 (DJR). Achilles … for Polyxena’s sake: In Greek mythology, Polyxena was the youngest daughter of King Priam of Troy and Queen Hecuba. Some ancient sources identify Polyxena as the beloved of Achilles, who is said to have fallen for her either at the negotiations for the ransom of the body of Hector, or while spying on her brother Troilus. the Grecian Gods … Philonis Deioneus’ daughter’s sake: Philonis, the famously beautiful daughter of the Phocian king Deion (or Deioneus), was loved by Hermes and Apollo – by whom, respectively, she gave birth to Autolycus and Philammon.
Peter Aretine’s Lucretia: See above, n. 21 (3.1.1).

Acontius: In classical mythology, a beautiful young man from the island of Ceos. Sappho … on Phaon the fair: An allusion to the story told by Ovid (Heroides 15) of the unrequited love of Sappho (born in Mytilene or Eresus on Lesbos) for Phaon, the ferryman who had been given a rejuvenating and beautifying ointment by Venus (Aphrodite) after carrying the goddess from Lesbos to the mainland, and the poet’s suicidal leap from the Leucadian cliffs – on which, see below, n. 134 (3.2.5).
Well might Stesichorus … so fair a creature: See above, n. 9 (3.2.1).
Those mutinous Turks … absence: ‘Mahomet’ in note ‘f’ refers to Sultan Mehmed II.
Roxane, a poor man’s child: According to the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus (8.4.23), the beautiful Roxane was actually the aristocratic daughter of the illustrious Sogdian satrap Oxyartes.

Orlando was mad for Angelica: Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (1532) describes the unrequited love (and consequent madness) of the Christian knight Orlando for the pagan princess Angelica. condole: See above, n. 133 (DJR).
Thisbe died for Pyramus: The mythical tragic tale of these beautiful Babylonian lovers is told in the fourth book of Ovid’s Metamorphoses.

Mars videt hanc, visamque cupit: This quotation from Ovid (Fasti 3.21) refers to the desire of Mars for the Vestal virgin Rhea Silvia, who gives birth to Romulus and Remus after being raped by the god.

so Matthew Paris … Cologne: Isabella of England (1214–41) – whose procession in Cologne after her wedding in 1235 to the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II is described by the English historian and polymath Matthew Paris – is here mistaken for Matilda of England (1102–67), who married the Holy Roman Emperor Henry V at Worms in 1114.
curious: See above, n. 30 (2.2.4). O fortunate God Mars … for her sake: See above, n. 10 (3.1.1) and n. 3 (3.2.2).
When fair Autolycus … discerned and expressed: See above, n. 10 (3.1.1).

Achilles … fair Briseis: In Homer’s Iliad, Briseis is the fair-haired girl abducted by Achilles, who fell in love with her after killing her husband and three brothers while destroying the settlement of Lyrnessus in Mysia. Ajax by Tecmessa: In classical mythology, the Phrygian princess was said to have been taken by Ajax as his concubine after he had killed her father in the Trojan War. Judith … Holofernes: Judith 10:23, 11:20–23. Delilah, Samson: Judges 16. Roxolana, Suleyman the Magnificent: Roxolana (or Hurrem Sultan, c. 1505–58), was the famously beautiful chief consort of the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I (1494–1566).
lapt: See above, n. 30 (DJR).
Clitophon: The protagonist, who falls in love with his cousin Leucippe, of the second century CE Greek novel Leucippe and Clitophon by Achilles Tatius.
that Thracian Rodophe: A reference to the legendary courtesan in Naucratis (in the sixth century BCE) more commonly known as Rhodopis, who was said to have made a fortune from her beauty.
Xenopithes a Philosopher: A fictional character in the Erotic Letters of Aristaenetus (1.17).
Stratocles the Physician: See above, n. 55 (2.2.4).
adamant: Loadstone.
blent: Flinched, shrank.
Xenophon’s description of Panthea: See above, n. 29 (3.2.2).

Urit te Glycerae … aspici: In this quotation from Horace (Odes 1.19), the name Glycera is that of a courtesan, named after the famous Athenian Glycera (fourth century BCE), who was alleged to have been the lover of the poet Menander.
the sale-piece: Possibly, the sample attracting buyers.
Non dum … crinem: See above, n. 25 (2.3.5).
Polyxena: See above, n. 62 (3.2.2). and Hero the fair … her hair: Lines from the first ‘Sestiad’ of Marlowe’s Hero and Leander (1598).

Guithera: One of the many spellings now usually standardized to ‘Guinevere’; for her blondness, see below, n. 8 (3.3.4). Clodoveus that lovely King of France: Clovis I (465–511), king of the Franks and founder of the Merovingian dynasty, in which long hair was a traditional privilege of the royal family.
our Venetian Ladies … so much: Venetian women were particularly renowned in the Renaissance for their use of blond hair dye. calamistrate: Curl, crisp or frizzle.
Pyracmon: In this mythological quotation from Virgil (Aeneid 8.425), Pyracmon was a Cyclops employed in the workshop of Hephaestus (Vulcan). a black man: A man with a swarthy complexion.

Dirt-dauber: See above, n. 84 (1.2.4). a Brontes: Like Pyracmon, and also mentioned in Aeneid 8.425, one of the divine blacksmiths of Hephaestus. ruddleman: Or ‘raddleman’, a digger or dealer of ‘raddle’ (red ochre) – but alternatively, an inhabitant of Rutland in England. that Huntsman Meleager in Philostratus: In the Imagines of Philostratus the Younger (15.5), the mythical hero and hunter Meleager is described as physically stout, with strong and well-developed limbs;
cf. below, n. 55 (3.4.1). Nireus: In classical mythology, the famously handsome king of the island of Syme and one of the Greek leaders in the Trojan War.

Justin’s wife … by chance: In Galen’s account (On Prognosis 6) it was the wife of a Roman actually called Justus who fell in love with Lucius Aurelius Pylades, a mimic dancer from Cilicia who was famous in Rome in the time of the emperor Augustus.

Faustina the Empress: Annia Galeria Faustina Minor, or Faustina the Younger (130–76 CE), wife of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, is said in the Augustan History (19) to have fallen in love with a gladiator (‘fencer’), who was consequently executed.
Fowlers: Bird-catchers. shoeing-horns: See above, n. 119 (1.2.2).
facetely: See above, n. 35 (1.2.4).
Touch box: The box for holding a musket’s ‘touch-powder’ (or priming powder).

as men catch dotterels … arm: The dotterel is a species of plover; it was traditionally said to be easily caught because of its habit of imitating human actions, which was exploited to distract it from the net.
the Poet … his Mistress: Horace, whose Art of Poetry (37) is quoted in the following line, in which the poet actually refers to himself.
Alcmena: See above, n. 88 (2.2.4).

Triton in his Melaene … formosa mihi: The quotation, which is taken from the dialogue ‘Galatea, Melene, Proteus’ by the Ferrarese humanist polymath Celio Calcagnini (1479–1541), refers to the love of Triton – on whom, see above, n. 18 (3.2.1) – for Melaene (or Melaine), who in Greek mythology was a water nymph and daughter of the river-god Cephisus.
interview: Mutual view of each other.
visio fit intra mittendo … images sent within: See above, 1.1.2.6, and n. 34 (1.1.2).

as that Ephesian … Philostratus speaks: When an elderly beggar in Ephesus was stoned by the Ephesians at the instigation of Apollonius of Tyana – on whom, see above, n. 55 (DJR) – he was revealed to be a malevolent, plague-causing demon with fiery eyes (Philostratus, Life of Apollonius of Tyana 4.10).
the patient’s: The receiver’s.
she complained in Apuleius: The unnamed second wife of the owner of the narrator Lucius’ lodging, who has fallen in love with her stepson (Metamorphoses 10.3).

that Marrhusian Phaedrus and Theban Lysias: The passage quoted here from Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plato’s Symposium (1484) recreates a scene that is set before the beginning of Plato’s Phaedrus, in which the famous orator Lysias (c. 459/8–c. 380 BCE) has an erotic encounter with the eponymous character of the latter dialogue, who was born in the district of Myrrhinus in Attica.
as he sings … not whom: The English poet George Wither, in his Faire-virtue, the Mistresse of Phil’arete (1622).
gloat: Gaze amorously. participate: Have a share in; possess or enjoy in common.
eduction: Excretion, expulsion.
Exornations: See above, n. 54 (DJR).

In beauty … that of favour: In this quotation in note ‘a’ from Francis Bacon’s essay ‘Of Beauty’ (1612), ‘favour’ means ‘face’, ‘countenance’ or ‘feature’; ‘colours’ means ‘complexions’; and ‘decent motion’ means ‘decorous’ or ‘graceful bearing’.
weeds: Garments distinctive of someone’s social status or profession.

Set out: See above, n. 29 (DJR). Indy bone: Ivory. cherry: The translation here of the term cerussata (‘painted with white lead’), from Martial’s Epigrams (1.72.6), seems to derive partly from its similarity to the word cerasus (‘cherry’).
coats: See above, n. 153 (DJR). stomachers: Ornamental chest coverings, worn under the lacing of bodices. guarded: Ornamented, as with lace or embroidery.
turgent: Swelling. lawn: A kind of fine linen, like cambric. tiffanies: Thin, transparent silks.
When Pallas … golden apple: See above, n. 193 (DJR).
plausible: Gratifying, ingratiating.
fond: See above, n. 103 (DJR).

Dulce ridentem Lalagen … discoursing: In this quotation from Horace (Odes 1.22.23–4), Lalage (Greek for ‘Chatterbox’) is a fictional courtesan, whose services would have typically included companionship and conversation, to whom the poet playfully expresses his devotion.

Galla’s sweet smile … Faustus the Shepherd … subrisit ocellis: Allusions to the fictional pastoral characters in the first eclogue of the Adolescentia (1498) by the Italian poet Mantuan (Battista Spagnoli Mantovano). The quotation is a line spoken by Faustus in the same poem.

Daphnis in Lucian … Crobyle: In the passage from Lucian’s fictional Dialogues of the Courtesans alluded to here (2–3), the poor widow Crobyle actually refers to Lyra, who in the dialogue is the daughter of Daphnis. brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR).
complement: A quality or accomplishment which ‘completes’ a gentleman.
the Prophet Isaiah a Courtier himself: According to Isaiah 1:1, the prophet attended the courts of various kings of Judah, including Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
a springe to catch woodcocks: Figuratively, a trap set for a person, especially someone easily tricked (a ‘springe’ is a snare used to catch birds or small game).

Sow-gelder: Someone who spays sows. Note ‘b’ refers to the sound made by the horns commonly blown by sow-gelders to announce their arrival at a place and offer their services. In Beggar’s Bush, a comedy by John Fletcher and Philip Massinger (and perhaps also Francis Beaumont), probably first performed at Whitehall Palace in 1622, a group of drunken beggars sing a song ‘like a sow-gelder’ – that is, in a crudely rhythmic manner. perstringe: Dazzle.

Apelles was enamoured with Campaspe … naked: According to Pliny the Elder (35.36.86–7), Campaspe (or ‘Pancaspe’) was a mistress of Alexander the Great, who commissioned a nude portrait of her from Apelles of Cos. When Apelles fell in love with Campaspe, Alexander presented her to the artist as a gift.

Cestius Gallus: The Roman senator Gaius Cestius Gallus, consul in 35 CE. Carolus Pugnax: Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy (1433–77), actually had a reputation for military valour rather than lasciviousness.
dance friskin: Dance in a frolic, a lively or playful encounter.
The Tuscans: See above, n. 138 (1.2.3).
Antoninus Caracalla … married her: See above, n. 50 (3.2.1); ‘mother-in-law’ here means ‘stepmother’. in cause: Blameworthy.
malkin: Slut.
lethalem arundinem, a fatal reed: An allusion to the coating of reeds with lime in bird-catching.
unstaid: Unrestrained.
tires: See above, n. 63 (1.2.3). shadows: Headdresses projecting forwards to shade the face. rebatoes: Large, stiffened collars standing around the neck.
falls: Bands or collars that fall flat around the neck. cauls: Netted caps or headdresses designed to hold the hair. tinsels: Pieces of cloth interwoven with gold or silver thread.
strength: Active property, or power.
tires: See above, n. 169 (DJR).

Nero’s Poppaea: Poppaea Sabina, the lover of Nero who became his second wife, was famous for her beauty and extravagance (she was said have bathed daily in the milk of 500 asses); see above, n. 13 (3.1.2). Ahasuerus’ concubines: See above, n. 17 (3.2.2), and Esther 2:2–17. pruning: Preening its feathers.
dress: Groom. shop book: Account book. day net: See above, n. 19 (DJR). stoop: See above, n. 1 (2.2.3).
setting-sticks: Rods used for stiffening the pleats of ruffs.
far-fetched: See above, n. 140 (1.2.4).
bands: Collars or ruffs. farthingales: Hooped petticoats.
the whore in the Proverbs … or other: Proverbs 7.
as an Ivy-bush is to a Tavern: Traditionally, a bush of ivy (or a depiction of one) placed outside an inn indicated the availability of wine.
circumvent: See above, n. 336 (DJR).
cornutos: Cuckolds. light housewives: See above, n. 18 (1.3.2).
tow: The fibre twisted into a wick on lamps or candles.
When Venus stood before Anchises … variegata: See above, n. 12 (3.2.1). spires: Spirals or coils. ouches: Ornamental clasps, buckles or brooches that hold the two sides of a garment together.

in Plutarch, when the Queens came … Antony: According to Plutarch (Antony 24), this occurred when Mark Antony travelled to the East, leading to his meeting with Cleopatra at Tarsus (in southern Turkey), in 41 BCE.
Bacchus shapes: That is, as priests or worshippers of Bacchus.

riot: See above, n. 263 (DJR). Et matutino … funera: In this quotation from Juvenal (Satires 4.108–9), Crispinus was an Egyptian who rose through the ranks, perhaps from slavery, to serve as an important official under Domitian.
extinct: Extinguished, destroyed. jet: Mince or strut around. Antics: See above, n. 41 (1.1.2).
hangers: Straps or loops on sword-belts for hanging swords. points: Tagged ribbons or cords used for fastening garments or shoes.

Lex Valeria and Oppia, and a Cato to contradict: The Lex Oppia (215 BCE) was an ancient Roman sumptuary law restricting women’s dress. It was actually abolished by the Lex Valeria Fundania, against the wishes of Cato the Elder – on whom, see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries) – in 195.
Lucullus’ wardrobe: See above, n. 48 (1.2.2). put down: Lowered in estimation, surpassed by comparison.

Isaiah’s Prophecy: Isaiah 3:16–24, prophesying punishments for the luxurious behaviour and dress of the daughters of Zion. sweet-balls: Balls of scented or aromatic substances. favours: Ribbons or cockades.
Christ’s yoke: See Matthew 11:29–30.
prank up: See above, n. 112 (DJR). minion: Or ‘minium’, cinnabar. ceruse: See above, n. 19 (2.2.1).
pricks: Skewers.

Cornelia … Roman Lady: Cornelia (b. c. 190 BCE), the daughter of the elder Scipio Africanus – see above, n. 147 (DJR) – and Aemilia Tertia, and mother of the heroes of Roman populist politics, Tiberius and Gaius Sempronius Gracchus, was renowned in antiquity as a Roman matron with an exemplary lifestyle. May-Lady: Or ‘May Queen’: a woman brightly dressed and crowned with flowers who presides over the May Day festivities.

as Jerome said of Blaesilla: See above, n. 32 (1.4.1). Furius … Numantia: The Roman general and statesman Marcus Furius Camillus celebrated two triumphs after victories over the Gauls, in 390 and 367 BCE; Lucius Papirius Cursor, an important general in the Second Samnite War (326–304 BCE), celebrated triumphs in 319 and 310; and after the successful siege of Numantia (133/2 BCE), which resulted in the total destruction of the Spanish city, Scipio Aemilianus – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) and n. 87 (1.2.4) – celebrated a triumph at Rome and acquired the unofficial epithet ‘Numantinus’.
As she said in Suetonius … ambiunt: The reference is apparently misremembered. Its real source may be the Chronica majora of Matthew Paris, who gives a very similar speech to King Lear.
dizzard: See above, n. 96 (DJR). Uxorem ducat Danaen: On this quotation in note ‘b’, see above, n. 67 (1.2.4).

Tidore: An island in the Maluku archipelago (the Moluccas), in what is now eastern Indonesia – here mentioned alongside Jakarta as far-flung, exotic destinations. Gelasimus de monte aureo: A character, whose name means ‘Mr Laughable of Golden Mountain’, from The Comedy of Timon, written c. 1602–3 by an unidentified author. Sir Giles Goosecap: The foolish knight in an English comedy of the same name, probably by George Chapman and published in 1606. Sir Amorous La-Fool: The idiotic knight in Ben Jonson’s Epicoene (1609/10).
Lycia: Actually Joessa, who in Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans gives her boyfriend Lysias a list of her various suitors.
dust-worms: See above, n. 124 (1.2.3).
That proud … Bishop of Ely: William de Longchamp (d. 1197), whose relatively modest knightly background was exaggerated and criticized by contemporary chroniclers.

Vortigern King of Britain … her dowry: Vortigern was a leader of the Britons in the fifth century CE; Hengist and his brother Horsa were the semi-legendary leaders of the Jutes, and the reputed founders of the kingdom of Kent and its royal house.

Jagello … Hedinga: After his baptism in 1386, the grand duke of Lithuania Jogaila (c. 1351–1434) married the twelve-year-old Queen Jadwiga (or Hedwig; ruler of Poland 1374–99) and became Władysław II Jagiełło. The union of their two realms was strategically devised to resist Russian and German expansion.

Charles the Great … the West: The planned marriage of the Holy Roman Emperor Charlemagne (742–814 CE) to the Byzantine Empress Irene of Athens (c. 752–803 CE), which was reportedly proposed in 802 and would have unified the Western and Eastern Roman Empires, did not take place.
event: See above, n. 149 (DJR).
Menelaus had with Helen … Messalina: On the figures in these unhappy unions, see above, n. 27 (2.2.6), n. 10 (3.1.1), n. 10 (3.2.2), n. 35 (3.2.1) and n. 24 (2.2.2).
as the Queen in Ariosto … Dwarf: In Orlando furioso (28.34–7), the queen of Lombardy cuckolds the handsome King Astolfo through adultery with a dwarf at his court.
colling: Embracing, hugging.
Potiphar’s wife … Joseph: See above, n. 3 (2.3.4).
Ille dies lethi … fuit: This quotation from Virgil’s Aeneid (4.169–70) refers to the fatal day on which Dido and Aeneas consummate their relationship while sheltering from a storm in a cave.
Illic Hippolitum pone, Priapus erit: In this line from Ovid’s Amores (2.4.32), Hippolytus – on whom, see above, n. 10 (3.2.2) – represents someone chaste and Priapus represents someone lustful.
compressed: Embraced sexually. a fine son, called Pyrrhus: Or Neoptolemus – see above, n. 135 (DJR).

Peter Abelardus … any other Lecture: The passionate love affair between the French philosopher and theologian Peter Abelard (1079–1142) and the nun and scholar Héloïse d’Argenteuil (d. 1164), recorded in their correspondence, had been famous since the fourteenth century.
guilty to herself: Conscious, cognizant.
gull: See above, n. 83 (DJR).
rivelled: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3).
pique-devanted: With a short beard trimmed to a point.
Parthenis was so taken … love me again: In the Erotic Letters of Aristaenetus (2.5), Parthenis is a lovesick virgin who is enamoured of a singer who lives next door to her.
If thou didst but hear her sing … follow her: Lucian’s character Polystratus is referring to Panthea – see above, n. 29 (3.2.2).

Those Samian singing wenches … Agathoclea: Agathoclea (d. 203 BCE) was the mistress of Ptolemy IV Philopator (245/4–204 BCE) of Egypt. Her mother, Oenanthe (d. 203), was the wife of the crown prince of Syracuse, Agathocles, and later the concubine of Ptolemy III Euergetes (reigned 246–222). Nothing is known about Aristonica, but presumably she also attended the royal court at Alexandria.

Argus had an hundred eyes … his head: In classical mythology, Argus was the many-eyed guardian of Io – who after being seduced by Zeus (Jupiter) had been turned into a cow by the jealous Hera (Juno). In order to abduct Io, Hermes (Mercury) lulled Argus to sleep with his flute and then killed him.
Dione’s: In Greek mythology, Dione was the mother of Aphrodite, by her husband Zeus – see above, n. 36 (3.1.1). In Latin literature, however, she was commonly identified as Venus.

Shore’s wife … Edward the Fourth: Elizabeth (sometimes referred to as Jane) Shore (d. 1526/7) had her marriage to the London mercer William Shore annulled in 1476 and was sometimes said to have been a mistress of Edward IV. This rumour, along with her reputation for great wit, was established by Thomas More in his History of Richard III (c. 1513–18).

belie: Counterfeit, pretend. Corybantiasmi: Imitators of the Corybantes, on whom, see above, n. 346 (DJR). Thrasonean Rodomonts or Bombomachides: Thraso is a boastful soldier in Terence’s Eunuch; Rodomonte is the courageous but conceited Saracen leader in Matteo Maria Boiardo’s Orlando innamorato (1583) and Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (1532), and the source of the English terms ‘rodomont’ and ‘rodomontade’; and Bombomachides is the eponymous character in Plautus’ Braggart Soldier. Lucian’s Leontichus: A military braggart in Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans.

Amadis de Gaul … Knight of the sun: See above, n. 249 (1.2.3). Suidas … Philaenis and Elephantine: According to the tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia now known as the Suda, the sex manual by Astyanassa (the maid of Helen of Troy) was subsequently imitated by the courtesan Philaenis of Samos (fourth century BCE) and the poet-physician Elephantis (first century BCE), and their works became influential in the Greek and Roman worlds. those light tracts of Aristides … in Crassus’ army amongst the spoils: According to Plutarch (Crassus 32), some of the licentious ‘Milesian Tales’ of Aristides of Miletus, which influenced later authors from Petronius to Boccaccio, were found in the baggage of Roman prisoners after the Parthian victory at Carrhae – on which, see above, n. 53 (2.3.3). with such-like pictures, as those of Aretine: A notorious series of erotic engravings, known as I modi, after drawings of sixteen sexual positions by Giulio Romano, and often referred to in English as Aretino’s Postures because of their publication in I sonetti lussuriosi (1527) by Pietro Aretino – on whom, see above, n. 32 (1.2.4).
Thetis’ marriage: Nuptial scenes depicting the beautiful water nymph Thetis and Peleus, the king of Phthia, were frequent subjects in ancient Greek and Roman art – see above, n. 193 (DJR).

Non dat basis, dat Neaera nectar … mel: The quotation in note ‘h’, taken from the Liber basiorum (1541) by the Dutch poet Johannes Secundus (Johannes Everard), refers to the author’s Spanish mistress, who is given the pseudonym ‘Neaera’ – perhaps after a character in Horace. Gillyflower: Clove, or a clove-scented plant.
osculum charitatis: Or the ‘kiss of peace’, a traditional Christian greeting; see 1 Peter 5:14.

bill: Stroke one bill with another. as she gave to Giton … invadens: In Petronius’ Satyricon (20), quoted here, the youthful slave Giton is playfully kissed by an unnamed young girl. An orgy ensues shortly afterwards.
those that he spake of … 7 suavia: The reward offered by Mercury, in Apuleius’ Metamorphoses (6.8), for the return of the runaway princess (and servant of Venus) Psyche.

abstinere … nuptiarum interdicitur: Weddings had been forbidden in the penitential period of Lent by the Council of Laodicea (Canon 52) in the fourth century CE; the source here is the medieval scholar of canon law, Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–96). In early modern England, almost 40 per cent of the year was customarily regarded as unsuitable for weddings, although in the seventeenth century the various prohibitions in the religious calendar had become controversial.
that notable tale in Petronius … in her Cabin: See above, n. 27 (2.3.5). A ‘cabin’ here is a bedroom.

take a green gown: Engage in lovemaking or be deflowered (literally: have a dress stained green by rolling in the grass with a lover). let their Coats: Loosen or take off their skirts or petticoats. surly: Haughty or disdainful.
personated: Put (a person) forward in an assumed character; cf. above, n. 1 (DJR).
spend himself: Ejaculate – but also, perhaps, ‘exhaust his money and resources’.
Philinna in Lucian: In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans (3), the courtesan Philinna discusses her seduction techniques with her mother. corrival: See above, n. 17 (3.2.1).
as Ampelis informs Chrysis: In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans (8), Ampelis dispenses amatory advice to the younger courtesan Chrysis.
come off roundly: Pay in full.
in the said Lucian, Melissa: In the Dialogues of the Courtesans (4), the courtesan Melitta (spelled ‘Melissa’ in Renaissance Latin translations) relates this anecdote to her friend Bacchis.

Eugenia drew Timocles … and thence came love: The sources for these allusions – all added in the third edition of 1628 – remain untraced; the first refers to the traditional custom of drawing names on St Valentine’s Day, and the second, apparently, to the ancient Greek sage Myson of Chen.
conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).

Decius, and Valerianus … Church: The Roman emperors Decius Traianus (ruled 249–51 CE) and Valerian – on whom, see above, n. 97 (1.2.3) – both of whom implemented persecutory laws and measures against Christians in the Roman Empire.
Godwin, that subtle Earl of Kent: Godwin (d. 1053), the father of Harold II of England, had also been made the first earl of Wessex by King Cnut (Canute).
sped: See above, n. 136 (1.2.4).

John the Monk … the days of Theodosius: In Burton’s source, which is by the German Lutheran theologian Georg Major (or Meier, 1502–74) not the Scottish historian John Major (or Mair, c. 1467–1550), this story refers to an anonymous monk, although it is included in the biography of the hermit John of Egypt (c. 305–94 CE), who lived during the reign of the Roman emperor Theodosius I.
intend: Intensify.

Another terms it the companion … obscene actions: This quotation combines excerpts from St Ambrose’s On Virgins (3.5.25) and Luther’s commentary on the sixth commandment in the Decem praecepta Wittenbergensi praedicata populo (1518). Gaditanian: Of Cadiz (from the Latin name for the city, ‘Gades’).
King Ptolemy’s riot: That is, of Ptolemy IV Philopator.

Thais in Lucian … a dance: In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans (3), Philinna relates how her fellow courtesan Thais danced in the company of both Lamprias and Philinna’s own client Diphilus, but it was the latter who responded to the seduction.

Herodias so far pleased Herod … a platter: Mark 6:22. In some biblical manuscripts, the woman more usually referred to as Salome, the daughter of Herod and Herodias, is identified as Herodias herself.

Robert Duke of Normandy … that night: The lewd response of Herleva (also known as ‘Arlotte’ as well as ‘Arlette’, and probably a tanner’s daughter) to the overtures of Robert, which led to the birth of William the Conqueror, was reputed to have been the origin of the English word ‘harlot’. In note ‘e’, ‘smock’ means ‘undergarment’, or ‘chemise’.

Owen Tudor won Queen Catherine’s affection: The marriage of Owen Tudor (c. 1400–1461) and Catherine of Valois (1401–37) led eventually to the establishment of the Tudor dynasty (via the birth of Edmund Tudor, the father of Henry VII of England).
new Rome: Constantinople, sometimes referred to by this name after its designation as the imperial capital by Constantine I in 324 CE.

Xenophon in Symposio … dance of Dionysius and Ariadne: Xenophon’s Symposium (9.2–7) describes a mimetic dance representing the mythological marriage of Ariadne, the daughter of King Minos and Pasiphae, to the god Dionysus.
oppugner: See above, n. 73 (1.1.2).
general Councils: Ecclesiastical assemblies convened to regulate religious doctrine. Fathers: Church Fathers. Siracides: See above, n. 140 (1.2.3).

Domitian forbad the Roman Senators to dance … the Senate: An exaggeration: according to Suetonius (Domitian 8), Domitian only expelled a former quaestor from the senate because of the latter’s obsession with dancing and acting.
Sempronia: The wife of Decius Junius Brutus (consul in 77 BCE), and one of the Catilinarian conspirators – see above, n. 227 (DJR).
Galliard: A quick and lively dance. tracing: Taking a step (in a dance). swimming: In a smooth waving motion.
The Sun and Moon … Bourbonian planets: For the astronomical terms used in this passage and the next, see above, nn. 86, 100 (2.2.3), and n. 105 (2.2.4). ♀ and ☿: Venus and Mercury.
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).
as one saith … burning lust: The quotation is from Theodoret.
censure: See above, n. 59 (DJR). tempestively: Seasonably, opportunely.

take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR). Semierus: According to William Camden, ‘Semier’ (Jean de Simier, Baron de Saint-Marc) was ‘a refined Courtier’ sent by the duke of Anjou in 1578 to visit Elizabeth I to woo her on his behalf. Camden says that the queen ‘received [him] very lovingly’.

Et Claros & Tenedos, Patareaque regia servit: This line from Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.516) refers to the sanctuary of Apollo at Claros, in the Lydian city of Colophon; the Aegean island of Tenedos, described in the Iliad (1.452) as being ruled by Apollo; and the Lycian port city of Patara, the site of one of the most important Apollo cults in the Greek world.

Thornax hill … the same place: Mount Thornax, subsequently called Coccygium (‘Mount Cuckoo’), was near the city of Hermione (modern-day Ermioni) in Argolis. ‘Telia Juno’ is the Latin version of ‘Hera Teleia’, where the epithet refers to her role as the goddess of marriage.

Charmides in the said Lucian loved Philematium … December: In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Courtesans (2–3), when the courtesan Tryphena tells the young man Charmides about Philematium’s real age and accompanying physical defects, he immediately loses his desire for her.

Fallere credentem … puellam: This misquotation from Ovid’s Heroides (2.63–4) inverts the sense by omitting the term non; in the original, deception is said to be ‘not hard work’ (non est operosa). Perhaps sarcasm was intended.

stick to crack: ‘Hesitate to boast’. as he did in Petronius: Apparently an allusion to the Satyricon (102–3), where Encolpius and Giton disguise themselves as the slaves of Eumolpus in a ruse to escape a ship under the command of their enemy, Lichas of Tarentum. pricklouse: Contemptible, worthless (a term specifically applied to tailors). cog: See above, n. 164 (DJR). foist: cheat. caroches: Luxurious coaches. sharkers: See above, n. 3 (2.3.8).

swear by the Genius of Caesar: This ancient oath was used in the cult of the Roman emperors; on the meaning of the term ‘genius’ here, see above, n. 22 (DJR). Hymen’s deity: In classical mythology Hymen was a god of marriage ceremonies.

a lovely Crown … shines: The ‘crown’ of Ariadne was said to be represented by the constellation Corona Borealis. Chequins, Florins, Crowns: Chequins were gold coins originally minted by the Venetian Republic, and used throughout Europe; florins and crowns were originally gold as well. Angels: Or ‘angel nobles’, gold coins minted in England from 1465 until about 1642, depicting the Archangel Michael killing a dragon. stamps: Coins marked with a device, coin medals.
every foot: On every occasion, frequently.
muscadel, or malmsey: See above, n. 30 (1.2.2).
collogue: See above, n. 31 (DJR). poses: Posies, small bouquets.

Haec scripsi … Chelidonium to Philonides: In the Erotic Letters of Aristaenetus (2.13), the courtesan Chelidonium expresses her anxiety that her lover Philonides has left her because of her profession.
Quartilla in Petronius: See above, n. 51 (3.2.1).
the Spanish Bawd: The eponymous protagonist, a former prostitute turned go-between, in La Celestina (1499) by Fernando de Rojas.

those eleven thousand Virgins: The legendary followers of St Ursula (d. 383), reputedly a British princess, who were said to have been martyred with her in Cologne by the Huns, after refusing them sexual intercourse. Milo’s wife in Apuleius: The immoral witch Pamphile, the wife of the narrator’s miserly relative and host Milo, in the Metamorphoses (2.5).
cautelous: Cautious, wary.
receipts: See above, n. 10 (2.1.2).
Flectere si nequeunt … movebunt: See above, n. 10 (2.1.1).
he said of old Croton … be inveigled: See above, n. 160 (DJR).
liberal science: See above, n. 7 (DJR).

occult: Secret. Steganography, Polygraphy: Both forms of cryptography. Nuntius animatus: A slightly inaccurate reference to the Nuncius inanimatus (‘The Inanimate Messenger’), which discusses magnetic telegraphy, by the English bishop (and Christ Church graduate) Francis Godwin (1562–1633). Burton added the reference in the third edition (1628), so he must have read or heard about Godwin’s tract before it was published in 1629. Juno’s jealousy: Described as such by Ovid (Fasti 5.231–2), about the birth of Minerva (Athena) from the ear of Jupiter (Zeus) without her services as goddess of childbirth. Danae’s custody: See above, n. 67 (1.2.4). Argo’s vigilancy: Argus is intended here.

as that Catanian Philippa … Naples: Philippa of Catania, the nursemaid of Giovanna I of Naples, was reported to have arranged the murder of the queen’s husband, András of Hungary – see above, n. 32 (3.2.1).
wise woman: A woman who deals in lesser forms of magic or charms, usually of a benevolent nature.
the Island of Zante: Zakynthos, in the Ionian Sea, was called Zante by the Venetians, who had annexed it as a colony from the Ottoman Turks in 1484.
white Devils: Literally, devils pretending to be virtuous beings; figuratively, evil people who feign virtue.
nets which Lucretia … Susanna: On the subjects of these allusions, see above, n. 48 (1.2.3), n. 10 (3.2.2), n. 264 (1.2.3), n. 8 (3.1.1).
catchpoles: Long poles with snares or nooses attached to one end, used to capture and restrain animals (or people). Pluto: See above, n. 117 (DJR).
sleepy: Sleep-inducing, soporific.
Eumenides: Literally, ‘kindly ones’ – the ancient euphemistic name of the (extremely unkind) Furies.
Empirics: See above, n. 76 (DJR).
Satyrions: See above, n. 46 (2.5.1).
They can: ‘They know of’, or ‘they have learned’.
Limiter: A friar with a licence to preach, hear confessions and beg.

goodwives: See above, n. 44 (1.1.1). the good Abbess in Boccace … veil or hat: In Decameron 9.2, an abbess rises early in an attempt to catch a nun with her lover, but mistakenly puts on the breeches of her own bedfellow.
Paulina, a chaste matron … Anubis: See above, n. 42 (3.2.1).
inescate: Allure, entice.
no other fascination … of which I have formerly spoken: See above, 3.2.2.2.
It was given out of old … King Philip: This story, about Philip of Macedon and his wife Olympias (c. 375–316 BCE), is taken from Plutarch’s Advice for a Bride and Groom (23).
skill of: Have knowledge of, skill in.
Characters, Knots: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1).
Hilarion: St Hilarion (291–371 CE) was an anchorite who lived in the desert in Palestine, in imitation of St Anthony.
as Apollo … Daphne: In classical mythology, while fleeing the affections of Apollo, Daphne was turned into a laurel tree by her father Peneus. Apollo then used its branches for his crown.
Corse: See above, n. 78 (1.2.1).
Ache: Aachen in Germany, traditionally known in England as Aix-la-Chapelle.

Marcus the Heretic: The founder of the early Christian Gnostic sect known as the Marcosians, and a disciple of the Egyptian Gnostic theologian Valentinus (d. c. 165 CE). The Marcosians flourished in the Rhône valley. Lady Katharine Cobham … her husband: Eleanor (not Katharine) Cobham (c. 1400–1452) controversially married Humphrey (1390–1447) in 1428, but was eventually imprisoned after being found guilty of treasonable necromancy in 1441; cf. above, 1.2.3.4, p. 257.

Sicinius Aemilianus … his wife: Aemilia Pudentilla was the widow of the brother of Sicinius Aemilianus. The latter’s charge of magic against Apuleius, probably made in 158/9 CE, was heard in Oea (modern-day Tripoli) by the governor of Africa, Claudius (not Gnaeus) Maximus, and it was apparently unsuccessful.

the Hyperborean Magician … fine feats: In Lucian’s Lover of Lies, or The Doubter (13–15), the character Cleodemus describes the feats of a magician from the lands of the Hyperboreans (a mythical people said to have lived at the edge of the world), which included flying, walking on water and through fire, reanimating corpses, summoning spirits and moving the moon.

pullen: Poultry. mala insana: Literally, ‘mad-apples’ – aubergines, sometimes thought to cause insanity. Mandrake roots, Mandrake apples: See above, n. 160 (1.2.4). mala Bacchica: ‘Bacchic apples’, as mentioned in 3.2.2.1, pp. 728–9. panis porcinus: Sow-bread, a plant of the Cyclamen genus. Hippomanes: Either a small black membrane said to be found on the forehead of a newborn foal, a slimy humour flowing from a mare on heat, or a plant supposed to put mares on heat.

that fountain Salmacis … drank of it: The spring of Salmacis in Caria, near Halicarnassus, was actually reputed to have had enervating powers, deriving, as Ovid relates, from its association with the myth of Hermaphroditus, the son of Venus (Aphrodite) and Mercury (Hermes). In this tale (Metamorphoses 4.285–388), the water nymph Salmacis sees Hermaphroditus at the spring, and when he resists her attempt to rape him they are merged together into a single being of both sexes, who curses the waters. According to Vitruvius, who is misquoted in note ‘e’, the spring did not have this effect (On Architecture 2.8.12). Aix in Germany: See above, n. 272 (3.2.2).
Et qui tenebant … micant: This quotation from Seneca (Phaedra 379–80) describes the lovesick Phaedra; see above, n. 10 (3.2.2).

green sickness: Chlorosis: a disease thought to afflict young, virginal women, causing a greenish discoloration of the skin and other symptoms. Cachexia: See above, n. 45 (1.2.2). habit: See above, n. 26 (1.1.1).
ut occluso stillat ab igne liquor: The Latin quotation is found in several Renaissance emblematic representations of love, which depict Cupid working at his still (and using fire to produce tears).
when she … son-in-law: See above, n. 104 (3.2.2).

When Antiochus … blushed besides: This apocryphal tale, taken from Plutarch’s Life of Demetrius (38) and involving the ancient Greek anatomist and physician Erasistratus, was frequently recycled in the Renaissance. Seleucus I – see above, n. 127 (1.2.1) – did marry the famously beautiful Stratonice in his old age, but his personal doctor was actually Erasistratus’ father Cleombrotus.

Galen brags … Pulse and Countenance: A conflation of Galen’s account (On Prognosis 8.21) of his cure of the wife of one of his patrons, Flavius Boethus, who was suffect consul before 163 CE, with the same author’s story about Pylades and the wife of Justin – see above, n. 91 (3.2.2). as Poliarchus did at the name of Argenis: In John Barclay’s novel Argenis (1621), Poliarchus is one of the suitors of the princess Argenis; their eventual marriage restores stability to the kingdom.

totus Parmeno … hanc: An aside delivered to the slave Parmeno by the young Athenian Phaedria, at the entrance of his beloved prostitute Thais, in Terence’s Eunuch (83–4). Maiden blush: A delicate shade of pink.
merry-conceited: Wittily ingenious. facete: See above, n. 35 (1.2.4). bewray: See above, n. 43 (DJR).

huc ades O Thelayra: The first line of a love song presented in Girolamo Fracastoro’s Naugerius sive de poetica dialogus (1549). Come kiss me Corinna: A slight misquotation of the comedy Τεχνογαμία, or The Marriages of the Arts (1618) by the poet Barten Holiday, which had been performed at Christ Church in February 1617 when its author was a Student there. The name ‘Corinna’, which was frequently used in Renaissance love poetry, alludes to the narrator’s beloved in Ovid’s Loves.

first give an hundred … more, &c.: A quotation from The Forest (6.8–13) by Ben Jonson, which appeared in the first folio edition of his works (1616). The reference in note ‘a’ to him as ‘our arch-Poet’ (poet-laureate) is slightly misleading, as he was never formally given this title, but he had been granted a royal pension in February 1616.
culling: Embracing, cuddling. courage: Sexual vigour, lust.

Philippides her in Aristaenetus: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (1.16), it is actually the character of Lamprias, confessing to his friend Philippides, who has enjoyed a kiss with his (unnamed) beloved. saluted: Kissed, or greeted with a kiss.
the old man in the Comedy … inserere: Chremes, addressing his son Clitipho in Terence’s Self-Tormentor (863–4).

Ixion: In classical mythology, when Jupiter (Zeus) brought the Thessalian king Ixion to Olympus, the latter attempted to assault Juno (Hera) indecently; but Jupiter tricked Ixion into having intercourse with a cloud made in her shape instead.

as Apollo on Leucothoe: In classical mythology, the sun-god Helios (Sol), sometimes identified as Phoebus Apollo, fell in love with the Persian princess Leucothoe and raped her. the Moon … Chariot to be stayed: See above, n. 13 (2.3.1). This quotation from Lucian’s Dialogues of the Gods (19.1) refers to the Latmus mountain range, of which Endymion was the local hero, in Caria.
Adamant: See above, n. 80 (3.2.2).
Aristaenetus of Euxitheus: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.2), Euxitheus declares his love for Pythias, whom has met while praying in a temple. wistly: Intently.
as Martial’s Mamurra … comedit, &c.: The fictional Mamurra is portrayed as a pretentious connoisseur (and voyeur) in Epigrams 9.59, quoted here.

The Sultan of Sana’s wife in Arabia: According to Ludovico di Varthema (Vertomannus), he had actually been imprisoned by the Sultan of Rada’a (now a district in Yemen), who left him in charge of one of his wives while on a military campaign against the Sultan of Sana’a. Varthema says that he subsequently feigned madness, and managed to escape by persuading the sultan’s wife to let him visit a physician to treat him.
hem: Clear the throat (here, to attract attention).
sleeveless: Pointless.

Hospita Demophoon … Demophoon were approaching: In Ovid’s Heroides (2.1–2), the mythical Thracian princess Phyllis (‘Rhodopeia’ in the quotation refers to the Rhodope mountain range in western Thrace) addresses her beloved, the king of Athens Demophoon (or Demophon). Troilus to the City gates … Criseyde: See above, n. 168 (1.2.3).
kens: Looks, scans.
Sphinx’s wings: According to Plutarch, in a fragment (136) quoting the Oedipus of Euripides, the Theban Sphinx – see above, n. 119 (1.2.2) – had multicoloured wings.
a torment … as he calls it in the poet: Alcesimarchus, a young man from Sicyon who has fallen in love with Silenium, in Plautus’ Casket Comedy (203–10).
The Comical Poet … lovesick son: Terence, in his Brothers (696–8).
Vos O dii … Theocles prays: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.8), Theocles has fallen in love with his mother-in-law.
gales: Talk, speeches.
Calisto was … such delight: See above, n. 82 (1.2.4).

Love is a fiend … repentance dwell: Note ‘c’ is a quotation from the English poet and translator Robert Tofte’s Blazon of Jealousie (1615) – itself a version of the Lettura sopra un sonetto della gelosia di mons. Dalla Casa (1545) by the Italian humanist scholar Benedetto Varchi; the note was present only in the first edition of 1621, but has here been restored. The omission in later versions was probably due to an error by the 1624 compositor, who had to deal with extensive additions to this part of the text. Burton rarely removed material from new editions without an obvious reason. castaway: See above, n. 2 (1.1.1).
mournful Amyntas … careful Amyntas: Amyntas is the shepherd beloved of Menalcas in Virgil’s Eclogues.
stool-ball: A rural game similar to cricket, played mainly by young women. barley-break: See above, n. 69 (2.2.4).
the Elysian fields: See above, n. 59 (1.1.2).
stern: Rudder, or helm.

Tulipant … our Herbalists call Narcissus: The ‘tulipant’ (tulip) was sometimes referred to in contemporary botany as ‘narcissus’ because of its apparent propensity
to hide its flowers at sunset or in poor weather conditions (putatively echoing the shy retreat of the mythical Narcissus from the attentions of the nymph Echo). Carolus Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua: According to the Imprese illustri (1584) of Girolamo Ruscelli, the emblem of Carlo Gonzaga (d. 1456) was accompanied by the Spanish motto ‘Syn sus rayos mys desmayos’ (‘Without its rays I faint’). Impress: See above, n. 19 (2.3.7). inamorates: Lovers. Primum mobile: See above, n. 52 (1.2.1). anima informans: Literally, ‘informing soul’, or ‘soul giving form’. In scholastic philosophy, the ‘form’ is the essential determinant of matter, which actualizes its potentiality – as in the common definition of the soul as the ‘form of the living body’: see above, n. 25 (1.1.2).

Cynosure, Hesperus & Vesper, his morning and evening Star: ‘Cynosure’ is the Pole Star; ‘Hesperus’ and ‘Vesper’ are both names for the evening star, the planet Venus in the evening; and the ‘morning star’ is the same planet in the morning. The description of the beloved as a celestial body is common trope in classical erotic literature.
His Laura: An allusion to Laura (probably Laura de Noves, 1310–48), the beloved of Petrarch in his poetry.

Juno, nec ira … illapsus: The original source of the quotation in note ‘b’, the Punica (15.94–5) of Silius Italicus, refers to the power of ‘Voluptas’ (Pleasure), who is portrayed in a struggle with ‘Virtus’ (Virtue). Burton has substituted Juno as the Roman goddess of love and marriage.

Mount Gargarus … stems: In this quotation, from the Amnon tragoedia sacra (1617) by the Ghent Benedictine monk Jacobus Cornelius Lummenaeus à Marca, Mount Gargarus is the higher part of Mount Ida in Crete. As the birthplace of Zeus (Jupiter), its abundance of ‘stems’ (‘lines of descent’) alludes to his numerous offspring.

When the King of Babylon … consume himself: According to Philostratus (Life of Apollonius of Tyana 1.36), the courtier, who had slept with one of the wives of the Parthian king Vardanes I (d. 45 CE), was a eunuch. Apollonius – on whom, see above, n. 55 (DJR) – counselled that the pain of continuing to live with frustrated desire would itself be the right punishment.

flux: See above, n. 4 (1.2.1). accede ad hanc ignem: The ungrammatical substitution of the feminine pronoun hanc for the masculine hunc, found in some versions of Terence’s Eunuch (85), suggests that the ‘flame’ (ignis) being referred to is the courtesan Thais. inextinguible: Inextinguishable.

Nam amor saepe Lypareo Vulcano … solet: In antiquity, the god Hephaestus (Vulcan) was associated with the Liparian island Vulcano, as the site of his forge; see above, n. 55 (1.2.1) and n. 36 (2.2.3).
For when Nero burnt Rome, as Calisto urgeth … 100,000 bodies: The comparison with the Neronian conflagration in 64 CE is drawn by the courtly lover Calisto in the first act of Rojas’s Celestina.
drench: Medicinal potion.
amain: See above, n. 5 (Preliminaries).
Empedocles: See above, n. 92 (DJR). sod: See above, n. 32 (1.2.2).
radical moisture: See above, 1.1.2.5.
pendent opera interrupta … coelo: This quotation, from Aeneid 4.88–9, refers to the building works started by Dido in Carthage, which are left incomplete when she falls in love with Aeneas.

Palladis telae vacant … manus: From Seneca’s Phaedra (103–4). In classical mythology, Minerva (Athena) was portrayed as the patroness (and sometimes the inventor) of the crafts of spinning and weaving, which were typical domestic tasks for women.
the shepherd in Theocritus: The lovesick Aeschinas, in Idylls 14. flag: See above, n. 6 (1.3.1). pranking: See above, n. 112 (DJR).
Uritur oblitus pecorum … formae: In note ‘f’, the quotation from Ovid (Metamorphoses 13.763–4) refers to the myth of the Cyclops Polyphemus and his beloved nymph Galatea.
amort: Lifeless, dejected.
Schools: Universities.
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR).
betwixt hawk and buzzard: Between a good and a bad thing of the same kind.

as Medea did … doth neither: Ovid’s Metamorphoses (7.19–21) describes Medea’s agonizing after falling in love with Jason in Colchis. Burton’s rendering of the quotation is loose to the point of misleading; Medea actually says, in a literal translation of the Latin text, that ‘I follow the worse’.

precipitates: Hurls down into a bad position, ruins. Jupiter into a Bull: See above, n. 20 (3.2.2). Apuleius an Ass: In Apuleius’ Metamorphoses, the protagonist Lucius (named after the author) accidentally turns himself into an ass. Lycaon a wolf: See above, n. 41 (1.1.1). Tereus a Lapwing: The mythical Thracian king Tereus was turned into a hoopoe (often confused with lapwings in the Middle Ages and Renaissance) as a punishment by the gods for raping Philomela, the sister of his wife Procne. The sisters were turned into a swallow and a nightingale, after Procne had retaliated by killing her son Itys and feeding him to Tereus. Callisto a Bear: There are different explanations in classical mythology for the transformation of Callisto, an Arcadian nymph (or princess, and daughter of Lycaon) into a bear. In some accounts it is a punishment by Artemis (Diana), or Hera (Juno), for losing her virginity after falling in love with Zeus (Jupiter) and being seduced or raped by him; in others, she is turned into a bear by Zeus in order to conceal his deed from Hera. She is also said to have become the constellation of the Great Bear after being killed by Artemis. An immodest woman is like a Bear: Note ‘a’ draws on the association, common since the Middle Ages, of bears with violent lust. The bear was also a traditional symbol of unchastity. Elpenor and Gryllus … Circe: See above, n. 189 (DJR).

Feram induit … se redeat: The allusion to Apuleius’ Metamorphoses in note ‘b’ refers to the crown of roses eaten by Lucius in a religious ceremony, which transforms him back into human form at the end of the novel.

tallow-faced: Pale or yellowish-white faced. a swollen Juggler’s platter face: A broad, round, flat face with puffed-out cheeks, like a face pulled by a jester or buffoon. chitty: Lean and pinched. clouds: Dark spots. squized: Squeezed or squashed. sparrow-mouthed: Wide-mouthed. gubber-tushed: With large projecting teeth. Bavarian poke: See above, n. 129 (1.2.1). lave-eared: With drooping or hanging ears. bloody-fallen fingers: Fingers with sores, pustules or ulcerated chilblains. aufe: A goblin child, or a changeling left by the fairies (and so a misbegotten, deformed child, or a simpleton). savours: Stinks. incondite: Crude, unrefined. tit: A disreputable young woman. fustilugs: A gross, foul-smelling woman. truss: A baggy, shapeless person. raw-bone: A very thin or gaunt person. sneaker: A shifty, stealthy person. mard: See above, n. 26 (2.3.2). rammy: See above, n. 5 (2.2.1). Irus’ daughter: Daughter of a poor man – on Irus, see above, n. 61 (2.3.3). Thersites’ sister: See above, n. 107 (DJR). Grobian’s scholar: A coarse, crude person (in Renaissance satire, ‘St Grobian’ was the fictional patron saint of the vulgarly ill-mannered).

Ipsa haec … Agnae: In this quotation from Horace (Satires 1.3.39–40), ‘Balbinus’ may refer to one of the victims of the proscriptions issued in 43 BCE after the assassination of Julius Caesar. ‘Hagna’ has not been identified, but this was a common name among Roman freedwomen.
carrack: Galleon. caskanet: An ornamental collar or necklace, a carcanet. myriads of crowns: See above, n. 15 (3.1.3).

Panthea, Cleopatra, Tarquin’s Tanaquil, Herod’s Mariamne, or Mary of Burgundy: A list of famously beautiful (and/or wealthy) queens: on Panthea, see above, n. 29 (3.2.2); Cleopatra VII of Egypt; Tanaquil, according to Roman tradition, was the noble Etruscan wife of Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome; Mariamme I (b. 53/2 BCE) was the beautiful second wife of Herod the Great; Mary, Duchess of Burgundy (1457–82 CE), the daughter of Charles the Bold (‘Carolus Pugnax’ in note ‘b’), was sometimes known as ‘Mary the Rich’.
Vincet vultus … bella: In this quotation from Seneca’s Octavia (775–6), the chorus refers to Poppaea Sabina – on whom, see above, n. 13 (3.1.2) and n. 137 (3.2.2).

Larissean Coronis: In classical mythology, the famously beautiful princess, daughter of Phlegyas (king of the Lapiths), beloved of Apollo and mother of Asclepius. Apollo kills her after discovering through a raven, his messenger, that she has slept with Ischys. Babylonian Thisbe: See above, n. 69 (3.2.2). Polyxena: See above, n. 62 (3.2.2). Laura: See above, n. 37 (3.2.3). Lesbia: Catullus’ beloved, a pseudonym for Clodia – possibly the married sister of Publius Clodius, on whom, see above, n. 183 (DJR). counterfeit: Fictional.

Dicebam Triviae … Dianae: The Roman goddess Diana was often associated (and sometimes identified) with Trivia, goddess of crossroads and witchcraft, and the Roman equivalent of Hecate – on whom, see above, n. 22 (1.2.4).
Hebe: In classical mythology, the daughter of Zeus (Jupiter) and Hera (Juno), and the personification of beauty in youth.
Euhemerus in Aristaenetus … her behalf: In the Erotic Letters (1.12), Euhemerus is enamoured of the courtesan Pythias, whom he presents as beautiful and virtuous.
as Triton … Sea-God: On this allusion and the verse immediately following, see above, n. 99 (3.2.2).
by odds: See above, n. 34 (1.3.1).
Elogies: See above, n. 54 (DJR).
I not: Or ‘I noot’ – ‘I don’t know’.
Whiter Galat: The name ‘Galatea’ means ‘milky white’ in Greek. withywind: Or ‘withwind’: bindweed, a species of the genus Convolvulus. wanton: See above, n. 18 (1.3.2).
conceited: See above, n. 20 (DJR).
Doris: The mother of Galatea and the other Nereids. Burton is referring to the first of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Sea-Gods.

when a country fellow … absolute and perfect: This story from a fragment of Plutarch (134) refers to the Greek painter and sculptor Zeuxis (fl. c. 435/25–390 BCE), whose painting of Helen in the temple of Hera Lacinia in Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily was famous in antiquity, and Nicomachus (fl. c. 360–320 BCE), who was another important painter, possibly from Thebes.

British Bunduica: Boudicca (or Boadicea, d. 60/61 BCE), whose name has many different spellings in this era: the queen of the Iceni, a Brittonic tribe whose territory included parts of East Anglia. Sostrata’s bitch: The original copies of the Anatomy have ‘Sostratu’s bitch’. Given the subsequent reference to Parmeno, ‘Sostrata’, the name of the widow in Terence’s Brothers, was probably intended (although Burton possibly misremembered this as ‘Sostratus’). Parmeno’s sow: Probably a reference to the slave Parmeno from Terence’s Brothers. But it may also refer to an ancient proverbial saying about popular delusion, ‘Nothing compared to Parmeno’s sow’; according to Plutarch, this originated in the imitation of a pig’s squeal given by Parmeno (probably a comic actor), which gained more applause than that of a real pig. Venerilla: A little Venus. Quanto quam Lucifer … Herce: In note ‘a’, the quotation from Ovid (Metamorphoses 2.723–4) refers to Mercury
(Hermes) falling in love with Herse, one of the daughters of the Attic king Cecrops in classical mythology.
M. D.: Note ‘b’ refers to the poet Michael Drayton – on whom, see above, n. 35 (1.2.3). Thou art my Vesta … my heart: Vesta was the ancient Roman goddess of the domestic hearth-fire.

nec pulchrae … Stratonices: This quotation, a Latin translation of an epigram by the Greek poet Nicander of Colophon, alludes to the deification of Stratonice – the wife of Seleucus I Nicator – and her frequent identification with Aphrodite (Venus), in several Greek cities after her death. Dulcinea: The imaginary beloved of Cervantes’s Don Quixote. Antiphila: The beloved of Clinia in Terence’s Self-Tormentor.
Veneres: See above, n. 65 (1.2.4).

Quintus Catulus … Roscius: References to the Roman statesman and poet Quintus Lutatius Catulus (c. 150–87 BCE), and the famous (and reportedly handsome) actor Quintus Roscius Gallus (d. 62), who was defended by Cicero in a civil trial.
curiously: See above, n. 125 (DJR).

Margareta speciosa … delight and darling: In the original source, Barth’s Latin translation of Celestina (1624), Calisto actually addresses his beloved Melibea as his ‘most precious pearl’ (‘pretiosissima margarita’). In extracting and rendering the quotation, Burton substitutes ‘Margaret’, which is etymologically derived from margarita.

as Rodomont courted Isabella: See above, n. 189 (3.2.2). After falling in love with Isabella, the daughter of the king of Galicia (who has vowed to remain faithful to the Scottish prince Zerbino, killed in a duel), Rodomonte’s attempted seduction fails when she tricks him into killing her.
undressed: Here, probably ‘casually dressed’, rather than ‘naked’.
fonder: See above, n. 103 (DJR). parasangs: See above, n. 42 (DJR).

Come to me … beyond all others: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (1.24), the courtesan Musarium (Mousarion in Greek versions), who has been criticized by a group of suitors for restricting her affections to the unexceptional Lysias, expresses her devotion to her beloved.
Mopsus: The young poet whose marriage to Nysa is celebrated in Virgil’s Eclogues (8.26–30).
enamorate: Lover.
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
congee: See above, n. 187 (1.2.3).
Areusa: One of the prostitutes in Rojas’s Celestina.

Roscida per tenebras Faunus … venit: In this line from Ovid’s Fasti (2.332), Faunus is the Roman god of the outdoors, equivalent to the Greek Pan. Here, the goat-like deity is on his way to rape the Lydian queen Omphale, but inadvertently molests Hercules (Heracles) instead.

Hercules served Omphale … and spun: As part of his punishment for killing his host Iphitus, Hercules performed the duties of the slave for Omphale. In the Latin versions of the myth, he is forced to carry out the typically female work of spinning wool, and is sometimes said to have become her lover.

Polyaenus when his Mistress Circe … not resist: An allusion to Petronius’ Satyricon (130), where Encolpius, who has assumed the identity of a slave called Polyaenus (an epithet of Odysseus), has been sexually humiliated in failing to satisfy the desire of ‘Circe’ – see above, n. 23 (3.2.2) – and attempts to redeem himself.

with that Centurion in the Spanish Celestina … Areusa: In Act 15, after being insulted by Areusa, the rogue Centurio says that he would prefer her to order him to kill ten men rather than travel a league on foot.

Galeatus of Mantua … was drowned: In the Morosophiae … liber alter (1620), the German scholar Gaspar Ens says that Galeatus (Galeazzo) was a Milanese
merchant who lived in the time of Louis XII’s campaigns in Italy (1494–1504), and that he killed his beloved Lucretia before committing suicide.
Ticinum: Now Pavia, on the River Ticino in northern Italy.
Aeolus to Juno: In Virgil’s Aeneid (1.50–86), quoted after this allusion, the Homeric ruler of the winds, Aeolus, accedes to Juno’s request to send a storm that will sink Aeneas’ fleet.
Pindus’ tops: The Pindus is a mountain range in northern Greece, on the border of Thessaly and Epirus.

Callicratidas in Lucian … hold us both: In the pseudo-Lucianic Affairs of the Heart (46), the Athenian Callicratidas is actually referring to an idealized boy, as part of a speech proving the superiority of male homosexual love.

Abrocomas in Aristaenetus … Delphis: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.21), Abrocomas – in Greek ‘Habrocomes’, named after the romantic protagonist in a novel by Xenophon of Ephesus (second century CE) – expresses his desire to love Delphis forever.

Sciron and Procrustes: Two terrifying Attic bandits who ambushed travellers in Greek mythology: Sciron, who forced his victims to wash his feet before hurling them into an abyss inhabited by a human-eating turtle; and Procrustes, who tortured travellers to death by stretching them and hitting their limbs with a hammer until they fitted his enormous (‘Procrustean’) bed. Both were killed by Theseus while he was crossing the Isthmus of Corinth. coulters: The iron blades fixed in front of the share in a plough; cf. 3.3.2.1, p. 952.

as Zerbino slain … Brandimarte in Barbary: In Orlando furioso, Zerbino dies in the arms of Isabella, and Brandimarte expires after being mortally wounded on the island of Lipadusa (near the coast of Africa), in the middle of saying the name of his beloved wife Fiordiligi. as Arcite did his Emily: In Chaucer’s ‘Knight’s Tale’, the knight Arcite, whose last words are quoted immediately after this allusion, dies when he is thrown from his horse after winning a contest for Emily’s hand with his rival Palamon.
ne: Nor.

Thirteen proper young men … by a slight: In Greek mythology, when a prophecy claimed that Oenomaus would be killed by his son-in-law, the king decreed that his daughter’s hand in marriage could be obtained only after defeating him in a chariot-race, in which failure meant death. Many suitors were killed, but Pelops won by sabotaging the axle of Oenomaus’ chariot.
As many gallants … obtained his suit: See above, n. 60 (3.2.2).

Sabea: The ancient kingdom of Sheba, whose territory lies in what is now Yemen (although Burton’s source actually states that the events occurred in a Libyan city called Silene). the golden legend: See above, n. 123 (DJR).

Squire of Dames: A comic character in Spenser’s Faerie Queene. Knight of the Sun: See above, n. 249 (1.2.3). Sir Bevis of Southampton: Bevis of Hampton (or ‘Sir Bevois’), an English hero found in many medieval romances. that renowned peer, Orlando … undertake: Orlando (the Italian form of Roland) was one of the ‘Paladins’, or ‘Twelve Peers’ – warriors who served Charlemagne and were celebrated in The Song of Roland as paragons of Christian virtue.
pour: Make great effort, give their all. stour: Armed contest. rivelled: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3).

the great Cham’s court: See above, n. 111 (1.2.4). Candish: See above, n. 7 (2.3.4). serve twice seven years … Rachel: Genesis 29:18–28. Gismunda the daughter of Tancredus … died: In Decameron 4.1, Guiscardo is killed by Tancred, who sends Ghismonda his heart in a golden cup. Ghismonda pours poison into the cup and drinks it, and rather than eating the heart, she places it on top of her own as she lies down to die. as Artemisia drank … powder: See above, n. 47 (3.2.1). more torments than Theseus or Paris: On Theseus, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3). In the Trojan Epic
(10.223–335) by the Greek poet Quintus of Smyrna (third century CE), Paris died in prolonged agony after being shot by the Thessalian hero Philoctetes with two of the arrows of Heracles, which had been dipped in the poisonous blood of the Hydra.
well apaid: Well satisfied, contented.
busk point: The lace and tag securing a corset’s busk (the supporting frame attached to its front section).

As Laodamia did … to war: In Greek mythology, the hero Protesilaus was the first Greek to be killed at Troy, as soon as the army landed. After his death, according to Hyginus (Fables 104), his grieving wife Laodamia made a bronze image of him and devoted herself to it, and when her father Acastus tried to end her misery by burning the image on a pyre, she killed herself by jumping into the fire. The tomb of Protesilaus at Elaeus, on the Thracian Chersonesus (the modern Gallipoli peninsula), was the site of a famous devotional cult and site of pilgrimage in antiquity.
coast: See above, n. 291 (DJR).

Ovid would be a Flea … a Ring: In Loves (2.15), Ovid expresses his desire to be the ring worn by his beloved. The references to the flea and gnat derive from spurious works: the pseudo-Ovidian Pulex (‘The Flea’) and, probably, the pseudo-Virgilian Culex (‘The Gnat’).
fain: Well pleased.
hap: Fortune, luck. Lawn: See above, n. 114 (3.2.2).

they that saw Hero in Musaeus: In the Hero and Leander (54–85) of the Byzantine poet Musaeus (sixth century CE), the crowds who have gathered in the Thracian city of Sestos for the festival of Aphrodite are stunned by the beauty of Hero as she passes through the temple of the goddess. Salmacis to Hermaphroditus … lecti: See above, n. 277 (3.2.2).

her break out … bedfellows: In Plautus’ Braggart Soldier (65), the parasite Artotrogus flatters the pompous Pyrgopolynices by reporting that a woman said this about him. as she said of Cyrus … but a night: In the anecdote related in Xenophon’s Cyropaedia (5.2.28), these words were actually said about an anonymous young man by a concubine of Abradatas, the (fictitious) king of Susa, who promptly had him castrated.
Nectarean: Sweet as nectar.
as Potiphar’s wife did by Joseph: See above, n. 3 (2.3.4).

as King John … at Dunmow: The legendary infatuation of King John of England (1167–1216) for Matilda Fitzwalter culminated in her taking refuge in Dunmow Priory, where the king had her poisoned with a poached egg. The story was a popular subject in English poetry and drama in the late Renaissance.

atque aliquis de diis … &c.: The quoted passage from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (4.186–8) continues ‘prayed that he might be shamed this way’ – having discovered Mars (Ares) and Venus (Aphrodite) ‘disgracefully bound together’: see above, n. 10 (3.1.1). so did Lucian’s Mercury wish: In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Gods (17.1–2), Hermes (Mercury) says that he is jealous of Hephaestus (Vulcan), who married Aphrodite as well as Charis (or Aglaea, the youngest of the Graces), but admits that he has himself had intercourse with the former goddess.
Old January in Chaucer … my felicity: In ‘The Merchant’s Tale’, the elderly knight January, having decided to marry the beautiful young virgin May, reflects on wedded bliss (1637–54).
rash: Clash together. rail: Pour, gush. sprent: Spurted.

that famous buckler of Argos: The particular explanation given by Erasmus in his Adagia of the proverb, ‘He’s boasting as if he’d carried off an Argive shield’, refers to the holy shield possessed by the city of Argos, which could only be moved with great difficulty.

as Serranus the Spaniard … Spinola: Don Mateo Serrano (c. 1550–1616) was governor of Sluis in the Low Countries, which was successfully besieged by Dutch and English troops in 1604. The Genoese aristocrat Ambrogio Spinola (1569–1630) was commander-in-chief of the Spanish army in Flanders.
The nine worthies: See above, n. 165 (1.2.3). Oliver and Roland: Both ‘Paladins’ of the court of Charlemagne. proof: Impenetrable, invulnerable.

as that fatal Dog, and fatal Hare … never make an end: In Greek mythological interpretations of astronomy, the constellation of Canis Major (the ‘Greater Dog’) was commonly represented as being in perpetual pursuit of the Hare, the constellation Lepus. ‘Fatal’ here means ‘condemned by fate’ or ‘doomed’.
