Castilio thinks Ferdinand … multitude of Moors: This reference, from Baldassare Castiglione’s Libro del Cortegiano (1528), is to the conquest of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, by the joint forces of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile in the Granada War (1482–91).
Sir Walter Mauny: Mauny (c. 1310–72) was a soldier and commander acclaimed for his gallantry and disregard of his own safety in Edward III’s campaigns in Scotland and France.
a proper man of person: See above, n. 52 (1.1.1).

smock: See above, n. 216 (3.2.2). a Burgomaster’s daughter: A ‘Burgomaster’ – an anachronistic term when used in an ancient context – was technically the chief magistrate of a Dutch or Flemish town. More loosely, it denoted a similar functionary in another foreign country. complements: See above, n. 121 (3.2.2).
Idiot: See above, n. 207 (DJR).
Grobians: See above, n. 59 (3.2.3).
a Novizza or Venetian Bride: In Renaissance Venice, a future bride was called a ‘Novizza’.
nice, and too curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR). terse: See above, n. 217 (DJR).
smugs up: Smartens. band: See above, n. 141 (3.2.2). twires: Twirls.
tire-woman: Lady’s maid. artificial impostures: Illusory ornaments.

As Mother Mamaea … people first: Julia Avita Mamaea (d. 235 CE) was actually the mother of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander. Herodian observes that during the festival of the sun-god Elagabalus, the emperor of the same name – whose mother Julia Soaemias Bassiana (d. 222) was Mamaea’s sister – used to parade around in ‘disgusting make-up’ (History of the Empire 5.7).
brave: See above, n. 47 (DJR).

lovelock: Or just ‘lock’ – a lock of hair worn longer than the rest, hanging forward over one shoulder, as was fashionable among male courtiers. Ganymede: See above, n. 41 (3.2.1). as Heinsius writ to Primerius: Daniel Heinsius’ letter of July 1607 to his fellow poet and scholar Jacob Primerius has the title ‘Qualis viro literato ducenda sit uxor? &, an ducenda?’ (‘What kind of wife should be taken by a learned man? And should he take one?’) prune: See above, n. 137 (3.2.2). pique-devant: See above, n. 182 (3.2.2). Julian the Apostate … Misopogon: In his satirical Misopogon (‘Beard-hater’), written in 363 as a reply to Christian critics in Antioch, Julian begins by quoting their ridicule of his beard and contrasting his shaggy, philosophical appearance with that of the smooth-skinned, sophisticated citizens of the city – before turning the abuse on to them. to follow mine author: Burton has returned to Heinsius. in Print: Perfectly, precisely, neatly.

Jupiter perceived Mercury … Philologia: In this reference to the late-antique Carthaginian encyclopaedist Martianus Capella, ‘Mercury’ and ‘Philologia’ represent eloquence and learning respectively. Suadela: The Roman goddess of Persuasion.

distilling: Trickling down, dripping. Callistratus by the help of Daedalus … a-dancing: Callistratus, in his account of the statue of Eros (Cupid) by the celebrated fourth-century BCE Athenian sculptor Praxiteles (Descriptions 3.12–15),
says that its features made him believe that the mythical craftsman Daedalus, famous for his lifelike sculptures, had fashioned a troupe of dancers that really had movement and sensation (itself an allusion to the dance-floor Daedalus made for Ariadne in Crete: Iliad 18.590–93); ‘many’ here means ‘company’ or ‘retinue’.
the Hours: See above, n. 198 (DJR).

Amphitrite: In classical mythology, a sea-goddess and ruler of aquatic creatures, and the mother of the sea-nymphs known as the Nereids. Hymenaeus: The ancient name for a wedding song. strawing: Scattering.

in Saint Mark’s Garden in Rome … wench asleep: The sculpture, which is included in a list of sculptures from Roman tombs by Heinrich Kornmann in De miraculis mortuorum (1610), has not been identified, but it was presumably once located in the gardens of the Palazzo San Marco (now the Palazzo Venezia).
View of Fr.: Note ‘f’ refers to The View of France (1604) by the English courtier Sir Robert Dallington.
mum: Perform as a mummer, act in a mime. Comus: The classical god of festivity. Hymen: See above, n. 235 (3.2.2).

public Professor: That is, a university professor, employed by the whole institution rather than a constituent college or a subsidiary body. In the course of his life, the philosopher Agostino Nifo (Niphus, c. 1469–c. 1546) had taught at Padua, Pisa, Naples and Salerno.

virginal Jacks: The blocks of wood holding the quills that plucked the strings of a virginal, moving up and down as the instrument was played. Trenchmore: A boisterous English country dance. prinkum-prankum: Another name for the cushion-dance: see above, n. 59 (2.2.6).
entreated: See above, n. 2 (1.2.4).

an hundred sesterces … Lais of Corinth: According to Aulus Gellius (1.8), Lais – on whom, see above, n. 158 (1.2.4) – charged 10,000 drachmas, or 10,000 denarii (one unit of each roughly corresponding to the average wage of a day-labourer). The figure of a hundred sesterces, which has evidently resulted from a mistranslation of the Latin terminology, undersells her services dramatically. as Mundus to Paulina: See above, n. 42 (3.2.1).
likely: See above, n. 38 (DJR).
Poetaster: Inferior poet.
Colewiz: Chemnitz.
Herebertus Archbishop of Cologne: Heribert of Cologne (970–1021).

Crommyomantia: The name or initials inscribed on the first onion to sprout were taken to indicate the girl’s first suitor. fasting on St. Anne’s Eve: This should be the Eve of St Agnes, the patron saint of young girls and chastity, which is 20 January. Fasting on this occasion was said to induce a dream of the future husband. Alphitomantia … by beans in a Cake: Alphitomancy, divination using barley meal or barley cakes, and the similar practice of crithomancy, which used baked barley cakes. Both involved the interpretation of patterns found in the flour, or in the smoke produced when they were burned.
exornations: See above, n. 54 (DJR).
Atellans … Fescennines: See above, n. 24 (3.1.1).

Danaus the son of Belus … heard of: According to Hyginus (Fables 273), the celebrations put on by the Libyan king Danaus for the wedding of his fifty daughters (the ‘Danaids’) included singing contests and the hymenaeus (‘wedding song’). The rest of the myth, in which under their father’s instructions they decapitate all but one of the bridegrooms on the wedding night, is not mentioned.

’Tis true, Vulcan … dearly loved. A version of the classical myth of the necklace made by Vulcan for the goddess Harmonia (the daughter of Mars and Venus, not Hermione), which he had cursed in revenge for his cuckolding – see above, n. 10 (3.1.1). The account given by Parthenius of Nicaea (Sufferings in Love 25), from
the Hellenistic historian Phylarchus, refers to the necklace’s passage, through the hands of the sons of the mythical Arcadian king Phegeus, down to the fourth century BCE and to the Phocian general Phayllus and the wife of Ariston, a leader of the Oetaean tribe in central Greece. Calamity eventually strikes: her son goes mad and burns their house down, killing Ariston’s mother and destroying their possessions. On ‘ouche’, see above, n. 147 (3.2.2).
Orders of the Garter, Golden Fleece: See above, n. 27 (3.1.1). The Order of the Golden Fleece is a Catholic chivalric order founded by Philip the Good, duke of Burgundy, in 1430.

Boyards, authors of Arcadia, Urania: References to the Italian Renaissance poet Matteo Maria Boiardo (c. 1441–94), author of Orlando innamorato (1483), and two English writers, Sir Philip Sidney (1554–86) and Lady Mary Wroth (c. 1587–c. 1653), the latter being the author of the prose romance Urania (1621).
porteous: Portable breviary, manual.

Non me carminibus … Linus: These lines from Virgil (Eclogues 4.55–6) refer to the mythical musician Linus, the son of Apollo and one of the Muses (sometimes identified as Terpsichore), brother of Orpheus and the music teacher of Hercules (who killed him in a fit of rage).

Astrophel’s Stella: In Astrophil and Stella, the sonnet sequence written by Sir Philip Sidney in the 1580s. Roses, Violets, Lilies … etc.: The list of terms is taken from the criticisms given by the Italian humanist scholar and physician Julius Caesar Scaliger, in his Poetices libri septem (1561), of the verbal repetitiveness of Giovanni Pontano’s Tumuli (1505), a collection of poems addressed to dead friends and relatives. ‘Costus’ is the root of a variety of thistle (Saussurea costus), native to northern India; the oil from its root was used in medicine as well as perfumery.
hog rubbers: See above, n. 8 (3.1.2). Menalcas and Corydon: Generic names for shepherds in pastoral poetry.
accurate: See above, n. 86 (2.2.4). Wakes, Whitsun ales: See above, n. 68 (2.2.4). roundelays: Folk dances in which the dancers form a circle. lovers’ knots: See above, n. 39 (3.1.2).

Corydon’s Phyllis … Sir Tophas: No source has been traced for this couplet, which may be Burton’s invention. Some of the allusions to characters from pastoral poetry may be specific – for example to Nicholas Breton’s Pastorall of Phyllis and Corydon (1600). ‘Dousabel’, whose name derives from ‘douce et belle’, is mentioned in Ben Jonson’s Alchemist (1610) as the beloved of Face (3.3.41). ‘Sir Tophas’ is a braggart soldier comically infatuated with a sorceress in John Lyly’s Endymion (1588).

O the Broom … bonny Broom: The title of a song included in John Playford’s English Dancing Master (1651), but also a line from the traditional love ballad ‘The Broom of Cowdenknows’. Bess a Bell she doth excel: A folk song sometimes entitled ‘Bessy Bell she doth excel’. indite: See above, n. 2 (Preliminaries).

Cis: A fictional milkmaid, addressed with these lines by a putative lover in The Letting of Humours Blood in the Head-vaine (1600) by Samuel Rowlands (cited in note ‘b’). Gammer Gubbins’ house: ‘Gammer’ here means ‘old woman’ or ‘grandmother’. ‘Gubbins’ was the name of the inhabitants of a Devonshire village of the same name, sometimes said to be lawless savages.

Lady Cressetlight … Sir Trolly Lolly: The figures of ‘Lady Cresset-light’ and ‘Sir Trollelollie’, in the fourth satire of Rowlands’s Letting of Humours being quoted here, are versions of Troilus and Cressida. A ‘cresset’ is a fire-basket of the kind commonly used to provide light at a wharf; ‘trolly lolly’ was slang for a fashionable type of coarse lace.

Xerxes gave to Themistocles … his diet: See above, n. 18 (1.4.1). ‘Myunte’ here refers to the small Ionian port of Myus, reportedly granted to the exiled Athenian
politician and general Themistocles for its abundance of fish (Diodorus Siculus, Library of History 11.57.7).
The Persian Kings … her hood: According to Cicero (Against Verres 2.33.76), the wives of Persian and Syrian kings were provided with specific adornments by different towns in their territories.
to buy her pins: That is, as ‘pin money’ – an allowance for clothing and personal expenses.

Antinoe: More usually Antinopolis, now Sheikh Ibada, on the east bank of the Nile. Constellations … Antinous: The constellation named by Hadrian after Antinous – on whom, see above, n. 107 (1.2.4) – is now obsolete in astronomy, and is regarded as part of Aquila.
set out his Hephaestion to all eternity: That is, adorn him for his funeral. On Hephaestion, see above, n. 162 (1.2.3).
sectator: Follower, disciple. under the plane tree: An allusion to Plato’s Phaedrus, which is set under a plane tree outside the walls of Athens, on the banks of the River Ilissus.
R. T.: On the attribution in note ‘a’, see above, n. 30 (3.2.3).
So for Lucian’s Mistress … hanged themselves: Note ‘b’ alludes to Panthea – see above, n. 29 (3.2.2).

Coresus and Callirhoe: In Greek mythology, the tragically unrequited love of the Dionysian priest Coresus for Callirhoe led to the Aetolian city of Calydon being cursed by the god with madness, and culminated in the suicides of both lover and beloved. Theagenes the Philosopher: In Lucian’s Passing of Peregrinus, the Cynic philosopher Theagenes of Patrae (second century CE) is reported to have assisted the suicide of his philosophical master, Peregrinus Proteus (c. 100–165 CE) – which Lucian says was motivated by a love of glory. & mihi fortis … vulnera vires: Spoken by Thisbe in Ovid’s Metamorphoses (4.149–50).
every while: Continually.

Catiline killed his only son … recusaret: According to Sallust (The War with Catiline 15) and Valerius Maximus (9.1.9), it was the grown-up stepson of Catiline – on whom, see above, n. 227 (DJR) – who was killed, because he was feared by Catiline’s future second wife.
Laodice the sister … she loved: Laodice’s attempt to poison her brother and spouse Mithridates VI – on whom, see above, n. 78 (1.2.2) – failed, and she was executed in 105 BCE.
Alexander to please Thais: See above, n. 175 (DJR) and n. 30 (2.2.4).

Nerius’ wife … Nobleman in Venice: This anecdote, taken from the ninth book of the Histories (1556) by the Byzantine historian Laonikos Chalkokondyles, involves Chiara Zorzi (d. 1454), the widow of the duke of Athens, Nerio II Acciaioli (1416–51), and the Venetian senator Bartolomeo Contarini, son of the governor of the colony of Nauplion in Greece, Priamo Contarini (1430–1511).

Constantine Despota: Constantine Palaiologos (c. 1280–1334), the son of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos (1259–1332). Nikephoros does not report that he killed his first wife, who died childless; Michael was his illegitimate son by his eventual second wife, the beautiful daughter of the imperial protosecretarius (‘chief secretary’).

Leucophrye betrayed … enemy’s Camp: According to Parthenius (Sufferings in Love 5.6), Leucophrye betrayed Magnesia (in southwestern Asia Minor) to an army commanded by her beloved Leucippus, a Lycian (or Carian) descendant of Bellerophon.

Pisidice the Governor’s daughter … father’s enemy: Parthenius (Sufferings in Love 5.21) reports that Pisidice, the daughter of King Lepethymnus of Methymna (a city on the northern coast of Lesbos), was stoned to death for this, on the orders of Achilles himself.

Diognetus did as much … Polycrita: According to Parthenius (Sufferings in Love 9), the virgin heroine Polycrite saved her hometown of Naxos, which was under siege by Milesian and Erythraean forces, by inducing the Erythraean leader Diognetus to betray his allies. Sadly, the grateful Naxians strewed so many celebratory garlands on to her that she suffocated and died.
Sine Cerere & Baccho: That is, without food and wine.
molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).
go woolward: Wear wool (rather than linen or cotton) next to the skin, especially in penance.
Tenterbellies: Gluttons, people with distended bellies.
Oracle: Divine revelation. This kind of devil … prayer: Matthew 17:21.

those Pauls, Hilarys, Antonys: On Paul of Thebes, see above, n. 38 (1.3.1). The other hermits referred to here are Hilary of Galatea (d. 558 CE) and probably Anthony the Great (d. 356), but the hermit Anthony of Lérins (c. 468–c. 520) is also possible. Hilarion: See above, n. 269 (3.2.2).
those Indian Brachmanni: See above, n. 91 (DJR). Redshanks: A derogatory term for Scottish highlanders or Irishmen (because they do not wear shoes or stockings).
such meats formerly mentioned … lust: See 3.2.2.1 above.

those old Egyptians abstained from Wine … the Giants: According to Plutarch (Isis and Osiris 6), the Egyptian kings believed that vines had first grown up from the earth where the blood of those who had once battled with the gods had been spilt.

Eryngoes: Candied roots of the sea holly (Eryngium maritimum), considered to be aphrodisiac. The original quotation from Ovid (Remedies for Love 799) refers to ‘lustful rocket’ (‘erucas … salaces’); see 2.4.1.3, p. 624, and 3.3.2.1, p. 729.
Ammi: See above, n. 10 (2.5.3). Vitex, or Agnus castus: See above, n. 27 (2.4.1).

Thesmopheries: The Thesmophoria, the ancient Greek festival of Demeter and Kore, celebrated throughout the Greek world exclusively by women. Hanea: Presumably a corruption, via ἁγνεία (‘chastity’) of ἄγνος, the Vitex agnus-castus or chaste tree, the branches of which were used in the Thesmophoria in the manner stated here.
wained: Transported, conveyed.
Mercurialis … amongst the Indians: In the Variae lectionum in medicinae scriptoribus (1576), the learned Italian physician Girolamo Mercuriale refers specifically to the Amazonian Indians.
opium Thebaicum: Or ‘Thebaic extract’ (laudanum), so named after its cultivation in Thebes by the ancient Egyptians.

Sussilite obsecro … sanguinem: In these lines from Plautus’ Curculio (151–2), the young man Phaedromus, who is infatuated with the slave-girl Planesium, sings to the door of the house of her owner, the pimp Cappadox.
Jerome so much … Nepotian: On Jerome and Paula, see above, n. 32 (1.4.1). His letter (52) to the young priest Nepotian warns of the dangers of clergy letting women into their homes.
the Canticles: The Song of Solomon.
averte oculos … saith David: Psalm 118:37 in the Latin Vulgate. intend: Fix the mind on, turn thoughts towards.
offends: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
scald: Scabby.

Myrtala in Aristaenetus … embrace him: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (2.16), Myrtala (Myrtale in Greek) tries to extinguish her passion for the young man Pamphilus, whose attention has been caught by another prostitute, Thais.
unstaid: See above, n. 132 (3.2.2). amain: See above, n. 5 (Preliminaries). blazing star: See above, n. 54 (1.2.1) and n. 36 (3.2.3).
bravely: See above, n. 47 (DJR).
Araspas in Xenophon … to see her: See above, n. 29 (3.2.2).

Scipio a young man … city in Spain: According to Livy (26.50), this occurred during the siege of Carthago Nova (now Cartagena) in 210 BCE during the Second Punic War. The woman had been betrothed to a leader of the Celtiberian tribe in Old Castile. that Grecian Charinus: Most likely an erroneous reference to Cleinias (cousin of Alcibiades), a discussion of whose beauty was composed by Xenophon in his Symposium. He has apparently been confused with the young lover Charinus from either Terence’s Girl from Andros or Plautus’ Merchant. Homer’s Nireus: See above, n. 90 (3.2.2).
Xenocrates lay with Lais … touch her: See above, n. 10 (DJR) and n. 158 (1.2.4).

Petrarch that had so magnified his Laura … accept of her: Petrarch had dealings with several popes, but the source of this tale is untraced. He says in the third book of his Secretum that his beloved Laura steadfastly refused his advances, but also, in his letter ‘To Posterity’ (Seniles 18.1), that he renounced lust after she died.

Gilbertines: The religious order, including both men and women living separately, founded in Lincolnshire (c. 1140) by Gilbert of Sempringham. The order had been defunct since the dissolution of the monasteries in England in the 1530s.
Xenophon prescribes Critobulus: See above, n. 26 (2.3.5).
Heinsius merrily inculcates … his friend Primerius: See above, n. 142 (3.2.3).
Isaeus … of Assyria: See above, n. 195 (1.2.3).
as Dido fled from Aeneas: That is, as a ghost in the underworld (Aeneid 6.472–4).
put: Send away, get rid of.

Petrarch hath such another tale … found yours: In a letter to the rhetorician Bruno di Firenze, Petrarch describes this as a ‘popular love story’ (Epistolae familiares 7.14). advice: See above, n. 53 (DJR).
convent: Monastery. The term could refer to any institution for the ‘religious’, including monks and friars as well as nuns.
pristine: Former.

So Zephyrus hated Hyacinthus … Apollo: In classical mythology, the beautiful Spartan hero Hyacinthus was accidentally killed by a discus thrown by his lover Apollo. In some versions, it was deliberately diverted by Zephyrus, the personification of the west wind, out of jealousy.
falling sickness: See above, n. 32 (1.1.1). strangury: See above, n. 15 (2.4.1). tetters: See above, n. 4 (2.3.2).

gull: See above, n. 83 (DJR). hath a wolf in his bosom: The sense of this phrase is clarified by its fuller form, given in a sermon from 1661 by the Anglican clergyman William Bell: ‘A wolf in the bosom that eats out the heart of its maintainer.’ It derives from the proverbial endurance of a Spartan boy who carried a stolen fox under his cloak, and silently let it gnaw out his bowels (Plutarch, Lycurgus 18).

Hypatia Alexandrina … liberavit: Note ‘c’ in the corresponding Latin passage refers to the Neoplatonic philosopher Hypatia of Alexandria. She had a high
reputation for her strict morality, but was killed by a crowd of Alexandrian Christians in 415 CE.

there’s as much difference of haec as his ignis: That is, ‘these flames are basically the same as those’. as Paris lost Oenone’s love by seeing Helena: In classical mythology, the first love of Paris was Oenone, a nymph from the Troad, but he spurned her after seeing Helen. Cressida forsook … Diomede: In the fifth book of Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde, the Greek warrior Diomede lures Criseyde away from Troilus. as Theseus left Ariadne … fortune: After being abandoned by Theseus, Ariadne married the god Dionysus.
Nunc primum Dorida … dowdy to this: In Petronius’ Satyricon (126), when Encolpius is introduced to ‘Circe’ – see above, n. 23 (3.2.2) – he disdains his former lover Doris.
Apologer: Fabulist.

Which those seven Persian Princes … the love of others: In Esther 1:10–2:4, the Persian queen Vashti is dismissed after refusing the summons of her husband Ahasuerus – on whom, see above, n. 17 (3.2.2). His advisers, the seven Persian and Median princes, arrange for her replacement to be found by bringing beautiful young virgins from all around the kingdom to the palace.

Pausanias in Eliacis: That is, in the description of the region of Elis by the ancient Greek traveller and geographer Pausanias (fl. c. 150 CE). one Cupid … drives out another: In the Description of Greece (6.23.5), the painting, in one of the gymnasia in the city of Elis, is actually said to have represented Eros and Anteros – see above, n. 19 (3.1.2).

Tully 3 nat. deor …. differing in office: According to Cicero (On the Nature of the Gods 3.23.60), the first Cupid is the son of Mercury and Diana; the second is the son of Mercury and Venus; the third is Anteros, the son of Mars and Venus. Cicero’s interlocutor in this part of the dialogue is Gaius Aurelius Cotta – on whom, see above, n. 69 (2.3.3).
motioned: Proposed.

Euryalus would admit … Lady of his Court: The fictional Historia de duobus amantibus (1444) of Enea Silvio Piccolomini – on which, see above, n. 16 (3.1.1) – is set in Siena, at the time when the city was home to the Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund – on whom, see above, n. 198 (1.2.3).
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
intempestive: See above, n. 313 (DJR). Nectarines: Nectar-like drinks. Homer’s Nepenthes, or Helena’s Bowl: See above, n. 95 (2.2.4) and n. 27 (2.2.6).
hardly: With difficulty.
saith Tryphaena … in Lucian: See above, n. 232 (3.2.2).
poller: See above, n. 186 (DJR). supplement: Supplier.
pocky: Pock-marked (indicating syphilis) – and, more loosely, worthless.
Hercules: See above, n. 9 (1.4.1). Holofernes: See above, n. 74 (3.2.2).
Mercury-reason: In Renaissance astrology and magic, the planetary god Mercury was associated with the power of reason. In classical antiquity, the god was also the patron of rhetorical persuasion.
as Lycinus in Lucian told Timolaus: See above, n. 286 (DJR).
for a piece of good: ‘For money’.
a most absolute form: ‘A perfect beauty’.

weed: See above, n. 111 (3.2.2). colly: Dirty with coal-dust or soot. Opopanax, Sagapenum: Both fetid gum resins used medicinally (like asafoetida), and derived, respectively, from the root of Opopanax chironium and the concrete juice of Ferula persica. all-to berayed: Utterly befouled.
rivelled: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3).
sparrow-mouthed: See above, n. 59 (3.2.3).
tires: See above, n. 63 (1.2.3)

like Aesop’s Jay: In the fable ‘The Jay and the Peacock’, a jay tries to beautify himself with peacock feathers. Cantharides: ‘Spanish fly’ – see above, n. 17 (1.2.5) – which according to Pliny the Elder (29.30) was fatally toxic when imbibed in a potion. Non redolet … solet: The second line of the epitaph reportedly inscribed on the tomb of Rosamund Clifford – on whom, see above, n. 49 (3.2.2).

Thersites: See above, n. 107 (DJR). Marcolphus: In the popular late medieval Dialogus Salomonis et Marcolfi, the Old Testament king converses with an ugly and misshapen – but strikingly intelligent – dwarf.

Seleucus … Stratonice’s bald pate: On Seleucus and Stratonice, see above, n. 5 (3.2.3). The legend of the queen’s baldness, due to illness, is recorded in Lucian’s Essays in Portraiture Defended (5), to which the detail about the king’s revulsion is a later addition.
Raimundus Lullius the Physician: See above, n. 109 (2.2.4).

Philip the French King … her father: Philip II of France (1165–1223) married Ingeborg (1174–1237), daughter of the Danish king Valdemar I, in 1193. Philip refused her the French crown, but it was eventually granted to her in 1213.
Margaret the King of Scots’ daughter … French King: See above, n. 35 (3.1.2).
by-respects: See above, n. 43 (3.1.2).
Saturni podex: A derogatory phrase for something old, numb or decayed – as Erasmus explained in his Adagia. In antiquity, the Roman god Saturn was traditionally depicted as an old man.
Veneres: See above, n. 65 (1.2.4).
a Venice glass, quickly broken: Venetian mirrors were made from plate glass that was notoriously fragile.
that fair flower Adonis … Anemone: See above, n. 56 (3.2.2).

Ariston … creature of the world: According to Pausanias (3.7.7), the woman married by Ariston, the son of the Spartan king Agasicles (sixth century BCE), had once been the ugliest in Sparta, but had been changed by Helen into the most beautiful.
as she asked her sister … well judge: In Aristaenetus’ Erotic Letters (1.11), these words are addressed by an unnamed woman to her maid.

Anacreon his Bathyllus: See above, n. 37 (3.2.1). Lumina sint Melitae … dominae: In these lines by the ancient epigrammatist Rufinus, which Burton has adapted from a collection edited by the sixteenth-century Flemish humanist Lucas Fruytier, Melita is the poet’s beloved.

Let her head be … complements and endowments: The saying recorded in Heinrich Bebel’s Proverbia Germanica (1508) has the hands (and legs) of the ideal woman coming from Cologne and the buttocks from Swabia; it makes no mention of the Spanish, Venetian and Italian elements, but does say that the ‘private parts’ (pudibunda) should come from Bavaria.

as Lucian deciphers … Panthea: See above, n. 29 (3.2.2); on ‘deciphers’ see above, n. 209 (DJR). Euphranor: Euphranor of Corinth (fl. 364–361 BCE), an ancient Greek painter and sculptor, famous for his image of the ‘Twelve Gods’ (that is, the Olympians) in Athens. as Venus gave Phaon … over the Ford: See above, n. 64 (3.2.2). distemperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR). Erinnys: One of the classical Furies, whose repulsive, gorgon-like appearance is described in the Eumenides of Aeschylus. rivels: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3). the black ox hath trodden on her toe: Figuratively, ‘been beset by adversity or misfortune’ – an English proverb, used by the character of Venus in John Lyly’s Sapho and Phao (1584), referring to an unhappy marriage. Its origins are obscure, but the black ox perhaps represents death or the devil.
lapt: See above, n. 30 (DJR). morphew: See above, n. 3 (1.4.1).
Bona-roba: A courtesan, or what John Florio more literally calls, in his Italian/English dictionary A Worlde of Wordes (1598), ‘good stuff, that is a good wholesome plum-cheeked wench’.
freckens: Freckles. neves: Marks on the skin. scabredity: Scabbiness.
gadder: One who ‘gads about’, or roves around idly. pranker: Prancer.

reaks: Pranks, tricks. Bacchos’ or Elenoras’ presence: ‘Baccho’ may be a reference to ‘Bacchis’ – the name of a prostitute in the comedies of Terence, and also of a beautiful woman in Athenaeus’ Learned Banqueters (13.594B) and Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love (9). ‘Elenora’ may be the notoriously beautiful, worldly and (in some accounts) immodest Eleanor of Aquitaine (c. 1122–1204).
naeves: Blemishes. private: See above, n. 24 (DJR).
Apologues: See above, n. 114 (DJR).

as Diogenes concludes in Nevisanus … habeat Quid: In his misogynistic Sylva nuptialis (1516), the Italian jurist Giovanni Nevizzano attributes the saying – about wives rather than women – to Diogenes, but while the ancient Greek Cynic was reportedly hostile to marriage, this is not one of his. The full adage, apparently a medieval invention, was sometimes given as ‘Nulla tam bona uxor non invenias, quod queraris’ (‘There’s no wife so good that you’d find nothing in her to complain about’).
liquorish: See above, n. 323 (DJR). Chideress: A quarrelsome woman, a scold.

When Leander was drowned … Anteros: In the mythological story of Hero and Leander, when their marriage is forbidden by Hero’s parents, Leander swims across the Hellespont (now the Dardanelles strait) from Abydos to Hero’s tower in Sestos every night, where she holds a torch to show him the way. One night the torch goes out, Leander drowns and Hero throws herself out of the tower. On Anteros, see above, n. 19 (3.1.2).
Mercurius Britannicus: See above, n. 5 (DJR).

like Passus’ picture … to be painted: (Pseudo-)Lucian’s story (In Praise of Demosthenes 24) involves the ancient Greek painter Pauson (fifth century BCE) and one of his (unidentified) patrons. passant: Walking. at that site: In that position.

a fever hectic: The type of fever which accompanies consumptive diseases, causing flushed cheeks and hot, dry skin. Libyc: The Libyan Sea (Mare Libycum), the portion of the Mediterranean separated from the Aegean by Crete.
litigious: See above, n. 215 (1.2.3).
with that Vestal virgin … dulce est: In the Controversies (6.8), the elder Seneca discusses the case of a Vestal virgin accused of unchastity because she wrote this verse.
give me my yellow hose again: The refrain of an English folk-song, in which a married man laments the lost freedom of his bachelorhood.

When those wild Irish Peers … too late: This anecdote, told by the English historian Richard Stanihurst in his De rebus in Hibernia gestis libri quatuor (1584), refers to Henry II’s lavish Christmas celebration in Dublin, following the Norman invasion of Ireland, in 1171. The event was designed to impress the Irish chieftains, commonly portrayed as barbarous in early modern English sources; many of them are reported to have submitted to his rule at the feast.

bear it out sometimes by the head and shoulders: That is, ‘sometimes repel violently’. The more usual contemporary expression is ‘bear it off by the head and shoulders’, where ‘bear off’ is a nautical language for ‘thrust away’.
In sober sadness: See above, n. 215 (DJR). like Epaminondas … two daughters: On the victories of Epaminondas mentioned in note ‘c’, see above, n. 166 (1.2.3). impinge: See above, n. 130 (1.2.3).
undiscreet: See above, n. 40 (DJR).

Uxor nomen … not of pleasure: Lucius Aelius Caesar (d. 138 CE), according to the Augustan History (5.11), said this to his wife in response to her complaint about his philandering. Note ‘g’ reproduces the erroneous name from this source, where he is referred to as Verus (who was actually his son, the emperor Lucius Verus, who ruled 161–9). snatch: Slang for sexual intercourse, especially of an
illicit kind or with a prostitute. fly out: See above, n. 81 (2.3.3). Lex Julia, which Caesar … as he would: According to Suetonius (1.52), Julius Caesar instructed one of his friends, the tribune and poet Helvius Cinna, to propose a bill making it lawful for Caesar to marry any woman he wished – and as many – in order to produce offspring. This anecdote is being confused with either or both of the Lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus (18 BCE) – which, among other things, prohibited marriage outside one’s class – and the Lex Julia de adulteriis, passed shortly afterwards, which outlawed extramarital intercourse by a respectable free woman. Irish divorcement: Divorce had been legal in Ireland for many centuries and remained so throughout the early modern era.

Pythias, Echo, Maenades: ‘Pythias’ here should be ‘Pitys’, like Echo a mythological mountain nymph constantly pursued by Pan; on the Maenads, appearing here because of Pan’s shared propensity with Dionysius for wild behaviour, see above, n. 346 (DJR).

Which the Satirist said of Iberina … one man still: In Juvenal’s Satires (6.53–4), the speaker refers to a probably fictional woman (whose name is spelled ‘Hiberina’ in modern editions) in support of his claim that there are no chaste women in Rome.

true Trojans: Colloquially, merry and dissolute people. mine host’s daughter … in Ariosto: An allusion to Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (1532): Fiammetta, the daughter of a Valencian innkeeper, is loved by both Astolfo and Giocondo but contrives to sleep with her own beloved, her father’s servant ‘il Greco’ (28.52–71). Messalina: See above, n. 24 (2.2.2).
as good husbands as Nero himself: Nero banished his first wife, Octavia, then had her murdered in 62 CE; see below, n. 62 (3.3.1). On his second wife, see above, n. 13 (3.1.2).

Xanthippe … Socrates: See above, n. 159 (DJR). Elenora to St. Lewis: Actually not King Louis IX of France, but Louis VII, whose marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine was annulled in 1152. Isabella to our Edward the second: Isabella of France (1295–1358) was notorious for her adultery and her implication in the apparent murder of her husband King Edward II of England in 1327. Mariamne to Herod: According to Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 15.213–36), Mariamme – on whom, see above, n. 62 (3.2.3) – was wrongfully executed by Herod in 29 BCE after his sister Salome had maliciously cast suspicion on her faithfulness. Serena to Diocletian: Serena, according to the spurious Acts of St Cyriacus, was the wife of the Roman emperor and persecutor of Christians Diocletian (241/4–c. 313 CE), and was later canonized as a Christian martyr. Theodora to Theophilus: The Byzantine empress Theodora (d. 867) was married to the emperor Theophilus (d. 842) and is venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church for maintaining her Christian piety in the face of her husband’s destruction of its sacred images. Thyra to Gurmunde: The Christian Thyra was married to Gorm the Old, who ruled in the tenth century as the last pagan king of the Danes.
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).

the Reed and Fern in the Emblem: In Joachim Camerarius the Younger’s Symbolorum et emblematum, ex re herbaria desumtorum centuria una collecta (1590), the title of this emblem is ‘Disparem vites’ (‘Avoid What’s Different’), and refers to the traditional belief in the mutual repugnancy of ferns and reeds. According to Pliny the Elder (18.45), ferns cut with a reed do not grow back.

If she be barren, she is not ––––––: It is not clear whether this is a self-censored obscenity, perhaps referring to a woman’s desire for intercourse, or an open invitation to the reader to complete the thought. Joseph Swetnam’s Araignment of Lewd, Idle, Froward, and Unconstant Women (1615) suggests that ‘if she be barren, thou wilt loathe her’.

O utinam aut … Suetonius: According to Suetonius (2.65), this saying was expressed by Augustus at any mention of his grandson (and adoptive son) Agrippa Postumus, his daughter Julia or his granddaughter Julia – all of whom he banished from Rome. It adapted a line from the Iliad, originally delivered by Hector to Paris.
Jacob had his Reuben … Adonijah: Old Testament filial disappointments, described in Genesis 49:3–7, 2 Samuel 13, 2 Samuel 16–18 and 1 Kings 1–2.

froward: See above, n. 48 (1.1.1). roaring like Juno in the Tragedy: Seneca’s Hercules opens with a lengthy diatribe delivered by Juno, who is angry about Jupiter’s love affairs and the successes of Hercules in his labours. See also below, n. 107 (3.4.2).

Malo Venusinam … Cornelia mater: In this quotation from Juvenal (Satires 6.167), Venusia is a small Roman provincial town, now Venosa. Modern editions prefer ‘Venustina’, which is probably the name of a prostitute. On Cornelia, see above, n. 159 (3.2.2).
Cornuto: See above, n. 145 (3.2.2).
Casimirus … deformed: The marriage of the Polish king Kazimierz III, or Casimir the Great (1310–70), to Adelaide of Hesse (c. 1324–71) lasted unhappily from 1341 to 1356.
the Tercel of a goshawk: Male hawks were called ‘tercels’ as they were reputed to be a third smaller than females.
housewife maid: Housemaid. smock: See above, n. 216 (3.2.2).
that Philosopher: Thales – see above, nn. 91, 192 (DJR) – as recorded by Diogenes Laertius (1.26).
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
no cure to serve: No duty to perform (as a servant).
Elias, Eliseus, John Baptist: Elijah, Elisha and John the Baptist are selected here probably because of their status as (virtuous) prophets.
miscarried: Suffered misfortune.

Arruntius and Haterius: The men named Arruntius and Haterius, and described by Seneca in On Benefits (6.38) as legacy hunters, cannot be identified with certainty. In the Annals (1.13), Tacitus mentions the senators Quintus Haterius (d. 26 CE) and Lucius Arruntius (d. 37 CE), who were older contemporaries of Seneca.
good personate: Well personified.

as another seconds him … undone me: The unnamed source here might be the Flemish humanist Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), who used the phrase quoted in the following sentence (‘uxor intumuit’) in a letter to Ludovicus Carrionus, discussing the domestic travails of their compatriot and fellow scholar Janus Lernutius (1545–1619).
συζυγία ob Xantipismum: Married to a harsh, nagging woman – after Xanthippe, the wife of Socrates: see above, n. 159 (DJR).
Phoroneus the lawyer: In Greek mythology, Phoroneus was a very ancient Peloponnesian king who was said to have been the first to organize families into cities (‘lawyer’ here means ‘lawgiver’).
take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR). Ligatures: See above, n. 2 (2.1.1). Characters: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1). as a wound with the spear of Achilles: See above, n. 16 (1.2.1).
magnetical medicines: See above, n. 3 (2.1.1).
Indian gymnosophist: See above, n. 91 (DJR).
Chaldeans: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2).

ex Sigillis Hermetis … sparsos: In his Antrum magico-medicum (1526) the Italian philosopher Marcantonio Zimara discusses magical seals designed to induce love, including those of Hermes (one of which has a picture of a woman), Solomon and the legendary ancient Hebrew physician Chael – sometimes identified as Bezalel, the chief artisan of the Tabernacle in Exodus 31:1–6.
Protesilaus’ tomb: See above, n. 113 (3.2.3).

Leucata Petra … Saint Maura’s: The white cliffs of the promontory of Cape Lefkatas, the southernmost tip of the Ionian island of Lefkada (or ‘Leucadia’), home to the castle of Santa Maura since the early fourteenth century. In antiquity the cliffs were the location of a sanctuary of Apollo, where in an annual ritual a criminal, with birds attached, would be thrown off the cliff. In mythology, the leap was a traditional means by which unhappy lovers released themselves from their misery.
Protela, Degonetus’ daughter: In Strabo’s account (Geography 10.2.9), actually Pterelas, the son of Deioneus, mythical king of Phocis. On Cephalus, see above, n. 20 (3.2.2).
Hic se Deucalion Pyrrhae … chased quite away: On Deucalion and Pyrrha, see above, n. 347 (DJR).

Cyzeni: The inhabitants of Cyzicus – see above, n. 21 (2.3.5). Amor Lethes … the river: ‘Amor Lethes’ here literally means ‘Love-Forgetfulness’; cf. above, n. 55 (1.1.2). the Temple of Venus Elusina: This should be the temple of Venus Erycina (‘Aphrodite from Eryx’), which was located on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, and also associated with prostitution.

Pausanias in Phocicis: That is, in his description of the Greek region of Phocis. at Naupactus in Achaia (now Lepanto): Naupactus (modern day Nafpaktos) was actually in West Locris, on the north coast of the Gulf of Corinth.

in Achaicis: In his description of the region of Achaia. the river Senelus: Actually the River Selemnus, near Patrae (now Patras). Here Burton follows the spelling given in Antoine du Verdier’s 1581 Latin translation of Vincenzo Cartari’s Immagini degli Dei degli antichi. as he holds … auro pretiosior: Burton is quoting the account of the Selemnus given by the Italian humanist Ludovico Ricchieri (Caelius Rhodiginus) in his Lectionum antiquarum libri triginta (1550), as cited in note ‘b’.
make an head: Make a stand, rally.

Et pariter torulo bini … Lavinia wed: This quotation from the De cerebri morbis (1549) by the Dutch physician Jason van der Velde (Pratensis) alludes to Lavinia, the heir to the throne of Latium in the Aeneid. Despite being betrothed to Turnus, king of the Rutuli tribe, her affections are eventually won by Aeneas, who marries her and names the city he founds ‘Lavinium’ in her honour.
look babies in one another’s eyes: Gaze at their own reflections in the other person’s eyes (and so, gaze closely and lovingly at each other).
Lady Elizabeth … daughter: Elizabeth of York (1466–1503), who married Henry Tudor in 1486.
Fortune my Foe: A popular traditional English ballad.
curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
descents: See above, n. 35 (2.3.3).
as slatters sort their slats: That is, as slaters arrange slates (when assembling a roof).
e contra: See above, n. 8 (3.1.2).

Pan loved Echo … Lyda: A mythological sequence of unrequited lovers taken from the Greek bucolic poet Moschus of Syracuse (mid-second century BCE), referring to the traditional erotic association between the god Pan and the nymph Echo, and perhaps a version of the story later reworked by Ovid into the tale of Faunus (Pan) and Omphale – see above, n. 92 (3.2.3).
as he complains … Ismariis immotior: The complainant here is Pamphilus, from the medieval pseudo-Ovidian story of Pamphilus and Galatea, which was related in the Carmen bucolium (1538) of Erasmus.

Phillida flouts me: An allusion to the traditional English ballad ‘Phillida and Corydon’. Caute, feris … Euridice: From the song of Orpheus composed by the Italian poet Celio Calcagnini in his Apologi (1544).
nice: See above, n. 125 (DJR).
boggle: Hesitate, demur.
prank up: See above, n. 112 (DJR). T. H.: Note ‘a’ refers to Thomas Hobbes, whose poem on the wonders of the Peak District, De mirabilibus Pecci (1627), is quoted here.
as Atalanta … not won: See above, n. 60 (3.2.2).
irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR).

stand in their own light: Cut themselves off from their own light (and so, figuratively, harm themselves). Stroza’s Gargiliana was … comfort too: This epigram by the Italian poet Ercole Strozzi (c. 1473–1508) is addressed to a woman, otherwise unidentified, called ‘Gargiliana’.

that generous Mare in Plutarch … an Ass: The passage in Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love (9) alluded to here draws on the ancient Greek belief that shearing the manes of mares deprives them of vigour. On ‘great horses’, see above, n. 24 (2.2.4); ‘generous’ here means ‘of a good breed’.
The Fox in the Emblem … be had: In Aesop’s fable ‘The Fox and the Grapes’, a fox fails to reach some grapes on a vine and then scorns them as undesirable.
Genius: See above, n. 173 (DJR).

embezzled: See above, n. 225 (1.2.3). Phanaretae ducet … naso: An adaptation of the exchange between the young man Clitipho and his mother Sostrata in Terence’s Self-Tormentor (1060–62), where the former protests against the match, arranged by the latter, with the ugly daughter of a neighbour (actually Phanocrates). The conversation, with Clitipho’s father joining in, continues in the passage that immediately follows.

All which Livy exemplifies … most worth: Livy actually locates this story in Ardea, a city of the Rutuli tribe in Latium and an ally of Rome. His account (4.9) explains how disagreement over the marriage escalated into a civil war, which then drew in the Romans and their Volscian enemies, thereby demonstrating the danger of the internal opposition between the nobility and the plebs.
Minion: See above, n. 331 (DJR).
feral: See above, n. 147 (DJR).
Civilians: See above, n. 230 (DJR).
the Comical old man: Megadorus, in Plautus’ Pot of Gold (479–82).
Eubulides in Aristaenetus … quickly: Unfortunately, Eubulides reports that his newly rich wife has become so insolent and demanding that he has decided to kick her out (Erotic Letters 2.12).

Acontius coming to Delos … married unto him: In the ancient myth, the oath inscribed on the apple is actually a cunning ruse by Acontius, since Cydippe inadvertently binds herself to it by reading it out. In the version of the story told by the poet Callimachus (mid-second century BCE), the encounter takes place at the festival of Artemis at Delos, which hosted a famous temple of the goddess.
Masinissa was married … otherwise of her: See above, n. 17 (1.4.1).

in the golden world … domineer: In Greek mythology, Ogyges (or Ogygus) is a primeval king, commonly said to have ruled Boeotia; his name and era became bywords for remote antiquity. Ninus, in Graeco-Roman tradition, was the founder of the Assyrian Empire and the builder of its capital city, Nineveh. The ‘golden world’ here is the golden age – on which, see above, n. 25 (3.1.3).

Leontius a Philosopher of Athens … Theodosius: The marriage of Athenais (Aelia Eudocia) to the Christian Roman emperor Theodosius II took place in 421 CE. Eudocia was later renowned for her piety, ascetic lifestyle, and poetry, as well as for her influence on the emperor, which allegedly led to the sidelining of Pulcheria (399–453).
Rodophe … married to the King: That is, Rhodopis – see above, n. 77 (3.2.2). The story of her marriage to the Egyptian king Psammetichus I (ruled 664–610) is false.

Danaus of Lacedaemon … any more ado: In his account of Sparta (3.12.2), Pausanias actually says that after the scandalous outcome of the first marriages of the daughters of Danaus – see above, n. 161 (3.2.3) – the king announced that any suitors would be free to marry the daughter whose beauty they found most pleasing, but then arranged foot-races to decide the order of their choices.

Crales a Serbian Prince … Emperor himself: This story refers to Stefan Milutin, king of Serbia (c. 1253–1321) – Burton’s source refers to ‘Crales Serviae’, where the former term is a Latinization of the Serbian term for king (Kralj). Eudocia (c. 1265–1302) was the sister of Andronikos II Palaiologos (1259–1332), and Simonida (c. 1294–1336) was his daughter.

Galeatius the second … was ended: These details, taken from Paolo Giovio’s Vitae illustrium virorum (1549), concern Galeazzo II Visconti, ruler (but not duke) of Milan 1349–78; his son, and first duke of Milan, Gian Galeazzo Visconti (1351–1402); Isabella, countess of Vertus (1348–73) and daughter of John II of France; and Galeazzo’s daughter Violante (1354–86), who married Lionel of Antwerp, the first duke of Clarence (1338–68) and the second surviving son of Edward III of England.

Collegiates: See above, n. 122 (1.2.2). States of lives in Copyholds: That is, the ‘estate of life’ (or a duration of one lifetime) in ‘copyhold’ tenure – on which, see above, n. 217 (1.2.3). Widows were customarily permitted to remain in the occupation of the holding if they did not remarry.
Tantalus a labris, &c.: The full quotation (Horace, Satires 1.1.68–9) is given in 2.2.4.1, p. 498.
cornutum sophisma: The ‘horned fallacy’ (or ‘horned question’), a dilemma in which respondents are caught out irrespective of whether they answer yes or no to a particular question.

Hieronymus Wolfius: The German humanist scholar Hieronymus Wolf (1516–80). illustrator: Interpreter, elucidator. triplicity: Or astrological ‘trigon’, a combination of three of the signs of the zodiac, with each being 120° apart. The triplicity of Venus was thought to influence a person’s marital status. the seventh house the Almutens: In astrology, the ‘houses’ were numbered from one to twelve in the direction of increasing longitude, beginning at the ‘ascendant’ – see above, n. 13 (DJR); the ‘almutens’ were planets prevailing or ruling in a horoscope. a ☉d & ☾a: ‘From the sun descending and the moon ascending’: the astrological symbols signify the future coming together of husband and wife.

deploring their misery … in Libanius: An allusion to Libanius’ Preliminary Exercises (26), which is an imaginary speech given by a eunuch who has fallen in love. with Jephthah’s daughter … virginities: Judges 11:37–8.

mastupration, satyriasis, priapismus: See above, n. 25 (1.3.2) and n. 86 (1.2.2). Bale’s Catalogue … in England: See above, n. 26 (1.3.2). that which Ulricus writes … by repentance: This dubious story about Gregory VII (pope 1073–85) is recounted in the Epistola de continentia clericorum, an anonymous late eleventh-century defence of clerical marriage that was spuriously attributed either to the Swabian Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg 923–73, or to the Italian Ulrich, bishop of Imola 1053–63. The story was used in several Protestant polemics in the sixteenth century.
Essei: The Essenes, an ancient Jewish sect famous for their celibacy and other ascetic practices. Montanists: Early Christian ascetics who followed the second-century prophet Montanus.

Anno 1419 … chose to die: The Portuguese bishop and cardinal James of Coimbra, who was born in 1433, actually died in 1459 (and Pius II was pope 1458–64). Better marry than burn: 1 Corinthians 7:9. Papinian: Aemilius Papinianus (d. 212 CE), a famously authoritative Roman jurist (and author of a work On Adultery).
Titmouse: One of the tit family of songbirds, or chickadee. election: See above, n. 62 (1.1.2). Whereas hem list, about environ: ‘Wherever it pleases them, all around’. kind: Nature.
hard stound: Hard time, time of trial or pain. pretence: Assertion of a right or claim. I wis: Truly, certainly (‘iwis’ in Middle English).
Terra Australis incognita: See above, n. 80 (DJR).
Orpheus Junior’s Golden fleece: See above, n. 52 (2.2.3).
the Isle of Maragnan: See above, n. 133 (1.2.1).

Vibius the Spaniard … imprisoned: This anecdote, taken from Plutarch’s Crassus (5), refers to the period after Lucius Cornelius Cinna had seized power in Rome in 85, which Crassus – see above, n. 103 (1.2.1) – spent in exile in Spain on the property of Vibius Paciacus.

Surenas the Parthian general: Surenas, or Suren, was the name of one of the seven great Parthian families, which held the hereditary right to military command. ‘The Suren’ may well have been the generic title of the king’s military commander, but the specific reference here is to the general who defeated the invasion of Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BCE – see above, n. 53 (2.3.3). as the Swiss Soldiers … their wives: Burton may be thinking of the German mercenaries (Landsknechte), who were commonly depicted alongside their women in sixteenth-century woodcuts, and whose camp followers typically included women (including prostitutes) and children. However, some images of the Swiss Reisläufer also included women.

Jus trium liberorum … contributions: ‘The right of three children’, a Roman legal privilege introduced with the marriage laws of the emperor Augustus – see above, n. 101 (3.2.5) – to encourage upper class families to raise children. The description given by Burton is misleading: having three children in Rome qualified parents for exemptions from the provision of public works and from acting as guardians (or, in the case of women, being subject to them). Four children were required for these exemptions for freed slaves and residents in Italy, and the figure was five for those in the provinces.
A woman shall … children: 1 Timothy 2:15.

O my sweet son … de luctu: In A Relation of a Journey (1615), the English poet George Sandys quotes Lucian’s On Mourning (13), which imagines a father lamenting the death of a son who has died before marrying and having children.
except: See above, n. 21 (DJR). as Theophilus the Emperor … he liked best: The customary bride-show took place in Constantinople in 830.
sponsi Penelopes: See above, n. 264 (1.2.3). wistly: See above, n. 17 (3.2.3).

she will bring him … horn-book: That is, turn him back into a child. A ‘horn-book’, which was used to teach small children to read, was a leaf of paper displaying the alphabet, pasted to a wooden board and covered with a plate of translucent horn. Bononian: Bolognese.

rambler: Slang for a person who goes out looking for sex. that sixth Satire of Juvenal: Notorious for its misogyny, and frequently quoted and imitated by Renaissance poets. dicteries: Witticisms. Stesichorus: See above, n. 9 (3.2.1). Martia did by Hortensius, Terentia by Tullius, Calpurnia to Plinius, Pudentilla to Apuleius: A list of rather patchy ancient pairings: Marcia, the daughter of Lucius Marcius Philippus (consul in 56 BCE), was initially the wife of Cato the Younger, who ceded her to the orator Quintus Hortensius Hortalus (114–50) on his request, and married her again in 50 after Hortensius’ death; Terentia was the first wife of Cicero, but they were divorced after their marriage broke down in 46; Calpurnia was probably the third wife of Pliny the Younger; and on Pudentilla and Apuleius, see above, n. 274 (3.2.2).

our Latin Homer: That is, Homer in Latin translation, as quoted immediately above. The lines (Odyssey 6.183–4) are probably taken from the anthology of
Stobaeus, in the translation by Conrad Gessner in the Sententiae ex thesauris Graecorum delectae (1559). as the Indian women … presently for him: A reference to the traditional Hindu practice of ‘sati’.

Admetus King of Thessaly … desired or expected: This tale from classical mythology ends happily with the return of Alcestis, after Hercules overpowers Thanatos (death) at the grave (in some versions she is saved by Persephone).
honest: Respectable or befitting.
naught: See above, n. 322 (DJR).

Pelopidas: See above, n. 88 (2.2.4). Trismegistus to his son Tatius: In the Hermetica, the son of Hermes Trismegistus is called ‘Tat’, although in the passage quoted here (2.17), Hermes is actually addressing Asclepius. Georgius Wicelius: The unconventional German priest and theologian Georg Witzel (1501–73), whose marriage to Elizabeth Kraus after his ordination cost him his vicarage in Vacha.
Metellus Numidicus: The Roman general and politician Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus, reported to have given this speech when he was censor in 102 BCE.

pathetically: Eloquently. motives: Persuasive arguments. Adjutorium simile: Note ‘a’ quotes God’s description of Eve in Genesis 2:18. Moses Curseth … Matrimony: Leviticus 20:20–21. Jacobus de Voragine: Rather than any work by Voragine – on whom, see above, n. 123 (DJR) – the source seems to be the Loci theologici (1545) by the German Lutheran theologian Urbanus Rhegius. Burton may have mixed up notes from Urbanus with some taken from Voragine’s discussions of marriage in Sermones quadragesimales (1575).
Anti-parodia: A specific type of parody that inverts the content of the original. In classical and Renaissance literary theory, a parodia is an imitation that closely resembles the original.
graft horns: See above, n. 345 (DJR). Paul commends marriage … single life: 1 Corinthians 7:1–9; Ephesians 5:22–33.

curious and nice: See above, n. 125 (DJR). Venus’ Vigil: A reference to the Pervigilium Veneris, cited in note ‘c’: an anonymous Latin poem, probably dating from the fourth century CE and sometimes attributed to Tiberianus, that presents itself as a processional song for the eve of a Venus festival in the Sicilian city of Hybla. Its opening, which announces the festival and praises spring, is quoted immediately below.
ask their Banes: Proclaim the banns (of their intended marriage), thereby inviting any objections.

Rhodanthe and Dosicles: The eponymous protagonists of the romantic novel by the Byzantine writer Theodore Prodromos (twelfth century CE). Clitophon and Leucippe: See above, n. 76 (3.2.2). Theagenes and Chariclea: See above, n. 15 (3.1.1). Poliarchus … Argenis: See above, n. 6 (3.2.3). Lysander Calista: The lovers in The Wandring Lovers (1623), a tragicomedy by John Fletcher, later revised (probably) by Philip Massinger as The Lovers’ Progress; they were also the subject of the Histoire tragi-comique de notre temps (1615) by Vital d’Audiguier, translated into English in 1627. potiturque … Iphis Ianthe: In the mythological tale told by Ovid (Metamorphoses 9.714–97), Iphis is the daughter of the Cretan Ligdus, mistakenly given a male name after her father is deceived by a prophetic dream of Isis into believing she is a boy. After lamenting her passion for Ianthe, the daughter of Telestes of Dicte, she is transformed into a boy by Isis and marries her beloved.

And Troilus … heart sweet: Note ‘d’ is misleading, as these lines are from the conclusion of the third book of Troilus and Criseyde. By the end of the story, Criseyde has abandoned Troilus for Diomede, and the narrator describes the death of Troilus in battle.
passed the pikes: Run the gauntlet, passed through dangers.
Epithalamium: See above, n. 115 (2.2.4).
Hymen O Hymenaee … Hymenaee: In this quotation from Catullus (62), the wedding song employs variants of the name of Hymen – see above, n. 235 (3.2.2).

Turtles: See above, n. 116 (1.2.4). hap: See above, n. 117 (3.2.3). Ravens’ years: The longevity of ravens was an ancient poetic commonplace that derived from antiquity (for example in Horace, Odes 3.17.13). According to a riddle of Hesiod reported by Plutarch (The Obsolescence of Oracles 11), the raven’s life could span 108 human generations (11,664 years).

Let the Muses sing … comfort increase: This continues the quotation from Erasmus’ Epithalamium (1524), cited in note ‘f’, and which was written in 1514 to celebrate the marriage of his friend Pieter Gillis (Petrus Aegidius) to Cornelia Sandrien.
entreat or make diminution: This should be ‘increase or make diminution’ (that is, ‘amplify or shorten’). The error is present in many early modern editions of Chaucer’s works. rather: Earlier.
Equivocations: See above, n. 47 (1.1.1).
obnoxious: See above, n. 9 (1.1.3).
latitude: See above, n. 18 (2.4.1). prerogative: Pre-eminence, superiority.
bastard branch: An unwanted shoot or sucker growing (typically) from the base of a tree.
foreigner: See above, n. 72 (2.4.1).
As the old man in the Comedy … adopted son: The elderly Athenian Micio, concerned for Aeschinus, in the opening lines from Terence’s Brothers.
Aegeus was so solicitous … foiled: See above, n. 108 (1.2.4).
emulators: See above, n. 224 (DJR).
Hadrian the Emperor … emulators: The Augustan History describes how Hadrian persecuted his friends and supporters after raising them to honours, and compelled several of them to commit suicide.
Saul envied David: 1 Samuel 18:1–16. Domitian Agricola … fame: See above, n. 61 (1.2.3)

Juno turned Proetus’ daughters … for beauty: See above, n. 40 (1.1.1). Cyparissae King Eteocles’ children … Memories: This tale, deriving from the Geoponika (11.4.2), may refer to the Boeotian king Eteocles of Orchomenus – rather than the Theban king: see above, n. 156 (1.2.4) – although his daughters were more commonly identified as the three Graces: see above, n. 25 (3.1.2).

Niobe, Arachne, and Marsyas can testify as much: Punishments for hubris (presumption or insolence towards the gods) in classical mythology: on Niobe, see above, n. 140 (DJR); Arachne was turned into a spider after failing to defeat Athena (Minerva) in a weaving contest; on Marsyas, see above, n. 185 (DJR).
Phalaris, Dionysius, Periander: Three ancient Greek tyrants – see above, n. 18 (1.1.1), n. 72 (1.2.3) and n. 223 (DJR).
turn … out of the hinges of: See above, n. 4 (1.2.3).

Selimus killed Corcutus … diverse others: Selim I – on whom, see above, n. 254 (DJR) – is said to have eliminated his brothers Korkut and Ahmed when he ascended the throne. Koca Mustafa Pasha, Grand Vizier under Selim’s predecessor Bayezid II, was also executed in 1512. On the term ‘Bassa’, see above, n. 162 (DJR).
Bajazet the second … caused him to be slain: See above, n. 162 (DJR).
Suleyman the magnificent … Son Mustapha: The Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I (1494–1566) had his son Sehzade Mustafa killed in 1553, when the latter had been implicated in a plot to assassinate his father.
Valens the Emperor … his Empire: Valens was emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire from 364 to 378 CE, and was succeeded by Theodosius I, who then ruled until 395.

Jo. Basilius, that Muscovian tyrant: Ivan IV Vasilyevich, or ‘Ivan the Terrible’ (1530–84), grand prince of Moscow, and Tsar of Russia from 1547 until his death. He was rumoured to have murdered his eldest son and heir, Ivan Ivanovich.

Antoninus and Geta … well-wishers: Antoninus Caracalla (188–217 CE) and Geta (189–211) were the sons of the emperor Septimius Severus (145–211) and Julia Domna – on whom, see above, n. 50 (3.2.1). After a series of conflicts while they were co-emperors, Caracalla is reported to have murdered Geta in the arms of their mother during a feigned reconciliation ceremony, and then to have ordered the slaughter of 20,000 of his brother’s friends and supporters.
Maximinus … bore to him: On Maximinus Thrax and his predecessor Severus Alexander, see above, nn. 11, 36 (2.3.2), and n. 35 (2.2.1).

When Alexander in his fury … of another: A reference to Alexander’s regret for his drunken murder of his friend, the military commander (and provincial satrap) Cleitus ‘the Black’, for insulting the king at a feast in 328 BCE.

Henry the third of France … own chamber: An important event in the French Wars of Religion (1562–98), when the leader of the Catholic League, Henry I, duke of Guise (1550–88), was assassinated by the bodyguard of Henry III (1551–89) at the Château de Blois, in the presence of the king.
Lewis the eleventh … of him: On Louis XI, see above, n. 24 (1.3.1).
watchet: Light blue. oillet holes: Or ‘eyelets’ – spy-holes usually placed in walls, but also small holes worked into the cloth of garments.
R. T. notis … jealousy: Note ‘f’ refers to a saying reported in the side notes of Robert Tofte’s Blazon of Jealousie (1615). cracked: Flawed, unsound.

our fortunate Prince: In the first two editions of the Anatomy, this was James I (the quotation following this comment is from a 1603 panegyric by the English poet Samuel Daniel). But by the time of the third edition (1628), Charles I was on the throne. The passage would have had an ironic flavour for the first readers of the posthumously issued edition of 1651, when England was a republic under the rule of the ‘Rump Parliament’.
communion: That is, sharing (a beloved).
Stephanus Bathorius … Poland: István Báthory, ruler of Transylvania (1571–6) and king of Poland (1576–86).
eke: Also. bode: Omen, premonition.

those old Egyptians … a Camel: In his Hieroglyphica (1556), the Italian scholar Pierio Valeriano does not refer this symbolic meaning to the Egyptians. The traditional symbolism perhaps derives from Aristotle’s History of Animals (6.18), where male camels are said to be aggressive if a human approaches them at the time of mating.
a strange tale to that purpose: In which a crocodile attacks a sailor who has killed its mate.

Another story of the jealousy of dogs … animalium: In which the goddess Hera (Juno), herself no stranger to jealousy – see above, n. 186 (3.2.2) – takes a dog on to her lap and strokes it, provoking her own dogs to bark and then attack it. The origin of this story is obscure.
bite off one another’s noses: That is, reply curtly or angrily to each other.

Lacerat lacertum … those parts: When the politician and orator Lucius Licinius Crassus (consul in 95 BCE) put the popular politician Gaius Memmius on trial for extortion in the late second century BCE, he argued that the walls of the city of Terracina (in southern Latium) were inscribed with the letters ‘L.L.L.M.M.’ Cicero says (On the Orator 2.49.240–41) that Crassus invented his explanation of the
graffito, which may have been an electoral notice, as a reference to the quarrel between Memmius and Largus over a woman. fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).

Constantine in the eleventh book … broke her neck: ‘Pineus’ here should be Pan, identified in the Geoponika (11.10) as the rival of the wind-god Boreas for the love of the nymph Pitys (Pinus in Latin), who is pushed off a cliff by the latter and turned into a stone pine.
Sir Geoffrey Chaucer … tale: In ‘The Knight’s Tale’; see above, n. 103 (3.2.3).
Giovanni de la Casa … styles him: The sonnet about jealousy quoted by Varchi (and his translator Robert Tofte) is Della Casa’s ‘Cura che di timor ti nutri e cresci’. See above, n. 39 (3.2.1).
naught: See above, n. 322 (DJR).
the significators to their several promissors: See above, n. 116 (1.2.1).

when he was Ambassador … not with us: On Bodin’s visit to England, see above, n. 34 (2.2.4). The Spanish ambassador was Bernardino de Mendoza (d. 1604), who was expelled from England in 1584 for his involvement in the Throckmorton Plot against Elizabeth I. The ‘Master of Requests’ (a leading officer of the English Court of Requests, which dealt with petitions for relief to the monarch) was the civil lawyer and diplomat Valentine Dale (c. 1520–89).
Licinius the Emperor: See above, n. 130 (DJR).
diverb: See above, n. 103 (2.2.4).

Trebius the Lawyer: An invented character whose name probably suggests erudition and authority by alluding to the famous Roman jurist Gaius Trebatius Testa (c. 84 BCE–c. 4 CE); but it also echoes an impoverished client from Juvenal’s fifth satire.
corse: See above, n. 78 (1.2.1).
she did not complain … her goodman: One of the sisters of Psyche, jealous of the latter’s marriage to Cupid. ‘Goodman’ here means ‘husband’.
fly out: See above, n. 81 (2.3.3).

Signior Deliro on his Fallace: See above, n. 346 (DJR). effeminate: Compassionate, tender. the Tibareni: A group of ancient tribes from northeast Anatolia. The mythical account of their customary practices at childbirth related here derives from Apollonius of Rhodes (Argonautica 2.1010–11), where it is stated that they are neighbours of the Amazons.

fondlings: ‘Fonds’, or fools – but also, those who are fondly loved or fondled. the Comical Poet: The ancient Athenian playwright Philemon (fl. c. 300 BCE), in the comedy The Tail of the Garment. lay out: Spend money.
minx: A lewd woman, mistress, or prostitute.
as Apollo set a Raven … Coronis: See above, n. 64 (3.2.3).
Lucretia: See above, n. 48 (1.2.3). Clytemnestra made Agamemnon cuckold: See above, n. 119 (DJR).
Abstemius: The fitting Latin name of the Italian writer Lorenzo Astemio, author of the collection of Latin fables entitled Hecatomythium (1495).

genis gratus … Apollo in Apuleius: A reference to the parody of incompetent rhetoric in the Florida (3.9) of Apuleius, where Marsyas tries to present these qualities as faults in his contest with Apollo – see above, n. 185 (DJR).

Mutius opinor & Trebatius hoc negassent: The anecdote in note ‘c’, from the Dutch poet and scholar Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), alludes to the Roman lawyers Trebatius Testa and Quintus Mucius Scaevola (consul in 95 BCE). fuzzled: Intoxicated. Hippocrates Cous: ‘Hippocrates of Cos’. went current: ‘Was accepted’. goodfellow: See above, n. 68 (2.2.6). those Criticisms … Festus or Pollux: That is, philological restorations or amendments to obscure or corrupt parts of the lexical works of Sextus Pompeius Festus and Julius Pollux, both from the second century CE.
yellow: Jealous.
cornute: Make into a cuckold.
Abraham was jealous … she was fair: Genesis 12:11–13.
Saxola his friend: The Florentine humanist Sassuolo da Prato (Saxolus Pratensis, c. 1416–69).
snout-fair: Fair-faced.
well-given: See above, n. 20 (1.3.2).

Nero … a base quean: According to Tacitus (Annals 13.12), Nero left his first wife Octavia because of his passion for Acte, a freedwoman from Asia Minor who had formerly been an imperial slave; see above, n. 105 (3.2.5). in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).

Cerinthus rejected Sulpicia … servant-maid: Sulpicia was the granddaughter of Servius Sulpicius Rufus (consul in 51 BCE) and the author of six poems in the Corpus Tibullianum expressing her love for a man with the pseudonym ‘Cerinthus’. In one of these (3.16), she complains about his infidelity with a ‘whore or country-girl loaded with a wool-basket’.

to hunt by stealth … their own: In the hunting metaphors here, a ‘walk’ is a haunt, or the usual place in which an animal is found, and the ‘course’ is the pursuit; ‘at game’ means ‘engaged’ (in an entertainment or pastime).
Nessus the Centaur … shot him to death: See above, n. 9 (1.4.1).

Neptune saw by chance … him cuckold: An allusion to Lucian’s Dialogues of the Sea-Gods (13), where the river-god Enipeus is angry with Poseidon (Neptune) for disguising himself as Enipeus and having intercourse with his beloved, the mortal princess Tyro.
Tarquin heard Collatine … he went: See above, n. 48 (1.2.3).

Theseus stole Ariadne … an husband: Plutarch’s Life of Theseus relates several mythological tales about the hero’s abductions of women, including Anaxo, a girl from his birthplace Troezen, and Helen of Troy, and also the story that he married and had a son (Hippolytus) with the Amazon queen Antiope (according to Pindar, however, he had also abducted her).

he was a counterfeit Amphitryon … shower: In classical mythology, Zeus (Jupiter) assumes the form of Amphitryon in order to have sex with the latter’s wife Alcmene, who subsequently becomes the mother of Heracles (Hercules). For his other transformations, see above, n. 11 (3.2.1).

which Suetonius … one ring: The full saying, that ‘the names and portraits of all the good emperors could all be engraved on a single ring’, actually comes from the Augustan History (The Deified Aurelian 42), where it is attributed to a jester from the time of the emperor Claudius.

Caesar: See below, n. 72 (3.3.1). Mahomet the Turk, that sacked Constantinople: Mehmed II – on whom, see above, n. 129 (DJR) – took Constantinople in 1453, and was reported by the Byzantine historian Laonikos Chalkokondyles to have had an affair with the prince of Wallachia, Radu III the Fair (1437/9–75). Ladislaus … besieged Florence: Ladislaus the Magnanimous (1377–1414) was rumoured to have been killed after the siege by a Florentine doctor, who delivered his beautiful daughter to the king along with a handkerchief laced with poison. doers: Slang for ‘philanderers’.

Urbani servate … adducimus: According to Suetonius (The Deified Julius 51), this was the first line of a couplet shouted by the soldiers of Julius Caesar during his Gallic triumph in 46 BCE. The second line was ‘Aurum in Gallia effutuisti, hic sumpsisti mutuum’ (‘You fucked away in Gaul the gold you borrowed here {in Rome}’). Curio: Gaius Scribonius Curio (d. 53 BCE), censor in 61 and an opponent of Caesar’s (like some, but by no means all, of the husbands of the women named).
Inter alios honores … jungendi: See above, n. 101 (3.2.5).
private History: That is, the history of someone’s personal life.
Philippus bonus: See above, n. 201 (DJR).
Laurence Medices: See above, n. 98 (2.2.4).
Castruccius Castrucanus: See above, n. 59 (2.2.6).

like Milo’s wife: See above, n. 243 (3.2.2). Martial’s Sota … Clitum marito: In Epigrams 4.9, it is actually Labulla, the daughter of the physician Sotas, who leaves her husband (all are fictional characters).
Fastidious Brisk: See above, n. 79 (1.2.4). lock: See above, n. 142 (3.2.3). cringe: See above, n. 121 (DJR).
bravely: See above, n. 47 (DJR). rammy: See above, n. 5 (2.2.1). dizzard: See above, n. 96 (DJR).
Senae: Siena.
pranks up: See above, n. 112 (DJR).
another Socrates … transcendere metas: Socrates here is a personification of practical wisdom and self-restraint.
yoke-fellow: Partner, spouse.

precise: See above, n. 125 (DJR). as he follows it … some goodfellow: That is, the Italian humanist Bartolomeo Sacchi, known as ‘Il Platina’ (1421–81), whose Dialogus contra amores, ad Ludovicum Stellam Mantuanum is quoted here.

Augusta Livia, non nisi … tollebat: That is, only had sex when pregnant. According to Macrobius (Saturnalia 2.5.9) this was actually said by Julia, the daughter of Augustus (rather than his wife Livia), in response to people who had said that given her infidelities, her children looked surprisingly similar to her husband Agrippa.
e contra: See above, n. 8 (3.1.2).
amphibological: Ambiguous, equivocating.
Noah … soberness: Genesis 9:20–21.

Lot lay with his daughters … drink: Genesis 19:30–38. as Cinyras with Myrrha: In Ovid’s version of the story of Myrrha and Cinyras – see above, n. 50 (3.2.1) – the latter is drunk with wine when Myrrha first enters his bedroom (Metamorphoses 10.438).
intended or remitted: See above, n. 35 (1.1.1).
gloats: See above, n. 107 (3.2.2). maundering: Muttering, grumbling.

Et miser in tunica … that thou dost wear: The quotation here of the English poet Robert Tofte’s translation of Propertius omits some of the sense of the Latin quotation, the last two lines of which read: ‘I’m wounded if your mother gives you lots of kisses,/Or your sister, and also when you sleep with a girlfriend.’
false key: Skeleton key, or picklock.

Argus did not so keep his Cow: See above, n. 186 (3.2.2). that watchful dragon the golden fleece: The Colchian Dragon, the serpent which guarded the Golden Fleece in the sacred grove of Ares in Colchis. Cerberus the coming in of Hell: See above, n. 254 (1.2.3).
calls … all to naught: Attacks verbally, denounces passionately.
like Juno in the Tragedy: See above, n. 112 (3.2.5).
Joanna Queen of Spain: Joanna of Castile (1479–1555), also known as ‘Joanna the Mad’ because of her melancholy, was the wife of Philip I of Castile, also known as ‘Philip the Handsome’ (1478–1506).
naught: See above, n. 322 (DJR).

as Henry the second’s importune Juno … at Woodstock: The jealous ‘Juno’ here is Eleanor of Aquitaine, who married Henry of Anjou (later Henry II of England) in 1152, and was reputed to have poisoned his mistress, Rosamund Clifford – see above, n. 49 (3.2.2) and n. 65 (3.2.5).

Agrippina by Lollia … Claudius: These jealousies of Julia Agrippina, or Agrippina the Younger (15–59 CE), the niece and fourth wife of the emperor Claudius, are reported by Tacitus (Annals 12.22). Lollia Paulina, who had previously been married to Publius Memmius (consul in 31 CE) and the emperor Caligula, had once been suggested as a possible match for Claudius, and was viewed as a rival by Agrippina. Lollia was banished and eventually killed in 49. Calpurnia was a noblewoman driven into exile by Agrippina after Claudius praised her beauty, but she returned to Rome after Agrippina died.
Alcoran: See above, n. 123 (DJR). entreat: See above, n. 2 (1.2.4).
the Sophies … Tartarian Moguls: See above, n. 64 (2.2.6) and n. 72 (1.2.2). In the Renaissance, ‘Tartary’ referred to several different regions of Asia.
Shereefs of Barbary: See above, n. 17 (3.2.2).
Quiloa in Africk: An Islamic sultanate (now the island of Kilwa Kisiwani, off southern Tanzania), which was briefly ruled by the Portuguese in the early sixteenth century.
those old Jews … nocte videant: Deuteronomy 22:17. Zacynthus, or Zante: See above, n. 252 (3.2.2).

those Vestal virgins … Senators: The Vestal Virgin who legendarily carried water with a sieve to prove her chastity was actually called Tuccia; the episode is usually dated to c. 230 BCE, but in any case the year given here, 47 CE, is incorrect. In the Renaissance, the sieve became a symbol of chastity. Aemilia, virgo innocens: A Vestal Virgin (second century BCE) famous for her miraculous rekindling of the sacred fire of Vesta, after another Virgin she had entrusted to keep it alight on her behalf had let it die out. Emma, Edward the Confessor’s mother … spectator: According to some reports, Emma of Normandy (d. 1052) – who became queen of England through her marriages to Æthelred II and King Cnut (Canute) – had an affair with Ælfwine, bishop of Winchester, but cleared her name by successfully walking over nine red-hot ploughshares placed in Winchester Cathedral.

Chunegunda the wife of Henricus Bavarus Emperor: St Cunegund of Luxembourg (c. 978–1033), wife of the Holy Roman Emperor Henry II (formerly the duke of Bavaria). coulters: See above, n. 102 (3.2.3). Charles the third … hot irons: When the Holy Roman Emperor Charles the Fat (839–88) accused his wife Richardis of adultery, she successfully endured trial by fire.

Pausanias saith … burning coals: This should be a reference to Strabo (Geography 12.7), who is describing reports about the priestesses at the temple of Perasian Artemis in Castabala (in the region of Cilicia).

Feronia’s Temple … Memnon’s statue: Feronia was an ancient Italian goddess associated with the forces of nature, whose main temple was in the grove of Capena in Etruria; in her annual sacrificial rites, cult followers walked barefoot across hot coals. The colossi of Memnon were two statues of the Pharaoh Amenophis III (ruled 1392–1355 BCE), on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes. Vocal sounds were said to have emanated from one of the statues every day at sunrise, which were interpreted as greetings to the dawn and sometimes given oracular significance (but an association with chastity is not attested in ancient sources).
old St. Wilfred’s needle in Yorkshire: The ability to pass through this narrow passage in the crypt of Ripon Cathedral was regarded as a proof of chastity.

as Phaerus that blind king of Egypt: The Latin translation of Herodotus (2.111) by the Italian humanist scholar Lorenzo Valla (1407–57) gives his name as ‘Pheron’, which probably mistakes the title ‘Pharaoh’ for a personal name, and identifies him as the son of Sesostris (the Greek name of three Egyptian rulers of the Twelfth Dynasty). The anecdote is told in more detail below in 3.3.3.1, p. 953, note ‘f’.
those wild Irish … pleasures: See above, n. 101 (3.2.5).

Phaerus of Egypt: See above, n. 21 (3.3.2). Cephalus and Procris: In classical mythology, Procris suspected her husband Cephalus of infidelity, and was killed while following him on a hunt when he mistook her for a wild beast. Tereus, Atreus, and Thyestes: Also in classical mythology, Procne punished her husband Tereus for the rape of her sister Philomela by tricking him into eating the flesh of his son Itys, and Atreus took revenge on his brother Thyestes for seducing his wife Aerope by killing Thyestes’ sons and serving their flesh to him unawares at a banquet. These events caused a series of marital and familial murders among their descendants, including that of Agamemnon – see above, n. 119 (DJR).

Alexander Pheraeus: The Thessalian tyrant Alexander of Pherae, who ruled from 369 to 358 BCE. Antoninus Verus … Lucilla: The Roman emperor Lucius Aurelius Verus was married to Lucilla, the daughter of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, in 164 CE; the Augustan History (10) reports two different rumours of her involvement in his murder. Demetrius the son of Antigonus, and Nicanor: Probably Demetrius the Fair (third century BCE), who was the half-brother and father, respectively, of the Macedonian kings Antigonus II Gonatas and Antigonus III Doson, and who was assassinated at the instigation of his wife Berenice because of his affair with her mother Apama. Burton may be confusing him with the Seleucid king Demetrius II Nicator (d. 125 CE), whose wife allegedly had a hand in his death, although the text could also be referring separately to both Demetriuses.

Hercules poisoned by Deianira: See above, n. 9 (1.4.1). Caecina murdered by Vespasian: According to Aurelius Victor, the Roman general Aulus Caecina Alienus – on whom, see above, n. 62 (1.2.3) – was killed by the emperor Titus in 79 CE on suspicion of infidelity with the emperor’s wife, the Jewish queen Julia Berenice (who was actually his mistress).
