Justina a Roman Lady: From an anecdote related in more detail below in 3.3.4.2, p. 972, which derives from the report of an epitaph inscribed on the floor of the Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament in St Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican.
Amestris, Xerxes’ wife … her daughter: In this tale from Herodotus (9.108–12), the Persian king Xerxes I (ruled 486–465 BCE) was having an affair with his niece Artaynte (Masistes was his brother).
Chilpericus the first: See above, n. 32 (3.2.1).

wand: Walking stick, or (in slang) penis. The double entendre is present in Burton’s source, the De rebus gestis Francorum (1516) of the Italian historian Paolo Emilio, which uses the Latin term virga.

Jerome Osorius … bloodshed: The protagonists in the story told by the Portuguese historian Jerónimo Osório in his De rebus Emmanuelis Regis Lusitaniae … libri duodecim (1571) are Fernão Caldeira – a page of Afonso de Albuquerque (c. 1453–1515), the duke of Goa – and Guterre de Monroy (c. 1479–c. 1550), the Portuguese captain of Goa.
kell: A long cloak or garment; alternatively, a caul – see above, n. 32 (1.1.1).

Jonuses Bassa and fair Manto his wife: The Ottoman administrator, governor and general Yunus Pasha (d. 1517) is said to have killed his Greek wife Manto in a fit of jealousy. that of Joanna of Spain: See above, n. 7 (3.3.2).
fits of the Mother: See above, n. 18 (1.2.5).

Switzers … Walloons: Like the Swiss, the Walloons (from the southeastern provinces of the Low Countries) were famous for their mercenaries, to the extent that their name could be used to refer to mercenaries of any kind.
Qui timet … salvus erit: In this quotation from Ovid (Remedies for Love 545–6), Machaon was one of the sons of Aesculapius and a famous physician and surgeon in his own right.
macerates: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

Celia in her Epistles: The Lettere amorose di Madonna Celia gentildonna Romana, scritte al suo amante (1562), sometimes attributed to the Italian poet, playwright and musician Girolamo Parabosco (c. 1524–57).

Argentocoxus, a British prince: Argentocoxus was a Caledonian chieftain during the reign of the emperor Septimius Severus; his wife’s exchange with the empress Julia Domna, said to have occurred in 210 CE, is recorded by Dio Cassius (77.16.5). naught: See above, n. 322 (DJR).
Actaeon’s badge: Actaeon, who became ‘horned’ when turned into a stag by Artemis (Diana) – see above, n. 320 (DJR) – was figuratively associated with cuckoldry.

Agamemnon … Antoninus: For Agamemnon, see above, n. 119 (DJR). Menelaus was the famously long-suffering husband of Helen of Troy. In some accounts, Philip of Macedon sought to divorce Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, on the grounds of her infidelity. Ptolemy here is most likely Ptolemy XIII Dionysius, the brother-husband of Cleopatra VII, mistress of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. Clodia, the wife of Lucius Licinius Lucullus – on whom, see above, n. 48 (1.2.2) – was rumoured to have had incestuous relations with her brother Publius Clodius. Caesar divorced his second wife, Pompeia, when rumours of Clodius’ interest in her became public, on the grounds that ‘Caesar’s wife must be above suspicion’. Pompey the Great’s third wife, Mucia Tertia, was widely believed to have been one of Caesar’s many conquests – see above, n. 72 (3.3.1). Cato the Younger – see above, n. 51 (1.1.1) – divorced his wife Atilia because of her unseemliness. The future emperor Augustus later justified his hurried divorce from his second wife, Scribonia, on the grounds of her immorality. Mark Antony turned against his wife Antonia when she was suspected of a liaison with his dissolute friend, the tribune Publius Cornelius Dolabella. And Faustina, the wife of the emperor Marcus Aurelius (‘Antoninus’), was accused in the Augustan History of multiple infidelities; see above, n. 92 (3.2.2). Bulls’ feathers: Horns (and so marks of cuckoldry).

the nine worthies: See above, n. 165 (1.2.3). was unworthily served by Mordred: In the version told by Geoffrey of Monmouth in the Historia regum Britanniae (c. 1136). Guithera or Helena Alba his fair wife: Guinevere. The English antiquary John Leland (c. 1503–52) referred to her as ‘Guenhera’, thereby etymologically associating her name with ‘Helena’ and ‘alba Leonora’ – where ‘alba’ (‘white’) refers to her ‘fair’ beauty. arrant honest: Of wayward virtue (or, as Burton’s source here says, of ‘doubtful chastity’).

fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR). a knave Gallus to watch: Probably an allusion to the cuckold Gallus in Martial’s Epigrams (2.56), although a similar reference to Catullus (78) is also possible. In ancient Rome, the ‘Galli’ were the voluntarily castrated priests of Cybele. that Roman Sulpicia … videat: These lines by a Roman poetess named Sulpicia (fl. late first century CE), who was a contemporary of Martial and happily married to a man called Calenus, were preserved in Probus’ scholia to Juvenal (6.537).
Town Bull: See above, n. 58 (3.2.1).
quit: Repay, or avenge.
diverb: See above, n. 103 (2.2.4).

base Irus, poor Seius, or mean Maevius: Three ancient proverbial figures: on Irus see above, n. 61 (2.3.3); Gnaeus Seius owned a horse said to have brought misfortune to him and all its subsequent possessors (which included Mark Antony, who had Seius proscribed); Maevius was a wretched poet, one of the unsuccessful rivals of Virgil and Horace. like Hercules he hath any two fathers: That is, having been raised by Amphitryon but with Zeus (Jupiter) as his biological father – see above, n. 69 (3.3.1).
fondly: See above, n. 103 (DJR).
St. Francis … charity left: In Thomas More’s Dialogue concerning heresies (1529), St Francis witnesses an unspecified young man kissing a girl.
Mr.: ‘Master’ (rather than ‘Mister’).

Lucretia to Collatinus: See above, n. 48 (1.2.3). Laodamia to Protesilaus: See above, n. 113 (3.2.3). credit: See above, n. 36 (1.2.4). Phocion’s wife in Plutarch: The second wife of Phocion – on whom, see above, n. 72 (1.2.3) – was famous in Athens for her sobriety and simplicity, according to Plutarch (Phocion 19).
goodman: See above, n. 46 (3.3.1).
as Octavia writ to her Antony: See above, n. 25 (1.2.4).

In the time of Valens the Emperor: See above, n. 18 (3.3.1). one Archidamus … accept of it: In Augustine’s account (The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount 1.50), this takes place in the reign of Constantine I (306–37 CE), the governor of Antioch is identified as (Septimius) Acindynus, and it is actually an unnamed rich man who offers the gold. After she sleeps with him, however, he swindles her out of the money, and the governor expresses remorse for placing the woman in this predicament by imprisoning her husband.
When one commended Theano’s fine arm … husband: Theano was the wife of the philosopher Pythagoras. This anecdote comes from Plutarch’s Advice for a Bride and Groom (31).

Bilia had an old man … strong as his: Bilia was married to the Roman military commander Gaius Duilius, a hero in the First Punic War after guiding the Roman fleet to victory at the Battle of Mylae in 260 BCE.

Tigranes and Armena … for her sake: In this anecdote from Xenophon’s Cyropaedia (3.1.41), Tigranes, the king of Armenia, addresses his wife simply as ‘Armenian {princess}’ – which was rendered as ‘Armenia’ in the Renaissance Latin translation by Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481).
meuses: Gaps in fences or hedges providing a means of escape.

patient Grizels: ‘Patient Griselda’, the wife in Chaucer’s ‘Clerk’s Tale’, is based on the character Griselda whose great patience and obedience in the face of provocative testing by her husband is narrated in the last chapter of Boccaccio’s Decameron (which, as note ‘b’ records, had been translated into Latin by Petrarch).

Nova Francia: ‘New France’, the area in North America colonized by the French in the sixteenth century, stretching along the St Lawrence River and including the provinces of Quebec and Acadia. as Leah, Rachel … Jacob: See above, n. 258 (1.2.3). In Genesis 12:15–20, Sarah becomes the concubine of Pharaoh. Livia seconded … Augustus: Suetonius reports that Augustus’ wife Livia supplied him with virgins to deflower in his old age (The Deified Augustus 71). Stratonice wife to King Deiotarus … her own: Plutarch explains that since Stratonice was unable to have children, she did this to provide Deiotarus, king of the Galatians (d. c. 40 BCE), with a successor (Bravery of Women 21).

Tertius Aemilius’ wife, Cornelia’s mother: Aemilia Tertia (or Aemilia Paulla, d. c. 162 BCE), actually the wife of Scipio Africanus the Elder – on whom, see above, n. 147 (DJR) – rather than Scipio Aemilianus; on her daughter Cornelia, see above,
n. 159 (3.2.2). According to Valerius Maximus (6.7.1), Aemilia turned a blind eye to her husband’s affair with a slave-girl to avoid his accusing her of a lack of self-restraint.
pickthank: Sycophantic, telltale.
take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR).
when that Macedonian Philip … a jest of it: See above, n. 7 (3.3.4).

Eumenes King of Pergamus … heard or done: This story, taken from Plutarch’s On Brotherly Love (18), refers to Eumenes II of Pergamum and Perseus of Macedon – on whom, see above, n. 80 (2.3.3) and n. 100 (1.2.4) respectively. Attalus succeeded Eumenes as Attalus II Philadelphus and reigned 159–138 BCE.
borne a man: Removed a piece in a game of backgammon (‘tables’).
as Arnoldus Tillius … his wife: The famous story of Martin Guerre had been circulating in English sources since the beginning of the seventeenth century; the trial took place in 1560.

much better be Cornelius Tacitus, than Publius Cornutus: Latin wordplay with the names of two ancient Roman historians (‘Cornutus’ is listed in the tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia now known as the Suda as an inferior contemporary of Livy): better to be ‘Horned and Silent’ than to be ‘Public Cuckold’.
wittol: See above, n. 176 (DJR).

be an ass, as he is an ox: That is, ‘be a fool, as he is a cuckold’ (oxen being both horned and castrated). as Gabba the Roman … his wife: Plutarch (Dialogue on Love 16) tells how Gabba, one of the court jesters of the emperor Augustus, allowed Maecenas – on whom, see above, n. 111 (DJR) – to fondle his wife at the dinner table by pretending to be asleep. But when one of Gabba’s slaves tried to sneak some wine away, he suddenly awoke, saying, ‘Don’t you know that I’m only asleep for Maecenas?’ – a literary allusion to the poet Lucilius which Burton has himself echoed a few lines earlier. Plutarch also relates the story, set in Argos, of Phayllus smuggling his beautiful wife past the soldiers of his rival Nicostratus so that she could sleep with Philip V of Macedon – on whom, see above, n. 168 (1.2.3). molest: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

which Henry … comfort himself: This was actually the advice of Louis XII of France, according to the second part of Thomas Danett’s 1600 translation of the Mémoires of the French diplomat and historian Philippe de Commines (1447–1511). the Pope’s curse: Excommunication.

Lethe in Trophonius’ den: The ‘water of forgetfulness’, drunk by those who consulted the oracle in the cave of Trophonius – on which, see above, n. 28 (1.3.1) – before having a draught of ‘the water of memory’, according to Pausanias (9.39.8).
R. T.: On the attribution in note ‘c’, see above, n. 30 (3.2.3).

The Nicholaites … Nicholas the Deacon: Early Christian heretics of the second century CE. Mentioned in Revelation 2:6 and 2:15 as advocates of a return to paganism, they may have been a Gnostic sect. Later, patristic authors identified the founder of Nicolaism as Nicholas of Antioch (from Acts 6:5), and the term was applied to married priests by those who believed in clerical celibacy. those Anabaptists in Munster … moved them: See above, n. 141 (DJR). Alcoran: See above, n. 123 (DJR).

one Picardus a Frenchman … as Adam did: The Picards were an early fifteenth-century religious sect present in Bohemia and Flanders, once thought to have been founded by Picard of Flanders. They revived the practices of the Adamites, an early Christian North African sect, but were suppressed by Jan Žižka – on whom, see above, n. 81 (DJR).

Mambrinum: Probably Luserna San Giovanni, at the eastern end of the Val Pellice in northwestern Italy. as I read … Malcolm’s time: Possibly a reference to the reforms to marriage and other social customs implemented under Malcolm III (ruled 1058–93) at the instigation of his queen, Margaret of Scotland.
Ut Agetas Aristoni … prostituit: Note ‘e’ refers to the story that Ariston – on whom, see above, n. 162 (3.2.3) – obtained the wife of his friend Agetus by trickery.
Calicut: See above, n. 47 (2.4.1). Biarmi: Brahmins.
those Essei and Montanists: See above, n. 182 (3.2.5).
constuprated: See above, n. 121 (1.2.4). satisfaction: Reparation.
Hieron king of Syracuse: See above, n. 327 (DJR). Ptolemy … wife: See above, n. 175 (DJR).
Eugubine: Gubbio, in the central Italian province of Perugia.

Combabus: In ancient mythology, the founder of the temple of the goddess Atargatis in Hierapolis (southwestern Anatolia). The story related here is said to have been the origin of the practice of self-castration among the eunuchs in the temple; on Seleucus and Stratonice see above, n. 5 (3.2.3).

as that Bellerophon … Proetus her husband: In classical mythology, while the hero Bellerophon was staying at the court of King Proetus of Argos, the latter’s wife Stheneboea (or Antea) slandered Bellerophon after he rejected her love. admiration: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).

Pseudo-Catholics: A pejorative term for Roman Catholics, used by Protestants to denigrate their supposed claim to comprise the authentically ‘Catholic’ (that is, universal) body of true Christian believers. punks and pleasant sinners: Both terms for prostitutes. Colleges: Here, slang for ‘brothels’.
Of Cato’s mind: Cato the Elder – see above, n. 6 (Preliminaries).
stout: Magnificent, splendid. cautelous: See above, n. 244 (3.2.2).
Night-crows: Night owls, sometimes thought to be evil omens.
him in Petronius … Achillea: Encolpius, in the Satyricon (129).

Alecto … ululat: A quotation from the ninth book of the De republica Anglorum instauranda libri decem (1579) by Thomas Chaloner. It refers to Alecto, one of the three Furies, associated with anger and the castigation of moral transgressions; on Hymen, see above, n. 235 (3.2.2).
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR).

though Tiberius deny it: According to Suetonius (5.23), Tiberius added a clause to the marriage law enacted by the Lex Papia Poppaea that prevented men over sixty from having children. Jurists, however, regarded it as the final part of the earlier legislative programme enacted by Augustus – on which, see above, n. 101 (3.2.5). Acherontic: Infernal, gloomy; cf. above, n. 10 (2.1.1).

our Lady’s match they call it: According to an early Christian tradition, Joseph was much older than the Virgin Mary. cras erit mulier … as he said in Tully: According to Quintilian (6.3.75–6), Cicero himself said this when he was reproached as a sixty-year-old for marrying his young trustee Publilia, in 46 BCE.

Cato the Roman: See above, n. 146 (1.2.4). Critobulus in Xenophon: In Xenophon’s Symposium (4.12–16), Critobulus expresses his love for Cleinias, the young cousin of Alcibiades. Tiraquellus of late: The French judge and professor of law André Tiraqueau (c. 1480–1558) married Marie Cailler, the young daughter of a legal officer from Fontenay, in 1512; he also published an influential treatise on marriage law, the De legibus connubialibus, in the following year. Julius Scaliger: In 1529 the forty-five-year-old Italian humanist scholar and physician married the sixteen-year-old Andiette de Roques-Lobejac. e contra: See above, n. 8 (3.1.2).
Charon’s match between Cascus and Casca: That is, a hell-bound match of (literally) ‘Old Man’ with ‘Old Woman’.

old Vetustina … to boot: Vetustina is an aged prostitute (probably a fictional character: her name derives from vetustus, Latin for ‘old’), insulted in this quotation from Martial’s Epigrams (3.93.2–5). emmet’s crest: See above, n. 106 (DJR).
Apuleius gives out of his Meroe: Meroe is an ugly witch who, in the tale told by Aristomenes in the first book of the Metamorphoses, seduces the character of Socrates.

Francis Sforza … naked first: The story told by Arnisaeus (De doctrina politica 1.3) actually refers to the duke of Milan, Galeazzo Maria Sforza (1444–76), who was the son of Francesco I Sforza. Galeazzo was contracted to marry Susanna Gonzaga (1447–81), the daughter of Ludovico Gonzaga, marquess of Mantua; but when Susanna developed a deformity of the spine that compromised her ability to bear healthy children, the contract was annulled, and a new one was put in place that arranged for her sister Dorotea to marry Galeazzo instead. On ‘curious’ in this passage see above, n. 125 (DJR). Lycurgus: See above, n. 243 (DJR).
fair-snout: See above, n. 60 (3.3.1).

Cassandra’s Temple … deformed maids: This alters the description given in Burton’s source, Niccolò Leoniceno’s Varia historia (1531). The temple of Cassandra, according to the third-century BCE Greek poet Lycophron (Alexandra 1126–40), was built by the Daunian people of Apulia as a sanctuary for girls who wanted to refuse marriage to men who had hair fashionably styled like Hector (what would now be called a ‘mullet’) but were deformed or of low birth.
as the bragging soldier … nimis: Pyrgopolynices, in Plautus’ Braggart Soldier (68).
blowze: A fat, red-faced prostitute.

buys a horse in Smithfield … Paul’s: Smithfield cattle market in London was proverbially associated with exchanges in which sellers took advantage of buyers in so-called ‘Smithfield bargains’ (a term later applied to marriages of convenience). The area around St Paul’s Cathedral in London was a notorious haunt of criminals and vagabonds.

Cat to her kind: A version of the traditional proverb, ‘Cat will after kind’ – that is, live up to its nature. The saying was frequently used to refer to sexual activity, due to its proximity to the expression ‘doing the deed of kind’ (having sexual intercourse).

Creden’ Pasiphae … Tauripetam: A quotation from Thomas Chaloner’s De republica Anglorum instauranda (1579), where the example of Pasiphae is used to warn against marrying a woman brought up in a sexually immoral household because she is likely to be adulterous. On Pasiphae, see above, n. 35 (3.2.1).
good cheap: See above, n. 26 (2.3.5). curtain-sermons: Reprimands given by wives to husbands in bed.

fly out: See above, n. 81 (2.3.3). Turdus malum sibi cacat: The thrush was once thought to defecate bird-lime, an adhesive used for trapping birds, from its diet of mistletoe berries. Candaules did … naked: In the story told by Herodotus (1.8–13), the Lydian king Candaules wanted to prove his wife’s beauty to Gyges – on whom, see above, n. 180 (DJR) – so he allowed him to see her naked. When the wife confronted Gyges with the choice of suicide or murdering Candaules, Gyges chose the latter and took the throne.
Phidias: See above, n. 77 (2.2.4). Elis: See above, n. 46 (3.2.5).
to be baptized, married, and buried: A proverbial saying that circulated in Italy and Portugal.
cample: Quarrel.
Fair water: See above, n. 7 (2.2.2).
froward: See above, n. 48 (1.1.1).

Apollonides Cous … buried alive for it: According to the Greek historian Ctesias (late fifth century BCE), the physician Apollonides of Cos fell in love with Amytis – actually the sister of Artaxerxes I (ruled 464–424/3 BCE) and the widow of Megabyzus, who had been a commander under Xerxes I (ruled 486–465 BCE) – while treating her for a minor illness. When Amytis told her mother
Amestris – on whom, see above, n. 4 (3.3.3) – about the affair, Apollonides was imprisoned and then, on the day that Amytis died, buried alive.
Cornuto: See above, n. 145 (3.2.2).
The like measure … Lacedaemonians: Agis II ruled Sparta 427–400 BCE; on Alcibiades see above, n. 72 (1.2.3).
Viriplaca Dea: Literally, ‘the placater of man’, a surname given to Juno as the restorer of harmony in marriage. indifferent: Impartial.

hostile or dominant aspect: See above, n. 14 (1.1.1). antiscions: Signs of the zodiac on opposite sides of the celestial equator (and thereby mutually harmonious). Characteristical: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1). Raguel: In Judaic tradition, the archangel of justice and vengeance. natural magicians: Magicians who manipulate the ‘occult’ (secret) forces of nature.

that law of Constantine … divorce: Legislation passed by the Roman emperor Constantine I in 331 CE imposed heavy penalties (especially financial ones) upon those who divorced unilaterally without what was stipulated as a serious cause; but it preserved the long-standing right to sue for divorce when a woman had committed adultery, poisoning or pandering, or when a man had committed murder, poisoning or tomb robbing. The penalties and restrictions were modified by Theodosius II and Valentinian III in the mid-fifth century, but the right to sue for divorce was preserved. In early modern England, divorce was impossible, although a marriage could be legally annulled on various grounds (for example, if it had never been consummated).
Empiric: See above, n. 76 (DJR). I am not willing to publish it … ear: Presumably because of its obscenity or hazardousness.
precisely given: See above, n. 125 (DJR).

Plato in Convivio … two distinct furies: The distinction between two kinds of μανία (‘madness’, usually rendered as furor in Renaissance Latin), the first arising from human disease and the second being a ‘divinely inspired release from customary behaviour’, is made in the Phaedrus (265A). Burton is probably misremembering the division of two ‘loves’ – see above, n. 36 (3.1.1). Neoterics: See above, n. 62 (DJR).

Apollo’s Priests … right wits: The temple of Apollo at Delphi and the sanctuary of Zeus in Dodona (in Epirus), the locations of two of the most famous oracles in ancient Greece. The ability to prophesy is explained by Plato as a form of divinely inspired ‘fury’ or madness.

Pythonissas: Seeresses; cf. above, n. 35 (1.2.1). Sibyls: See above, n. 18 (1.3.1). Enthusiasts: See above, n. 17 (1.1.3) and 3.4.1.2–3 below. stupend: See above, n. 138 (DJR). latitude: See above, n. 18 (2.4.1).
Euripes: See above, n. 46 (1.2.3) and n. 2 (2.2.3). Halcyonian seas: See above, n. 85 (1.2.3).
vindicate: Lay claim.
principalities, powers: See above, n. 46 (1.2.1).
admirable: See above, n. 50 (1.1.2).
plausible: See above, n. 116 (3.2.2).
spike: See above, n. 11 (2.5.3). calamus: See above, n. 10 (2.5.3).
gold of Ophir: See above, n. 29 (2.2.3).
no tongue can tell … Paul saith: 1 Corinthians 2:9 (paraphrased).
a strong object overcometh the sight: By its emission of correspondingly powerful visual ‘species’: see above, n. 34 (1.1.2).
we shall hereafter … he is: 1 John 3:2.
No man … the other: Matthew 6:24.
Cant.: ‘Canticles’ – see above, n. 6 (3.1.1).
by-respects: See above, n. 43 (3.1.2).
Atheism: The category of ‘atheism’ in this period was flexible and expansive, and often included general impiety and irreligious behaviour as well as disbelief in the existence of God.
supererogate: See above, n. 124 (DJR).
the Law: See above, n. 7 (1.1.1). those Evangelical Counsels: Or the Roman Catholic ‘counsels of perfection’ – poverty, chastity and obedience.
Ethnics: Pagans.
curious: See above, n. 125 (DJR). Idiots: See above, n. 83 (1.2.4).
secure: Sinfully complacent. in a reprobate sense: See above, n. 131 (1.2.4).
as shall be showed in the Symptoms: See 3.4.1.3 below.

Lictor: An attendant of a magistrate in ancient Rome, who had the power to inflict corporal or capital punishment upon offenders. Sergeant: An enforcement officer of a court, or of another person in authority (and so the English equivalent of a Roman lictor). aut lita … primitive Church: An allusion to the edict passed in 250 CE by the Roman emperor Decius, compelling all Roman citizens (except Jews) to make sacrifices to the official Roman gods, which triggered the persecution of many Christians.

as a good Christian prince … tutus est: Pope Pius II addressing Mehmed II – on whom, see above, n. 129 (DJR); the letter is quoted in several Renaissance sources, for example the Epistolarum Laconicarum atque selectarum farragines duae (1554) by Gilbert Cousin. as Phalaris writ to Alcander: See above, n. 216 (1.2.3). ‘Alcander’ (literally, ‘Strong Man’) was the name of various historical and mythical individuals, but may refer here to the tyrant who came to power in Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily after the fall of Phalaris in the mid-sixth century BCE.
Si Deus … nos: Romans 8:31.
horn of … salvation: That is, the mighty means or power of salvation (commonly said of God or Christ).

as Paul saith … wretched: 1 Corinthians 15:19. as Lucian that Antiochian Priest … Religion himself: The Latin translation of Eusebius’ Ecclesiastical History (9.6) by Rufinus quotes an oration, said to have been given in Nicomedia in 312 CE by the early Christian martyr Lucian of Antioch, in defence of his faith and before his execution by the Roman emperor Maximinus II (who ruled 305–13).
in respect: See above, n. 94 (DJR).
compinged: Compressed, confined.
Cimmerian darkness: The Cimmerians were ancient nomads from the area around Crimea, and in mythology were said to have lived in perpetual darkness near the land of the dead.
Magellanica: See above, n. 8 (2.2.3).

China, great Cham … Japan: A list of powerful East Asian kingdoms: on ‘Cham’, see above, n. 111 (1.2.4); ‘Pegu’ was a kingdom in what is now southern Myanmar (Burma); ‘Deccan’ refers to the Muslim sultanates in the region of the Deccan Plateau, stretching across southern India; ‘Narsinga’ is the empire of Vijayanagara in southern India, called Bisnegar or Narsinga by the Portuguese. Gentiles: See above, n. 38 (1.2.1). Manamotapa: See above, n. 48 (2.2.3). Terra Australis incognita: See above, n. 80 (DJR).
Sus: One of the four traditional kingdoms of Morocco (alongside Marrakesh, Fez and Tafilalet).
the great Mogul: See above, n. 72 (1.2.2). the Sophy of Persia: See above, n. 64 (2.2.6).

those at odds … as Leo Afer reports: Divisions which eventually led to the Sunni–Shia schism. The ‘four Doctors’ here are the first four caliphs, described by Samuel Purchas as ‘the four great Doctors of the Mahumetan law’ in Purchas his pilgrimage (1613), who ruled in the period 632–61 CE: Abu Bakr (c. 573–634), Umar ibn al-Khattab (c. 583–644), Uthman ibn Affan (576–656) and Ali ibn Abi Talib (601–61).
Presbyter John in Africk: See above, n. 7 (2.2.3).

Thomas Didymus: Thomas the Apostle (often also known as Didymus, ‘the Twin’, or as ‘Doubting Thomas’) was sometimes said to have proselytized in India, and was thereby associated with the origins of the kingdom of Prester John (Ethiopia being confused with India in this tradition).

Nestorians: Followers of the Syrian patriarch Nestorius (386–450 CE), and subsequently associated with the ‘Church of the East’, who believed that the human and divine natures of Christ were separate. Jacobins: Or Jacobites, a sixth-century sect that followed Jacob Baradaeus of Edessa, who held the ‘monophysite’ view that Christ had a single divine nature. Wallachia: A region in Romania, between the Danube and the southern Carpathians. Illyricum: Illyria, a region in the western Balkans, bordering the eastern shore of the Adriatic. Slavonia: A region in eastern Croatia. Rascia: Raška, a major administrative district in southwestern Serbia (now often considered the forerunner of the modern state of Serbia).
Hispania nova: See above, n. 247 (DJR). Castella Aurea: Panama, then named literally ‘Golden Castle’ after the gold found there by the Spanish. Peru: See above, n. 247 (DJR).

Zeilan: See above, n. 48 (2.2.3). Ormus: Probably Ormoc, the port city in the Philippines which Magellan was said to have visited in 1521, rather than the island of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. land-leaping: See above, n. 237 (1.2.3). Melinda: Malindi (formerly Melinde), on the eastern coast of Kenya. Quiloa: See above, n. 14 (3.3.2).

Samosetans: Followers of Paul of Samosata (bishop of Antioch, 260–68 CE), who espoused the heretical ‘Monarchian’ belief that God is one person, not three. Socinians: Followers of the Italian theologian Fausto Sozzini (Socinus, 1539–1604), who held a number of heretical beliefs associated with the rationalist theology of early Unitarianism, and rejected orthodox teachings about the Trinity, the divinity of Christ and salvation. Photinians: Followers of the heretic Photinus (d. 376 CE), bishop of Sirmium (now in Serbia), who rejected the incarnation of Christ. Arians: Followers of Arius – on whom, see above, n. 149 (1.2.4). Anabaptists: See above, n. 141 (DJR).

what Tacitus … Religion: Of the Jews (Histories 5.13), where the phrase ‘religionibus adversa’, rendered by Burton as ‘contrary to Religion’, is more accurately translated as ‘hostile to religious rites’ or ‘propitiatory rites’ (that is, the traditional Roman ones).
Pilapians: The Finns.
defecate: Spiritually purified.

Brownists, Barrowists: English followers of the religious separatists and Congregationalists Robert Browne (c. 1550–1633) and Henry Barrow (c. 1550–93) respectively. Familists: Members of the ‘Family of Love’, a clandestine religious sect, founded by the German mystic Hendrik Niclaes (1502–80), which (like Anabaptism and Socinianism) also had a foothold in England.
paradoxes: See above, n. 3 (DJR).
We are taught … may devour: 1 Peter 5:8.

Indies: Here, the Asian or East Indies. Apollo Alexicacus, Apollo λοίμιος: The epithets ‘Alexicacus’ and ‘Loimius’ refer to Apollo’s power to avert evils, and to spread or deliver from plague. The latter was given to Apollo at Lindus in Rhodes, but Burton is presumably thinking of the great ‘plague of Athens’ – on which, see above, n. 45 (2.5.1). Spectrums: See above, n. 15 (DJR).

Adonided: Or Tammuz, the Mesopotamian deity of food and vegetation, often associated (as in Ezekiel 8:14) with the Greek god Adonis. Adramelech: According to 2 Kings 17:31, the cult of the ancient Mesopotamian sun-god Adramelech was brought into Samaria by the Sepharvites (the ‘Capernaites’ are the inhabitants of Capernaum in Galilee). Asiniae: Ashima, a Semitic goddess of fate secretly worshipped, according to 2 Kings 17:30, by the Samaritans in the city of Hamath. Astartes … Dagon with the Philistines: See above, n. 67 (1.2.1). Tartary with the Hevaei: Actually Tartak, a god (according to 2 Kings 17:31) worshipped by the Canaanite tribe of the Avvites (‘Hevaei’ in the Latin Vulgate) and thought to have taken the form of a donkey. Melchonis: Or Moloch, on whom, see above, n. 86 (1.2.1). Beli: Possibly a corruption of ‘Belit’, the female form of Bel, on whom, see above, n. 67 (1.2.1); but Burton may be thinking of Bel Marduk, the patron deity of Babylon. Beelzebub: Described as the god of the Philistine city of Ekron in 2 Kings 1:2–3. Baal: A variation of ‘Bel’ used by the Canaanites, referring to their chief deity. Apis: An ancient Egyptian god worshipped as a bull and venerated as a protector of the dead. Isis and Osiris: See above, n. 67 (1.2.1). Apollo Pythius: See above, n. 35 (1.2.1) and n. 66 (1.2.4). Jupiter in Crete … Pallas at Athens: These classical deities were associated with these locations as their birthplaces, or places where they were venerated as patrons. Juno was sometimes identified with Astarte, the patron goddess of Carthage; the Romans conducted a ritual appeal (evocatio) for her to leave the city before they destroyed it in 146 BCE.
witty: See above, n. 49 (DJR).
the Lady of Lauretta: See above, n. 87 (DJR).
the battle of Cannae: See above, n. 130 (DJR).

Oeneus reigned in Aetolia … Meleager: In Homer’s Iliad (9.528–99), when Oeneus, the king of the city of Calydon, angers Artemis by refusing her the traditional sacrifice, she sends the Calydonian boar, which is eventually killed by his son Meleager – on whom, see above, n. 90 (3.2.2). A war then breaks out between Calydon and the nearby city of Pleuron over the boar trophies.

Mithridates King of Pontus … army: Mithridates VI – on whom, see above, n. 78 (1.2.2) – unsuccessfully besieged the Mysian town of Cyzicus – on which, see above, n. 21 (2.3.5) – in 73 BCE. Aristagoras, in Plutarch’s tale, is the town-clerk.

Trophonius’ Den … Lebadea: See above, n. 28 (1.3.1). Jupiter Ammon in Egypt: The god Ammon (Amun) was the chief divinity of ancient Egypt and so was naturally identified by the Greeks and Romans with Zeus or Jupiter. There was an oracle of Ammon at the Siwa oasis (ancient Ammonium) in the Libyan desert. Amphiaraus: A seer who was descended from Melampus – on whom, see above, n. 9 (2.4.1) – and venerated at a sanctuary near Oropus, on the border of Boeotia and Attica.

Juno’s Image, and that of Fortune spake: See above, nn. 29, 35 (1.2.1). Castor and Pollux … Hannibal’s army: Cicero (On the Gods 2.2.6) records the Roman legend that the Dioscuri – on whom, see above, n. 54 (1.2.1) – had caused their victory over the Latin League (not the Carthaginians) at the Battle of Lake Regillus in 499 or 496 BCE.
pseudo-catholics: See above, n. 51 (3.3.4). Sichem … St. Thomas’ Shrine: See above, nn. 87, 121 (DJR).

St. Sabine … Ariulphus Duke of Spoleto: Ariulf (d. 602), the Lombard ruler of Spoleto in central Italy, was said by the Lombard monk and historian Paul the Deacon (c. 720–99) to have attributed his victory over the Byzantines at Camerino in 592 to assistance from St Sabinus of Spoleto, the martyred third-century bishop of Assisi. St. George … the Castilians: At the Battle of Aljubarrota (1385), in which John I of Portugal (1357–1433) defeated John I of Castile (1358–90). St. James for the Spaniards in America: St James ‘Matamoros’ (‘Moor-slayer’), originally portrayed as presiding over the Spanish conquest of the Moors, was later described as the patron saint of the conquistadores.

Bannockburn … St. Philanus’ arm: The relic of St Fillan (Fáelán Amlabar or ‘Fillan the Mute’, 641/2–724), was said to have assisted the Scots at Bannockburn (1314). cap-case: See above, n. 125 (1.2.3). another time … St. Magnus fought for them: On the day of the Battle of Bannockburn, according to the Renaissance Scottish historian Hector Boece, St Magnus (Magnus Erlendsson, earl of Orkney, 1075/6–c. 1116) was said to have appeared as a knight in shining armour, riding through Aberdeen and announcing a Scottish victory.

the Legend, out of purgatory: See above, n. 9 (1.2.3), but the reference to purgatory here may refer more generally to revelations from souls who have come out of purgatory – as mentioned in 1.2.1.2, p. 194.
Scaevola: See above, n. 55 (3.3.1). diverb: See above, n. 103 (2.2.4).

Zaleucus praefat legis … Deos: Note ‘a’ refers to a legal code said to have been written by Zaleucus, a legendary lawgiver (seventh or sixth century BCE) from Locri in Italy, whose introduction is recorded by Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 12.20) and quoted here.
Politicians: See above, n. 201 (DJR). ingeminate: See above, n. 4 (2.2.2).

Captain Machiavel … obedience: Machiavelli is here identified as the ‘Captain’ (the leading authority) on this subject because of his remarks on the political function and manipulation of religion in the Discorsi sopra la prima deca ti Tito Livio (1531) and Il Principe (1532).
this error of his: That is, of Machiavelli. This passage was not adjusted when the preceding sentence quoting Cardano was added in the fourth edition (1632).

Zalmoxis’ stratagem amongst the Thracians: According to Herodotus (4.95), Zalmoxis was a former slave of Pythagoras who became wealthy and preached his beliefs about immortality to the Getae, a Thracian tribe living on the lower Danube, who then worshipped him. Numa’s plot … Aegeria: See above, n. 23 (DJR). Sertorius with an Hart: According to Plutarch, Sertorius – on whom, see above, n. 31 (2.2.1) – ruled the populace in Spain with the help of a white deer which he claimed communicated with the goddess Diana (Sertorius 11).
So Mahomet … were made: An allusion to the first revelation of Muhammad (610 CE) from the archangel Jibril (Gabriel in English), after which he began to write the Qur’an.
that Syrian Pherecydes: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2).

Aeacus, Minos, and Rhadamanthus: In Greek mythology, the three judges of the dead in the underworld, originally mortal kings renowned for their just rule. Stygian lakes, fiery Phlegethons, Pluto’s kingdom: See above, n. 34 (1.2.2), n. 37 (2.2.3) and n. 117 (DJR) respectively.
Cocytus: The ‘river of wailing’ – another of the rivers of the Greek underworld.

The Turks in their Alcoran: See above, n. 123 (DJR). John Baptista Alfaqui: The Moorish Valencian convert to Christianity and former faqih – see above, n. 234 (DJR) – Johannes Andreas, who became a Catholic priest in 1487.
Nunquir and Nequir: Actually Munkar (‘the Denied’) and Nakir (‘the Denier’).
Senex de montibus: The Old Man of the Mountains was the title of the leader of the medieval Islamic sect of the Assassins (or ‘Hashashin’), the Nizari Ismailis.

Carnificinam exercent … one saith: Lactantius, in the Epitome of the Divine Institutes (54), referring to the persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire by pagans ‘who consider themselves pious and just’.

Chaldeans: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2). Brachmanni … Ethiopia: See above, n. 91 (DJR). the Turditans in Spain: The Turdetani, an ancient tribe that inhabited the valley of the Guadalquivir River in southern Spain, noted for their advanced civilization by Greek and Roman commentators. Amphiaraus: See above, n. 57 (3.4.1).

that high Priest of Rome: The title of pontifex maximus, which was held by the chief priest of the ancient (pagan) Romans, was also used by the popes.
bull-bellowing Pope: A satirical reference to papal edicts (‘bulls’). that three-headed Cerberus: A reference to the triregnum, the papal tiara, which comprises three crowns.

those Praetorian soldiers, his Janissary Jesuits: Disparaging remarks about the militaristic character of the Jesuits asserting their resemblance to the ancient Roman Praetorian Guard, which had the reputation for sternly enforcing state power, and the Janissaries, which were the branch of the Turkish infantry that formed the guard of the Sultans. dissociable: Segregative, divisive. dromedaries and asses: Like ‘ass’, ‘dromedary’ could mean ‘stupid person’ as well as ‘beast of burden’.

they hold there is no God … Julius 2nd: According to Protestant polemicists, these popes either held heterodox and atheistic beliefs or were generally impious and worldly: Leo X – see above, n. 57 (1.1.2) – who was alleged by John Bale in the Acta Romanorum pontificum (1558) to have described the Gospel as fable that had been very profitable ‘for us’ (the Medici) and ‘our circle’; Gregory VII (Hildebrand of Sovana, reigned 1073–85), who had been accused by his opponents of necromancy and atheism; Alexander VI (Rodrigo Borgia, reigned 1492–1503), whose corruption had been fiercely denounced by Savonarola, and whose multiple mistresses and illegitimate children were the subject of scandal; and Julius II (Giuliano della Rovere, reigned 1503–13), who had been widely criticized for corruption, and famously denounced in the satirical Julius Exclusus (1514), often attributed to Erasmus but probably written by the English humanist Richard Pace (d. 1536). Lucianists: Followers of Lucian (and so, atheistical scoffers).
gullish: See above, n. 83 (DJR).
Seeking their own … Christ’s: Note ‘d’ paraphrases Philippians 2:21.

Peter’s patrimony … Bishop: In early Christianity, the ‘Patrimony of St Peter’ comprised the property and possessions of the Church of St Peter in Rome, and belonged to the pope as the bishop of Rome. Canonists: Professors of canon law.
The Laity suspect … mortmain: In note ‘g’, statutes of mortmain regulate the terms of the ownership of property held inalienably by an ecclesiastical (or other) corporation.

Three Princes Electors in Germany Bishops: The electoral college that appointed the Holy Roman Emperor comprised seven prince-electors, three of which were archbishops (of Cologne, Mainz and Trier). Magdeburg, Speyer … Bamberg: All German prince-bishoprics, which had bishops (prince-bishops) as their civil rulers.
Walsingham in England: Walsingham, in the county of Norfolk, was a famous site of medieval pilgrimage and home of the shrine of Our Lady of Walsingham, until the latter was destroyed in 1538.
Delos: See above, n. 19 (2.3.5).

magnanimous: See above, n. 58 (1.1.1). combustion: See above, n. 340 (DJR). Demetrius … pull him in pieces: According to Acts 19:24–35, the silversmith Demetrius started a movement to resist Paul’s preaching because of its impact on those craftsmen who, like him, made silver shrines of Artemis (Diana) to sell to pilgrims attending her great temple in Ephesus.

Peter’s keys: According to Catholic tradition, the keys of St Peter (or the ‘Keys of Heaven’), which were given by Jesus to Peter, granted the divine authority of ‘binding and loosing’ on earth and in heaven – see above, n. 105 (2.2.3) – to the Church of Rome.

’Tis a wonder, saith Machiavel … endure: After the murder of the archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Becket, in 1170, Henry II (1133–89) eventually performed public penance at the door of the cathedral and submitted to various demands made by Pope Alexander III (ruled 1159–81). In his Istorie fiorentine (1.4) Machiavelli is concerned with the papal requirements that the king should affirm
his innocence to his own barons, send and accompany an army to Jerusalem, grant his subjects the right to appeal to Rome, and annul any laws deemed unfavourable to the Church.

Henry the fourth … Canossus: In the struggle between ecclesiastical and civil power known as the ‘Investiture Controversy’, the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV (1050–1106) was excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII in 1076. In the following year, with his wife Bertha of Savoy (1051–87), Henry performed barefoot penance lasting three days in the snow, in front of the castle of Canossa (in Reggio Emilia, northern Italy) to remove the punishment.

Frederick the Emperor … Alexander the third: The Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa (1122–90) kissed the feet of Pope Alexander III in a rite of reconciliation in 1177. In some accounts, Alexander proceeded to bring his other foot down on to the emperor’s neck to humiliate him.

Another held Adrian’s stirrup: Reportedly Frederick I, who was compelled to hold the stirrup of Pope Adrian IV in Rome in 1155. King John … the Pope’s Legate: King John of England submitted to Pandulf Verraccio, papal legate and bishop of Norwich, at Ewell (near Dover) in 1213.
animate: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3).
circumvent: See above, n. 336 (DJR).

Pelagians, Manichees: Two forms of heresy that had been frequently denounced by Christian theologians. Pelagianism, a movement traced to the British-born Christian theologian Pelagius (c. 354–c. 425), emphasized the freedom of the human will to such an extent, according to its detractors, that unacceptable limits were placed on the power of divine grace and the sacraments. On Manicheanism, see above, n. 188 (1.2.3). just: See above, n. 26 (DJR).

Lucian’s Alexander: The prophet Alexander of Abonoteichus (second century CE), portrayed as a fraud in Lucian’s Alexander the False Prophet. Simon Magus: See above, n. 62 (1.2.1). Simoni deo sancto, &c.: According to the early Christian apologist Justin Martyr, this was inscribed on a statue of Simon on Tiber Island. However, a statue discovered there in 1574, bearing the inscription ‘Semoni Sanco Deo’, indicates that it was actually dedicated to the obscure ancient Sabine god Semo Sancus. Apollonius Tyanaeus: See above, n. 55 (DJR). Cynops: See above, n. 62 (1.2.1). Eumo: correctly ‘Eunus’ – a Syrian who, according to Florus’ account (2.7) of the First Servile War in Sicily (135–132 BCE), incited his fellow slaves to revolt by faking a frenzy inspired by the goddess Atargatis (Syria Dea). Eudo de stellis: See above, n. 104 (1.2.1).

John Beheim … come from heaven: A summary of the story of Hans Böhm (or Böheim, d. 1476), an illiterate Franconian herdsman who was also a piper or drummer (and sometimes called ‘the Drummer of Niklashausen’). He turned anticlerical preacher after claiming to have had visions of the Virgin Mary and sparked a peasant revolt in the village of Niklashausen, near Würzburg.
Ignes fatui: See above, n. 54 (1.2.1).
Limbus Patrum: See above, n. 38 (2.2.3).
coast: See above, n. 291 (DJR).

as he in Euripides … sive aliud quid: A slightly distorted Latin version, found in several Renaissance works, of a fragment from a lost tragedy of Euripides, preserved in Plutarch’s Dialogue on Love (13).

Now for those idolaters … a Christian: The following passages refer to the imperial succession from the late third to the mid-fourth century CE, during which time Christianity became established as the state religion of the Roman Empire. The emperors Maxentius and Licinius were rivals to Constantine I – see above, n. 22 (1.4.1) and n. 130 (DJR) – and were eventually defeated by him.

Qui Christum negant … ter decies: According to the Italian cardinal and ecclesiastical historian Cesare Baronio in the third volume of his Annales ecclesiastici
(1592), these were among the chants made by the people in response to a speech by the Roman emperor Constantine I in 324 CE. Constantius: The Roman emperor Constantius II (317–61 CE). Jovinianus: This should be ‘Jovianus’: the Roman emperor Jovian (331–64 CE), who ruled after Julian the Apostate.
Publicans: Tax-collectors (and figuratively, impious heathens).

God and the Emperor: There may be a more specific source for this allusion, but the idea that submission was due simultaneously to God and the Roman emperor, which sometimes cited 1 Peter 2:13–17, was influentially formulated by the early Christian bishop and historian Eusebius (d. c. 359), and was frequently reiterated in the Byzantine Empire.
collapsed: Those that have ‘lapsed’ from the faith (or, alternatively, just ‘ruined’).
Marcus and Valentinius: See above, n. 273 (3.2.2).

Friar Cornelius of Dort: The Dutch Franciscan Cornelis Brouwer of Dordrecht (1521–81), a famous preacher in Bruges and a vehement critic of Calvinism. Rumours that he had stripped and beaten women as part of their penance originated in an anonymous anti-Catholic satire of 1569.
bayards: Blindly reckless people; see also above, n. 4 (2.4.2).
collogue: See above, n. 31 (DJR). soothe up: See above, n. 116 (1.2.2).
never hobby so dared a Lark: In hunting, a hobby (a small kind of falcon) used to be flown at larks and other small birds to ‘dare’ (daze or fascinate) them so that they could be captured.
swell: See above, n. 108 (DJR).
fondly: See above, n. 103 (DJR).

Donatus … turned heretic: The Numidian priest Donatus Magnus (d. c. 355 CE) became bishop of Carthage later, in 313, as well as the leader of the Donatist sect. so did Arian … advanced: In the early fourth century, Arius – on whom, see above, n. 149 (1.2.4) – was involved in a protracted controversy with Pope Alexander I of Alexandria over the doctrine of the Trinity. experiments: See above, n. 107 (1.2.2).

take place: See above, n. 52 (DJR). Alexander in India after his victories: That is, Alexander the Great, after his campaign in the Indian subcontinent, which included a famous victory over the Indian king Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE).
nuzzled: Trained, indoctrinated. mortified: Insensible. perfection: Holiness. going woolward: See above, n. 3 (3.2.5).
macerate: See above, n. 14 (DJR).

used, by such parties … Apostles: Deuteronomy 9:9; 1 Kings 19:4–8; Daniel 1:8; Matthew 4:2–4; Matthew 9:15. On ‘Elias’, see above, n. 121 (3.2.5). Castigo corpus meum: Note ‘a’ quotes 1 Corinthians 9:27 in the Latin Vulgate. as one saith, Plus respiciunt … in corde: A reworked quotation from the account of John Chrysostom given by the English theologian (and president of Magdalen College, Oxford) Laurence Humphrey, in his Jesuitismi pars secunda Puritanopapismi (1584). temperature: See above, n. 194 (DJR).
rivel: See above, n. 34 (1.2.3).

Hilarion, as Jerome reports … Antonius: See above, n. 269 (3.2.2). for want of vapours … sleep: Sleep, as is mentioned in 1.1.2.7 above, was thought to occur when the hot vapours produced by digestion moved upwards from the stomach to the head, where they inhibited the ‘animal spirits’ and caused the ‘common sense’ to stop functioning. idle-headed: Delirious, crazy.
the devil’s bath melancholy: See above, 1.2.1.2, p. 200.

such Sibylline prophecies: The ‘Sibylline Oracles’, a set of prophecies purportedly made by the ancient Sibyls – see above, n. 18 (1.3.1) – but actually deriving from pagan, Jewish and Christian sources in late antiquity, were considered by some to bear testimony to the coming of Christ. They had been the subject of heated
debate since they were printed for the first time in 1545. except at: See above, n. 21 (DJR).

Saint Francis’ five wounds: See above, n. 19 (1.2.3). that which Matthew Paris relates … saw as much: See above, n. 9 (1.2.3). Walsingham of him … Saint Julian: Possibly a misremembrance of the Gesta abbatum monasterii Sancti Albani by the medieval chronicler Thomas Walsingham (c. 1340–c. 1422), which reports the appearance of the ghost of a malicious dead monk called Nicholas Goudeby in the monastery of St Albans, of which St Julian was the patron saint.

Beda lib. 5 … strange visions: Bede’s Ecclesiastical History reports a comforting vision seen by Sebbi of Essex (ruled 664–c. 696), the joint ruler of the East Saxons with his cousin Sighere, on his deathbed. Alexander … Enthusiastical prisoner: In his Genialium dierum libri sex (1591), the Italian humanist Alessandro de’ Alessandro presents what he calls a ‘barely credible’ tale of man who had escaped from prison in a town in the central Italian region of Paelignia, and when he was recaptured claimed that he had returned from hell, which he described in detail. that of Eris Armenius … strange wonders: The tenth book of Plato’s Republic narrates the eschatological myth of the Pamphylian warrior Er, who comes back from the afterlife after being killed in battle, and reports on his descent to the underworld. those tales Ulysses related to Alcinous in Homer: In book 7 of the Odyssey. Lucian’s vera historia: The True History is a satirical parody of ancient travellers’ tales.

Florilegus hath many … delude him: The Flores historiarum of the English historian and polymath Matthew Paris tells the story of St Guthlac (674–715 CE), an aristocratic soldier who became a hermit and withdrew to the island of Crowland, where he was tempted and abducted by devils, but then rescued by St Bartholomew.
In the same author … fasting and meditation: In the Flores historiarum, as the date suggests, the vision is actually given to Charles III (Charles the Fat), ruler of the Carolingian Empire 881–8.

Strabo Geog. lib. 14 describes Charon’s den … be done: According to Strabo (Geography 14.1.44), the sick would travel to Acharaca, a village on the road between the towns of Tralleis and Nysa in Caria, to live near the Charonium (the ‘cave of Charon’) while priests slept inside it on their behalf and dreamed of their cures. Sometimes the patients were brought into the cave to fast and dream of their own cures, which could be interpreted by the priests if required.
that Chaldean Mithrobarzanes: The magus who guides Menippus to the underworld in Lucian’s Menippus, or The Descent into Hades.
promiscuous: See above, n. 106 (DJR).
pyx: The box which holds the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.

Mesquitas: Mosques. Varius mappa … poterat: Note ‘b’ quotes Horace, Satires 2.8.63–4, where the amusement of his friend the poet Lucius Varius Rufus is provoked by an exchange at a dinner party between the host Nasiedenus and the parasite Nomentanus. When the former reacts melodramatically to a wall-hanging collapsing on to the fish course, the latter pretentiously laments the cruelty of fortune.
condole: See above, n. 133 (DJR).

have and hold, de lana caprina: See above, nn. 72, 120 (DJR). fit for Calpurnius … to laugh at: The reference to Calpurnius – presumably the Roman bucolic poet Calpurnius Siculus (first century CE) – is puzzling, but may have been taken from the second edition of John Foxe’s Acts and Monuments (1570), in which an account of a ‘ridiculous pageant’ involving a monk from Gloucester College in Oxford is accompanied by a marginal note that is near-identical to note ‘c’ here.

As Merlin … what it meant: In the Prophecia Merlini, written by Geoffrey of Monmouth (c. 1135), Vortigern, who is under attack by the Saxons, consults Merlin. In the magician’s prophetic vision, a white dragon, representing the Saxons,
overcomes the red dragon, representing the Britons. However, the red dragon returns and ultimately defeats the white dragon. Merlin explains that, with the assistance of a boar from Cornwall, the Britons will be victorious. On Vortigern, see above, n. 167 (3.2.2). wishing mine eyes … Jeremy did: Jeremiah 9:1.

Tot mundo superstitiones … one saith: No source has been traced for this exact saying, but it may be an adaptation of a phrase in Jean Calvin’s Praelectiones in librum prophetiarum Jeremiae (1563), which comments on Jeremiah 11:13 – the subject being the multiplicity of deities worshipped by the Jews.
private: See above, n. 46 (1.2.2). Vatinian hate: See above, n. 161 (DJR).

what factions … many years: References to the French Wars of Religion (1562–98) and to the Thirty Years War in continental Europe (1618–48), which was ongoing when the first five editions of the Anatomy were published (although England, as the Civil War would show, was hardly immune). The ‘hurly-burly’ of more general religious–political factionalism and conflict was prevalent throughout Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
the ten general persecutions: See above, n. 139 (DJR).
as our Saviour saith … against son: Matthew 10:35.

Tentyra and Ombos: Towns in Upper Egypt denounced by Juvenal (Satires 15.33–92) for their savagery in religious conflict. Tentyra is now Dendera; Ombos was the Greek name for the Egyptian city of Nubet, near the larger Kom Ombos on the eastern bank of the Nile.
Giaours: A Turkish term of reproach for non-Muslims, derived from guebre (a pejorative name for a Parsee or Zoroastrian).

those Marian times: The period of the persecution of Protestants in the reign of the English Catholic Mary I (1553–58). those miserable slaughters … Cabrieres: In 1545 the Protestant Waldensian inhabitants of these two Provençal villages were massacred with the approval of the papacy and the French king. the Duke of Alva’s tyranny in the Low countries: See above, n. 139 (DJR). the French Massacres: See above, n. 136 (DJR).

Fee-simple: Absolute and perpetual possession. peculiar donation: Possibly an allusion to the Donation of Constantine – on which, see above, n. 23 (2.3.3); ‘peculiar’ here means ‘belonging exclusively to them’. entailed: Bestowed as an inalienable possession. per funem aureum … doctrina: A line from Lucretius (On the Nature of Things 2.1553) which employs the Homeric image of the ‘golden chain’ – see above, n. 38 (3.1.1).
conversations: See above, n. 110 (DJR).

Separatists: More specifically, in England, sects such as the Brownists and Barrowists. peculiar Churches of Amsterdam: Several religious sects, such as the Mennonites, were permitted to worship in seventeenth-century Amsterdam, which is also where the Familists were founded; ‘peculiar’ here means ‘exempt from ordinary ecclesiastical jurisdiction’.

as some Jews did … observationem: In the Jewish Antiquities (18.3), Josephus records that Pilate, the procurator of Judaea, sparked protests in Jerusalem in 27 CE by bringing images of the Roman emperor into the city and then threatened the protestors with death.

Ratholde the Frisian Prince: Radbod (or Redbad), king of Frisia (d. 719), who attempted to expel Christianity from Frisia. According to the eighth-century Life of Wulfram of Sens by the monk Jonas of Fontenelle, Radbod refused baptism after asking whether he would see his ancestors in the afterlife, and being told that, while he would be in heaven, they would be in hell.
Banians: Hindu traders from Gujarat, though the term was sometimes applied to all Hindus in western India.

in divinis … admiranda: Burton took this from the 1613 English translation, possibly by the poet William Barksted, of the Pneumologie, ou discours des esprits (1587) by the Dominican prior Sébastien Michaelis, where it is attributed to ‘a certain ancient father’ (‘quelque bon & ancien pere’ in the original). The presumably patristic source has not been traced.

Ipse dixit … ‘he himself said it’: And so, an unproved assertion depending solely upon authority. According to Cicero (On the Nature of the Gods 1.5.10), whenever the followers of Pythagoras were questioned about the rational grounds of their assertions, their response was to state this – referring simply to the sayings of their master.

that pontificial consubstantiation: The Roman Catholic doctrine, disputed by Protestants, of the real substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ together with the Eucharistic bread and wine. Vide Samsatis … Milesium: Note ‘c’ refers to a letter remarking on the impossibility of various Christian doctrines, written by a Persian Muslim from Isfahan to a monk called Meletius, who had been converted from Islam to Christianity by the Byzantine emperor John VI Kantakouzenos (c. 1295–1383). The letter was included in later printed Latin editions of the emperor’s Contra Mahometicam fidem Christiana & orthodoxa assertio.
Golden Legend: See above, n. 123 (DJR).
feral: Dismal.
Amosis: The Pharaoh Ahmose I (or Amosis I), founder of the Eighteenth Dynasty, who ruled Egypt in the sixteenth century BCE.

In the city of Bubastis … Storks: According to Herodotus (2.67), dead cats were given sacred burial in the Egyptian town of Bubastis, where the primary deity of the city was Bastet (originally a lion-goddess but later worshipped as a cat). Herodotus also mentions ibises, which were revered by the Egyptians, particularly the ‘sacred ibis’ (Threskiornis aethiopicus), which was worshipped as the holy animal of Thoth – for whom, see above, n. 47 (1.2.1). an Ox (saith Pliny): The Egyptian bull cult of Apis, which in Memphis involved the worship of a live bull, is discussed by Pliny the Elder (8.71.185–6). Leeks and Onions … deos colis: The cult of Serapis and Isis at Alexandria is discussed by Macrobius in his Saturnalia (1.20.13–18), but the reference to allium-worship comes from the Roman Christian writer Prudentius’ Reply to the Address of Symmachus (2.866), quoted here. It is probably groundless, although Juvenal (Satires 15.9) says that the Egyptians regarded eating leeks or onions as sacrilegious.

Indigetes: See above, n. 87 (1.2.1). Lares, Lemures: See above, n. 23 (1.2.1). Dioscuri: See above, n. 54 (1.2.1). Soteres: ‘Saviours’ or ‘preservers’ – titles given to gods and rulers in Greek-speaking countries. Parastatae: ‘Supporters’ or ‘helpers’: titles given to Greek gods, especially the Dioscuri – see above, n. 54 (1.2.1). Pax … Neptunia Doris: Roman gods or goddesses: of peace (Pax); rest (Quies); health (Salus); liberty (Libertas); happiness (Foelicitas); either physical vigour or new year’s gifts (Strenua, also sometimes a variant of Strenia); arousal (Stimula); possibly good fortune, youth, gardens and agriculture, or exhortation to virtue (our knowledge of Horta is uncertain); goatherds and shepherds (Pan); the forest (Sylvanus); fertility and sexuality (Priapus); the flowering of plants (Flora); purification (Cloacina) – see above, n. 3 (2.1.3); the manuring of soil (Stercutius); fevers (Febris); fear (Pallor) – cf. 1.2.3.5, p. 258; envy (Invidia); wantonness (Protervia); Laughter (Risus); suffering and silence (Angerona) – see 1.2.3.5, p. 258; sensual pleasure (Volupia); countryside and leisure (Vacuna) – see above, n. 357 (DJR); marital harmony (Viriplaca). ‘Veneranda Pales’ (‘Venerable Pales’), quotes Virgil’s Georgics (3.294), referring to Pales, a Roman god of shepherds and herds; ‘Neptunia Doris’ was the name sometimes given in Renaissance sources to Doris – on whom, see above, n. 74 (3.2.3) – although she was the daughter of the sea-god Oceanus rather than Neptune.
Aesculapius: See above, n. 86 (1.2.1). Tiresias: See above, n. 18 (1.3.1). Mopsus: See above, n. 18 (1.3.1).

ex homine daemon evadit: For the Neoplatonist philosopher Maximus of Tyre (second century CE), once the soul divests itself of the body after death, it is called (and in some sense becomes) a demon (Orations 9); cf. 1.2.1.2, p. 182. disparaged: See above, n. 27 (DJR). variety: Variation.
Genius: See above, n. 22 (DJR).

Cuna: Actually Cunina, the Roman goddess who protected children in the cradle (cuna or cunae). Deverra: The Roman goddess who presided over the threshold of a house where a woman was giving birth, armed with a broom to protect against the god Sylvanus. Nodina: Or Nodutus, the Roman god presiding over corn, who brought the stem on as far as its knots (nodi). Prema, Premunda: See above, n. 3 (2.1.3). Comus the god of goodfellows: See above, n. 149 (3.2.3) and n. 68 (2.2.6). Hebe goddess of youth: See above, n. 66 (3.2.3). Mena menstruarum: The Roman goddess Mena presided over menstruation.
As Jeremy told them … Cities: Jeremiah 11:13.
babies: See above, n. 104 (DJR).

When Romulus was made away … Romans: The mythical deification of Romulus, dated by Livy (1.16) to 716 BCE, was said to have occurred when the king was reviewing his army on the Campus Martius and disappeared in a storm. Livy reports contemporary rumours that he had been secretly murdered by his senators.

Syrophanes of Egypt … for a god: This fable, about the otherwise unknown Syrophanes, was commonly cited in medieval and Renaissance discussions of the origins of idolatry. It derived from the Mythologies (1.1) by the Christian writer Fulgentius (fl. 500 CE).
This did Semiramis for her husband Belus: Semiramis was actually fabled to be the wife of King Ninus, son of the Assyrian king Belus; see above, n. 342 (DJR).

Flora … amongst the rest: The origins of the ancient Roman festival known as the Floralia, which honoured the goddess Flora and involved prostitutes and indecent farces, are obscure. Its dedication day was 28 April, and games were celebrated annually until 3 May.

Venus Barbata: Literally, ‘Bearded Venus’, a Roman cult in which Venus was represented as androgynous. According to the tenth-century Byzantine encyclopaedia now known as the Suda, Venus was honoured with a bearded statue by the women of Rome after they had been afflicted with a pestilential itch and compelled to shave off their hair.

Alabanda a small town in Asia Minor: The city of Alabanda, in the ancient region of Caria in western Anatolia, was caught up in the Third Macedonian War (172–168 BCE) between the Romans and the last Macedonian king, Perseus – on whom, see above, n. 100 (1.2.4). The Alabandans built the temple, according to Livy (43.6.5), in 170.

Tully writes to Atticus … deserved it: In letters written shortly after the death of his daughter Tulliola (45 BCE), Cicero describes his efforts to build a shrine to her and says that he has ‘many ideas for her deification’ (Letters to Atticus 275, 276).

those Lupercals of Pan: An ancient Roman festival with various carnivalesque elements (including a wild chase through the Forum) that was held annually in February in honour of Lupercus, a god usually identified with the Greek Pan. Bona dea: See above, n. 42 (3.2.1). Anna Perenna: The Roman goddess of the ‘healthy year’ (her name is derived from amnis perennis, ‘perennial river’), honoured at the Ides of March in a festival involving both sexes drinking wine together in tents and grass huts. Saturnals: See above, n. 309 (DJR). bald: Meaningless.
olim truncus eram: A quotation from Horace (Satires 1.8.1), where a wooden statue of the god Priapus reminisces about its origins. stupid: Inanimate.

Jupiter with a ram’s head … three heads: Allusions to representations of the following gods: Zeus-Ammon (Jupiter-Ammon), which combined the Graeco-Roman and Egyptian gods, the latter being traditionally depicted with the head of a ram; Hermes (Mercury), who was sometimes identified in the Greek world with the Egyptian god Anubis, typically portrayed as a man with a dog’s head; Pan, who was often identified in Greek and Roman sources with the goat-like satyrs, and in Egypt with gods in the form of goats; and Hecate, the goddess of magic and ghosts, who was commonly represented with three heads in classical sculpture (alluding to her epithet ‘Troiditis’ or ‘Trivia’ and her association with crossroads and liminal spaces). that of Minerva … Athens: The ancient wooden cult statue of Athena Polias in the Erechtheum on the Acropolis.

Apollo and Neptune … Phrygia: In classical mythology, when Apollo and Poseidon (Neptune) failed in their revolt against Zeus (Jupiter), they were condemned to enter the service of the Trojan king Laomedon for one year. Poseidon built the city walls of Troy, while Apollo guarded Laomedon’s cattle. kept sheep: Pan, the god of shepherds, also tended sheep according to the Homeric Hymns (19). Hercules emptied stables: See above, n. 284 (DJR). as Isis for her son … weeping Priests: The renowned grief of the goddess Isis is actually for her brother and husband Osiris, who had been murdered by Set (or Typhon), and the lamentations of Isis and her sister Nephthys for Osiris were included in Egyptian religious rituals. ‘Cynocephalus’ (literally, ‘dog-head’) refers to the god of funerals and the afterlife, Anubis, the son of Nephthys and Osiris. According to Plutarch (Isis and Osiris 44), Nephthys had given birth to Anubis after disguising herself as Isis in order to seduce Osiris, and left him to die for fear of Typhon, but Isis then adopted him as her son. Mars in Homer … crying: See above, n. 53 (2.3.3) and n. 10 (3.1.1).
Diagoras: Diagoras of Melos, an ancient Greek poet, sophist and notorious atheist of the fifth century BCE.

Hecatombs: Large public sacrifices, originally made by the ancient Greeks and Romans, and properly of a hundred oxen. Marcus, Julianus … Tauricremus: The emperors Marcus Aurelius and Julian the Apostate.
invention: Solution. to sacrifice in Lucian’s time … Troja to Pylus: This passage from Lucian’s On Sacrifices (2) alludes to the opening of book 3 of Homer’s Odyssey.
Turtle: See above, n. 116 (1.2.4).

Croesus regum omnium … maris: Note ‘f’ derives from Herodotus’ account (1.47) of how Croesus tested various Greek oracles by requiring them to state his actions at particular times in the recent past. The Pythian oracle at Delphi correctly reported, in verses that opened with ‘I know the number of grains of sand, and the measures of the sea’, that at the stated time Croesus had been cooking a tortoise with lamb in a copper pot.
exploded: See above, n. 45 (DJR).
To the roof of Apollo Didymeus’ Temple … did not suffice: See above, n. 41 (3.2.2). According to Strabo (Geography 14.1.5), the temple was too large to be given a roof.

the Capitol: The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (Jupiter Capitolinus), on the Capitoline Hill at Rome. the Serapeum at Alexandria: The famously magnificent temple of the Egyptian god Serapis, built by Ptolemy III Euergetes (reigned 246–222 BCE). Apollo’s Temple at Daphne … Antioch: See above, n. 25 (2.2.4).

The great Temple at Mexico … Pantheon of Cuzco: The Templo Mayor in the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán in Mexico, and Coricancha, the temple of the sun in Cuzco, Peru. The Spanish Jesuit missionary, philosopher and theologian José Acosta compares the latter to the Roman Pantheon in his Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590).

Helena built … holy Land: Among the churches built by the Roman empress St Helena (d. c. 330 CE), mother of the emperor Constantine I, was the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, on the site of her presumed discovery of the ‘True
Cross’ (the relics of the cross on which Christ was crucified). Bassa: See above, n. 162 (DJR).

Arras in Artois: The Augustinian abbey of St Vaast (or Vedast) in Arras, the capital of Artois in northern France. Fulda in Germany: The Benedictine abbey of Fulda, in Hesse, central Germany. Saint Edmundsbury in England: The Benedictine abbey, now the site of St Edmundsbury Cathedral, in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk.
donaries: See above, n. 295 (DJR). pendants: See above, n. 13 (2.1.3).
Alexander … king of Macedonia: Alexander I, who ruled in the first half of the fifth century BCE, and was the son of Amyntas I.
The Leucadians … undergo it: See above, n. 134 (3.2.5).
The Decii … manibus: See above, n. 3 (3.1.3). Curtius did leap into the gulf: See above, n. 3 (3.1.3).

Nicias that … captain of the Greeks: The commander of the Athenian expedition whose attempt to invade Sicily (415–413 BCE) in the Peloponnesian War was a catastrophic failure, resulting in the annihilation of the Athenian forces and his own death.

when Pompeius besieged Jerusalem: In 63 BCE, bringing the end of the independence of Judaea and establishing Roman control of the territory. some Jewish Christians in Africk … vanquished: Presumably during the Vandal conquest of North Africa (429–39 CE), which led to the destruction of the Christian churches there. ‘Jewish Christians’ were Jews who combined Jewish practice with belief in Christ.
the Dibrenses … any conditions: The inhabitants of the city of Debar, in what is now North Macedonia, were Greek Orthodox Christians, some of whose rituals involve the drinking of blessed water.
Praetor: Mayor, or chief civic official.

the Indies: The Asian or East Indies. the mountains betwixt Scanderoon and Aleppo: The Kurd Mountains, or Kurd Dagh, in what is now northwestern Syria and southeastern Turkey; on ‘Scanderoon’, see above, n. 219 (DJR). Kurds coming of the race … hurt them: Possibly a reference to Kurdish Zoroastrianism, in which Angra Mainyu, the main evil adversary of the creative spirit Spenta Mainyu, was deified in an annual ritual.

as they did infants … of old: A reference to the Curetes, classical mythological beings said to have sacrificed children to Kronos (often identified with the Roman god Saturnus), in the cave of Mount Dicte on Crete, in order to protect his infant son Zeus (Jupiter). Agamemnon’s Iphigenia: In classical mythology, Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to Artemis (Diana), in order to dispel the unnatural calm that had delayed the Greeks’ departure for Troy.

their Idols made of flour and men’s blood: These details are taken from the description of the idols in Tenochtitlán given by the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés (1485–1547) in a letter to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, written in 1520. They were made from ground leguminous plants and amaranth seeds, but what Cortés thought was human blood may have been the juice of the prickly pear cactus.
Cham: See above, n. 111 (1.2.4).
as Cleombrotus Ambraciotes’ Auditors of old: See above, n. 106 (1.2.3).
dizzards: See above, n. 96 (DJR).
Essei: See above, n. 182 (3.2.5). Rabbins’ ridiculous Comments: See above, n. 123 (DJR).

a great bird … seven years: This fable about the Ziz, a giant bird in Jewish mythology, is attributed to the grammarian Elia Levita (1469–1549) by Johann Buxtorff in his Synagoga Judaica (1604). when a Roman Prince … Joshua ben Hananiah: The Babylonian Talmud details conversations between the Roman emperor Hadrian and the Jewish sage Joshua ben Hananiah (c. 50–c. 130 CE). the wood Ela: The dwelling-place of the tigris, the gigantic (and very dangerous) lion of the forest of Bei-Ila’i in the Talmud.
Calenders, Dervishes, Torlaquis: Sufi mystics in Turkey and Persia (the Qalandars and Torlaks are both orders of dervishes).
miraculous: Capable of producing miracles.
Mahomet’s Temple: The Kaaba, in the Great Mosque of Mecca.
cast: See above, n. 73 (2.2.3).
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
Christians have that shield … resist: An allusion to Ephesians 6:10–17.

Antichrist: The claim that the pope was Antichrist had become commonplace among English Protestants after the publication of John Foxe’s Acts and Monuments (1563), although earlier figures, such as the theologian John Wycliffe (d. 1384), had also expressed this view. plays his prize: See above, n. 53 (1.2.3).
dementate: See above, n. 347 (DJR).
only: See above, n. 14 (DJR). nose of wax: See above, n. 154 (DJR).
irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR). duplications, triplications: See above, n. 69 (DJR).
taken themselves by the noses: See above, n. 3 (Preliminaries).

Nicholaites: See above, n. 40 (3.3.4). Montanists: See above, n. 182 (3.2.5). Tatians: Ascetic followers of Tatian of Adiabene, an early Christian Assyrian theologian of the mid-second century. Severians: A sect of Gnostic ascetics, also from the second century. Adamians: Or ‘Adamites’, see above, n. 41 (3.3.4). Circumcellions: See above, n. 30 (1.4.1).
Eliases: See above, n. 121 (3.2.5).
satisfactions: See above, n. 295 (DJR).

Cosmus and Damian: See above, n. 28 (1.3.1). Gallus: St Gall, whose Latin name means ‘cockerel’. Wenceslaus: This should be Wendolinus (d. 607 CE), an Irish hermit and shepherd. Pelagius: Actually St Pelagia – on whom, see above, n. 21 (1.4.1). suitors: Regular visitors, petitioners, or followers. St. Nicholas’ Bourges in France: The medieval cathedral at Bourges has a famous stained-glass window depicting St Nicholas (d. 343), but the Basilica of Saint-Nicolas-de-Port, a famous pilgrimage centre that held relics of St Nicholas, is probably meant here. Genoa: The shrine of Nostra Signora della Guardia, in the mountains near Genoa, was a famous site of pilgrimage, as was the shrine of St John in Genoa Cathedral, said to hold the relics of John the Baptist. Lyons: The shrine of Our Lady in Lyons Cathedral, another important pilgrimage site. Pratum: Prato Cathedral in Tuscany hosted the ‘girdle of Thomas’, said to have been received by St Thomas the Apostle (Didymus, ‘the Twin’, or ‘Doubting Thomas’) when the Virgin Mary dropped it during her assumption into heaven. St. Denis: The Basilica of St Denis, containing his relics, and situated north of Paris. our Lady’s Church at Bergamo: In note ‘d’, the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore.
Blase: St Blase (or Blaise), whose feast-day is 3 February in the Latin Church.

tumble with St. Francis … hogs: According to the medieval chronicler Roger of Wendover (d. 1236), when Francis visited Innocent III at Rome, the pope was unimpressed at his shabby appearance and instructed him to win his favour by rolling in the mud with some pigs – which he duly did.
Punks: See above, n. 51 (3.3.4).
quis expedivit psittaco suum χαῖρε: A quotation from the prologue to Persius’ Satires, which supplies the answer – ‘the belly’ (a reference to the motivational power of hunger).
that ridiculous fable of St. Ursula … martyred: See above, n. 243 (3.2.2).

Obs and Sols: See above, n. 333 (DJR). tropological: A figurative interpretation (of Scripture) that posits an underlying moral message. Quodlibetaries: Academic disputations. Feribrigge and Strode: Two Oxford philosophers famous for their works on logic, Richard Feribrigge (fl. 1361–7) and Ralph Strode (d. 1387). ampliations: Extensions, amplifications. Sorbonists: The Sorbonne had long been regarded (sometimes contemptuously) as a bulwark of scholastic philosophy. Minorites: The Franciscans (‘Friars Minor’) were famous for their contributions to scholastic philosophy in the medieval period, but are singled out here perhaps because of the reputation of John Duns Scotus, nicknamed ‘the Subtle Doctor’.

Whether he can produce … term: A question, expressed in scholastic logical and metaphysical terminology, which refers to theological debates about God’s omnipotence and relation to the world – can God create a relation (‘respect’, relatio) without real grounds (‘foundation’, fundamentum) for that relation, or indeed without a real object (‘term’, terminus) to which he could be related? When the ‘subject’, ‘term’ and ‘foundation’ are all real, it is described as a ‘real relation’ (that is, independent of the mind); when either the ‘term’ or ‘foundation’ is not real (that is, produced by the mind), it is called a ‘relation of reason’. According to Thomas Aquinas in the Summa theologiae, the relation between creation and God is real, but that between God and creation is rational because it is without a real ‘foundation’ (since God and creation are of an entirely different order).
Fetch Trajan’s soul … and how: See above, n. 105 (2.2.3).
clout: Mend with a patch.

200 Commentators on Peter Lombard … sentences: Peter Lombard’s Sententiae, written in the twelfth century, was a standard theological textbook in medieval and Renaissance universities. Scotists, Thomists, Reals, Nominals: See above, n. 68 (1.2.3).
defecate: See above, n. 36 (1.2.2).
Precisians: Puritans, often said to be excessively ‘precise’ – see above, n. 125 (DJR).
humane learning: See above, n. 28 (DJR). things indifferent in themselves: See above, n. 125 (DJR). snuff: Sniff contemptuously. stone-horse: Stallion.
Counsels: In medieval and Renaissance theology, the twelve advisory declarations of Christ and the apostles stipulating the means of moral improvement.
Apocalypses: Prophetic revelations.

some call God … Vorstius and Socinus: The German theologian Conrad von der Vorst (1569–1622) sympathized with the controversial views of Fausto Sozzini (Socinus). His Tractatus theologicus de Deo sive de natura et attributis Dei (1610) was condemned by the theologian David Pareus, his former supporter, for its Socinian ideas about the nature of God’s being, the divinity of Christ, predestination and atonement.
Krechting, Knipperdoling: Bernhard Krechting and Bernhard Knipperdolling, two of the leaders of the Münster Anabaptists in the early decades of the sixteenth century; see above, n. 141 (DJR).

In Poland 1548 … the Commons: In his Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (1578), the historian Alessandro Guagnini dates the appearance of this character, identified as the nobleman (and civic official of Brest) Jakub Melsztyński, to the start of the reign of Sigismund I (1506–48).
One David George an illiterate painter: The Anabaptist leader David Joris (c. 1501–56), who also went by the names of Jan Joriszoon and Jan van Brugge.

Lavat. de spect …. Prophet Elias: In the De spectris (1570), the Swiss Protestant theologian Ludwig Lavater gives the full name of this individual as Joannes Leonardus Sartorius, and says that he thought he could prove the truth and universality of ‘our religion’ by a miracle in a manner similar to Elijah.

Hacket … burned at Norwich: The maltster William Hacket and his fellow prophets, the puritan gentlemen Edmund Coppinger and Henry Arthington, were arrested for treason in 1591, after Hacket had proclaimed himself the new messiah and instituted a plot against Elizabeth I; Hacket was executed in July of the same year. According to Burton’s source, William Camden, the puritan Peter Burchet was executed in 1573 (in London, not Norwich) after stabbing the naval commander Sir John Hawkins (1532–95) with a dagger, in a case of mistaken identity. The wheelwright Matthew Hamont (Hovatus) was accused of Arianism and burned as a heretic in 1579.

Bodin … civil wars: In the fifth chapter of his Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem (1566), Jean Bodin simply observes that the English had suffered many defeats at the hands of the Scots. Burton seems to be thinking of the English Wars of the Roses. Pharsalian fields: See above, n. 137 (DJR). velitations: Skirmishes.
