In Cyprian’s time … present calamities: The Apologia ad Demetrianum of Cyprian (d. 258 CE), probably written in 252–3, replies to the accusation, made by an otherwise unknown person called Demetrianus, that plagues and famines had been caused by the Christian abandonment of the pagan gods.
scanted: Inadequately supplied. default: See above, n. 14 (DJR).
sensible creatures: In note ‘a’: see above, n. 85 (DJR).

Others are so strict … against God: For the context of this remark in note ‘b’, added in the fifth edition (1638), see above, n. 68 (2.2.4). Nuda ac tremebunda … jusserit Io: The quotation in note ‘c’ from Juvenal (Satires 6.525–6) is taken from a description of an absurdly superstitious Roman woman, here depicted as a worshipper of Io (who had been temporarily turned into a white cow by Juno, and is probably being conflated with the Egyptian goddess Isis).
Sabbatarians: Especially contemporary puritans, who strictly observed the Sabbath.
Millenaries: Millenarians.
Mogullians: The Mughals – see above, n. 72 (1.2.2).
as Cornelius was formerly accepted: The conversion to Christianity of the Roman centurion Cornelius is described in Acts 10.

Sua cuique civitati (Laeli) … nobis: In this quotation from Cicero’s speech In Defence of Flaccus (69), Cicero is addressing Decimus Laelius, the lead prosecutor in the trial of (the younger) Lucius Valerius Flaccus (59 BCE).
Demonicus: See above, n. 16 (3.1.2). Caecilius in Minucius: See above, n. 38 (1.2.1). ordination: Ordinance, law.

in some time of the reign of Maximinus … cultum: A reference to the decree restoring rights to Christians issued by the emperor Maximinus II shortly before his death in 313 CE; this followed the Edict of Serdica, issued in 311 by the emperor Galerius (c. 260–311) which ended the persecution of Christians under Diocletian. Formalist: See above, n. 126 (DJR).

The like Edict … Arcadius and Honorius: The sons of Theodosius I and emperors, respectively, of the eastern and western portions of the Roman Empire, from 395 to 408 and 393 to 423 CE; they issued several joint edicts designed to suppress pagan worship.

Symmachus the Orator in his days: The Roman politician and orator Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, who argued vigorously for the toleration of the traditional pagan cults, lived in the second half of the fourth century CE, and probably died in 402.

This tenet was stiffly maintained … Rustan Bassa: Rüstem Pasha (c. 1500–1561) was the Grand Vizier of Suleiman the Magnificent (1494–1566). His conversation with the Flemish diplomat and author Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq took place when the latter was ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, for the second time, in 1556.
Toleration of non-Muslim religious practices had been institutionalized in the millet system, which divided the population into different religious and ethnic groups, in the reign of Mehmed II in the fifteenth century.
Theodosius is commended … silence: The Christian Roman emperor Theodosius I (ruled 379–95) passed many laws against heresy.
club-law: Use of the club (or physical force) to enforce obedience.
Servetus: See above, n. 11 (2.3.5). Castellio … Martin Bellius: ‘Martin Bellius’ was actually the pseudonym of Sebastian Castellio – on whom, see above, n. 135 (1.2.1).
post unam … devita: Titus 3:10. as Paul did by Hymenaeus: 1 Timothy 1:20.

Sadducees: Those who deny the resurrection of Christ and the immortality of the soul – named after the ancient Judaic religious group opposed to the Pharisees. Herodians: Those who are motivated purely by self-interest, named after the New Testament opponents of Christ and supporters of the dynasty of Herod the Great. Libertines: See above, n. 75 (1.2.4). secure: See above, n. 23 (3.4.1). in a reprobate sense: See above, n. 131 (1.2.4).
credat Judaeus Apella: A quotation from Horace (Satires 1.5.100) referring to the reputed superstitiousness of the Jewish population in Rome. Lucian’s Alexander: See above, n. 97 (3.4.1).
that Cyclops in Euripides: Polyphemus, the title character of Euripides’ Cyclops.
Their God is their belly, as Paul saith: Philippians 3:19.
at all adventure: By chance, randomly.

with Nero, Me vivo fiat: According to Suetonius’ life of Nero (38), these words (‘Let it be while I’m alive’) were uttered by the emperor in response to someone saying, ‘When I’m dead, let the earth be consumed by fire’ (perhaps a quotation from the lost Bellerophon of Euripides), after which he set fire to Rome (in 64 CE). as Paterculus said … executi: Velleius Paterculus (2.24) says this of Gaius Flavius Fimbria – see above, n. 187 (DJR) – who in 85 murdered the general Lucius Valerius Flaccus, took control of his army, and defeated Mithridates VI of Pontus in battle, but was forced to commit suicide shortly afterwards by Sulla – on whom, see above, n. 101 (1.2.3). ‘Caitiffs’ here means ‘villains’ or ‘despicable wretches’.
Lycaon-like: See above, n. 41 (1.1.1). exenterate: See above, n. 51 (2.5.1). Cadmus’ soldiers: See above, n. 17 (1.1.1).

with Pentheus they neglect … the Gods: See above, n. 5 (1.2.1). socii deorum: A phrase, drawing on the primary meaning of ‘socii’ as the allies of Rome, that is later misattributed to Seneca (it probably derives from his Epistles 92.27, which refers to human beings as the ‘socii’ of God).

Apries an Egyptian tyrant … from him: Apries was a pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, who ruled Egypt from 589 to 570 BCE. According to Herodotus (2.169), after expressing this hubristic view he was defeated in battle and strangled.
Mahomet the second, that sacked Constantinople: See above, n. 129 (DJR).

Bulco Opoliensis … Vratislavia: Probably Bolko V (c. 1400–1460), duke of Opole-Głogów in Upper Silesia. Bolko was one of the Hussites – see above, n. 81 (DJR) – whose rejection of the authority of the papacy and criticism of lay authorities led to their being condemned as heretical. The quotation here is from the Asiae Europaeque elegantissima descriptio (1531) by Enea Silvio Piccolomini (Pope Pius II). ‘Vratislavia’, and ‘Breslau’ in note ‘f’, both refer to Wrocław. turned them up: Abandoned or discarded them.

laterem lavas: ‘Washing {the colour out of} a brick’, a phrase found in Terence’s Phormio (186), was a proverbial expression for a futile endeavour. as Attabaliba that Indian Prince did Friar Vincent: The last emperor of the Incas, Atahualpa (d. 1533), whose exchange in 1532 with the Dominican friar Vincente de Valverde, later bishop of Cuzco, is recorded in Theodore de Bry’s Americae pars sexta, sive historiae … scriptae (1596).

Petronius in Tacitus … songs: The biographical details reported by Tacitus about Petronius are now widely accepted to be about the author of the Satyricon. His forced suicide in 66 CE, after being implicated in a plot against Nero, is portrayed by Tacitus as being consistent with his literary sensibility (Annals 16.18–19).
as mad as Hercules … children: See above, n. 21 (2.4.2).
exorbitant: Aberrant, monstrous.
Nullos esse Deos … thrives: Modern editions of Martial give the name of this fictional wealthy atheist as ‘Segius’.

There was a great plague in Athens … all alike: A slightly reworked quotation from the 1629 English translation of Thucydides by Thomas Hobbes, which Burton owned in a presentation copy, referring to the ‘plague of Athens’ – see above, n. 45 (2.5.1).
have and hold: See above, n. 120 (DJR).
Cousin-germans: See above, n. 117 (1.2.2). Deists: Those who believe in God on the basis of reason, but reject revealed religion. conversation: See above, n. 110 (DJR).

Averroist: A follower of the Arabic philosopher Averroes (1126–98), commonly associated in this period with the denial of the personal immortality of the soul, and thereby with atheism. Anima mea … Philosophorum: Note ‘d’ partially reports a saying commonly attributed to Averroes with regard to the Eucharist: ‘Quandoquidem Christiani adorant quod comedunt, sit anima mea cum Philosophis’ (‘Since the Christians eat what they worship, let my soul be with the philosophers’).

fatum Stoicum … inevitable necessity: Stoic philosophy was often seen in the Renaissance as (in modern terms) ‘causally determinist’, that is, explaining the present as being fully caused by past events – even as it placed strong emphasis on individual moral responsibility. The apparent paradox was the subject of much philosophical commentary. Chaldean Astrologers: See above, n. 54 (1.1.2). Nigidius Figulus: Publius Nigidius Figulus (d. 45 BCE), a Roman scholar notorious in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for his adherence to Pythagoreanism and a range of occult beliefs and practices. Priscilianists: The followers of Priscillian (d. c. 385 CE), a Spanish Christian ascetic and bishop of Ávila executed for practising magic, were subsequently condemned as heretics. questionaries: Questioners, especially in theological matters. Novem Judices: The popular medieval Latin compendium of judicial astrology – on which, see above, n. 106 (1.2.1) – known as the Liber novem judicum (‘Book of the Nine Judges’) and comprising the teachings of Arabic and Greek authors. Albumazar: The Persian astrologer Abu Ma’shar (787–886). Dorotheus: The astrologer Dorotheus of Sidon (first century CE). our Countryman Eschuidus: The fourteenth-century English astrologer John of Eschenden.
Intelligences: See above, n. 18 (1.2.1).
vertical: At their highest point.
advice: See above, n. 53 (DJR).
second causes: Or ‘secondary’ causes – see above, 1.2.1.4 and 1.2.1.5.
So Cotta argues in Tully: See above, n. 47 (3.2.5).

As the woman told Alexander … reign: A misremembrance of a story told by Dio Cassius (69.6.3) about the emperor Hadrian, not Alexander the Great. On the meaning of ‘causes’ here, see above, n. 232 (DJR).
ambidexters: See above, n. 165 (DJR). neutralists: Those who maintain neutrality between competing religious teachings.

the barbarous Getes worshipped Zalmoxis: See above, n. 68 (3.4.1). the Cilicians Mopsus: See above, n. 18 (1.3.1). the Thebans Amphiaraus: See above, n. 57 (3.4.1). the Lebadians Trophonius: See above, n. 28 (1.3.1).
Claudius the Emperor … hurt Jupiter: In On Anger (1.208–9) Seneca says this about Caligula, not Claudius.
Diagoras: See above, n. 175 (3.4.1). Demonax: Demonax of Cyprus, a Cynic philosopher (c. 70–170 CE). Mezentius: See above, n. 4 (2.3.5).
Scholar: See above, n. 55 (DJR).
vindicate: See above, n. 284 (DJR).

oppugns: See above, n. 6 (2.1.4). infoelix Brunus: The Italian friar and philosopher Giordano Bruno had been burned as a heretic by the Inquisition in February 1600. Caesar Vaninus … France: The heterodox Italian philosopher Lucilio (or Giulio Cesare) Vanini, whose De admirandis naturae reginae deaeque mortalium arcanis (1616) was condemned as heretical in 1618 and is referred to several times in the Anatomy; he was tried and executed in 1619. paradoxes: See above, n. 3 (DJR). Boccace, with his Fable of three rings: A parable about the plurality or unity of true religion, recounted by Boccaccio (Decameron 1.3).

that pestilent Book de tribus mundi impostoribus: The notorious atheistic treatise On the Three Impostors of the World was said to have criticized Jesus, Moses and Muhammad, and refuted Christianity, Judaism and Islam, although it appears not to have existed until fraudulent versions were written and printed in the early eighteenth century. mundi Cymbalam … Peresio: The anonymous Cymbalum mundi, almost certainly by the French humanist scholar and writer Bonaventure des Périers (first published in 1537), was a controversial set of dialogues that satirized pagan religious beliefs and practices, and was commonly interpreted as a free-thinking attack on Christianity.
Frederick the Emperor: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor (ruled 1220–50). Henry the Landgrave of Hessen: This should probably be Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia (Heinrich Raspe, 1204–46).
Formalists: See above, n. 126 (DJR). lukewarm Laodiceans: The Laodicean Church was one of the early Christian Churches of Asia Minor, and was criticized as ‘lukewarm’ in Revelation 3:15–16.
Omnis Aristippum … res: The quotation in note ‘a’ from Horace (Epistles 1.17.23) refers to Aristippus of Cyrene, on whom, see above, n. 97 (DJR).

simoniacal Contractors: See above, n. 229 (1.2.3). sonant vitium percussa maligne: A partial quotation of Persius (3.21–2), where the vicious person is compared to a misfired clay pot that betrays its flawed character when tapped with the finger.
Gripers: See above, n. 127 (DJR).
Curii: See above, n. 165 (DJR). Esau’s hands, and Jacob’s voice: An allusion to Genesis 27:22.
Salmoneus: See above, n. 69 (2.2.3).
Topic: Local.
just: See above, n. 26 (DJR). irrefragable: See above, n. 70 (DJR).

Hierom. Montanus: This should be a reference to Pontanus (the philosopher Girolamo Pontano), whose De immortalitate animae ex sententia Aristotelis was published in 1597. the Ambrosian College in Milan: See above, n. 35 (2.2.3).
Colophon: Conclusion, finishing touch.
forlorn: Doomed to destruction.

Fifteen thousand Locrenses … Crotonienses: In a battle fought in the mid-sixth century BCE on the River Sagra in southern Italy, the numerically inferior forces of the Greek city of Locri overcame those of the Greek city of Croton.
cui simile, saith Froissart … almost: Probably a recollection of Froissart’s comment about the Battle of Poitiers – see above, n. 32 (2.2.4) – since the chronicler was almost certainly dead in 1415.
desperatio facit Monachum … saying is: The medieval proverb, about the effect of adversity, is usually given as ‘Militem aut monachum facit desperatio’ (‘Despair makes a monk or a soldier’).

A Tuscan Soothsayer … desperately died: This story, taken from the Compendium of Roman History (2.7.2) of Velleius Paterculus, is set in the aftermath of the rebellion by Gaius Sempronius Gracchus and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus in 121 BCE, which had been brutally crushed by the consul Lucius Opimius (3,000 people are said to have been killed). The Fulvius mentioned here is the eighteen-year-old son of the ringleader, seized by Opimius when he was sent by his father to negotiate a surrender. He appears not to have followed the advice of the Etruscan (‘Tuscan’) soothsayer, and was later executed. ‘Door-cheek’ here means ‘door-post’.
animateth: See above, n. 164 (1.2.3). we of all others … this life: 1 Corinthians 15:19.
as in David … forsaken me: Psalm 22:1.
as he did Judas: Matthew 27:3–5; see also above, n. 103 (1.2.3).
the melancholy humour … Devil’s bath: See above, 1.2.1.2, p. 200. as in Saul … possession of us: 1 Samuel 16:14–23, 18:10–11, 19:9–10.
shoeing-horn: See above, n. 119 (1.2.2).
fact: See above, n. 148 (DJR).
cheverel consciences: Flexible consciences. Cheverel-leather (kid-leather) was noted for its pliability. molested: See above, n. 109 (DJR).

Many are called … miserentis Dei: Quotations and allusions referring, in the sequence presented here, to Matthew 20:16; Matthew 7:21; Luke 12:32; 1 Corinthians 10:12; Philippians 2:12; Luke 17:34; Matthew 7:14; Matthew 13:3–9; Romans 8:30; Romans 9:18; and Romans 9:16 in the Latin Vulgate.
as they did Luke 11. 46: The Pharisees and experts in the Law, so criticized by Jesus in Luke 11:37–53. lade: Load.
as he said … men’s souls: Probably a loose allusion to the remark reportedly made by Pope Leo X, cited in note ‘e’, which is discussed above, n. 80 (3.4.1).

indiscreet: See above, n. 40 (DJR). preterition: Omission from God’s elect. voluntary permission: The teaching that God may choose to permit the sinful effects of actions that have been freely chosen by men. intempestively: See above, n. 313 (DJR). auditories: Churches, or any places where sermons or spiritual instructions are heard (by ‘auditors’). thing indifferent: See above, n. 125 (DJR).

Parsons’ Resolution: The name given to the Catholic version of The First Book of the Christian Exercise, Appertaining to Resolution (1582; later editions were entitled The Christian Directory) by the Jesuit Robert Persons (or Parsons, 1546–1610). A popular Protestant adaptation, purged of Catholic doctrine, was published by the Calvinist Edmund Bunny (1540–1618) in 1584.
O miser Oreste: See above, n. 119 (DJR).

which those Egyptians … torture of it: In his Hieroglyphica (1556), the Italian scholar Pierio Valeriano actually says that some interpret the mill as a symbol of human social interaction (because millstones can only work together); and that the symbol for a spiritual conscience is a swan.
Dire: More commonly ‘Dire sisters’, another name for the Furies (‘Dirae’ in Latin). apparitor: A court officer. Sergeant: See above, n. 25 (3.4.1).
the statue of Juno … her eye: This description, from Lucian’s On the Syrian Goddess (32), refers to a statue in the temple of Atargatis (identified by Lucian as Hera) at Hierapolis in Syria.
tides: Times.
as the prodigal Son … in the end: Luke 15:11–32, where the parable actually ends happily. as bitter as wormwood: Proverbs 5:4.
as to Lucian’s tyrant … did bear witness: See above, n. 61 (1.2.4).

Kennethus King of Scotland … all his life: According to the historian George Buchanan in his Rerum Scoticarum historia (1583), Kenneth III (ruled 997–1005) had arranged the poisoning of his nephew Malcolm, one of the sons of King Dubh, because he saw him as a rival of his own son, also called Malcolm, to the throne.
Lewis the 11th … Alphonsus King of Naples: On Louis XI, see above, n. 24 (1.3.1); Charles VIII ruled France 1483–98; on Alfonso, see above, n. 16 (3.2.1).

Pausanias the Spartan Tyrant: Pausanias was actually the regent of Sparta, assuming this role in 480 BCE as the guardian of his cousin Pleistarchus. According to Plutarch (Cimon 6), he had invited a girl to his bedroom, but after falling asleep he mistook her for an assassin and killed her.
Why was Herod … Mariamne his wife: See above, n. 106 (3.2.5).

Why was Theodoricus … worthy Romans: Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths (c. 455–526 CE) and ruler of Italy from 493, executed the philosopher Boethius (his adoptive son) and the historian Symmachus for their supposed involvement in a treasonous plot. Later, according to the Byzantine historian Procopius (History of the Wars 5.1), Theodoric saw the face of Symmachus on the head of a large fish he had been served at dinner. Overcome by guilt, he died shortly afterwards.
Adrasteia, or Nemesis: Adrasteia (‘Inevitable’) was an ancient Greek goddess, often identified with Nemesis.

Eusebius: See above, n. 45 (3.1.2). Nicephorus … Maximinus and Julian: Examples of divine vengeance for the persecution of Christians that are commonly recycled from patristic sources. The chapter of the fourteenth-century Byzantine historian Nikephoros’ Ecclesiastical History cited here describes the gleeful divine vision of the ascetic Syrian monk Julian Saba (d. 367 CE) presaging the death of the emperor Julian the Apostate – whose last words after being mortally wounded in battle in 363 are quoted by Burton in 1.2.1.1, p. 180. Elsewhere (7.39), Nikephoros describes the gruesome and guilt-ridden death of the emperor Maximinus II – on whom, see above, nn. 29, 249 (3.4.1) – when he botched his suicide by poison in 313.

Popelius the second King of Poland: Prince Popiel II, the last of the mythical Popielid dynasty, and reputed to have been a cruel tyrant. Following the murder of his uncles at the instigation of his wife, Popiel and his princess were said to have been devoured by a horde of rodents. Hatto Archbishop of Mainz: Hatto II, who lived in the tenth century. His cruelty, according to popular legend, resulted in his death in the so-called ‘Mäuseturm’ (‘Mouse Tower’) on a small island in the Rhine, opposite Ehrenfels Castle in Hesse.

Such another example … lib. 2 cap. 2: Gerald of Wales (1146–1223) tells three stories of incidents that occurred in the northern Welsh region of Cemmaes: of a young man who was devoured by a plague of toads; of another devoured by rats; and of a rich man bitten by a viper after following directions for obtaining gold that he had received in a dream.

Jubilees: According to the tradition established by Pope Boniface VIII in 1300, these are years of remission from the penal consequences of sin, in which plenary indulgence can be granted for the performance of good works. gaol-deliveries: Clearing out prisoners from jails by bringing them to trial.

Taxa Camerae Apostolicae: Tariff lists with titles of this kind, issued by the papacy and designed for the selling of sacramental absolution for sins, were in wide circulation in the Renaissance – sometimes having been altered by Protestants for polemical purposes. Leo decimus: See above, n. 57 (1.1.2). sharking: See above, n. 3 (2.3.8). grosses: Foreign coins of relatively low value, such as the German Groschen or Italian grossi. dollars: The English name for German thalers, large silver coins. parable: See above, n. 200 (1.2.3).
ghostly fathers: Spiritual confessors.

What therefore Timanthes did … would himself: The Sacrifice of Iphigenia by the Greek painter Timanthes (fifth/fourth centuries BCE) was famous and influential in antiquity for its representation of emotion. On Iphigenia and Agamemnon, see above, n. 195 (3.4.1). Calchas, the seer and augur for the Greeks in the Trojan War, died from sorrow after his return from Troy when he was defeated in a prophesying contest by the seer Mopsus – on whom, see above, n. 18 (1.3.1). deciphered: See above, n. 209 (DJR).
angor: Anguish.
Chirurgery: See above, n. 20 (2.1.4).
All that is single … concur in this: That is, all the particular symptoms in the other forms of the disease are combined in this one.

Peter in his bonds … protected him: Acts 12:5–6. Tully makes it an argument … securely slept: With this and other arguments, Cicero successfully defended Sextus Roscius, a Roman citizen from Ameria (modern-day Amelia, in Umbria), against a charge of patricide in 80 BCE.
for the sight … fear of hearts: That is, because of terrifying sights and terror in their hearts (both sent by God).

Apollodorus in Plutarch … within him: According to Plutarch (On the Delays of the Divine Vengeance 10), Apollodorus, the notoriously cruel tyrant of Cassandreia (d. 276/5 BCE), once had a dream in which he saw himself being flayed and boiled in a cauldron by Scythians, and heard his heart say, ‘It was I that brought you to this.’

There is a most memorable Example … most mad: The case of Francesco Spiera, a jurist from Citadella (north of Padua) who had died in despair in 1548 after publicly abjuring Protestantism, was infamous among religious controversialists.
Bellovacus: Actually the Paduan physician Aloysius Bellocatus (Luigi Bellocato, 1501–75).

Springer a Lawyer: Actually the Scottish diplomat and book collector Henry Scrimgeour (c. 1505–72), later professor of civil law at Geneva, whose essay on Spiera was published with a preface by Calvin in 1550.
Cardinal Cresence: Cardinal Marcello Crescenzio, who had been the sole papal legate at the second session of the Council of Trent (1551–2), died on his way back to Rome.
Achitophel: Or Ahithophel, who advised Absalom in his revolt against King David and committed suicide when his counsel was rejected (2 Samuel 17:23).

paraenetical: See above, n. 2 (2.3.1). copious in this subject: In the first edition (1621), with the additional instruction to ‘Consult with them and such others’, the last Subsection of the Anatomy ended here. Most of what follows was added in the second edition (1624), but several new passages were incorporated in the third edition (1628) and a few additions were made in the fourth (1632) and fifth (1638) editions. cases of conscience: See above, n. 14 (2.1.1).

Mr. James Whitehall: In note ‘a’: James Whitehall had been awarded his MA at Oxford, and ordained as deacon at Checkley in 1609, becoming priest there in 1620. A manuscript miscellany written by him, containing quotations from Philip Sidney, John Marston and Shakespeare, suggests that he shared some of Burton’s literary as well as spiritual interests and concerns.
occur: Oppose.
Alexipharmacum: See above, n. 111 (2.2.4). Manasseh: The king of Judah (687–642 BCE), whose idolatry, repentance and forgiveness are described in 2 Kings 21.
as a Dog to his vomit … mire: 2 Peter 2:22; cf. Proverbs 26:11.
as our Saviour enjoined Peter … 77 times: Matthew 18:21–2.
The gods once … would himself: See above, n. 38 (3.1.1). maugre: Notwithstanding, in spite of.
deboshed: See above, n. 66 (DJR). Alexander the Copper-smith: The opponent of Paul’s ministry identified in 2 Timothy 4:14 (and perhaps also referred to in 1 Timothy 1:20).
obnubilates: See above, n. 9 (1.3.2).
vailable: Effectual.

I am troubled … believing heart: This imaginary exchange between the English Protestant martyrs John Careless (d. 1556) and John Bradford (d. 1555) concludes William Perkins’s Case of Conscience (1592), being quoted here.
explicite and implicite: See above, n. 99 (1.2.1).

As she raved in the tragedy … stellas habet: In her diatribe at the beginning of Seneca’s Hercules, Juno complains that after abandoning Jupiter for his adulteries she has been driven out of the heavens, and that her place has been taken by his ‘whores’; while others, such as the hero Perseus (the son of Jupiter by Danae, who has a constellation named after him), have maintained their position.

Marmoreo Licinus … esse Deos: Licinus was a famously wealthy freedman, notorious for his peculation as provincial governor of Gaul under Augustus. In the original verse (an anonymous Roman epigram thought to refer to Licinus’ actual grand tomb outside Rome), Licinus, a supporter of Julius Caesar, is contrasted with Caesar’s opponents Cato the Younger and Pompey the Great. Burton has substituted ‘Pomponius’, thinking perhaps of Cicero’s friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, or Gnaeus Pomponius (a famous orator killed in the civil wars), or of the Pomponius who was one of the trusted friends of the ill-fated populist hero Gaius Sempronius Gracchus.
offend: See above, n. 23 (DJR).
as our Saviour said … Avoid Satan: Mark 8:33, Matthew 16:23, Luke 4:8.
resist the Devil … from thee: James 4:7. sorrowful Hannah: 1 Samuel 1:8. pray continually, as Paul enjoins: 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

preposterous: Monstrous. such fatal tables: A reference to the tabular illustrations of the ‘lines of salvation and damnation’, found in some contemporary Calvinist theological works, depicting signs of election or reprobation.
Who knows, saith Solomon … dignus: Ecclesiastes 9:1.

as the Collier did … he left him: This traditional story, which draws on the proverbial association of a ‘collier’ (a coal trader or miner) with blind religious faith, may have been taken from Alabaster’s Conversion (1599) by the English clergyman William Alabaster (1568–1640).
he will triumph over the law: See above, n. 7 (1.1.1).
an adulterous cruel David: See above, n. 7 (3.1.1). an Apostate Solomon: 1 Kings 11:4–13.
particularity: Being personally singled out (here, for reprobation).

our late Arminians … universal grace: Followers of the controversial Dutch Reformed theologian Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), a critic of Calvinist interpretations of predestination, who emphasized the ability of all Christian believers to respond freely to the invitation of God to pursue their own salvation.
Many are called, few chosen: Matthew 22:14.
Christ came … sinners: 1 Timothy 1:15.
Caecilius urgeth: See above, n. 38 (1.2.1).

They were acceptable … Seneca: This list of virtuous pagans includes the Persian king Darius I (ruled 522–486 BCE), perhaps because of his funding of the restoration of the Second Temple of Jerusalem (although Cyrus the Great, who ended the Babylonian captivity in 539 BCE, may have been meant). The classical statesmen with reputations for incorruptible virtue are Aristides ‘the Just’, Cato the Younger and Manius Curius Dentatus – see above, n. 72 (1.2.3), n. 51 (1.1.1) and n. 165 (DJR). as Cornelius: See above, n. 246 (3.4.1).

the Valentinian and Basilidean heretics: The Valentinians were followers of Valentinus – see above, n. 273 (3.2.2); the Basilideans were followers of the second-century Gnostic, Basilides of Alexandria. Rustan Bassa: See above, n. 252 (3.4.1).
censured: See above, n. 59 (DJR).
my Author: Here, the heterodox religious reformer and writer Caelio Secondo Curione (‘Caelius Secundus’), in the De amplitudine beati regni Dei (1554), which has just been quoted and discussed above.
quid meruistis oves: A quotation from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (15.116), referring to sheep as sacrificial victims.

non ex corrupta massa, praevisa fide … as our Arminians: The Arminian doctrine of predestination ex praevisa fide – that God has foresight of the faith of the elect. but God’s absolute decree … which our Arminians will not admit: This passage refers to conflicting interpretations of the controversial doctrine of predestination – the ‘supralapsarian’ position (‘God’s absolute decree … or homo conditus’) that the divine decree of election and reprobation was made before the decree to create the world and human beings, and so also before the decree to authorize the fall of man; the ‘infralapsarian’ position (‘from Adam’s fall … est reprobationis’) that the decree of election and reprobation followed the decree of the fall; and the contemporary Calvinist doctrine of the ‘perseverance of the saints’ (‘perseverantia sanctorum’), according to which the elect can never totally or finally fall away from the state of grace.

all are invited … in a reprobate sense: A statement of the doctrine of ‘single’ predestination – that God has elected some for salvation, passing over (rather than actively choosing, as in ‘double’ predestination) the reprobate.

it is a forbidden question … censure: Burton added this passage in the fifth edition (1638). Long-running disputes about predestination, which typically pitted Calvinist positions against those of contemporary Arminians, had been escalating in England throughout the 1620s. In fact, discussion of predestination had already been forbidden by royal proclamations issued in 1626 and 1628.
Antics: See above, n. 41 (1.1.2).
humiliate: See above, n. 10 (1.1.1).
Cynthius aurem vellit: This quotation from Virgil (Eclogues 6.3–4) refers to Apollo, who was born on Mount Cynthus on Delos.
commencements: Degree ceremonies.

he corrects us all … mensura: An allusion to Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 61, which discusses the careful manner in which God contrives good from our evil as well as from our virtuous deeds: ‘When he permits, he permits by measure, number and weight’. the Lord will not quench … reed: Matthew 12:20.
as David said … death: Psalm 23:4.

non a delitiis ad delitias: A quotation from Jerome’s Epistles (118.6), which states the impossibility of passing from a life of worldly pleasures to heavenly bliss. as the old Romans … to that of honour: The first Roman temple of Virtus (Virtue), built to accompany the existing temple of Honos (Honour) near the Porta Capena, was completed in the late third century BCE.

Christ in the garden … forsaken me: The words here are those of Christ on the cross as recorded in Matthew 27:46, rather than, as the syntax suggests, during his agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37–42, Luke 22:39–44).
the King of Nineveh’s Sackcloth and ashes: Jonah 3:6, referring to the king’s self-abasement after Jonah had prophesied that God would destroy Nineveh for its wickedness; cf. above, n. 19 (2.3.5).
ex persona Dei: Literally, ‘from the person of God’ – that is, with a divine message from God.
Lazarus was poor … God: See above, n. 17 (2.3.3). Abraham did hope beyond hope: Romans 4:18.
exceptest: See above, n. 21 (DJR).
O my soul … within me: Psalm 43:5.
respected: See above, n. 9 (1.2.5).
The Paschal Lamb … herbs: An allusion to Exodus 12:8, where the festival of the Passover is instituted.
issue: End, termination.
Mormolukees: Or ‘mormos’ – imaginary monsters, hobgoblins.
as I have formerly declared … inward causes: See 1.3.3.1 above. terriculaments: Objects of unnecessary fear, bogeymen.
that Christian armour which Paul prescribes: Ephesians 6:10–17. he sets down certain Amulets: ‘He’ is the Dutch physician Levinus Lemnius (1505–68), not Paul.
hypericon … perforata herba: St John’s wort is known as Hypericum perforatum, on account of its dotted or perforated leaves.
accurate: See above, n. 86 (2.2.4). so Saul … David’s harp: 1 Samuel 16:14–23.

as the Angel taught Tobias: The archangel Raphael, calling himself Azarias, is the travelling companion of Tobit’s son in Tobit 6:6–7. The Book of Tobit was included in the apocrypha of the King James Bible (1611).
white bryony: Bryonia dioica, sometimes called red bryony.
opopanax: See above, n. 61 (3.2.5). galbanum: See above, n. 33 (2.4.2). castoreum: See above, n. 64 (2.5.1).
Characters: See above, n. 105 (1.2.1).

that absurd story … circumventing Friars: A reference to the account of the cases of demonic possession in the Ursuline convent in Aix-en-Provence (1609–11) given by the Dominican prior Sébastien Michaelis, who was also grand inquisitor in Avignon. According to Michaelis, when an aristocratic novice called Madeleine de Demandolx de la Palud exhibited signs of possession in 1609 – and other nuns began to follow suit – it was discovered that she had previously been seduced by a local parish priest, Louis Gaufridi, who had reportedly bewitched her. In November 1610 she and another novice, Louise Capeau, were taken to Saint-Baume, where they were exorcized with the assistance of the Flemish Dominican priest François Domps (Dompius); Gaufridi was executed in April 1611. In note ‘b’, ‘W. B.’ is the English translator of Michaelis’s account, The Admirable Historie of the Possession and Conversion of a Penitent Woman (1613), possibly the poet William Barksted.

Astrological elections: See above, n. 132 (1.2.4). habits: Here, probably, actions or behaviour (although monastic attire is also possible). fustian: See above, n. 54 (DJR). sesquipedal: Or ‘sesquipedalian’, polysyllabic. ambitious: Ostentatious, or convoluted. swelling: See above, n. 108 (DJR).
circumvents: Encompasses.
corollary: See above, n. 75 (2.3.3). tenderest: See above, n. 82 (1.2.2).
